official: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security; Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (DOJ's Middle District of Tennessee brought and prosecuted the underlying case)
offense_category: Vindictive Prosecution -- Bringing Criminal Charges in Retaliation for a Successful Civil Lawsuit Against the Government, a Due Process Violation a Federal Judge Found This Case Actually Met
incident_summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national living in Maryland with a U.S.-citizen wife and child, had been granted protection from deportation under a 2019 immigration court order after a judge found he faced danger from gang targeting of his family. In March 2025, **Trump administration officials deported him to El Salvador's CECOT mega-prison anyway, in violation of that court order** -- an error the administration itself later acknowledged in litigation while resisting court orders to facilitate his return. Abrego Garcia sued and won, forcing the government to return him to the United States by June 2025. DHS then issued an April 2025 press release describing a 'bombshell investigative report' alleging Abrego Garcia was a suspected human trafficker, based on a 2022 Tennessee traffic stop in which he was found driving with nine passengers and released with only a warning at the time. Prosecutors in the Middle District of Tennessee subsequently charged him with human smuggling and conspiracy to commit human smuggling. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly touted the indictment at a press conference, saying 'This is what American justice looks like.' U.S. District Judge Waverly Crenshaw Jr. first found in October 2025 that Abrego Garcia may have been charged out of prosecutorial vindictiveness, writing that 'the Government had a significant stake in retaliating against Abrego's success' in his deportation lawsuit, and ordered a hearing on the question. In May 2026, Judge Crenshaw dismissed the case outright, finding 'presumptive vindictiveness' and writing that 'absent Abrego's successful lawsuit challenging his removal to El Salvador, the Government would not have brought this prosecution,' concluding 'the evidence before this court sadly reflects an abuse of prosecuting power.' The Justice Department vowed to appeal the dismissal.
elements_required: The government violated an existing federal court order protecting a specific individual from deportation, then resisted court orders to correct the error
The individual sued the government and won, forcing his return to the United States

Criminal charges were subsequently filed against the same individual, based on conduct (a 2022 traffic stop) that had not previously resulted in charges despite being known to law enforcement at the time

A federal judge -- not merely the defendant or his advocates -- independently found the prosecution was likely brought in retaliation for the successful lawsuit, using the legal standard of 'presumptive vindictiveness,' and ultimately dismissed the case on that basis

status: Dismissed by the district court on May 22, 2026 on vindictive-prosecution grounds; the Justice Department has stated it will appeal. Abrego Garcia's underlying immigration status and the earlier deportation-error litigation are separate, ongoing matters not resolved by this dismissal.
rebuttal_anticipated: The administration could argue that the 2022 traffic-stop evidence independently supported a legitimate human-smuggling charge regardless of the timing relative to Abrego Garcia's lawsuit, that prosecutorial discretion permits charging decisions made at any point once evidence comes to light, and that Bondi's public statement reflected confidence in a case DOJ believed was meritorious rather than an admission of retaliatory motive.
comeback: A federal judge -- applying the specific legal standard for vindictive prosecution, which requires more than mere suspicion -- independently examined the same timeline and evidence and concluded not only that the prosecution may have been retaliatory but, after a full hearing, that it presumptively was: the government would not have brought this case at all absent Abrego Garcia's successful lawsuit. That is a judicial finding under a demanding legal standard, not a political characterization, and it followed a case the government's own senior law-enforcement official had already publicly celebrated as vindication before the court's own scrutiny concluded otherwise.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of the administration pursuing criminal or civil action against individuals who have publicly challenged or embarrassed it (see the Halligan entry for a separate, similarly-adjudicated instance) -- though this entry documents an immigration-enforcement-context case with its own independent judicial fact-finding, distinct from that entry's specific defendant and legal theory.

The case remains on appeal as of this entry, so the dismissal is not yet a final, unreviewable judgment -- frame as 'a federal district judge found presumptive vindictiveness and dismissed the case, with the government's appeal pending,' not as a conclusively settled matter.

official: George Cook, Acting Director, U.S. Census Bureau (no single official is named in sourcing as personally directing the AFPI placements; Cook is the agency's senior accountable office-holder, which has operated without a Senate-confirmed director since early 2025)
offense_category: Institutional Capture Through Politically Screened Placement -- partisan think-tank staff detailed into a nonpartisan statistical agency outside its normal vetted hiring process, producing a methodologically disputed report used to support voter-fraud claims; not itself a charged violation
incident_summary:
WIRED reported (September 16, 2026) that at least seven staffers from the America First Policy Institute (AFPI) -- a think tank aligned with President Trump -- have been detailed to the U.S. Census Bureau under the Intergovernmental Personnel Act (IPA), a mechanism historically used to bring in term-limited specialists from local governments, universities, and tribal organizations, not political-advocacy staff. The AFPI detailees were given access to sensitive Census population data.

On August 18, 2026, the Census Bureau published an anonymously authored report titled "Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election: A Beginning Analysis," which compared voter records against citizenship records and claimed to identify roughly 24,000 instances of noncitizen voting in the 2020 election. WIRED identified two of the report's authors, Matthew Jensen and Jeff McCrea, as AFPI staffers, and named at least five additional AFPI members detailed to the Bureau, including researcher Max Kossek and Ryan Montgomery. Independent experts and former Census officials raised methodology concerns: David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said "census data cannot reliably be matched to voter data," and other reviewers flagged the report's undisclosed authorship and the absence of clear false-match testing or sample validation to confirm how many of the flagged 24,000 records were actually ineligible voters. A Census employee told WIRED the AFPI staffers' role was "disrespectful to the institution," saying there had historically been "nothing close" to this level of outside-advocacy-group access.

House Oversight Democrats -- Reps. Robert Garcia, Maxwell Frost, and Raja Krishnamoorthi -- sent a letter to the Census Bureau on September 4, 2026 raising concerns about the report and the AFPI detailees' role in producing it.

Independent subject-matter experts and former agency officials identified specific, substantive methodology concerns with the report -- not merely a partisan disagreement with its conclusions
The report was produced and published without a Senate-confirmed Bureau director in place, during a period of documented leadership vacancy
Congressional oversight (a formal letter from House Oversight Democrats) has already been triggered by the report and the staffing arrangement that produced it

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the Intergovernmental Personnel Act is a lawful, routinely used mechanism for bringing outside expertise into federal agencies, the detailees' subject-matter work on election-integrity questions is within the Bureau's legitimate research mandate, and disagreement with the report's methodology is a normal part of academic/statistical debate rather than evidence of impropriety.
comeback: The IPA mechanism's normal use is for local-government, university, and tribal specialists on term-limited technical assignments -- not for embedding staff from a single, Trump-aligned political advocacy organization en masse inside a nonpartisan statistical agency to author an anonymously published, politically salient report on voter fraud. The methodology concerns here aren't a generic academic dispute: a named expert said the underlying data-matching approach is unreliable by design, and the report withheld its authors' AFPI affiliations from the public. A career Census employee's on-record description of the situation as "disrespectful to the institution" and without precedent underscores that this isn't ordinary interagency personnel-sharing.

What remains genuinely contested: whether the report's methodology is actually invalid (a substantive empirical/statistical dispute, not yet independently adjudicated) versus AFPI's/the administration's position that it identifies real noncitizen voting. The report is disputed: authored by undisclosed political-advocacy staff, criticized on methodological grounds by independent experts, not a proven fabrication.

A spokesperson for Ben Black stated: 'Ben Black had no personal or professional relationship with Jeffrey Epstein,' a denial that directly contradicts the documentary evidence in the DOJ records and Guardian's review of Epstein's own correspondence.

official: Scott Bessent, Secretary of the Treasury (also performing duties of acting IRS Commissioner)
offense_category: Potential Conflict of Interest / Improper Personal Benefit via Official Position (possible analogues: 18 U.S.C. §208, federal conflict-of-interest statute; or broader abuse-of-office concerns regarding personal tax benefit obtained through a settlement reached by subordinate DOJ/Treasury officials) — NOT charged; the settlement and Blanche's release order were published by DOJ, but Treasury has not detailed how they apply; appeals pending
incident_summary:
On May 18, 2026, the administration announced a settlement of Trump's lawsuit against the IRS that created a $1.776 billion compensation fund for individuals -- including the president's allies -- who claimed to have been unfairly targeted by the Biden administration; a release order signed the next day by Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche reportedly granted President Trump and his family immunity from IRS audits. On June 2, Blanche told Congress the fund would not move forward, without committing to end the audit protections. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who also performs IRS Commissioner duties during a vacancy, has repeatedly declined to confirm or detail the audit-immunity terms, citing ongoing litigation. Treasury General Counsel Brian Morrissey resigned on May 18, 2026, the day the fund was announced; the next day Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told senators "I don't know if it's a coincidence," and he and Vice President JD Vance declined to rule out payouts from the $1.8 billion fund to January 6 defendants, with Vance saying requests would be handled "case-by-case."

On July 13, 2026, Judge Kathleen Williams found the underlying lawsuit was brought for an "improper purpose" and in bad faith, found there was never a genuine case or controversy between the parties, and referred one of Trump's attorneys for bar discipline; her opinion specifically found that Bessent, IRS CEO Bisignano, and DOJ's litigators were structurally bound not to advance any position contravening the President -- though the court assessed monetary sanctions only against Trump's side and its lawyers and did not sanction Bessent personally, and no charges or finding of personal impropriety have been made against him. On July 31, 2026, Trump, his co-plaintiffs and their attorneys Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein filed a notice of appeal to the Eleventh Circuit. On August 5, 2026, Judge Williams denied Trump's request for an expedited ruling on his motion to stay her sanctions order, finding no "good cause" for expedited treatment, and ordered the court-appointed amici to respond.

Rather than withdraw the audit-immunity provision after Judge Williams' ruling, then-Acting Attorney General Blanche posted a document on X on August 2, 2026, stating that the audit deal applies only to the parties named in the lawsuit and only retroactively; outside tax-law experts at the NYU Tax Law Center say the clarification changes nothing substantive, and the underlying protections could shield Trump from as much as $100 million in back taxes and penalties tied to his Chicago skyscraper. After Blanche's August 8 confirmation as Attorney General, DOJ -- through newly installed Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter -- filed a brief at the Eleventh Circuit on August 12, 2026 formally joining Trump's side of the appeal, asking the court to stay Judge Williams' sanctions order and reassign the case away from her, arguing that reasonable members of the public would view her actions as improperly motivated. On September 11, 2026, McCotter filed a notice of appeal on behalf of the IRS and the Treasury Department, the defendants Bessent oversees, appealing the July 13 order themselves. On September 14, Judge Williams denied the stay motion outright, finding the movants had shown neither a likelihood of success on appeal nor irreparable harm. The Eleventh Circuit has not granted a stay and has directed the parties to brief whether the order is immediately appealable.

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (confirmed August 8, 2026; was Acting Attorney General at the time of this entry's original sourcing)
offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) -- underlying investigation into Brennan is ongoing and no charges have been filed; Blanche himself has not been personally charged with anything
incident_summary:
In July 2025, Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard declassified documents she said showed Obama-era officials fabricated the intelligence community's 2016 assessment that Russia sought to help Trump's campaign, plus a related criminal referral to DOJ. Retired CIA official Susan Miller, an author of the original 2017 assessment, publicly rejected that claim in a CNN interview reported July 26, 2025, saying the intelligence behind the Russia finding was verified, that the findings were not based on the Steele dossier, and that no one had told her team what conclusion to reach. Attorney General Pam Bondi nonetheless ordered federal prosecutors to convene a grand jury investigating the fabrication claim in early August 2025, formalizing the probe in Florida shortly after despite reports questioning the jurisdictional basis for doing so there. On August 20, 2025, Todd Gilbert, then U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Virginia, resigned after DOJ leadership pressured him to open a related grand jury investigation and to sideline a career prosecutor, Zachary Lee, who had concluded the case lacked evidentiary support; Gilbert refused, and reporting that October identified the Russia-probe pressure, not a routine personnel matter, as the real reason he was pushed out.

On September 26, 2025, on the government's motion, Chief Judge Cecilia Altonaga ordered two new federal grand juries empaneled beginning January 12, 2026, one in Fort Lauderdale and one in Fort Pierce. In late October 2025, Trump ally Mike Davis said the Fort Pierce grand jury, which he said U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones had moved to empanel, would investigate what Davis calls a decade-long conspiracy against Trump, and suggested Merrick Garland, Lisa Monaco, Chris Wray, and Jack Smith should be compelled to testify. The investigation became public on November 7, 2025, when former CIA Director John Brennan, along with Peter Strzok, Lisa Page, and, per CNN, former DNI James Clapper, was subpoenaed by the Miami-based U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida; Fox News reported that Quiñones was supervising the probe and that law enforcement sources expected up to 30 subpoenas in the coming days. On December 22, 2025, Brennan's attorney wrote to Chief Judge Altonaga alleging possible judge shopping -- that DOJ was steering the grand jury to Fort Pierce, whose only federal judge is Trump-appointed Aileen Cannon, to land any indictment before her -- and asking her to ensure the matter was not steered to Cannon; critics were already calling the expanding probe a fishing expedition relitigating ground covered by prior special-counsel and Senate Intelligence Committee investigations.

On February 17, 2026, the AP reported DOJ had issued a new wave of subpoenas to an array of former intelligence and law-enforcement officials, this time seeking records from the years since the 2017 assessment rather than only the months around it. Brennan's lawyers said he had been told he is a target but had not been given any "legally justifiable basis" for the investigation. On March 19, 2026, CBS News reported that Miami-based federal prosecutors had subpoenaed former FBI Director James Comey (whose separate earlier indictment had been dismissed in November 2025; tracked in a related entry in this database), that more than 130 subpoenas had been issued since the investigation began, and that McCabe had also received a subpoena, which his lawyer called "a vendetta in search of a crime." In April 2026, Maria Medetis Long, the career prosecutor overseeing the case in Miami, was removed after raising concerns about its evidentiary strength; Joseph DiGenova -- a Trump ally, former Trump campaign lawyer, and counselor to Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- was installed to lead the investigation in her place.

On May 12, 2026, Reuters reported the FBI had begun questioning current and former CIA officers about Brennan's role in the 2017 assessment -- despite multiple prior independent reviews having already affirmed Russia's 2016 election interference. On July 1, 2026, Brennan sued DOJ seeking a court order to preserve records related to both investigations, laying groundwork for an anticipated vindictive- or selective-prosecution defense should charges be filed.

In early September 2026, DOJ issued a new round of grand jury subpoenas, and Brennan's lawyers said he had now been told he is a target specifically over whether he falsely testified to Congress -- an allegation he and his attorneys have consistently denied -- with DiGenova still helping lead the investigation. On September 10, 2026, DiGenova abruptly resigned, submitting his resignation letter to Blanche that afternoon and telling CBS News only that "it was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department"; his wife and Fort Pierce team member, Victoria Toensing, left DOJ the following day. The same September 10 subpoena wave included Brennan himself: his attorney disclosed he had been ordered to appear before the Fort Pierce grand jury on October 15, 2026, named a "subject" of the broader conspiracy investigation while remaining a target only in the separate, narrower false-testimony probe. A DOJ spokesperson thanked DiGenova for "his work these past five months" alongside the Southern District of Florida prosecutors "led by U.S. Attorney Jason Reding Quiñones" but did not explain the departure. NBC News reported that no one would be named to replace him for now and, citing a source, that DOJ leadership had lost confidence in his leadership and hoped the Justice Department lawyers from Washington already on his team would get the probe back on track; days later, a person familiar with the matter told NBC the investigation was being run by Quiñones with support from Main Justice. The resignation came within days of grand jury witnesses' lawyers being notified of new subpoenas, and investigators separately began reaching out to lawyers for former FBI agents who had investigated Trump's own retention of classified records, requesting voluntary interviews. Bloomberg reported that on September 11, 2026, the investigation expanded further still, with new subpoenas issued including one seeking testimony from Clapper.

The day after DiGenova resigned, Kurt Olsen -- a Trump ally who had pressed DOJ in 2020 to back Trump's challenge to his election loss, later served as the White House's director of election security and integrity, and had since moved to the Miami-based prosecution team -- told Brennan's lawyers there were multiple "viable" grand jury investigations of their client, according to a declaration by Brennan's attorney Ken Wainstein in his records case, reported September 14, 2026: a "far-reaching" Fort Pierce investigation, covering "issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond," in which Brennan was a "subject," and a narrower investigation run from Washington into his statements to Congress, in which he was a "target" and which remained "still viable." On September 28 and 29, 2026, CBS News and ABC News, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Olsen had resigned from the Justice Department, and the AP that he had resigned from the investigation; CBS and ABC also reported that several other prosecutors had recently left the team, though one source said some had only been on temporary assignments that had ended and that new attorneys had been added. CNN, which had initially reported that Olsen had quit the department entirely, updated its story on September 30 to say he had left the investigation but that an email he sent DOJ leadership had been mistakenly read as a resignation; the same day, Attorney General Blanche told reporters Olsen "has not resigned" and is "still employed exactly where he was before," adding that the investigation remained "well-staffed." Later that day, a Justice Department official told CBS News that Olsen had announced in a September 28 email that he was leaving the case, that officials had misread the email as a resignation from the department, and that he would remain on staff as senior counsel but would not be assigned to the investigation. The investigation had still produced no charges.

The replacement lead (DiGenova) has documented political ties to Trump and the current DOJ leadership, rather than being an arms-length career assignment

The investigation targets a prominent, named Trump adversary (Brennan, who has been a vocal Trump critic) over conduct connected to the 2016 Russia-interference assessment, a subject of longstanding public presidential grievance

No indictment has yet been returned, despite the investigations having been open since November 2025 -- consistent with (though not proof of) an evidentiary basis weaker than the resources devoted to the case would suggest

As of September 2026, Brennan's lawyers say he has been told he is a target specifically over allegedly false congressional testimony -- a narrower, more concrete theory than the earlier general 'no legally justifiable basis' framing, relevant to whether the investigation has developed an actual prosecutable theory or simply narrowed its stated rationale without new evidence

DiGenova, installed in April 2026 specifically to advance the case after his predecessor's removal, himself resigned September 10, 2026 without ever bringing charges in either probe -- a second consecutive lead prosecutor exiting the case without producing a prosecutable result, relevant to whether the case has a genuine evidentiary basis or has instead cycled through leadership without one

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General
offense_category: Hatch Act Concern (5 U.S.C. 7323(a)(1), barring use of official authority or influence to affect an election) -- a sitting Attorney General speaking at Republican campaign events before the 2026 midterms; Senate-confirmed appointees may take part in politics in a personal capacity, so the dispute is whether he acted in his official role; complaints pending with the Office of Special Counsel, not charged (Hatch Act enforcement is administrative)
incident_summary:
Within weeks of taking office, Attorney General Todd Blanche spoke at a series of Republican campaign events ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, a break with the post-Watergate practice of attorneys general staying away from partisan politics. On August 14, 2026, four days after he was sworn in, Blanche spoke at an event at the Nassau County Police Academy in Garden City, New York, headlined by President Trump and Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, the Republican nominee for governor of New York. According to watchdog complaints, the event was billed as an official White House appearance on violent crime; Blanche was introduced as the sitting attorney general, identified himself as "attorney general of the United States," and said: "We just heard from our great Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman who's doing everything we need him to do to back the blue, support law enforcement and to make this county a safe county that we can all raise our kids in." Blanche later told the AP, "I will always say yes to speak when the president of the United States asks me to," and that he was "purely thanking cops."

On September 9, 2026, Blanche spoke at the Republican National Committee's 2026 midterm convention in Dallas, an event the committee said was held to support its slate of midterm candidates. The Justice Department said on social media that his "appearance this evening in his personal capacity is legal (and has been approved by ethics)"; the convention's on-screen graphic identified him as a "former federal prosecutor" rather than by his title. Former Attorney General Eric Holder called the appearance "unprecedented" and "disgraceful." On September 15, from the White House podium, Blanche dismissed Democratic lawmakers' concerns about artificial intelligence as "nothing but an effort to influence the midterms." **On September 16, at a North Carolina rally for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley, Blanche called Trump "the greatest president of our generation."** He told the crowd that people were safer than two years ago, "And that's President Trump and Vice President Vance delivering on a promise that they made to you." The AP reported that the speech also veered into the stock market, inflation and wage growth.

The Justice Department says the appearances are made in Blanche's personal capacity and do not get into agency policies or official business. "His appearances are reviewed and cleared by the Department's ethics officials," spokesperson Kiersten Pels told the AP, adding that travel expenses are reimbursed by the attorney general. The New York Times reported that those ethics rules had been loosened: in March 2026, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi rescinded a 2022 Garland-era policy that barred DOJ political appointees from partisan events even in a personal capacity, and the ethics office is now led by a former aide to Vice President JD Vance with no prior department experience. **Joseph Tirrell, DOJ's senior ethics official until he was dismissed in 2025, called the North Carolina appearance "terrible."** In his former role, he said, he would have told the attorney general: "That rally sounds like a Hatch Act violation to me, and I'd advise you not to do it."

At least four complaints about Blanche's political appearances have been filed with the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which enforces the Hatch Act: Public Citizen's in mid-August over the Long Island event; The Steady State's on September 4 over the same event (also naming FBI Director Kash Patel, with a referral to DOJ's Inspector General); The Steady State's in mid-September over his March 2026 CPAC appearance as Deputy Attorney General; and The Steady State's on September 28 over the Dallas convention speech. DOJ called the first complaint "baseless" and "a politically motivated complaint designed to weaponize the Hatch Act against the attorney general for his support of law enforcement."
elements_required: Blanche, while serving as Attorney General, spoke at partisan political events supporting Republican candidates or the Republican Party during the 2026 midterm campaign

In at least one appearance he was identified, or identified himself, by his official title, or spoke about the Justice Department's official work, such that a reasonable listener would see him acting in his official role (the Hatch Act's use-of-official-authority test, 5 U.S.C. 7323(a)(1))

The on-duty exemption for Senate-confirmed appointees (5 U.S.C. 7324(b)) applies only if no Treasury funds paid for the political activity, and does not permit use of official authority to affect an election
Complaints have been filed with the Office of Special Counsel, which has authority to investigate and make a finding

status: Ongoing: at least four Hatch Act complaints over Blanche's political appearances are pending with the Office of Special Counsel; no OSC finding reported. DOJ says the appearances were personal-capacity and ethics-cleared, with travel reimbursed.
rebuttal_anticipated: The Hatch Act lets Senate-confirmed appointees take part in politics in a personal capacity, and even on duty if the Treasury does not pay the costs (5 U.S.C. 7324(b)). The attorney general is not among the further-restricted officials barred from campaigning, so Public Citizen's premise is wrong. DOJ says each appearance was reviewed and cleared by ethics officials and avoided agency policy and official business, and that Blanche reimbursed his travel expenses; the Dallas convention identified him only as a 'former federal prosecutor.' NYU legal ethics professor Stephen Gillers told the Times his political statements are protected by the First Amendment and break no professional conduct rule: 'Any attempt to discipline him will fail.'
comeback: The exemption covers personal-capacity activity, not use of official authority to affect an election, and the test is whether listeners would reasonably see him acting in his government role. At the Long Island event, billed as an official White House appearance, he was introduced as the sitting attorney general and praised the Republican nominee for governor; at Dallas he recited DOJ enforcement results. Cynthia Shaw, DOJ's ethics chief in Trump's first term, told the Times that 'The bigger the job you get, the less personal capacity you have.' The ethics clearance DOJ cites came after Bondi rescinded the department's stricter policy and under an ethics office now led by a former Vance aide.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a pattern of senior officials campaigning in the 2026 midterms while complaints pile up at an Office of Special Counsel that has left them pending for months or closed them without discipline, as with RFK Jr.'s calls to Iowa candidates and his military-jet campaign trip. At DOJ it follows the loosening of the department's own guardrails, including the firing of ethics official Joseph Tirrell, and Blanche's stated view that the president should have a voice in individual prosecutions. An attorney general campaigning for one party while DOJ investigates the president's opponents weakens the appearance of impartial law enforcement.

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (confirmed August 8, 2026; was Acting Attorney General at the time of this entry's original sourcing)
offense_category: Press Freedom / DOJ News Media Policy Violation (28 C.F.R. § 50.10) -- a separate leak investigation from this tracker's other DOJ-journalist-subpoena entries, notable because DOJ has refused to withdraw it after backing down from comparable subpoenas of other reporters
incident_summary: DOJ subpoenaed Matthew Cole, a freelance journalist who co-wrote a 2025 New York Times story on a botched 2019 Navy SEAL Team 6 mission in North Korea (in which SEALs killed several unarmed North Koreans while attempting to plant a listening device, based on reporting from roughly two dozen unnamed sources), **demanding his testimony and more than two years of his notes and communications to identify his sources**. The subpoena was issued in Virginia in February 2026, while Pam Bondi was Attorney General; FBI agents attempted to deliver it in person at Cole's New York City residence, then delivered it to his lawyer when he was not home. Its existence was not made public until August 1, 2026, when The Times disclosed it at Cole's request -- the paper said it supported his decision to make public a subpoena the government had tried to keep secret, and is paying for his legal representation. Unlike DOJ's subpoenas of Wall Street Journal reporters (Iran war reporting), a Washington Post reporter (Venezuela coverage) and New York Times reporters (Air Force One security story), all of which DOJ withdrew after legal challenges, DOJ had refused to withdraw the Cole subpoena as of early October 2026.

The subpoena targeted a journalist specifically in connection with his newsgathering (identifying confidential sources for a national-security story), not as an ordinary case witness unconnected to his reporting
DOJ sought an unusually broad scope -- more than two years of notes and communications -- to identify sources for a single story

DOJ has maintained the subpoena even after withdrawing comparable subpoenas against Washington Post, Wall Street Journal and other New York Times reporters following legal challenges, indicating the withdrawals were not a general policy change

offense_category: Conflict of Interest -- Directing DOJ to Halt Cryptocurrency Enforcement While Personally Holding Crypto Assets an Ethics Agreement Required Him to Divest, Then Gifting Rather Than Selling Those Assets to His Own Children
incident_summary: At his March 2025 Senate confirmation, Blanche disclosed cryptocurrency holdings valued between $159,000 and $485,000, including Bitcoin ($100,000-$250,000), Solana, Ethereum, and Coinbase stock. His ethics agreement required him to fully divest those holdings within 90 days of confirmation and, until then, barred him from participating in any matter with a 'direct and predictable effect' on his crypto-related financial interests. In April 2025, Blanche issued a DOJ-wide memo titled 'Ending Regulation by Prosecution' that terminated Biden-era investigations into crypto companies, dealers, and exchanges, disbanded the National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team -- which had secured major convictions including a $110 million fraud case and a settlement with Binance's founder resulting in $4.3 billion in penalties -- and redirected DOJ's crypto-related focus away from platforms hosting illicit activity toward only direct prosecution of terrorists and drug traffickers. **Rather than selling his crypto holdings as the ethics agreement required, Blanche transferred assets valued between $116,000 and $315,000 as gifts to his adult children and a grandchild in late May and early June 2025**, separately selling only $5,000-$75,000 worth of additional holdings. Ethics experts said this method of 'divestment' defeated its purpose: Virginia Canter, a former White House and Treasury ethics lawyer, said 'if you are invested in that industry and now making a decision that could affect whether or not the DOJ is gonna pursue prosecutions, that's an obvious conflict of interest,' and Kedric Payne, the Campaign Legal Center's ethics director, said gifting the assets to adult children 'defeats' the law's purpose of eliminating even the appearance that an official's decisions are influenced by personal financial interests. Blanche's case was one instance of a broader pattern: ProPublica's analysis found the Trump administration's approximately 216 political appointees collectively held $175-340 million in cryptocurrency, compared to roughly two dozen Biden appointees holding under $7 million combined -- with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (formerly Cantor Fitzgerald's CEO, with billions in crypto investments) and SEC Chair Paul Atkins (who owned up to $6 million in crypto-related businesses) cited as other crypto-invested officials in directly relevant regulatory positions.

offense_category: Selective/Weaponized Enforcement -- DOJ installed a prosecutor who was on the Capitol grounds on January 6, 2021 -- in what a former DOJ Capitol Siege Section prosecutor called the restricted area -- to co-direct a task force prosecuting left-wing political violence as domestic terrorism, raising a direct double-standard concern -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary:
Brian Lynch has co-directed Joint Task Force Vanguard -- a DOJ task force that DOJ describes as central to prosecuting alleged left-wing political violence -- since March 2026, when Todd Blanche was still Deputy Attorney General (he became Acting Attorney General on April 2, 2026); the task force indicted 15 anti-ICE protesters in Minneapolis. Reporting revealed that Lynch, then three months into his job as an assistant U.S. attorney in Maryland, attended the January 6, 2021 march at the Capitol wearing a Trump 2020 hat and a shirt bearing an Afghanistan deployment service map. Images obtained by Talking Points Memo show Lynch standing near a crane on Capitol grounds in what a former federal prosecutor described as "definitely in the restricted area." A DOJ official confirmed Lynch "was present but never entered the Capitol, left the grounds after a brief period, and did not commit and was never accused of any violation of law." Michael Romano, former deputy chief of DOJ's now-disbanded Capitol Siege Section (which prosecuted January 6 cases), said he was surprised a prosecutor present that day continued working and was later promoted to lead a task force prosecuting political violence, noting "people were trying to stop the certification of the electoral college vote on January 6th." Lynch did not respond to requests for comment.

The case Lynch's task force built has since drawn a legal challenge leaning directly on his Jan. 6 presence. On August 13, 2026, defense attorney Kevin Riach filed a discovery motion on behalf of defendant Isaac Sant, one of the 15 Minneapolis anti-ICE defendants, calling Lynch's grand-jury conspiracy slide -- which named groups including the AFL-CIO and the Minneapolis Federation of Educators as co-conspirators "with no evidence" tying them to the defendants -- part of a "broad and irrational investigation," and signaled an intent to move to dismiss for selective prosecution. The motion draws on DHS undercover-surveillance reports the government produced in discovery, and on August 25, 2026, Riach filed a further batch of exhibits in support of it, including Homeland Security Investigations reports from its "Project Whipple Shield" investigation. A hearing was held August 27, 2026 before U.S. Magistrate Judge David Schultz on Riach's discovery motion; Sant told reporters outside court the motion sought "to reveal the scope of the spying" by DHS. Schultz did not rule from the bench and said he plans to issue an order on the motion soon, with no exact timeline given, FOX 9 reported. Court records show that after the hearing, Schultz allowed prosecutors to file supplemental briefing, which they filed September 10, 2026, and on September 16 he gave Sant's lawyer more time to respond.

offense_category: Prosecutorial Discretion Override / Corporate Accountability Failure -- DOJ senior leadership overruled its own Criminal Division's recommendation to pursue felony charges over infant hospitalizations and possible deaths, in favor of a civil settlement, against a company represented by a law firm with a pro-bono services deal benefiting pro-Trump causes
incident_summary: Federal prosecutors investigated Cronobacter bacterial contamination at Abbott Laboratories' Sturgis, Michigan infant-formula plant, where the FDA said **five infants were hospitalized with bacterial infections that 'may have contributed to death in two patients'**. Prosecutors reportedly recommended a felony charge that Abbott executives conspired to defraud the US, plus a separate Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act charge against the company. Tysen Duva, the DOJ Criminal Division's assistant attorney general, supported pursuing the felony charges, but was reportedly overruled by the Deputy Attorney General's office, then led by Todd Blanche, which ordered the criminal investigation closed. DOJ instead pursued a civil False Claims Act settlement, which a senior DOJ official called 'the best mechanism to achieve accountability, deterrence and protection of the public,' saying it included a 'significant' monetary penalty; on September 14, 2026, DOJ announced Abbott would pay $384,999,040, saying there had been no determination of liability. Sen. Adam Schiff opened an inquiry into the decision, writing to DOJ: 'Under your management, DOJ does not consider a case involving deadly risks to medically sensitive infants, after a recommendation of a felony charge, to be worthy of criminal prosecution,' and demanding an explanation for why prosecutors' advice was rejected. Abbott is represented by Kirkland & Ellis, one of the law firms that struck a deal with the White House providing pro-bono legal services to pro-Trump causes -- the same firm documented elsewhere in this tracker's entry on DOJ's subpoenas of law firms over Boris Epshteyn communications.

incident_summary: In an April 2026 NBC News interview, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche -- Trump's former personal defense attorney -- was asked about a communication in which Trump had publicly implored then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to indict several of his political enemies. Blanche said Americans should be 'happy' about it, calling it an example of the president being upfront with the public and making his 'high expectations' clear: 'That type of communication from President Trump should make every American happy,' Blanche said, adding it 'means that there's an executive, a chief executive, that is making sure every one of his Cabinet members are working as hard as they should.' Blanche described Trump as 'my boss' and characterized the investigations into Trump's political opponents as receiving 'outsized focus' only because 'they involve individuals that the president has had significant issues' with -- not because of their share of DOJ's actual caseload. Separately, Blanche suggested prosecutors could continue pursuing cases against a target even after a grand jury declines to indict, rather than treating a declined indictment as the matter's end -- 'You don't have to just take a "no true bill" from a grand jury and walk away,' he said. Legal commentary in Just Security later urged courts to adopt a 'no true bill' rule, devised by the chief judge of D.C.'s federal district court, requiring prosecutors to disclose a grand jury's prior refusal to indict before re-presenting a case elsewhere. The interview came as Blanche's own nomination for permanent Attorney General faced a contested Senate confirmation process.

offense_category: DOJ Weaponization Against the Legal Profession / Executive Privilege Misuse -- DOJ using civil-litigation subpoena power against private law firms to shield a presidential adviser's communications from a bar association's discovery request, while its own public justification concedes those communications are relevant
incident_summary:
Starting around February 2025, Trump used executive orders to strip lawyers at firms he viewed as hostile -- including firms that had represented his adversaries or investigated him -- of security clearances, government contracts, and building access. Rather than negotiating with government attorneys, targeted firms instead cut deals directly with Boris Epshteyn, Trump's personal lawyer, who by April 2025 had extracted commitments of close to $1 billion in free legal services for Trump-aligned causes plus changes to hiring practices, according to the Wall Street Journal; the nine firms that reached these deals, beginning with Paul, Weiss in March 2025, were Paul, Weiss, Skadden, Willkie Farr & Gallagher, Milbank, Kirkland & Ellis, Latham & Watkins, A&O Shearman, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, and Cadwalader, Wickersham & Taft; Bloomberg Law put their combined pledges at $940 million. In early July 2026 (the University of Wisconsin Law School's Lawyers and Democratic Decline tracker says the subpoenas were issued July 1; DOJ's notice to the ABA is dated July 2), the Justice Department subpoenaed 14 major law firms and their leaders -- the nine firms that reached deals pledging free legal services to the administration, the four firms that successfully challenged Trump's executive orders targeting them in court (Perkins Coie, Jenner & Block, WilmerHale, and Susman Godfrey), and Covington & Burling, which was targeted by a February 25, 2025 presidential memorandum -- seeking the firms' communications with Trump adviser Boris Epshteyn about those executive orders, plus any communications the firms had with the American Bar Association regarding Epshteyn. The New York Times reported the subpoenas on July 14, and DOJ disclosed them in a July 17 court filing in the ABA's ongoing lawsuit alleging its members face harm from the administration's law-firm policy; DOJ's stated position was that the ABA should seek this information from its own members or the firms rather than from the White House directly, while simultaneously invoking executive privilege to withhold Epshteyn's communications from direct disclosure, framing them as confidential presidential advice. DOJ's subpoena notice was filed under the name of Civil Division Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate and signed by trial attorney Adam S. Fox. On July 17, DOJ also moved to disqualify Susman Godfrey, one of the subpoenaed firms, as the ABA's counsel. The appeal of the underlying executive orders, already struck down for the four affected firms, remained pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which heard argument on May 14, 2026.

In a July 22, 2026 reply supporting its July 7 motion to compel, the ABA said the government's argument "leads to an absurd outcome," called its law-firm subpoenas "a huge waste of time (and resources) for everyone involved," and pressed for direct production by DOJ or a compliant privilege log. The subpoenas also called the 14 firms' leaders to depositions set for August 3, 2026; no account of those depositions has been publicly reported. Judge Amir H. Ali heard the motion to compel on July 31 and took it under advisement, and on August 3 ordered DOJ to identify the individuals and custodians at issue for several of the ABA's requests or assert privilege over them. On August 10, 2026, DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel issued a 21-page opinion to the Counsel to the President, signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser, concluding that executive privilege can extend to a president's communications with private advisers -- "anyone the President consults outside the Executive Branch" -- where the communications relate to official presidential decisionmaking, involve or reflect communications with the President or his direct advisers, and are confidential; the opinion does not mention the ABA case or Epshteyn. The Washington Examiner reported it on August 11. On August 17, DOJ formally asserted the presidential communications privilege over the non-public names of presidential advisers and custodians the court had ordered it to identify, saying the subpoenaed firms had "only just begun to produce records." On August 25, DOJ invoked the OLC opinion in its reply supporting the motion it had filed on July 2, on behalf of the Executive Office of the President and the United States, to quash the ABA's own document and deposition subpoenas to Epshteyn, turning what had been a litigation-filing assertion into a position backed by OLC's formal opinion.

offense_category: Prosecutorial/Grand Jury Overreach and Voter/Election-Worker Intimidation Pattern -- no criminal charge against Blanche personally; DOJ's subpoena was itself judicially found unreasonable
incident_summary:
Following an FBI search warrant executed at Fulton County, Georgia's election hub in January 2026 (seizing hundreds of boxes of ballots and other 2020 election records in an FBI investigation that, according to the FBI's own warrant affidavit, originated from a referral by Kurt Olsen, the White House's presidentially appointed Director of Election Security and Integrity, who had worked after the 2020 election to overturn Trump's loss), DOJ prosecutors issued a grand jury subpoena, dated April 17, 2026, demanding the names and personal contact information of every Fulton County employee and volunteer poll worker who worked the 2020 election. Fulton County moved to quash the subpoena on May 4, 2026, arguing it was meant to "target, harass and punish the President's perceived political opponents." On July 7, 2026, U.S. District Judge William Ray -- a Trump appointee -- quashed the subpoena, calling its scope "staggering" and writing that "given the low need for the subpoenaed information and the highly burdensome nature of the disclosure of the same, the Subpoena is unreasonable and must be quashed." Judge Ray added that while the grand jury works with federal prosecutors to investigate alleged crimes, "that does not give the DOJ the right to use the Grand Jury to do whatever the DOJ wants." Judge Ray found that the five-year statute of limitations for any crime arising from the 2020 election had run by January 7, 2026 at the latest, so the records "would not lead to information that could be used to charge anyone with anything, at least not any viable charge"; DOJ had argued that the limitations period did not bar the grand jury's inquiry. The court expressly did not reach Fulton County's argument that the subpoena was politically motivated.

A DOJ spokesperson said the same day as the ruling that the decision was "at odds with numerous holdings of the Supreme Court" and that the Department was "considering all options to challenge" it. DOJ followed through: on August 6, 2026, federal prosecutors filed a notice of appeal to the Eleventh Circuit (No. 26-12769). On September 11, 2026, the appeals court clerk granted DOJ a 30-day extension, making its opening brief due October 15, 2026.
elements_required: DOJ sought sweeping personal information (names and contact details of every 2020 Fulton County poll worker/employee) far beyond what a legitimate, narrowly-targeted investigation would require
A federal court independently found the subpoena's burden disproportionate to any legitimate investigative need -- not merely a characterization by the targeted party
The subpoena followed a documented pattern of DOJ action specifically targeting a jurisdiction Trump has publicly and falsely blamed for his 2020 loss

Blanche -- Acting Attorney General from April 2, 2026 and confirmed as Attorney General on August 8, 2026 -- is the accountable DOJ official (the subpoena is dated April 17, 2026, when Blanche was Acting AG) for the department's subpoena practices, whether or not he personally reviewed this specific request

incident_summary: In January 2026, in a separate leak investigation of a government contractor, the FBI searched the home of a Washington Post journalist and seized her electronic devices. On March 4, 2026, while Pam Bondi was Attorney General and Todd Blanche was her deputy, **DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas for the records of Wall Street Journal reporters**, seeking the sources of a February 23 Journal article on warnings from Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and others at the Pentagon about the risks of a war with Iran; the Journal disclosed them on May 11. DOJ also issued **grand jury subpoenas seeking to compel testimony from three Wall Street Journal journalists and Washington Post national security reporter Ellen Nakashima** (the Post's came in the spring); the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press says it is unclear when those were authorized, though CNN reported that Trump personally pushed Blanche, Acting Attorney General from April 2, to issue the subpoenas. The New York Times later reported that the Post subpoena concerned coverage of U.S. military operations in Venezuela. Both papers challenged the subpoenas in sealed proceedings in federal court in Virginia, and DOJ withdrew them in June 2026, under Acting Attorney General Blanche. DOJ's own media-subpoena policy requires the Attorney General's approval for subpoenas to journalists; Blanche declined to comment on the subpoenas or the decision to withdraw them, calling it a grand jury matter.
elements_required: DOJ policy (28 C.F.R. § 50.10) requires the Attorney General's personal, written approval before a subpoena compelling journalist testimony or records may issue

The subpoenas targeted working journalists specifically in connection with their newsgathering (national security reporting on the Iran war and, per The New York Times, on U.S. military operations in Venezuela), not as ordinary case witnesses unconnected to their reporting

DOJ ultimately withdrew the subpoenas following legal challenge, which is consistent with either an initial approval that did not survive scrutiny, or a decision that should not have been approved in the first place

The Attorney General in office at each step (Bondi when the March records subpoenas issued; Blanche, as Acting Attorney General, when DOJ withdrew the subpoenas in June) is the accountable official for DOJ's media-subpoena policy compliance, whether or not he or she personally signed each individual subpoena

offense_category: Potential quid-pro-quo clemency arrangement / abuse of prosecutorial discretion in connection with a convicted co-conspirator's cooperation, prison classification, and possible pardon (relevant concerns: 18 U.S.C. Sec. 201-adjacent bribery/gratuity principles do not directly apply to clemency itself, but the sequence raises conflict-of-interest and equal-justice concerns given Blanche's prior personal representation of Trump); not charged, no formal investigation into Blanche's own conduct identified in sourcing reviewed
incident_summary: On July 17, 2025, amid mounting pressure over DOJ's withheld Epstein files, Trump publicly directed Attorney General Pam Bondi to "produce any and all pertinent Grand Jury testimony"; the next day, July 18, DOJ under Bondi asked the Southern District of New York to unseal grand jury materials from Maxwell's criminal case; a parallel DOJ motion to unseal grand jury materials in the original Florida Epstein criminal case was denied on July 23, 2025 by U.S. District Judge Robin Rosenberg, who ruled that DOJ's rationales "are no exceptions" to grand jury secrecy under binding 11th Circuit precedent and wrote that the government itself "has effectively conceded that the Court's hands are tied." Amid mounting public and congressional criticism over DOJ's refusal to release the full Epstein files, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche -- Trump's own former personal defense attorney -- personally interviewed Ghislaine Maxwell, Jeffrey Epstein's convicted co-conspirator serving 20 years for sex trafficking, over two days (July 24-25, 2025) in Tallahassee, Florida, under a grant of limited/proffer immunity; Blanche had announced the outreach on July 22 in a statement Bondi posted on X: "President Trump has told us to release all credible evidence." Maxwell's attorney said she "answered every single question" and had been cooperating "100%." Asked in July 2025 about clemency for Maxwell, Trump said, "I'm allowed to do it, but it's something I have not thought about." Roughly a week after the interview, on August 1, 2025, Maxwell was quietly transferred from a low-security facility to FPC Bryan, Texas -- one of only three minimum-security federal prison camps in the country, ordinarily reserved for low-risk, often white-collar offenders -- a transfer multiple former federal prison officials called "highly unusual" for a convicted sex offender. On August 5, 2025, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced H.Res.635, expressing that Maxwell should not receive a pardon, commutation, or other clemency; it drew 14 Democratic cosponsors in all, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and has received no floor vote. Victims were given until August 5, 2025 to submit letters on DOJ's SDNY unsealing motion; on August 5 and 6 the court docketed six letters that representatives of victims and other witnesses had submitted. One victim, in a letter reported by CNN on August 4, called the push "political warfare" that shields powerful men while ignoring survivors and wrote that the government's continued handling of the matter was "eating at me day after day." A second, in a letter reported August 10, objected specifically to what she called Maxwell's impending "public legitimization," separately criticizing Maxwell's prison transfer, DOJ's private meetings with her, and clemency speculation, and accused the administration of retraumatizing survivors by moving to unseal without consulting them first. On August 11, 2025, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer -- the same judge who later denied Maxwell's habeas petition -- denied DOJ's unsealing bid in a scathing 31-page order, calling the government's central premise that the materials would reveal meaningful new information about Epstein's or Maxwell's crimes "demonstrably false," and separately faulting DOJ for failing to notify Epstein's and Maxwell's victims of the request in advance. On August 19, 2025, Democracy Forward sued DOJ and the FBI to force release of communications about the investigation, including any Epstein-Trump correspondence. On August 20, 2025, U.S. District Judge Richard Berman likewise denied DOJ's bid to unseal grand jury records from Epstein's 2019 New York case, finding that the information in them "pales in comparison to the Epstein investigative information and materials in the hands of the Department of Justice." On August 22, 2025, DOJ released the July 24-25 interview transcript (263 pages for day one, 66 for day two) and audio; in it, Maxwell said she "never saw" Trump "in any inappropriate setting" and disputed aspects of her own conviction, casting doubt on accuser Virginia Giuffre's allegations -- prompting Giuffre's family to say DOJ had given Maxwell "a platform to rewrite history." The Supreme Court declined to hear Maxwell's direct appeal on October 6, 2025. Reps. Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia each wrote to FPC Bryan Warden Tanisha Hall on October 30, 2025 seeking answers about her treatment; on November 8, 2025, NBC News reported on Maxwell's own emails from her first months at FPC Bryan, obtained by the House Judiciary Committee, in which she called herself "much much happier" and "safe," while separate Wall Street Journal reporting documented additional perks (dormitory meal delivery, late-night workouts, priority shower access) and inmates alleging retaliation, including one transfer, for discussing Maxwell with reporters. On November 10, 2025, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin disclosed that a whistleblower had come forward describing extensive special treatment FPC Bryan's warden was arranging for Maxwell: customized meals delivered to her cell, private visitor meetings in a cordoned-off area with refreshments, visitors permitted to bring computers (described as unprecedented), the warden personally handling her documents and correspondence, after-hours private exercise time in staff-only areas, and access to a service-dog-in-training for recreation that other inmates and staff were not normally permitted to touch. Raskin said the same whistleblower reported Maxwell was actively preparing a formal commutation application for submission to Trump with the warden's assistance. Raskin publicly demanded written answers from Trump on the extent of any clemency discussions and requested Blanche testify publicly before the Committee; no response from Trump, Blanche, or the Bureau of Prisons was identified in reporting reviewed. In November 2025, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One, "I don't talk about that. I don't rule it in or out." On December 9, 2025, after Congress passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, Engelmayer granted DOJ's renewed request to unseal the Maxwell-case grand jury materials, citing the Act, while again criticizing DOJ for moving without notice to victims. On February 9, 2026, appearing virtually for the House Oversight Committee's subpoenaed deposition, which Chairman James Comer had postponed in August 2025 until the Supreme Court acted on her appeal, Maxwell invoked the Fifth Amendment rather than answer questions; her attorney, David Oscar Markus, said she was "prepared to speak fully and honestly" if Trump granted her clemency. On July 29, 2026, the Senate agreed by unanimous consent to S.Res.608, sponsored by Sen. Jacky Rosen, expressing that Maxwell should not be granted a presidential pardon or any form of clemency. On August 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer denied her self-represented habeas corpus petition in a 67-page opinion calling her claims "meritless" and warning that further appeals would not be considered made in good faith.

official: Todd Blanche, Deputy Attorney General
offense_category: Weaponizing the Federal Clemency Process for Political Loyalty -- firing DOJ's career Pardon Attorney for declining a personal favor for a Trump ally, then installing a political appointee who has used the office to fast-track clemency for MAGA-aligned figures
incident_summary:
Elizabeth Oyer, DOJ's career Pardon Attorney since 2022, was fired on March 7, 2025 -- two days after Todd Blanche was confirmed as Deputy Attorney General. Oyer later testified, including before the Senate Judiciary Committee on July 16, 2026 during Blanche's own confirmation hearing to become Attorney General, that Blanche's office had asked her to recommend restoring gun rights to actor Mel Gibson, who lost that right after a 2011 misdemeanor domestic-violence conviction and who has a personal relationship with President Trump; Gibson's attorneys had written directly to senior DOJ officials citing a special appointment he had received from Trump. When Oyer declined and was pressed to reconsider, she was fired without any stated reason in a termination letter signed by Blanche.

On May 14, 2025, Trump appointed Edward "Ed" Martin Jr. -- previously interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, known for openly blending Trump's political goals with DOJ's clemency function -- as the new Pardon Attorney. Within two weeks of Martin's appointment, Trump pardoned more than two dozen MAGA-aligned loyalists and wealthy donors, including Culpeper County, Virginia Sheriff Scott Jenkins, convicted in December 2024 on federal bribery charges in a "cash-for-badges" scheme and sentenced to 10 years (Martin posted "No MAGA left behind" after the Jenkins pardon); reality-TV stars Todd and Julie Chrisley, pardoned May 28, 2025 after a 2022 conviction for defrauding banks of more than $30 million and evading federal taxes, after their daughter Savannah, a Trump-aligned media figure and RNC speaker, publicly and personally lobbied for their release and Trump called her directly to tell her the pardons were coming; and a commuted sentence for Larry Hoover, a Chicago gang leader (Gangster Disciples) serving multiple life sentences for conspiracy and drug-trafficking convictions -- a notable outlier from the wave's otherwise white-collar/MAGA-loyalist pattern, since Hoover's case is neither a fraud conviction nor an obvious political-donor connection. Martin went on to organize symbolic pardons for participants in the 2020 fake-elector scheme and to grant clemency or pardons to a number of Trump-connected officials and campaign donors; ProPublica reporting found no comparable path forward for ordinary clemency applicants under the restructured office. A June 17, 2025 House Judiciary Committee Democrats analysis, led by Ranking Member Jamie Raskin, quantified the pattern's scope beyond named individual examples: Trump's pardons and commutations -- more than 1,600 recipients, including white-collar and fraud convictions well beyond the MAGA-loyalist cases above -- had eliminated roughly $1.3 billion in restitution and fines owed to crime victims and taxpayers.

On December 3, 2025, Trump pardoned Rep. Henry Cuellar (D-TX) and his wife, ending a sitting Democratic member of Congress's active federal prosecution mid-case -- a materially different scenario from the wave above, which involved already-convicted or symbolic beneficiaries rather than a pending indictment against a sitting lawmaker. Cuellar and his wife had been indicted in 2024 on 12 counts of bribery, conspiracy, and money laundering centered on an alleged roughly $600,000 in bribes from Azerbaijan and a Mexican bank; two Foreign Agents Registration Act-related counts had already been narrowed under a separate Trump-driven policy sharply limiting FARA prosecutions before the pardon voided the remaining charges entirely. Cuellar's response undercuts any "reciprocal loyalty" framing of the pardon: he announced he would run for re-election as a Democrat, prompting Trump to publicly call the decision "a lack of LOYALTY" on social media -- itself evidence that the administration frames pardons as transactions expecting political fealty in return. Government watchdog group CREW sued for records on the pardon's origin, and Cuellar continued to face a separate House Ethics Committee investigation, opened May 2024 and reauthorized July 2025, unaffected by the federal pardon.

Martin's tenure as Pardon Attorney ended when Trump announced on August 21, 2026 that Martin was "leaving to go outside to fight Legal Battles for the upcoming Midterm Election, and the Presidential Election of 2028"; the announcement named no successor Pardon Attorney, with no reporting indicating a change of direction for the office's clemency practices. Martin's January 1, 2026 removal as head of DOJ's Weaponization Working Group, which CNN's sources tied in part to a DOJ review finding he improperly handled grand jury material, -- a related but factually distinct episode from the clemency-favoritism pattern described here -- is tracked separately in this database. On September 3, 2026, Oyer filed suit in federal court in Washington, D.C. against DOJ and Blanche, seeking a declaration that her removal was unlawful, reinstatement to federal service, and back pay.

official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (sued in his official capacity; was Acting Attorney General when the suit was filed and the June 2026 injunction issued, and as Deputy Attorney General signed DOJ's 2025-2026 letters to Congress on the files' production)
offense_category: Resisting a Federal Court's Orders to Comply With the Epstein Files Transparency Act -- a judge rejected DOJ's reasons for withholding FBI interview notes and never reviewing foreign-language files; no contempt finding has been made
incident_summary:
The Epstein Files Transparency Act, signed November 19, 2025, required the Attorney General to publish the Justice Department's unclassified Epstein and Maxwell files by December 19, 2025, with a written justification for every redaction published in the Federal Register. In a January 30, 2026 letter to Congress, then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said foreign-language materials had not been reviewed or produced because "it was not practicable for a first-level reviewer to determine the responsiveness of a foreign-language document." On April 27, 2026, lawyer and journalist Katie Phang sued Blanche, then Acting Attorney General, in federal court in Washington under the Administrative Procedure Act (Phang v. Blanche, No. 26-cv-1417), alleging DOJ had improperly redacted and withheld records the law required it to release, including notes of FBI interviews with a woman who alleged that, when she was about 13, Epstein introduced her to Trump, who then assaulted her.

On June 25, 2026, U.S. District Judge Emmet G. Sullivan granted Phang a preliminary injunction. DOJ had argued that Phang lacked standing and a right to sue but did not respond substantively to her merits arguments, which the court treated as conceded. The order required DOJ, by July 2, to unredact names in eight emails and two DOJ documents or show cause why not; to produce the handwritten FBI notes behind four FD-302 interview reports or show cause; to begin reviewing and producing foreign-language materials and notify the court; and to publish the redaction log in the Federal Register or explain why it could not. DOJ answered that the notes were "substantially similar" to the typed reports and hard to redact, and that the court should not "supplant Congress's acceptance" of its foreign-language explanation. At an August 13 hearing, where a DOJ lawyer could say only that the Federal Register publication was "forthcoming," Sullivan said "the public has a right to know what the hell is going on in this case," recalled holding Justice Department prosecutors in contempt in the Ted Stevens corruption case, and said "I don't want to do it, but I will do it to ensure justice is fairly administered." DOJ filed a notice of appeal on August 24 and, on August 27, published its February 14 report to Congress in the Federal Register as its redaction justification.

On September 16, 2026, after reviewing documents privately, Sullivan discharged the show-cause orders for seven documents and for the redaction log but **rejected DOJ's reasons for withholding the handwritten FBI interview notes and for never reviewing foreign-language Epstein files, and on the foreign-language files wrote that DOJ "cites no authority for the proposition that administrative inconvenience excuses him from meeting his statutory obligations."** He called a civil contempt finding "premature" because DOJ had now stated its rationale, set out the legal standard for contempt, and ordered Blanche, by September 24, to give the court redacted and unredacted copies of the notes and documentation for three disputed victim redactions, and to begin the foreign-language review and notify the court, seeking clarification by September 21 if he considered that order not "clear and unambiguous." In a separate order the same day, Sullivan found DOJ had missed its June 26 deadline to answer the lawsuit without seeking an extension, and ordered an answer by September 24.

DOJ appealed again and, on the evening of Friday, September 18, asked Sullivan to pause the foreign-language requirement, arguing that once documents are produced they "cannot be unproduced." On September 21 he denied the request because DOJ had not conferred with Phang's lawyers as local rules require, said he would have denied it on the merits anyway, and temporarily stayed only the foreign-language deadline so DOJ could ask the D.C. Circuit for a stay, which it did on September 22, arguing Phang has no right to sue. DOJ filed its answer on September 24, denying that it had failed to comply with the Act. MeidasTouch reported that Phang said on September 25 that a DOJ lawyer had told her by email that DOJ had given the judge the FBI notes by the deadline, though DOJ filed no public notice of what it submitted; the same report said, per Phang, that no foreign-language Epstein-file document had been publicly produced. The foreign-language deadline remains paused under Sullivan's temporary stay while the D.C. Circuit weighs DOJ's stay request; on September 25 Phang opposed that request and asked the appeals court to dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

offense_category: Conflict of Interest / Breach of Sworn Recusal Commitment (relevant standards: DOJ ethics regulations on personal/substantial participation in matters involving a former client; professional conduct rules, New York Rules of Professional Conduct, subject of a grievance complaint before New York's Attorney Grievance Committee, declined at staff level with reconsideration pending) — NOT charged criminally; this is a professional-ethics and conflict-of-interest matter, addressed via attorney grievance complaint and congressional inquiry, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary:
At his February 12, 2025 Senate confirmation hearing for Deputy Attorney General, Todd Blanche testified under oath: "I will follow the rules as told to me by the experts, career prosecutors in the department, if it comes to ever recusing." In March 2025, less than two weeks after he took office as Deputy Attorney General, DOJ's top career ethics lawyer, Joseph Tirrell, formally advised him that his recusal from cases involving Donald Trump in his personal capacity was necessary, given Blanche's prior work as Trump's personal defense attorney, CNN reported in May 2026. Reporting indicates he did not recuse himself from matters including a May 2026 settlement (Trump v. IRS), reached while he was acting Attorney General, that granted Trump and his family an IRS audit shield and was connected to a proposed $1.776 billion compensation fund; DOJ never contested Trump's claims in that litigation and never made a court appearance before settling. On June 22, 2026, Democracy Defenders Fund, Lawyers Defending American Democracy and 101 former federal and state judges filed a 73-page grievance complaint against Blanche with New York's Attorney Grievance Committee (Appellate Division, First Department), covering the settlement, the $1.776 billion fund and related conduct. Separately, the New York City Bar Association's July 13, 2026 letter urged the Senate Judiciary Committee to reject his nomination as Attorney General, calling him "unfit to lead the U.S. Department of Justice" and saying he had breached his confirmation commitment to follow career ethics staff's recusal guidance.

On July 13, 2026, Judge Kathleen Williams found the underlying IRS settlement was brought for an improper purpose and referred Trump's attorney to the Florida Bar for discipline; the personal tax-liability release for Trump and his family was left intact. By July 24, 2026, the New York Attorney Grievance Committee's chief attorney had declined to open an investigation into the grievance complaint, instead directing it to DOJ's own Office of Professional Responsibility; DDF and LDAD filed a request for reconsideration with the Committee's chair, arguing OPR's lack of independence given it reports to Blanche's own chain of command. On August 2, 2026, after Sens. Thom Tillis and John Cornyn demanded written assurances, Blanche issued an order stating that the May 18, 2026 order establishing the fund "is rescinded and shall have no force or effect"; DOJ also said that day that the settlement's audit protections apply only retroactively (CBS News, NPR) and are limited to Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization (NPR). Neither change was signed by the settlement's parties, which Senate Judiciary ranking member Richard Durbin said left them unenforceable (Roll Call).

The Senate confirmed Blanche as Attorney General by a 50-49 vote in the early hours of August 8, 2026. Sens. Collins and Murkowski (R) voted no alongside every Democrat, both citing independence concerns given Blanche's history as Trump's personal lawyer. With Sen. McConnell absent, the outcome came down to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R), Roll Call reported; NPR called his vote "crucial." In an August 7 floor speech, Cassidy cited what he called Blanche's "poor judgment in approving the anti-weaponization slush fund and exempting the president from IRS audits" and "episodes of apparent lawfare [with the] DOJ bringing suits against political enemies," then announced he would vote to confirm. The IRS settlement and fund were directly debated on the Senate floor and did not prevent confirmation, but the vote was not a finding on the merits of the recusal question.

incident_summary:
Alexander Smirnov, a former FBI confidential informant, was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison after admitting he fabricated a claim that Burisma, a Ukrainian energy company, paid Joe Biden and Hunter Biden a $10 million bribe. Prosecutors later wrote that when he was re-interviewed in September 2023, Smirnov changed parts of his account and "promoted a new false narrative after meeting with Russian officials"; DOJ stated in February 2024 that Smirnov admitted "officials associated with Russian intelligence were involved" in developing that new Hunter Biden narrative. The fabricated bribery claim had circulated among congressional Republicans and fueled impeachment-related attacks on President Biden before it was exposed as false.

In April 2025, prosecutor David Friedman told the court, with minimal explanation, only that "the United States intends to review the government's theory of the case underlying Defendant's criminal conviction," and jointly moved with Smirnov's own attorneys for his release pending appeal, which Judge Wright rejected from the bench with visible skepticism ("Seriously?"). Smirnov was nonetheless furloughed from custody by the Bureau of Prisons later in 2025, despite that denial, and was reported missing from the facility for months; his lawyer called it a medical furlough, and the Bureau of Prisons said in March 2026 that he was back in custody at Terminal Island. On March 4, 2026, DOJ filed its answering brief in the Ninth Circuit under the name of Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche (signed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Alexander P. Robbins), siding with Smirnov and asking the court to vacate the judgment and let him withdraw his guilty pleas. The Wall Street Journal noted that if an appeals court vacated the sentence, DOJ could then drop the charges entirely -- erasing Smirnov's own admission that the Biden bribery claims were fabricated.

The Ninth Circuit appeal (Nos. 25-400 and 25-408) proceeded with DOJ's active support. After briefing, the panel on July 31, 2026 ordered supplemental briefs on whether it had jurisdiction over the appeals and on the sentencing-guideline adjustment the government had described, then decided the case without oral argument, submitting it on September 17, 2026. On September 22, 2026, Judges Jacqueline Nguyen, Ryan Nelson and Roopali Desai dismissed the custody-credit claim for lack of jurisdiction, holding that a recommendation to the Bureau of Prisons is not part of a sentence and cannot be appealed, and affirmed the rest, finding that the plea agreement did not require a sentencing adjustment. The ruling rejected the argument Smirnov and DOJ had jointly pressed and left his guilty pleas and six-year sentence in place.

The fabricated claim was used by the sitting president's political opponents (congressional Republicans) to pursue impeachment-related attacks before being exposed as false
