official: Todd Blanche, Attorney General (confirmed August 8, 2026; was Acting Attorney General when the indictment was announced)
offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) -- DOJ criminally indicted a nonprofit civil rights watchdog organization long critical of the administration; SPLC's motion to dismiss on vindictive-prosecution grounds was denied August 7, 2026; no conviction, charges contested
incident_summary:
On April 21, 2026, a federal grand jury indicted the Southern Poverty Law Center on 11 counts -- six counts of wire fraud, four counts of false statements to a federally insured bank, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering -- announced by then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche. The indictment alleges that between 2014 and 2023, SPLC secretly funneled more than $3 million to "field sources" affiliated with extremist groups including the Ku Klux Klan, the National Socialist Movement, and the American Front, characterizing this as defrauding SPLC's own donors. In an April 30, 2026 letter reported May 1 by MS NOW and CNN, House Judiciary Democrats Jamie Raskin and Mary Gay Scanlon wrote that, according to whistleblower information, Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh ordered the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Middle District of Alabama to rush through the indictment despite serious concerns about the strength of the case.

On May 26, 2026, SPLC moved to dismiss the indictment, arguing the charges are "vindictive" and part of a broader "retribution campaign" against organizations and individuals the administration perceives as its enemies, and separately sought discovery into DOJ's prosecutorial motives. On June 2, 2026, the grand jury returned a superseding indictment charging the same 11 counts and alleging that $4.1 million in tax-exempt funds were used to pay informants inside extremist organizations (CBS News). U.S. District Judge Emily C. Marks denied both the motion and the discovery request in an order issued August 7, 2026, finding SPLC had not shown evidence of prosecutorial animus resulting in the prosecution -- a ruling that resolves this procedural motion but does not reach the underlying fraud charges, and does not foreclose SPLC raising the same argument again at trial or on appeal; no appeal of that denial has been identified.

On August 11, 2026, the grand jury returned a second superseding indictment adding former SPLC official Heidi Beirich as the first individually-named defendant (unsealed August 12, when she was arrested), charged with wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to submit false statements to a bank, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering -- bringing the case to 14 counts. It alleges SPLC funneled at least $4.1 million in tax-exempt donor funds between 2007 and 2023 (Fox News). Beirich was arraigned August 25. On August 31, Judge Marks denied SPLC's motion to be tried separately from Beirich and, on Beirich's motion, continued the joint trial from October 5, 2026 to February 1, 2027; on September 2, after SPLC's lead counsel said the February term was unworkable, she reset jury selection and trial for April 19, 2027 in Montgomery (court orders, Docs. 160 and 168). SPLC's lawyers argue law enforcement agencies have long known the organization paid informants to monitor hate groups' movements as part of its investigative and watchdog work, and separately allege that Blanche made a false statement, at a news conference and in interviews, when he claimed SPLC had not shared informant-derived information with law enforcement.

incident_summary: **Boeing's 2021 deferred prosecution agreement over the fatal 2018 Lion Air and 2019 Ethiopian Airlines 737 MAX crashes (346 deaths combined) was found violated** after the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout revived scrutiny of the company's compliance record, putting Boeing back on track for prosecution on the underlying fraud-conspiracy charge -- deceiving FAA regulators about a flight-control system (MCAS) implicated in both crashes. Judge Reed O'Connor rejected an initial revised plea-deal version in December 2024. Reuters reported May 17, 2025 that crash victims' families were preparing to formally object to a new tentative nonprosecution agreement the Trump-era DOJ had reached with Boeing, which would let the company avoid a felony conviction. The DOJ formally announced the agreement May 23, 2025, and the parties filed the final written Non-Prosecution Agreement on May 29, 2025: Boeing avoids trial and any felony conviction; pays a $487.2 million criminal fine (crediting $243.6 million already paid under the 2021 agreement); contributes $444.5 million to a new victims'-families compensation fund; and commits at least $445 million more to compliance, safety, and quality programs -- a total 'pay or invest' commitment DOJ said exceeds $1.1 billion. Boeing must retain a DOJ-selected Independent Compliance Consultant and cooperate with authorities for two years, but the agreement does not include the court-supervised independent monitoring the 2021 deal's compliance-oversight regime nominally provided. Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote Attorney General Bondi May 22, 2025 questioning the deal's adequacy. Victims' families -- relatives of those killed in both crashes -- formally objected, calling it 'a step backward' from real accountability. On November 6, 2025, Judge O'Connor granted DOJ's motion to dismiss the underlying criminal case, approving the agreement, but wrote that the families opposing it 'are correct' that it 'fails to secure the necessary accountability to ensure the safety of the flying public' and 'disregards the need for Boeing to be subject to independent monitoring' -- concluding, however, that he lacked legal authority to override DOJ's charging decision even though he disagreed the dismissal served the public interest. Families' attorneys said they planned to appeal to the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals.

incident_summary: In August 2025, the FBI searched former National Security Advisor John Bolton's Maryland home and Washington, D.C. office as part of an investigation into alleged mishandling of classified information; agents found records labeled 'confidential,' including material referencing weapons of mass destruction, the U.S. mission to the United Nations, and other strategic-communications documents. Reuters reported September 25, 2025 that Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office was pressuring career prosecutors in the Maryland U.S. Attorney's office and DOJ's National Security Division to present the case to a grand jury within days, despite those prosecutors' own view that more investigation was needed -- an escalation that came one week after the administration removed the top federal prosecutor in Virginia over frustration that DOJ was not moving fast enough against Trump critics including Bolton and then-FBI-Director-turned-critic James Comey (indicted around the same week). On October 16, 2025, **a federal grand jury in Greenbelt, Maryland indicted Bolton on 18 counts under the Espionage Act -- eight counts of transmitting national defense information and ten counts of unlawfully retaining it**, filed by U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes and Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Sullivan. Prosecutors alleged Bolton used personal AOL and Google accounts to send diary-style entries containing Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information to two unauthorized family members while serving as National Security Advisor, later storing printed copies at his Maryland home; some of the alleged material reportedly also appeared in drafts of his 2020 memoir, 'The Room Where It Happened.' Bolton's attorney, Abbe Lowell, characterized the seized records as 'the kinds of ordinary records...that would be kept by a 40-year career official,' noting some dated to his Bush-administration tenure (1998-2006). Bolton pleaded not guilty at his October 17, 2025 arraignment before U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang and was released on bond with standard conditions, without prosecutors seeking detention. Trump had publicly directed Attorney General Bondi the previous month to pursue his perceived enemies more aggressively; Bolton himself said Trump's retaliation 'began then, continued when he tried unsuccessfully to block the publication of my book...and became one of his rallying cries in his re-election campaign,' while Trump called Bolton 'a bad guy' in response to the indictment. On June 26, 2026, Bolton pleaded guilty, facing a maximum of 60 months in prison and agreeing to pay a $2.25 million fine.

offense_category: Concentrating Sole Certification Authority Over an Accelerated Capital-Appeals Process in the Attorney General, on an Honor-System Basis -- a proposed rule, not yet finalized; a due-process/executive-power-concentration accountability claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: DOJ proposed a rule making it easier for states to obtain certification for an accelerated federal review process for death penalty cases under a 1996 federal law (the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act's Chapter 154 opt-in provisions). Attorney General Pam Bondi argued that regulations implemented during the Obama and Biden administrations had improperly prevented states from using the law's fast-track option, which -- once a state is certified -- **cuts a death-sentenced prisoner's window to file a federal habeas petition from one year to 180 days and requires federal courts to prioritize capital habeas petitions over all non-capital cases**. Under the proposal, the certification decision (whether a state's system for providing competent post-conviction defense counsel meets the law's requirements) rests solely with the Attorney General, based substantially on the certifying state's own representations about the quality of its post-conviction counsel system -- a process critics, including the Death Penalty Information Center, describe as effectively an honor system that does not independently verify defense-counsel quality or consider opposing views before certification. Bloomberg reported the change is part of the Trump administration's broader push to expand use of the federal death penalty. Critics quoted by Davis Vanguard and other outlets warned the accelerated timeline and reliance on state self-certification increase the risk of executing people without adequate review of wrongful-conviction claims.

incident_summary: A ProPublica investigation, examining two decades of DOJ case-declination data, found **DOJ under Attorney General Pam Bondi closed more than 23,000 criminal investigations without prosecution in the first six months of the administration -- including cases involving terrorism, fraud, corruption, labor racketeering, drug trafficking, and environmental crimes** -- while ramping up immigration prosecutions. The majority of the declined cases had been referred to DOJ by law enforcement agencies, including under prior administrations, whose investigators believed a federal crime may have been committed. February 2025 alone, covering the first weeks of Bondi's tenure, saw nearly 11,000 declinations -- the most in a single month since at least 2004, when comparable data begins, and far exceeding the prior monthly high of roughly 6,500 declinations set in September 2019 during Trump's first term. ProPublica's analysis found the increase was not attributable to a larger inherited caseload or increased referral volume from law enforcement, indicating a deliberate shift in prosecutorial priority rather than a passive resourcing effect.

The February 2025 monthly declination total (~11,000) is the highest in at least two decades of comparable data, exceeding even the prior high recorded during Trump's first term

ProPublica's analysis ruled out caseload inheritance or referral-volume increases as explanations, supporting a characterization of the decline as a deliberate prioritization shift toward immigration enforcement

incident_summary: Three Alabama federal district judges, in an inquiry beginning in 2022 (predating this administration), examined whether Lambda Legal attorney Carl Charles and other counsel had engaged in 'judge shopping' while challenging Alabama's ban on gender-affirming medical care for transgender youth -- specifically, whether Charles called the chambers of a different judge to request the case be assigned to her as a related matter. Lambda Legal called the indictment 'an outrageous act of governmental overreach' and said it stood behind Charles; the New York City Bar Association and other advocacy and legal organizations publicly condemned the indictment as disproportionate and intimidating toward civil rights lawyers generally.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General Jan 2025-Apr 2026 (oversaw the dismantling); Todd Blanche, Attorney General since April 2026 (acting until August 10, 2026; Senate-confirmed August 8), has not restored the unit; Kash Patel, FBI Director (purged the FBI's CR-15 anti-corruption squad)
offense_category: Deliberate impairment of federal public-corruption enforcement combined with a pattern of pardons for politically-connected allies -- no criminal charge against Bondi or Blanche personally; this is an institutional-capacity and accountability-evasion claim, not a completed prosecution
incident_summary:
In late March 2025, Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche circulated a memo proposing to reorganize DOJ's Public Integrity Section, reassigning most of its personnel to individual U.S. Attorney's offices while keeping a core team of supervisory attorneys to administer the Justice Manual. The Washington Post reported May 17, 2025 that DOJ was considering, and Bloomberg Law reported was actively weighing, ending the longstanding requirement that federal prosecutors obtain the Public Integrity Section's approval before bringing corruption charges against members of Congress and other elected officials, and ending the requirement that U.S. Attorney's offices consult the section's career lawyers during such investigations -- a Watergate-era safeguard designed to prevent politically motivated prosecutions by letting career, non-political attorneys review case merits before politically appointed U.S. Attorneys could indict. The Justice Manual's requirement of the section's approval before charging a member of Congress for conduct related to public office (JM 9-85.110) remains in place; in June 2025, however, DOJ leadership suspended a separate requirement (JM 9-85.210) that prosecutors consult the section before opening campaign-finance, patronage and election-corruption matters, pending revisions.

Under Attorney General Pam Bondi, DOJ's Public Integrity Section -- the unit responsible for prosecuting public corruption by federal, state, and local officials -- was reduced from 36 full-time attorneys (NPR put it at around 40 full-time staff) handling 175-200 open matters at the start of the second Trump term to just two attorneys by September 2025, smaller than at any point since its 1976 creation; as of May 2026 it still had two full-time attorneys and about 20 open matters, per current and former DOJ officials. The staffing cut coincided with parallel rollbacks elsewhere in DOJ's anti-corruption infrastructure: a pause in enforcing the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act against U.S. executives who bribe foreign officials, disbanding of an FBI squad devoted to investigating congressional misconduct, disbanding of a task force pursuing Russian oligarchs' assets, and a pullback in enforcing the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Over the same period, Trump pardoned at least 15 people who had been charged with or convicted of public corruption, more than half of them Republicans or Trump supporters, though Democrats such as former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich and Rep. Henry Cuellar were also pardoned. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse sent Bondi a formal oversight letter on March 20, 2025 demanding answers on the section's dismantling. Bondi left DOJ in April 2026; Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal defense attorney, became acting Attorney General and has not publicly moved to restore the section's staffing.

On June 8, 2026, Vice President JD Vance referred Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison, both Democrats, to DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division -- a separate unit, not the Public Integrity Section -- for criminal investigation, citing a House Oversight Committee report alleging they failed to stop fraud in federally funded social programs; Ellison called the referral a political stunt by an administration that targets its perceived opponents. Todd Blanche was confirmed by the Senate as permanent Attorney General on August 8, 2026 (50-49, with Sens. Collins and Murkowski the only Republican defections) and sworn in; in his first address to DOJ staff (August 13) and subsequent remarks (August 16) he pledged to lead with "integrity" but explicitly declined to commit to DOJ independence from the White House. Rather than restaffing the Public Integrity Section, DOJ has instead expanded the National Fraud Enforcement Division, finalizing a rule in August 2026 that lets it prosecute any federal offenses uncovered during investigations that begin with suspected fraud; no public indication of Public Integrity Section restaffing has been identified.

ProPublica reported in September 2026 on one investigation that ended in the purge. Martin Kao, the former CEO of the Hawaii defense contractor Navatek, pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegal campaign contributions and loan fraud and then sat for interviews with FBI agents and prosecutors through September 2024, telling them he had traded campaign donations for defense research funding and handing over a 50-page document naming members of Congress, staffers and lobbyists; agents questioned him extensively about Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and her office. By late 2024 the two agents on the case, from the FBI's congressional-corruption squad known as CR-15, had come to believe there was enough evidence to warrant a broader investigation into bribery of members of Congress, according to a memo ProPublica reviewed, and agents were still examining Kao's dealings with Collins and her staff in early 2025. After Trump returned, FBI Director Kash Patel purged CR-15 agent by agent, Trump appointees ordered the remaining Public Integrity Section prosecutors to halt new corruption cases, the career attorney assigned to Kao's case quit, and the two agents were removed (one fired in October 2025, the other pushed out in early 2026). **ProPublica reported that these dismissals ended the review, which was still in its early stages, and that the investigation is now dead**; it did not report a specific order closing it. No one in Collins' orbit has been charged, and the allegations are Kao's, partly corroborated by records ProPublica reviewed. Collins denies wrongdoing and called the report "a political hit job"; her office says the matter was resolved in 2021, and an FBI spokesperson said the bureau had investigated claims against Collins years ago and "ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins' campaign"; the FBI did not respond to questions about the 2024 inquiry.

status: The Public Integrity Section's staffing collapse remains unreversed under Blanche, and DOJ is expanding the National Fraud Enforcement Division instead. ProPublica reports that the purge also ended an early-stage FBI inquiry into alleged congressional bribery.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue the staffing changes reflect a legitimate reorganization of prosecutorial priorities, that the pardon power is constitutionally unreviewable and each pardon can be defended on its individual merits, and that reduced headquarters staffing doesn't necessarily mean corruption cases aren't being pursued through U.S. Attorney's offices instead.
comeback: The scale of the cut (roughly 90%, from dozens of attorneys and 175-200 open matters down to two attorneys and about 20) is corroborated by multiple independent outlets citing named and unnamed DOJ officials, not a single source's characterization, and it happened in parallel with the dismantling of several other, unrelated anti-corruption units (FCPA, FARA, the oligarch-asset task force) -- a pattern harder to explain as ordinary reallocation than a single office's staffing change would be. Layering at least 15 corruption pardons, more than half of them for Republicans or Trump supporters, on top of that capacity cut is what former acting section chief John Keller describes as producing a chilling effect on prosecutors pursuing public corruption cases. And the claim that corruption work simply moved to U.S. Attorney's offices meets at least one documented counterexample: ProPublica reports that an FBI inquiry into alleged bribery of members of Congress ended after its agents and career prosecutor were purged or quit, rather than being picked up elsewhere.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Fits a broader pattern of DOJ shrinking its career-staffed corruption-enforcement capacity: the section's collapse began with the resignations over the Eric Adams case dismissal, and ran alongside a pause in foreign-bribery (FCPA) enforcement. Rather than restoring that capacity, DOJ has built up a fraud division run by a political appointee, which has since received a vice-presidential referral of two Democratic Minnesota officials. Trump's pardons of at least 15 corruption defendants (among them the Tennessee House speaker case and the Blagojevich pardon) are a separate presidential act, but they push the same way: fewer consequences for public officials, with more than half of those pardoned Republicans or Trump supporters.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (served 2025-2026, removed April 2026)
offense_category: DOJ Leadership Blocking Investigation of a Federal Agent's Fatal Shooting While Pressuring an Investigation of the Victim's Widow -- potential obstruction/prosecutorial-misconduct pattern, distinct from an ordinary declination decision
incident_summary:
ICE agent Jonathan Ross fatally shot Renee Nicole Good, a 37-year-old U.S. citizen and mother of three, in south Minneapolis on January 7, 2026, during Operation Metro Surge; Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said video evidence did not appear to support DHS's account that Good was using her SUV to run over an agent. Rather than pursuing a standard investigation of Ross's use of deadly force, top DOJ officials pressured the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota to instead investigate Good's widow, Becca Good, reportedly examining any ties she might have to activist groups. In response, First Assistant U.S. Attorney Joe Thompson -- the office's lead prosecutor on the high-profile Feeding Our Future fraud case, which had charged 78 people and secured 58 convictions -- resigned along with five colleagues (Harry Jacobs, Melinda Williams, Thomas Calhoun-Lopez, Ruth Schneider, and Tom Hollenhurst) in mid-January 2026, citing DOJ's reluctance to investigate the agent and the push to investigate Good's widow instead. In late January 2026, Tracee Mergen, a supervisor in the FBI's Minneapolis field office who had unsuccessfully attempted to investigate Ross, resigned, reportedly after pressure from FBI leadership in Washington to drop that inquiry. Eight additional assistant U.S. attorneys, including civil division chief Ana Voss, were reported in early February 2026 to be leaving the office, amid continued frustration with how DOJ was handling both the Good case and the separate fatal shooting of Alex Pretti by federal agents. CBS News reported the office's assistant U.S. attorney roster fell to as few as 17, down from 70 under the Biden administration, as the resignation wave continued into February 2026. The office lost at least 14 career prosecutors within a roughly three-week span.

The resignations extended beyond the Minneapolis U.S. Attorney's Office to DOJ headquarters itself. Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon, MS NOW reported, decided against a civil-rights investigation of Ross's shooting, and Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said there was "no basis" for a civil-rights (excessive-force) investigation into Ross's shooting -- a decision legal experts called highly unusual, noting DOJ's own manual calls for Civil Rights Division involvement in cases designated as a matter of "national interest." At least six leaders of the Civil Rights Division's criminal section, including its chief, principal deputy chief, deputy chief and acting deputy chief, announced their departures, a separate, headquarters-level wave distinct from the Minneapolis resignations; MS NOW reported they left in protest over the handling of the shooting, while a DOJ official said they had requested early retirement before it. DOJ instead treated the case as a potential assault on a federal officer, with prosecutors reportedly pressured to scrutinize Good's own conduct and her spouse rather than Ross's use of force, despite the video evidence Mayor Frey said didn't support the official account. This fits a broader documented pattern: Wired reported ICE agents have fatally shot at least 25 people since 2015 with no criminal indictments, and Fox 9 Minneapolis reported that records analyzed by The Trace showed at least 59 shootings, fatal and nonfatal, involving ICE agents from 2015 to 2021, with no evidence of an agent being indicted. The two figures measure different scopes rather than conflicting, and neither found an ICE agent indicted over the shootings it covered. Bondi was removed as Attorney General in April 2026, for reasons not confirmed by sourcing reviewed to be connected to this matter specifically.

Following Minnesota officials' June 2026 lawsuit to compel access, federal investigators turned over previously withheld hard drives and physical evidence, including Good's SUV, to Hennepin County and the Minnesota BCA, as Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced on July 13, 2026. Moriarty said review of the evidence was ongoing, with no timeline set for a charging decision on Ross; no public update on the reported federal investigation of Becca Good was identified. ProPublica reported September 2, 2026 that federal authorities had first agreed to a joint investigation of Ross's shooting of Good, but Justice Department officials later refused to cooperate with state police, deeming any review of the shooting unnecessary. Moriarty, who leads the state's ongoing review, publicly linked this to a separate DOJ decision to downgrade planned civil-rights charges against a different agent (DOJ charged him on September 3, 2026 with making false statements to federal investigators, MS NOW reported) in the legally distinct January 14, 2026 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, who was allegedly shot in the leg by ICE agent Christian Castro.

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: Potential Conflict of Interest / Appearance of Pay-to-Play via Selective Non-Enforcement of Federal Anti-Bribery Law -- NOT charged; a contested characterization, since the FCPA pause applied broadly and was not shown to be directed at benefiting any single donor
incident_summary:
On February 5, 2025, the day of her swearing-in as Attorney General, Pam Bondi issued a memorandum redirecting DOJ's corporate-enforcement priorities away from certain corporate crimes toward foreign bribery specifically tied to transnational criminal organizations and cartels. On February 10, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order, "Pausing Foreign Corrupt Practices Act Enforcement to Further American Economic and National Security," directing Bondi to halt new FCPA investigations and enforcement actions for 180 days and review existing matters -- the first pause of FCPA enforcement since the statute's 1977 passage.

Pilgrim's Pride, a poultry company that pleaded guilty to price-fixing in 2021 and is controlled by Brazilian billionaire brothers Wesley and Joesley Batista -- whose holding company J&F Investimentos pleaded guilty in October 2020 to conspiring to violate the FCPA itself and agreed to pay more than $256 million, over bribes paid to Brazilian officials; a parallel settled SEC order found that the Batistas' bribery scheme was carried out in part to facilitate JBS's 2009 acquisition of Pilgrim's Pride and that the brothers, J&F and JBS caused Pilgrim's Pride's violations of the FCPA's books-and-records and internal-controls provisions, with JBS paying about $27 million in disgorgement and each brother a $550,000 civil penalty -- was the single largest donor to Trump's 2025 inauguration, contributing $5 million, reported April 21, 2025. Ethics watchdogs raised concerns that a major donor with the Batista brothers' bribery history benefited from timing that coincided with the administration pausing the very federal law under which their past conduct had been resolved. On May 19, 2025, Reuters reported Sen. Elizabeth Warren sent a letter to the CEOs of Pilgrim's Pride and of JBS USA -- the U.S. arm of Pilgrim's Pride's Brazilian parent company, JBS -- asking whether company officials communicated with the Trump transition team or other Trump associates about the $5 million inaugural donation, and with the SEC, the White House or other agencies about a separate, long-delayed SEC approval for JBS's own dual-listing on the New York Stock Exchange, which had been approved just two days after a public FEC filing revealed Pilgrim's Pride as the inauguration's largest donor. Warren's letter also noted DOJ had two ongoing civil investigations into Pilgrim's Pride at the time, concerning its payment practices toward contract farmers and antitrust matters, separate from but concurrent with the FCPA-pause concern. No source reviewed confirmed whether JBS or Pilgrim's Pride ever responded substantively to Warren's letter, nor whether the SEC's own approval timeline was in fact influenced by the donation, as distinct from the appearance of the timing itself.

DOJ ended the formal pause on June 9, 2025, when Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche issued guidelines resuming FCPA enforcement with a narrower focus -- prioritizing cases touching U.S. economic/national-security interests, transnational criminal organizations and cartels, and individual (rather than corporate) misconduct. WilmerHale's year-end review counted seven DOJ FCPA actions in 2025 (only two against corporate defendants) and no SEC FCPA enforcement, the lowest level of publicly announced FCPA enforcement activity since the firm began formally tracking such actions in 2010. JBS completed its NYSE debut June 13, 2025, roughly six months after the donation.

Bondi herself, not just a donor, had a direct financial tie to a second potential beneficiary of the pause. Her financial disclosures showed $203,738 in 2024 income from the Fort Lauderdale law firm Panza, Maurer & Maynard, with Pfizer the only client she named for that work; Public Citizen noted in January 2025 that she had not disclosed the Pfizer representation on her Senate questionnaire or during her appearance before the Senate Judiciary Committee, and the Miami Herald reported the tie in early July 2025. official: Donald Trump, President; Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: Repeated Unlawful Appointments to Circumvent the Senate Confirmation Process for a U.S. Attorney Post -- multiple federal courts found the appointments unlawful; not a criminal charge against Bondi personally
incident_summary:
Alina Habba, a former personal defense attorney for Trump, was installed as acting/interim U.S. Attorney for the District of New Jersey. When Habba's interim term expired, New Jersey's own federal district judges exercised their statutory authority to appoint a replacement, choosing career prosecutor Desiree Grace rather than extending Habba. Trump responded by firing Grace and withdrawing Habba's own pending nomination as permanent U.S. Attorney, keeping Habba in the post without the judges' authorization; a federal judge later ruled the arrangement violated the Federal Vacancies Reform Act and, separately, that a structure allowing the administration to unilaterally extend her tenure past normal limits amounted to "a unilateral appointment in violation of the Constitution's Appointments Clause." The dispute first surfaced publicly when defendants facing narcotics charges argued in court that prosecutors could not proceed against them without a validly appointed U.S. Attorney in charge, triggering a wave of paused trials, postponed hearings, and delayed guilty pleas across the District of New Jersey as the authority question worked through the courts. Judge Matthew Brann's 77-page order found Habba had "exercised the functions and duties of the office... without lawful authority since July 1, 2025"; Brann declined to dismiss the narcotics defendants' cases outright, instead disqualifying Habba from participating in their cases and any other ongoing matters. An appeals court upheld the disqualification ruling, and Habba resigned in December 2025.

The most prominent case Habba's office brought under this disputed authority was her June 2025 indictment of Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-NJ) on three counts of assaulting, impeding, and interfering with federal officers during a May 9, 2025 congressional oversight visit to the Delaney Hall immigration detention facility in Newark, where McIver and other members of Congress were present to inspect conditions; prosecutors alleged she physically interfered with agents attempting to arrest Newark Mayor Ras Baraka, who was also arrested (and had charges against him separately dropped) during the same visit. McIver pleaded not guilty and argued Habba's unlawful appointment should void the indictment; the Third Circuit's December 1, 2025 ruling disqualifying Habba did not retroactively dismiss the case, and an August 2026 appeals ruling allowed two of the three charges to proceed to trial despite the authority dispute. McIver's prosecution was part of a broader wave of federal and local officials facing arrest, assault, or charges in connection with immigration-enforcement protests and oversight activity in mid-2025, including Sen. Alex Padilla, NYC Comptroller Brad Lander, and Wisconsin Judge Hannah Dugan, separately charged with obstruction for allegedly helping an undocumented defendant evade arrest in her courtroom -- a pattern Time magazine's June 2025 reporting characterized as officials facing consequences for opposing the administration's immigration crackdown.

Rather than nominating a Senate-confirmable replacement, Attorney General Bondi then appointed three individuals -- Philip Lamparello, Jordan Fox, and Ari Fontecchio -- to jointly divide the U.S. Attorney's responsibilities among themselves. A federal judge ruled this arrangement was also unlawful, finding DOJ had split the power of the U.S. Attorney's office among the three-person team specifically to route around the earlier disqualification ruling. The same judge, per AP News, threw a government prosecutor out of court and ordered the top officials running the New Jersey U.S. Attorney's Office to testify under oath, condemning DOJ's leadership structure there as "chaotic" and potentially unconstitutional. After that, the district court's own judges -- in consultation with DOJ leadership, a notable shift from the prior confrontational posture -- appointed career prosecutor Robert Frazer as acting U.S. Attorney on March 23, 2026, rather than DOJ nominating a Senate-confirmable replacement itself. A defendant separately challenged Frazer's appointment as unlawful; Judge Brann rejected that challenge on April 16, 2026, affirmatively ruling the appointment lawful.

offense_category: Vindictive/Selective Prosecution (violates Due Process; established legal doctrine, e.g. United States v. Goodwin) and Appointments Clause Violation (U.S. Const. Art. II, §2, re: unlawful appointment of the prosecuting U.S. Attorney) — the underlying CHARGES against James were brought and then dismissed; Bondi herself was not charged with anything personally
incident_summary:
Following repeated public calls by President Trump for Bondi's DOJ to prosecute New York Attorney General Letitia James, who had brought a civil fraud case against Trump and his businesses, DOJ pursued criminal charges against James. A federal judge dismissed the case after finding the interim U.S. Attorney who secured the indictment had been unlawfully appointed, and two separate federal grand juries also declined to indict James. Congressional Judiciary Democrats opened an investigation into the matter, characterizing it as retaliatory prosecutorial abuse.

On December 22, 2025, DOJ filed to reinstate the indictments against both James and James Comey, whose cases had been dismissed on the same Appointments Clause defect; the Fourth Circuit consolidated the two appeals for oral argument and disposition on January 12, 2026. On March 25, 2026, FHFA Director Bill Pulte -- who has separately pursued mortgage-fraud referrals against other Trump critics, tracked in a related entry in this database -- sent two new criminal referrals to federal prosecutors (Jason Reding Quinones, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, and Andrew Boutros, U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois), alleging James may have falsified information on homeowner's insurance applications to Universal Property Insurance (Florida) and Allstate (Illinois). James's attorney called the new referrals a political vendetta and accused Trump officials of recycling baseless allegations after the original federal case was dismissed and two separate grand juries had already declined to indict her. Bondi was removed as Attorney General in April 2026, for stated reasons related to Epstein files handling, not this matter specifically.

The Fourth Circuit's consolidated appeal of the dismissal remains unresolved; if the court reverses, the original indictments -- not merely the new Pulte-initiated insurance-fraud referrals -- could be reinstated and the case could proceed to trial. A three-judge Fourth Circuit panel heard argument on September 15, 2026; two of its judges questioned the government's claim that it could keep installing interim U.S. attorneys without Senate approval, and reporting described the panel as appearing poised to uphold the dismissals. No ruling had issued as of this update.

offense_category: Press Freedom / DOJ Media-Policy Reversal (rescission of the post-2021 policy restricting subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants against journalists in leak investigations) -- not itself unlawful (the Attorney General has discretion to set DOJ media policy), but the direct policy predicate for this tracker's later journalist-subpoena entries
incident_summary: On April 25, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi issued a memorandum rescinding Attorney General Merrick Garland's July 2021 policy, which had shielded journalists from compelled testimony and record seizures in leak investigations after it was revealed the first Trump administration's DOJ had secretly obtained or attempted to obtain records from at least nine journalists. Bondi's memo authorizes prosecutors to more readily seek subpoenas, court orders, and search warrants directed at journalists and news organizations to compel records and testimony related to leak investigations, provided such measures are approved by DOJ leadership, narrowly tailored, and preceded by advance notice to the journalist where feasible. Bondi framed the reversal as necessary to 'identify and punish the source of improper leaks' she said jeopardized DOJ's ability to 'uphold the rule of law, protect civil rights, and keep America safe.' Freedom of the Press Foundation condemned the decision and criticized members of Congress who did not prioritize passing a federal shield law in 2024; its advocacy director, Seth Stern, said every Democrat who put the PRESS Act "on the back burner" when they could have passed "a bipartisan bill codifying journalist-source confidentiality" should be ashamed. This memo is the specific policy predicate underlying this tracker's later, more developed entries on individual journalist-subpoena episodes (e.g. the 2026 grand jury subpoenas to Wall Street Journal and Washington Post reporters, weighed against 28 C.F.R. Section 50.10, and the FBI-run Air Force One leak probe that led to subpoenas of New York Times reporters), none of which had previously documented the April 2025 policy reversal itself as a discrete, dated action by a named official.
elements_required: A named DOJ official (Bondi) issued a formal, dated policy memorandum reversing a specific predecessor policy (Garland's July 2021 media-subpoena restrictions)

The reversed predecessor policy existed specifically because of a documented prior abuse (DOJ secretly obtaining or attempting to obtain records from at least nine journalists during the first Trump administration)

The new policy's stated safeguards (DOJ-leadership approval, narrow tailoring, advance notice) are self-administered by the same department whose leadership ordered the reversal, not externally enforced
This reversal is the specific policy authority subsequently invoked in this tracker's later, individual journalist-subpoena episodes

evidence.description: The New York Times reported that in March 2026 the administration demanded records from Wall Street Journal reporters to identify sources for an article on internal discussions about the risks of a war with Iran, that DOJ also subpoenaed a Washington Post reporter over coverage of U.S. military operations in Venezuela, and that after the papers challenged the subpoenas under seal in Virginia, the administration withdrew them in June after the judge indicated she was likely to quash them.

status: In effect since April 25, 2025; no report of it being rescinded or narrowed. Later episodes under it: 2026 subpoenas to Wall Street Journal and Washington Post reporters, withdrawn in June; to New York Times reporters, withdrawn in July; and to Times freelancer Matthew Cole, still active.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the Attorney General has clear discretion to set DOJ's internal media-subpoena policy, this is not a change to any statute, safeguards (leadership approval, narrow tailoring, advance notice) remain in the new policy, and leak investigations into unauthorized disclosure of sensitive government information are legitimate law-enforcement business regardless of which outlet receives the leaked material.
comeback: The safeguards Bondi cites are administered entirely within the same department whose leadership ordered the reversal -- there is no independent or statutory check, which is precisely the gap the 2021 policy and the still-unpassed PRESS Act were designed to close. **The predecessor policy did not exist in a vacuum: it was adopted specifically because the first Trump administration's DOJ had already secretly obtained or attempted to obtain records from at least nine journalists, and this reversal restores the department's ability to do exactly that.** The later, more developed episodes this tracker documents under this authority (the 2026 subpoenas to Wall Street Journal reporters over Iran-war coverage and to a Washington Post reporter over Venezuela coverage, withdrawn in June 2026 after the papers' sealed court challenges, once the judge indicated she was likely to quash them) show self-administered safeguards did not, in practice, prevent subpoenas a court later treated skeptically.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern, documented elsewhere in this tracker (Blanche's and Patel's individual journalist-subpoena and retaliation entries), of DOJ leadership treating leak deterrence as justification for expanding investigative reach into the press, with self-administered rather than externally enforced safeguards.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts (memo issued, date, what it rescinded, stated safeguards, Bondi's own quoted justification) -- corroborated across NPR, CBS News, Courthouse News, the U.S. Press Freedom Tracker, and two independent law-firm client-alert analyses (Ballard Spahr, Cleary Gottlieb), a broad and non-partisan sourcing spread for a DOJ-policy story. The precise published text of the new policy's safeguard language was not independently located in any source reviewed here -- described consistently across outlets but not confirmed against DOJ's own primary-document text. This entry documents the foundational policy action; the later individual subpoena/search episodes it authorized are each tracked in their own separate, already-existing entries rather than folded in here, to keep this entry's own scope to the policy reversal itself.

offense_category: Removal of an Aggressive Antitrust Enforcer Following White House Pressure Tied to a Presidential Pardon of a DOJ Antitrust Target -- raises accountability concerns about enforcement independence rather than alleging a specific criminal violation
incident_summary:
Abigail (Gail) Slater, Assistant Attorney General for the DOJ's Antitrust Division, was forced out in February 2026 after roughly a year leading the division, during which she pursued aggressive antitrust enforcement. Friction with the White House had been building for months: CBS News reported July 17, 2025 that Slater had already drawn criticism from colleagues and business leaders while leading active cases against Capital One, Apple, Google, and others, including friction over her office's handling of merger reviews -- Bondi's chief of staff Chad Mizelle had overruled her to accept a Hewlett Packard Enterprise/Juniper Networks merger settlement DOJ officials were confident was weaker than what the government could have won at trial. The two named officials who raised those concerns, Roger Alford (principal deputy assistant attorney general) and Bill Rinner (deputy assistant attorney general and head of merger enforcement), were placed on administrative leave in late July 2025 and fired outright on July 29, 2025 for alleged "insubordination" -- the officials Mizelle had overruled were themselves removed within days of that CBS News reporting. HPE had retained lobbyists with ties to the Trump White House to push the settlement through; Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison later moved to intervene in the federal court's Tunney Act review of the settlement, and House Judiciary Committee Democrats opened a probe into whether DOJ had ceded to lobbyists over its own antitrust experts' advice. Business leaders were reportedly unhappy after Slater warned them not to engage with the administration through Trump-aligned lobbyists and consultants seeking to influence pending antitrust matters; some administration officials defended her as principled and appropriately distrustful of well-connected allies attempting to sway confidential legal decisions.

In December 2025, Trump issued a "full and unconditional pardon" for Oak View Group co-founder Tim Leiweke, who had been indicted by Slater's own division earlier in 2025 -- undercutting an active enforcement action from within her own department. She had also lost the confidence of AG Bondi and Deputy AG Blanche, with a source telling reporters officials felt new leadership was needed to advance the President's agenda; a separate travel-rules dispute (an unauthorized trip to a Paris conference) led DOJ to cut off Slater's government credit card access. Slater suggested in a public post that she was leaving voluntarily, but CNN's sourcing characterized the departure as a firing. Bondi publicly thanked Slater for her service; DOJ named Omeed Assefi acting antitrust chief. House Judiciary Democrats sent a formal letter to Bondi regarding the Antitrust Division following Slater's departure; the letter's outcome was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed.

The Antitrust Division's Live Nation/Ticketmaster case -- the matter Slater had been pursuing aggressively before her departure -- was settled by DOJ in March 2026 for a $280 million payment and divestiture of roughly a dozen venues, short of the Ticketmaster breakup that had been the division's stated goal. A federal jury in a parallel case brought by a coalition of state attorneys general -- who continued litigating because they viewed DOJ's settlement as inadequate -- found Live Nation and Ticketmaster liable for illegal monopolization on April 15, 2026, with a separate remedies trial (potentially including a breakup) to follow before Judge Arun Subramanian. Former DOJ antitrust attorney Roger Alford testified before Congress in May 2026 criticizing the settlement on the record as enabling political-ally lobbying.

Live Nation and Ticketmaster have moved to overturn the April 15, 2026 jury verdict entirely (Rule 50(b) judgment as a matter of law) or, failing that, for a new trial (Rule 59); briefing closed July 2, 2026, and Judge Subramanian had not ruled as of the most recent reporting reviewed, with his questioning at a post-trial hearing focused on whether the states proved a legally distinct large-amphitheater market. Separately, the states' Tunney Act bid for discovery into the DOJ settlement's own adequacy was denied without prejudice by Judge Subramanian on August 4, 2026, with the states invited to return with narrower requests; the court's own Tunney Act ruling on the settlement is expected mid-September to mid-October 2026. The Rule 50(b)/59 post-trial motions remained unruled following a July 31, 2026 hearing.

incident_summary:
**On July 11, 2025, Attorney General Pam Bondi fired Joseph Tirrell, the career director of DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office, in a four-sentence termination letter that gave no reason.** Tirrell had spent nearly 20 years at the department and had led the ethics office since 2023, reviewing and approving financial disclosures, recusals, and conflict-of-interest waivers for DOJ leadership including Bondi herself, Deputy AG Todd Blanche, and FBI Director Kash Patel. His portfolio had also included advising then-Special Counsel Jack Smith on ethics matters during Smith's prosecutions of Trump, including approving roughly $140,000 in free legal fees Smith received from a major Washington law firm -- and, before the firing, requiring Bondi's own office to either pay for, return, or destroy gifts (cigars from Conor McGregor, a soccer ball from FIFA) that federal employees are barred from keeping; a DOJ spokesperson told the New York Times the ball was accepted and the cigars were destroyed after consulting ethics officials. Tirrell was fired the same day Bondi dismissed at least 20 other DOJ employees with ties to Smith's prosecutions team, as part of a broader purge. In the same November 2025 Times account, Tirrell said he also believed leadership "didn't want the ethics office calling them up and telling them what to do." A DOJ spokesperson responded that "any ethics advice received from career ethics officials has been followed and not overruled."

Tirrell, along with two other fired former DOJ officials (Michael M. Gordon and Patricia A. Hartman), filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (Gordon v. Executive Office of the President, D.D.C. 1:25-cv-02409, before Judge Jia M. Cobb) seeking immediate reinstatement and back pay -- noting that fired federal employees would normally appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board, but that the board had been left without a quorum after Trump removed one of its members, leaving them without the administrative appeal process Congress designed for exactly this situation; the complaint called MSPB review futile, though each plaintiff also filed a protective MSPB appeal. The Board's quorum was restored when a newly confirmed member was sworn in on October 28, 2025. The government moved to dismiss on November 25, 2025, arguing the Board is the proper forum; the plaintiffs opposed on December 23, 2025, arguing MSPB review would still be futile because the President now claims the power to fire Board members and its administrative judges and to direct how they construe the law, and the government replied on January 20, 2026. Tirrell has continued to write publicly on DOJ ethics policy, including a March 9, 2026 op-ed in Above the Law criticizing DOJ's decision to stop treating its senior political appointees as Hatch Act "further restricted" employees, which had limited their political activity. In April and July 2026 the plaintiffs flagged rulings in other Article II firing cases (Comans in the Eastern District of Virginia and Comey in the Southern District of New York) holding that such employees need not go to the MSPB first; on August 18, 2026 Judge Cobb ordered the government to address those rulings, and on September 15, 2026 the government responded that they were wrongly decided. The motion to dismiss remains undecided.

incident_summary: Federal prosecutors dismissed all charges against the 'Broadview Six,' a group of ICE-facility protesters, after a federal judge detailed prosecutorial misconduct during the grand jury proceedings that had produced the indictment. **Released grand jury transcripts showed prosecutors improperly 'vouched' for the case to grand jurors (suggesting the case wouldn't have been brought if it weren't just), a prosecutor had an improper conversation with a grand juror outside the jury room, and grand jurors who expressed skepticism about the case were prevented from participating further after an initial panel declined to indict.** Defense attorneys further alleged prosecutors intentionally redacted portions of the grand jury transcripts to conceal the misconduct from the court; presiding Judge Perry said she was 'incredibly shocked' by the government's redactions. U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Illinois Andrew Boutros personally attended the dismissal hearing to acknowledge the case was dismissed due to improper handling of the grand jury process by the lead prosecutor.

offense_category: Directing a Prosecutor to Open a Grand Jury Investigation and Freeze Bank Assets Over the Prosecutor's Own Professional Judgment That the Evidentiary Threshold Was Not Met -- an institutional-integrity and prosecutorial-independence claim, not a criminal charge against Bove
incident_summary:
Denise Cheung, the top criminal prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, resigned on February 18, 2025 after refusing an order from her Trump-appointed superiors -- acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove, directing Ed Martin (Trump's nominee for permanent D.C. U.S. Attorney) -- to open a grand jury investigation into a Biden-era Environmental Protection Agency funding decision and then use DOJ's authority to freeze the associated bank assets. Cheung and other experienced white-collar prosecutors in her office assessed the evidence on hand -- Bove's office cited a Project Veritas video as its basis -- and concluded it did not meet the legal threshold required to justify a grand jury investigation or an asset freeze. After she and her colleagues pushed back on the grand jury request, DOJ shifted to freezing the bank assets instead; the FBI in Washington, looped into the plan, sought legal backing from Cheung and ultimately wrote to the bank itself, and Martin objected that the FBI's letter was not explicit enough about a criminal investigation. In her resignation letter, Cheung wrote that she believed she lacked the legal authority to issue such a letter, cited her oath of office and legal-ethics obligations, and said that when she declined, she was asked to resign.

After Cheung left, then-Interim U.S. Attorney Ed Martin personally submitted a seizure warrant application without any other prosecutors in his office joining it; a D.C. magistrate judge rejected it, ruling, according to the Washington Post's sources, that the application and an accompanying FBI agent's affidavit failed to establish a reasonable belief that a crime had occurred. Bove then approached at least one other U.S. Attorney's office, in the southeastern United States, about opening a grand jury investigation and seeking a court order to freeze the Citibank funds, and prosecutors there also declined, the Post reported. The FBI also questioned EPA employees about the program, reportedly at the request of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida. Separately, in the parallel civil litigation over the underlying Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund grants (Climate United Fund v. Citibank and related suits by the grant recipients), U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan told a DOJ lawyer at an April 2, 2025 hearing: "Here we are, weeks in, and you're still unable to proffer me any information with regard to any kind of investigation or malfeasance" -- a judge's remark from the bench, separate from the prosecutor's own assessment, that DOJ had shown her no evidentiary basis. No indication in sourcing reviewed that the underlying grand-jury investigation into the EPA funding decision itself (as opposed to the asset-freeze mechanism) was ever formally opened or closed.

A divided en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled 6-4 on August 4, 2026 that EPA likely acted unlawfully in terminating the GGRF grants and clawing back disbursed funds, affirming the district court's preliminary injunction that a three-judge panel had set aside in September 2025. On August 6, 2026, the government filed an unopposed motion to stay the mandate pending a forthcoming Supreme Court cert petition; the court granted it, extending through November 9, 2026 the partial stay, in place since April 16, 2025, of the injunction's requirement that Citibank disburse funds, and directed that the stay continue pending the Supreme Court's final disposition if a petition is filed. No cert petition has been confirmed filed.

offense_category: Ordering Dismissal of a Pending Federal Corruption Indictment in Exchange for a Sitting Official's Cooperation on Unrelated Policy Priorities -- a federal judge found the arrangement carried the appearance of an improper quid pro quo; addressed here as an institutional-integrity and prosecutorial-independence matter rather than a criminal charge against Bove
incident_summary:
New York City Mayor Eric Adams had been federally indicted on charges including bribery, wire fraud, and illegal foreign campaign contributions. On February 10, 2025, acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove ordered federal prosecutors to move to dismiss the case without prejudice -- preserving DOJ's ability to revive the charges later -- citing concerns that the prosecution would interfere with Adams's ability to assist the administration's immigration-enforcement priorities and with his reelection campaign, rather than any evidentiary or legal weakness in the case. The order triggered a cascade of resignations: Acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Danielle Sassoon, who had held the post only three weeks, resigned rather than comply, writing that Adams's attorneys had effectively proposed a quid pro quo in a meeting with DOJ -- that Adams would cooperate with the administration's enforcement priorities only if the indictment were dropped. The then-acting chief of DOJ's Public Integrity Section and a deputy assistant attorney general also resigned rather than sign the dismissal motion.

U.S. District Judge Dale Ho ultimately dismissed the case on April 2, 2025 -- but with prejudice, permanently barring its revival, rejecting DOJ's request to dismiss without prejudice. Judge Ho wrote that "everything here smacks of a bargain: dismissal of the Indictment in exchange for immigration policy concessions," calling DOJ's claimed "virtually unreviewable" license to dismiss charges on that basis "disturbing in its breadth, implying that public officials may receive special dispensation if they are compliant with the incumbent administration's policy priorities," and that dismissing without prejudice would create "the unavoidable perception that the Mayor's freedom depends on his ability to carry out the immigration enforcement priorities of the administration." Senators Whitehouse and Blumenthal had filed ethics complaints against Bove with DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility and New York's attorney grievance body on February 27, 2025. On May 28, 2025, shortly after Bove's Third Circuit nomination was announced, the senators were notified that New York's Attorney Grievance Committee was transferring the matter to DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility as "better suited" to investigate and would take no further action. A June 2025 NBC News analysis situated the episode within a broader four-month pattern in which the new administration dismantled key parts of federal anti-corruption enforcement, including the Inspectors General purge and a pause in foreign-bribery enforcement documented elsewhere in this database.

Sens. official: Doug Burgum, Secretary of the Interior
offense_category: Statutory Violation — Commemorative Works Act (40 U.S.C. §§8901-8909) and 40 U.S.C. §8106 (unauthorized construction of a monument on federal land in the National Capital area) — NOT charged; this is a planning/permitting-stage dispute, not yet a completed unauthorized construction, and is most likely to be resolved via litigation or congressional action rather than criminal process
incident_summary:
The Interior Department, under Burgum, has advanced planning and historic-preservation review (a Section 106 Assessment of Effect and draft Programmatic Agreement) for a 250-foot "Triumphal Arch" at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery -- nicknamed the "Arch de Trump" by critics -- although the Commemorative Works Act allows a new commemorative work on National Park Service land in the capital only as specifically authorized by law, and Congress has enacted no such authorization for this project. In February 2026, three Vietnam veterans and architectural historian Calder Loth sued the President, the Executive Office of the President, Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley and the National Park Service (Lemmon v. Trump) to block construction absent congressional authorization, also objecting that the arch would obstruct the view between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial. In court, the government has claimed its authority from a 1925 law that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge; the plaintiffs call that reading meritless.

At an April 2, 2026 hearing, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan said she did not want ground broken while the case was pending, or to "wake up in the morning" to bulldozers at Memorial Circle. On April 8, she entered a consent order under which NPS may not authorize construction before posting notice on its planning website and must give at least 14 days' notice on the court docket before construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, begins; the plaintiffs' preliminary-injunction motion was denied without prejudice. The U.S. Commission of Fine Arts approved the arch's concept on April 16, 2026. On May 13, 2026, Burgum told the House Natural Resources Committee, under questioning from its top Democrat, Rep. Jared Huffman, that there was "no final agency action around building something" at the site and "not a proposal." The next day, as workers operated drilling equipment inside fenced-off areas of Memorial Circle -- site surveys such as geotechnical work, according to Interior -- Huffman accused Burgum of coming "pretty damn close" to perjuring himself and offered him the chance to revise his statements; Interior called the testimony "100% accurate." No perjury referral or charge has been identified. On May 21, the Commission of Fine Arts gave final design approval, except for the sculpture and statuary, after the design dropped an eight-foot base and four lion sculptures.

In a June 15, 2026 comment letter on the Section 106 review, Senators Angus King, Martin Heinrich and Jeff Merkley and Representatives Jared Huffman, Maxine Dexter and Yassamin Ansari, writing as ranking members of committees with jurisdiction over capital monuments, told Burgum and NPS officials that Congress has never authorized the arch, that Congressional Research Service analysis they requested in January reached the same conclusion, and that NPS has "no power to build" it, citing the Commemorative Works Act, 40 U.S.C. §8106 and the 1910 Height of Buildings Act. On July 9, 2026, the National Capital Planning Commission voted 8-1, with three members voting present, to give preliminary approval to the site and building plans, with comments to be addressed before final review; it suggested cutting the mezzanine to 130 feet and the observation level to 20 feet to meet the Height of Buildings Act, adding the 40 feet to the arch's Lady Liberty statue (bringing it to 100 feet) so the arch would still reach 250 feet. NPS issued a revised Section 106 Assessment of Effect on August 28, 2026.

On September 3, 2026, Burgum announced on X that Interior was "preparing to start, over the next two-week period, the excavation work necessary for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck." The plaintiffs sought a temporary restraining order the next day. The government answered that the planned work -- four archaeological test pits, starting no earlier than September 21 with the land restored by October 31 -- was predecisional information-gathering, not construction, and that NPS had issued no final agency action authorizing construction. On September 4, Chutkan ordered 48 hours' notice before any activity on Memorial Circle other than that archaeological information-gathering, warning that construction before a final NPS authorization or without 14 days' notice would violate her orders. On September 17 she denied the government's request to dissolve that order, clarifying that it covers only arch-related activity, and denied the restraining-order motion as moot; on September 18 the government gave notice that nine geoarchaeological borings would be added to the testing. A government motion to dismiss and cross-motions for summary judgment are fully briefed and pending. On September 24, 2026, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation notified NPS that it was terminating consultation on a Section 106 agreement for the arch -- before consultation was finished, according to the National Trust for Historic Preservation -- and said it would send formal comments to the Secretary of the Interior, whose response would conclude the review; it asked for public comments by September 29. NCPC has not given final approval, and the arch is not on the agenda for its October 1, 2026 meeting.

Separate violation alleged under 40 U.S.C. §8106 (a related capital-construction statute)

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the project remains in a preliminary planning/environmental-review phase, not actual construction, so no violation has technically occurred yet; in court, the government has claimed authority from a 1925 statute that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and it describes the current site work as archaeological testing, not construction, with no final NPS decision authorizing construction.
comeback: The 'planning phase, not yet a violation' framing inverts how the Commemorative Works Act works in practice: every comparable memorial built over the last forty years went to Congress first, before construction was permitted -- not as a post-hoc formality, but as the threshold requirement that opens the door to everything else. Proceeding with a formal Section 106 historic-preservation review and a draft Programmatic Agreement before securing that authorization isn't a minor sequencing issue to be cleaned up later; it's the documented departure from the Act's established practice. A CRS analysis -- nonpartisan, written for Congress, not an advocacy document -- concluded, according to the lawmakers who requested it, that building the arch without congressional authorization would not comport with the Act. The government's answer in court has been a 1925 statute that authorized the Arlington Memorial Bridge, and it has kept proceeding.

The White House ballroom, where the East Wing was demolished before courts could weigh in, is a separate project on a separate legal track, but it is the precedent Judge Chutkan and the plaintiffs pointed to in demanding advance notice here. The arch has also advanced in the same budget cycle in which the administration's fiscal 2027 request proposed a 40 percent cut to the National Park Service's maintenance budget and a $736 million cut to park operations; Burgum told senators the proposed $10 billion presidential capital fund would not pay for the arch, so the parallel is one of priorities, not a documented transfer of money. Burgum's role is that of the cabinet officer carrying out and publicly championing the project, including through his May 2026 testimony that there was no final agency action; he did not originate it.

offense_category: Authorizing Live Artillery Fire Directly Over a Major Public Interstate Highway for a Televised Political Spectacle, Resulting in a Malfunctioning Round Striking a State Patrol Vehicle
incident_summary: On October 19, 2025, the Marine Corps staged a live-fire demonstration at Camp Pendleton, California, commemorating the Corps' 250th anniversary and recorded for a future prime-time broadcast, attended by an estimated 15,000 invited guests including Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The demonstration included Marine forces moving from Navy ships offshore onto Pendleton's Red Beach, and howitzer artillery firing directly over Interstate 5 -- a major corridor between Los Angeles and San Diego, closed to traffic during the exercise -- intended to land far to the east in the base's Whiskey Impact Area. **One M795 high-explosive round detonated prematurely, at an altitude of roughly 1,480 feet, scattering shrapnel onto the closed roadway that struck and damaged a California Highway Patrol vehicle and motorcycle**; the patrol vehicle was part of Vice President Vance's own security detail. No injuries were reported. Military and police officials described firing live artillery directly over a public interstate as 'highly uncommon.' The day before the event, California Gov. Gavin Newsom called the demonstration 'dangerous' and 'unnecessary,' saying 'firing live rounds over a busy highway isn't just wrong -- it's dangerous,' and accused the administration of prioritizing spectacle over public safety; Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) countered that Newsom had improperly interfered with Marine Corps planning and staged 'a spiteful publicity stunt,' with his spokesperson dismissing media coverage as 'comic exaggerations.' Rep. Mike Levin led 26 House members and two senators in a formal letter demanding answers on who had authorized firing over the freeway and how the safety risk had been assessed beforehand; state Sen. Catherine Blakespear called the event 'posturing with militaristic bluster at the expense of the safety and well-being of the community.' A Marine Corps investigation, detailed in a 666-page report dated December 19, 2025, concluded there was 'no definitive answer' for why the round detonated early, characterized the malfunction as a 'one in a million' occurrence, and found no negligence or wrongdoing by Marine Corps personnel involved.

A state governor and dozens of members of Congress from both chambers formally characterized the underlying decision (not merely the malfunction) as reckless and demanded accountability for who authorized it

The military's own investigation, while finding no personnel negligence in the malfunction itself, could not identify why the round detonated early and did not address whether firing over a public highway was itself a sound safety decision

incident_summary: In September 2025, after Jimmy Kimmel's on-air remarks following the killing of Charlie Kirk, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said on a podcast, "Look, we can do this the easy way or the hard way," and warned of "additional work for the FCC ahead"; Disney briefly suspended Kimmel's show and reinstated it six days later. On April 23, 2026, Kimmel joked in a sketch that First Lady Melania Trump had "a glow like an expectant widow." After a shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner on April 25, the President wrote on Truth Social on April 27 that the joke was a "despicable call to violence" and that Kimmel should "be immediately fired by Disney and ABC." **The next day, April 28, the FCC's Media Bureau ordered all eight ABC-owned television stations to file license renewal applications within 30 days, although none of their licenses expires before December 2028 and two run to 2031.** The FCC had not called a license in early for more than half a century until the day before, when it did so for one small licensee, and according to ABC's complaint it had never called in a network's owned stations together. The order said early renewal was essential to the agency's investigation of Disney's employment and diversity practices, and Carr criticized Disney's diversity policies on a podcast as the order went out. The stations filed on May 28 under protest, and the public comment period closed August 5 with more than 150,000 comments, according to ABC's complaint. **After ABC declined to carry his July 16 address live, the President said during the speech that this "should mean a revocation of their licenses," and on July 22 Carr said he expected ABC's decision to be part of the agency's early review of the stations' licenses.** On August 18, ABC, Disney and the eight stations sued the FCC in federal court in Washington, alleging a retaliatory campaign against ABC "for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts," and moved for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to stop the FCC from designating the licenses for a hearing. Carr called it "a meritless case." On September 3, the FCC moved to dismiss, arguing that only a federal appeals court can review its licensing actions and that Disney's deficient responses to the discrimination inquiry, not ABC's speech, prompted the early renewals; it agreed to give at least 48 hours' notice before referring the licenses for a hearing. In a September 17 filing, ABC argued that Carr is carrying out the President's "specific directives aimed at curbing speech critical of the Administration," citing the President's August 30 post that NBC's Kristen Welker would be "reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment." The FCC replied on September 24, and Judge Loren L. AliKhan set a hearing on ABC's motion for October 6, 2026.

Separately, at least three people filed formal EEO discrimination/retaliation complaints against Chavez-DeRemer herself, alleging she created a hostile workplace, retaliated against the female staffers who reported her husband's conduct, fostered a climate in which staff feared punishment for speaking out or resisting directives they considered inappropriate, and directed staff to perform personal errands for her (including cleaning her closet).

The Inspector General's investigation broadened well beyond the husband incident: whistleblowers alleged Chavez-DeRemer had an affair with a member of her own security detail, used department resources for personal trips, and sent inappropriate personal messages to young staffers; the IG separately investigated her chief of staff Jihun Han and his deputy Rebecca Wright for alleged "travel fraud" -- setting up professional events as pretexts for her personal travel. It also recounted witness statements that career employees who raised travel-rule concerns were removed from travel-preparation duties at her direction. offense_category: Repeated Policy Flip-Flopping on Classifying Swastikas and Nooses as Hate Symbols, Followed by an Actual Swastika Incident at a Recruit Training Center -- documents an institutional policy failure rather than any single official's criminal conduct
incident_summary:
In November 2025, The Washington Post reported the Coast Guard would no longer classify swastikas and nooses as hate symbols under a new workplace-harassment policy, instead labeling them merely "potentially divisive." Within a day, the Coast Guard reversed course and said both would again be classified as hate symbols. Despite that public reversal, Commandant Adm. Kevin Lunday's order to maintain the hate-symbol classification was never actually incorporated into the policy for reasons that remain unclear, and the more lenient "potentially divisive" language was allowed to take effect in mid-December 2025 despite objections from members of Congress. Facing renewed uproar, the Coast Guard deleted the downgraded language again on December 18, 2025, restoring the hate-symbol classification for a second time.

Roughly two months later, on February 19-20, 2026, an instructor found a swastika hand-drawn on a bathroom wall at the Coast Guard's primary recruit training center in Cape May, New Jersey; Lunday personally flew to the base to address roughly 900 recruits and staff, condemning the symbol's use, and the Coast Guard referred the incident to its Investigative Service. The Coast Guard Investigative Service has not publicly released findings, identified a suspect, or announced any disciplinary/legal action from the Cape May incident; no further policy reversals have been identified since the December 2025 restoration of the hate-symbol classification.
