official: Doug Collins, Secretary of Veterans Affairs
offense_category: Defiance of a Federal Court Order -- Re-Terminating a Union Contract 13 Days After a Judge Ordered Its Reinstatement, on the Eve of an Enforcement Hearing -- a district court's contempt inquiry, held in abeyance and not a finding; VA disputes the characterization
incident_summary:
Government Executive reported that the administration, following Office of Personnel Management guidance, had assured federal judges that agencies would hold off on formally terminating union contracts until litigation over the underlying executive order concluded; in August 2025, the VA canceled its collective bargaining agreement covering roughly 320,000 employees (the figure Reuters and Federal News Network report; Government Executive has put it at more than 300,000, and the figure of more than 400,000 in some August 2025 reporting covers all five unions whose VA contracts were terminated that day) anyway, implementing Trump's executive order stripping collective bargaining rights from large parts of the federal workforce on stated national-security grounds -- drawing immediate accusations from labor leaders (AFGE President Everett Kelley among them) that the move was retaliatory, the same retaliation theory the contempt dispute below revisits in a more acute form. The employees' union sued, and on March 13, 2026, U.S. District Judge Melissa DuBose of the District of Rhode Island (a Biden appointee) issued a preliminary injunction ordering the VA to reinstate the bargaining agreement, finding the union likely to succeed on its claim that VA had canceled it in retaliation for the union's opposition to administration policies, and that VA had provided no evidence supporting its claimed national-security rationale. VA formally reinstated the agreement but, the union told the court, did not honor its terms, and the union moved on March 20 to enforce the injunction. On the night of March 26, 2026, the eve of the hearing on that motion, VA filed an after-hours status report announcing it had re-terminated the same contract, and argued at the hearing that the enforcement motion was now moot. At that March 27 hearing, DuBose said the position was "a blatant disrespect for not just this court's order but for the rule of law," granted the enforcement motion, gave the administration until Tuesday, March 31, to explain why VA should not be held in contempt, and scheduled a contempt hearing for April 3, 2026.

VA appealed the injunction and the March 27 enforcement order to the First Circuit that same day and on March 29 asked DuBose to stay both; on March 30, DuBose held the contempt proceeding in abeyance pending the appeal, and on April 6 she denied VA's stay request. In early April, VA's Central Office instructed facilities to return AFGE-represented employees to the contractual status quo, and no contempt ruling has been issued. On May 16, 2026, a unanimous First Circuit panel (opinion by Chief Judge David Barron) refused to stay the injunction, leaving the reinstatement in place, but stayed the enforcement order's directives that VA comply with the agreement "in both form and substance" and keep processing pending grievances and arbitrations, finding VA likely to succeed in challenging that part.

The dispute did not end there: Government Executive later reported this was VA's third attempt to scrap the same union contract. After VA itself moved in May 2026 to open negotiations on a successor agreement, it told AFGE on July 24 that it would terminate the agreement for all bargaining-unit workers on its scheduled August 8 expiration date, claiming the union had not met within 30 days of VA's request; AFGE disputed this, citing the contract's rollover clause and a series of negotiation letters exchanged in June and July. On August 7, 2026, Judge DuBose again ruled for AFGE, calling VA's 30-day claim "not well-taken" and its plan "in direct contravention" of her orders, and enforced the injunction in an order amended August 11. VA appealed that enforcement order to the First Circuit and asked DuBose to stay both it and the March injunction; she denied that request on August 28, 2026. No First Circuit ruling on that second appeal has been identified, and no ruling on the merits has been issued; DuBose's March finding that the union was likely to succeed on its retaliation and APA claims rested in part on Secretary Collins having exempted some unions, but not AFGE, from the executive order. The contempt proceeding remains in abeyance.

incident_summary: Beginning July 25, 2025, the House Oversight Committee, chaired by Rep. James Comer, subpoenaed Ghislaine Maxwell and the Department of Justice for Epstein-related files. On August 5, 2025, the committee issued deposition subpoenas to the Department of Justice and ten individuals across four administrations -- former Presidents Bill Clinton and Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, former Attorneys General Merrick Garland, William Barr, Loretta Lynch, Eric Holder, Jeff Sessions and Alberto Gonzales, former FBI Director Robert Mueller, and former FBI Director James Comey -- demanding files and depositions. **Notably absent from that list was Alex Acosta, the Trump-first-term Labor Secretary who, as the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, personally negotiated Epstein's 2008 non-prosecution deal.** Epstein victims' attorney Jack Scarola and others publicly questioned how a genuine investigation could omit him. After that criticism, the committee announced Acosta would appear for a voluntary interview (not a compelled subpoena) on September 19, 2025. Comer separately delayed Maxwell's own deposition until after the Supreme Court ruled on her appeal, while denying her requests for immunity or advance questions. On August 21, 2025, Comer called Bill Clinton a 'prime suspect' in the probe, citing unverified reports of visits to Epstein's island, and warned that non-compliance with the Clintons' subpoenas could trigger contempt proceedings enforced by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi. The Clintons initially refused to testify, calling the subpoenas 'invalid and legally unenforceable... an unprecedented infringement on the separation of powers'; the Oversight Committee voted to advance contempt-of-Congress resolutions against them in January 2026, after which the Clintons agreed to appear and testified in February 2026 that they had no knowledge of Epstein's crimes.
elements_required: Congressional investigative and subpoena power was deployed asymmetrically -- compelled process against the administration's political opponents, escalating to contempt-of-Congress votes when they resisted

The Trump-administration official with the most direct, legally consequential personal role in the underlying Epstein non-prosecution deal was initially omitted from the subpoena list entirely, and was added only after public criticism, and even then via a voluntary interview rather than a compelled subpoena or deposition

The chairman publicly characterized one subpoenaed opposition-party figure as a 'prime suspect' based on unverified reporting before any deposition had occurred, while applying no comparable public pressure to the Republican official who actually brokered the 2008 deal

offense_category: Selective/Vindictive Prosecution and First Amendment concerns -- DOJ indicted former FBI Director James Comey a second time, in a different federal district, over a social media post; Comey has moved to dismiss, arguing the post is protected speech and not a 'true threat'; contested, no conviction
incident_summary:
In April 2026, a federal grand jury in the Eastern District of North Carolina indicted former FBI Director James Comey over an Instagram post depicting seashells arranged on a beach to spell "86 47," which prosecutors characterized as a threat against President Trump. This is a legally separate indictment from the "lying to Congress" case tracked elsewhere in this database, which was brought in the Eastern District of Virginia by Lindsey Halligan and dismissed in November 2025 after a court found Halligan's appointment unlawful; the two cases share only their target and their connection to the broader pattern of prosecutions against Comey.

On May 26, 2026, Judge Louise Wood Flanagan granted a defense request to delay proceedings, setting arraignment for September 30, 2026 and trial for October 21, 2026 in New Bern, NC. In late May 2026, Matthew Petracca, the lone prosecutor from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina assigned to the seashells case, withdrew without public explanation; on May 29, DOJ filed a notice substituting Assistant U.S. Attorney Timothy Severo for him.

On July 27-28, 2026, Comey's legal team moved to dismiss the case on selective- and vindictive-prosecution grounds and separately argued the seashell image does not meet the legal standard for a "true threat"; it also moved for disclosure of grand jury proceedings and to suppress evidence from two search warrants. In a July 28, 2026 court filing, Comey alleged the Secret Service illegally surveilled him in connection with the case, further alleging Trump personally requested Secret Service updates on its interview of Comey and that a senior DOJ official ordered surveillance a Secret Service agent internally flagged as legally questionable.

DOJ filed its oppositions to Comey's motions on August 18, 2026, arguing the seashell post could reasonably be read as a threat to kill the President and that this is a question for a jury rather than the court; Comey filed his replies on September 1. On September 25, 2026, Judge Flanagan granted Comey's unopposed request to postpone the September 30 arraignment to January 2027, stating the court will set a trial date after arraignment; she had not ruled on the pending motions.
elements_required: A federal grand jury returned an indictment against a former FBI Director over a social media post, in a case legally and geographically distinct from the already-dismissed EDVA prosecution of the same individual, establishing this as a second, separate prosecutorial track rather than a continuation of the dismissed case

The image at issue (seashells forming '86 47') requires an inferential leap from arrangement to threat that Comey's defense argues fails the constitutional 'true threat' standard, a contestable legal question distinct from a factual dispute
The case's sole assigned lead prosecutor withdrew without any public explanation from DOJ, a documented, unexplained departure in a high-profile politically sensitive case
A separate court filing alleges Secret Service surveillance of Comey connected to this case, an additional, independently checkable factual claim

official: Thomas Dans, Chair, U.S. Arctic Research Commission
offense_category: Undisclosed Conflict of Interest / Potential Foreign Agents Registration Act Gap -- a Trump appointee promoting a foreign shipbuilder's business while it was under EU sanctions investigation for supplying Russia, without registering as a lobbyist or foreign agent; not itself a charged violation, and Arctic Research Commission members are not classified as federal employees required to file ethics disclosures
incident_summary:
President Trump appointed Thomas Dans -- a Texas venture capitalist and MAGA-aligned online influencer with no formal scientific background -- chair of the U.S. Arctic Research Commission in December 2025. Dans has long-standing personal and business ties to Russia dating to learning Russian as a child; he worked in finance in Moscow in the mid-1990s and previously held a $250,000-$500,000 investment stake in the company operating Papa John's restaurants in Russia. He has publicly advocated reestablishing closer U.S.-Russia relations and shared pro-Kremlin content online, and in 2023 attempted to buy Finland's Helsinki Shipyard -- where roughly half the world's icebreaker fleet has been built -- while it was chaired by Viktor Olerskiy, a former Russian deputy transport minister and former board member of Russia's state-owned shipping company, Sovcomflot.

In August 2024, before his Arctic Research Commission appointment, Dans announced he was "working with Damen Shipyards Group," a Dutch shipbuilder, publicly promoting its icebreaker capabilities. As Arctic Research Commission chair -- a position that helps shape U.S. Arctic policy, including federal icebreaker procurement -- Dans continued championing Damen while his own consulting arrangement with the company remained undisclosed and unregistered. ProPublica reported (September 15, 2026) that during Dans's engagement with Damen, Dutch prosecutors were investigating the company for supplying Russia with equipment usable for military purposes in violation of EU sanctions, and that one Damen executive Dans had publicly posed with, Rutger Dolk, was later detained by Dutch authorities. Damen terminated its agreement with Dans -- which would have paid him if the company won a federal icebreaker contract -- while ProPublica's reporting was still underway. Legal experts told ProPublica the arrangement may have required Dans to register as a lobbyist or foreign agent under the Foreign Agents Registration Act; he apparently did neither. Unlike most senior presidential appointees, Arctic Research Commission members are not classified as federal employees and are not required to file ethics disclosures; the commission has a conflict-of-interest policy, but ProPublica reported violations carry no penalties.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly defended Dans, saying "Tom Dans is doing a great job leading the Arctic Research Commission, and his shipbuilding expertise has helped him succeed in this role," and dismissed ethics concerns, saying "These so-called 'experts' have no idea what they are talking about." Dans declined ProPublica's interview request and did not respond to its written questions.
elements_required: A presidential appointee held a paid business arrangement with a company (Damen Shipyards) whose interests directly overlapped with the appointee's own federal policy role (Arctic/icebreaker policy)
That arrangement was not publicly disclosed or registered, despite legal experts identifying a plausible FARA/lobbying registration obligation

The foreign company involved was, during the same period, under investigation by its own government for sanctions violations tied to supplying Russia -- a fact the appointee did not disclose while publicly promoting the company

The appointee has a documented pattern of pro-Russia advocacy and business ties predating the appointment, relevant to assessing whether the conflict was an isolated oversight or consistent with a broader pattern
The regulatory gap itself is structural, not unique to Dans: Arctic Research Commission members are exempt from the ethics-disclosure requirements that apply to most senior appointees

status: No ethics investigation, FARA enforcement action, or removal has been identified as of this entry's addition. Damen terminated its agreement with Dans during ProPublica's reporting; the White House has publicly defended him and rejected the ethics concerns raised.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense (echoing the White House's own on-record statement): Dans's shipbuilding-industry experience is exactly the relevant expertise for an Arctic Research Commission chair focused on icebreaker capacity, and informal advocacy for a shipbuilder he'd worked with isn't itself unlawful absent a specific disclosure statute Arctic Research Commission members are shown to be bound by.
comeback: The defense doesn't address the specific gap ProPublica documented: legal experts said the paid Damen arrangement itself -- not just Dans's general industry background -- plausibly triggered a FARA or lobbying-registration obligation that wasn't met, and Damen was under active EU sanctions investigation for Russia-linked conduct at the time Dans was publicly promoting it in his federal policy role, a fact neither Dans nor the White House disputes. That the Arctic Research Commission's ethics rules happen to be unusually weak is a structural finding about the position, not a rebuttal to whether Dans's own conduct met even that low bar -- and the undisclosed payment arrangement was terminated only once a journalist began asking about it, not through any internal compliance process.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] An appointee with documented pro-Russia advocacy and undisclosed foreign business ties placed in a federal policy role with outsized influence over lucrative shipbuilding contracts, in a position exempt from the ethics-disclosure rules that would normally surface exactly this kind of conflict -- illustrating how appointments to lower-profile advisory bodies can carry real policy and national-security stakes with less oversight than higher-visibility Cabinet posts.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the underlying facts -- ProPublica's investigation is detailed, on-record (including the White House's own defense of Dans and confirmation that Damen ended the arrangement), and was independently republished/corroborated by Salon, Defense One, and Alaska Public Media's own follow-up reporting on the story. What remains genuinely unresolved: whether Dans's conduct actually violated FARA or any other specific statute -- ProPublica reports legal experts' view that registration was plausibly required, not a formal finding that it was legally mandated or that Dans broke the law. Dans's arrangement is a documented, undisclosed conflict of interest under a commission with unusually weak ethics rules, not a proven legal violation.

official: Darin Smith, Interim/Confirmed U.S. Attorney for the District of Wyoming
offense_category: Prosecutorial Misconduct Before a Grand Jury -- calling defendants 'murderers' to grand jurors, telling them deliberations 'won't take long,' and engaging in off-the-record conversations with jurors during breaks between indictments
incident_summary:
On May 15, 2026, three federal judges in the U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming jointly dismissed felony grand jury indictments against nine defendants -- Cheyenne Swett, Richard Allen, Michael Scott Hopper, Brian Joseph Johnson, Dennison Jay Antelope, Mathew Christopher Jacoby, Matthew Miller Jr., Wolf Elkins Duran, and Jose Benito Ocon -- citing "deeply concerning" misconduct by then-interim U.S. Attorney Darin Smith. The judges found Smith called defendants "murderers" to the grand jury, told jurors deliberations "won't take long," and had improper off-the-record conversations with jurors during breaks between indictments, writing that "this misconduct began with some of the first words spoken to the grand jurors" and calling it "one of the few rare cases that rises to the level of dismissal." The indictments, which included a murder charge, were dismissed without prejudice, allowing the U.S. Attorney's office to re-present the cases to a new grand jury; the judges stayed the order until May 20 to give the government the opportunity to appeal. Despite these findings, the U.S. Senate confirmed Smith as Wyoming's permanent U.S. Attorney days later, on May 18, 2026, in a party-line en bloc vote.

The grand jury impaneled on March 16 was discharged, and on May 18, 2026, the court impaneled a new one. On May 19, the judges denied defense motions to reconsider, rejecting requests to make the dismissal permanent (dismissal with prejudice) or to disqualify the entire Wyoming U.S. Attorney's Office from the cases; they wrote that the fresh grand jury was an adequate remedy and that "the problematic conduct, limited to the U.S. Attorney, will not be repeated." The new grand jury re-indicted all nine defendants in cases filed May 20, 2026. Michael Scott Hopper pleaded guilty on July 15, 2026, and on September 18 was sentenced to 30 months in prison, concurrent with any sentence in a Park County state case. Plea agreements were filed in June and July 2026 in the re-indicted cases of Wolf Elkins Duran, Dennison Jay Antelope and Mathew Christopher Jacoby, and presentence reports followed in August and September.
elements_required: A sitting federal prosecutor made inflammatory, prejudicial statements directly to a grand jury -- calling defendants 'murderers' before any conviction and pressuring jurors that deliberations 'won't take long' -- rather than simply presenting evidence

The misconduct was not an isolated lapse but, per the judges' own order, began with 'some of the first words' to the grand jury and continued through improper off-the-record conversations across multiple indictments

Three separate federal judges, acting jointly, found the cumulative misconduct left 'grave doubt' the indictment decisions were free of its influence -- a threshold the judges themselves described as meeting one of the 'few rare cases' warranting dismissal, not a routine or borderline call
The U.S. Senate confirmed Smith to the permanent U.S. Attorney position after these findings were public, with no reporting reviewed indicating any consequence to his confirmation

A new grand jury re-indicted all nine defendants within five days of the dismissal order, and the judges declined to impose any stronger remedy (dismissal with prejudice or office disqualification) despite the misconduct findings, limiting the practical consequence to procedural delay

rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue that dismissal without prejudice (rather than with prejudice) reflects that the underlying cases may still have merit, and that the misconduct finding concerns process, not the guilt or innocence of the nine defendants.
comeback: The dismissal-without-prejudice distinction doesn't diminish the misconduct finding itself: three federal judges, acting jointly and describing the case as one of the 'few rare' instances warranting dismissal, found the prosecutor's own conduct -- not a technicality -- compromised the grand jury process from its opening words, and the Senate confirmed him to the permanent post regardless. The re-indictment five days later, without any disqualification of Smith's office, means the practical consequence of the misconduct finding was limited to a brief procedural reset rather than any lasting check on the same office trying the same cases again.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Smith told the Senate Judiciary Committee he had no experience appearing in court in a criminal or civil case or questioning witnesses before a grand jury, yet the Senate confirmed him in an en bloc vote days after three judges found his conduct before a grand jury serious enough to dismiss nine indictments. That fits a pattern in this tracker of U.S. Attorney posts going to politically connected appointees without prosecutorial experience whose grand jury presentations then drew judicial criticism: in the Eastern District of Virginia, a magistrate judge flagged statements that interim U.S. Attorney Lindsey Halligan, a former Trump personal attorney, made to the grand jury in the Comey case as apparent "fundamental misstatements of the law." The confirmation also shows the Senate treating a judicial misconduct finding as no bar to a permanent appointment.

offense_category: Proposing, and Later Publicly Threatening, Extrajudicial Killings and Military Strikes on Sovereign Mexican Territory Without Congressional Authorization
incident_summary: In the opening weeks of Trump's second term in early 2025, after the administration designated numerous Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations, DEA Acting Administrator Derek S. Maltz advocated internally for targeted killings of cartel leadership and drone strikes on drug production infrastructure inside Mexico -- telling colleagues he supported 'hitting the production labs and command control leaders in Mexico.' The proposals, coordinated in part through White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller's interagency discussions, alarmed officials at the Pentagon and elsewhere in the White House, who warned Congress had not authorized military force against drug cartels and that a terrorist-organization designation alone doesn't create authority to 'fire anything.' Officials also raised the risk of American or civilian casualties and noted the Coast Guard already had sufficient legal authority for drug interdiction under Title 14. The Washington Post reported the internal dispute September 19, 2025, describing the plans as 'fairly conceptual' and lacking 'a robust legal framework'; NBC News had separately reported in April 2025 that drone strikes were under consideration. No strike in Mexico was carried out following Maltz's proposal. The idea resurfaced at the presidential level months later: on January 9, 2026, Trump told Fox News's Sean Hannity, after touting the separate Caribbean/Pacific maritime strike campaign's toll, 'we are going to start now hitting land, with regard to the cartels,' calling cartels a force 'running Mexico.' Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum publicly rejected the possibility, saying she didn't believe the U.S. was 'taking seriously' an invasion and that organized crime required Mexican, not foreign, solutions -- reasserting Mexico's sovereignty. As of this entry, no U.S. land strike inside Mexico has been reported; instead, the two governments' cooperation has taken the form of intelligence-sharing through the Joint Interagency Task Force-Counter Cartel, which reportedly assisted the Mexican military's own raid killing cartel boss 'El Mencho' in 2026, alongside continued U.S. maritime strikes against alleged drug-trafficking vessels (tracked separately in hegseth-boat-strike-kill-order-2025-09.json) and drone-defense operations at the border.

incident_summary: On May 12, 2025, DHS's Los Angeles Homeland Security Investigations office subpoenaed Los Angeles County for all records related to California's Cash Assistance Program for Immigrants (CAPI), a state-funded (not federally funded) program providing **cash assistance to aged, blind, and disabled legal immigrants who are ineligible for Supplemental Security Income (SSI) due to their immigration status**. DHS publicly stated it was investigating whether California was providing federal benefits to individuals in the country illegally. The subpoena, issued to the LA County Department of Public Social Services, requested personal information including applicants' names, dates of birth, and proof of SSI ineligibility, covering January 2021 to the present. DHS's own May 12, 2025 press release framed the action as investigating California generally for 'providing federal benefits to illegal aliens,' even though CAPI itself is state-funded and specifically serves legal immigrants ineligible for federal SSI, not undocumented individuals receiving federal funds. As of a late-May 2025 inquiry from LA Public Press, LA County had not turned over applicants' personal information, instead responding to DHS with program eligibility-criteria information and requesting a meeting -- neither complying with nor formally litigating against the subpoena as of that reporting.

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Gutting Internal Civil Rights and Detention Oversight Offices While Immigration Enforcement Expands -- eliminating the internal check mechanisms specifically designed to catch abuse in the enforcement activity documented elsewhere in this tracker
incident_summary:
On March 21, 2025, DHS ordered a work stoppage and issued Reduction-in-Force notices to nearly all staff at three offices: the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, the Immigration Detention Ombudsman -- which investigates complaints about conditions and treatment in ICE detention -- and the Citizenship and Immigration Services Ombudsman; these are DHS's own internal oversight mechanisms, specifically created to catch and address civil-rights violations and detention-condition abuses within the department's own operations, distinct from external oversight bodies like the Inspector General or Congress. The RIF notices prompted an April 24, 2025 lawsuit from Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights, the Southern Border Communities Coalition, and the Urban Justice Center. DHS publicly announced on May 23, 2025 that it would not formally abolish the three offices, but the reduction in force itself went ahead; the court later noted that it "has already occurred."

In February 2026, Mother Jones reported that a February 2 letter from 22 Democratic members of Congress to Secretary Noem highlighted that staffing for the Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and the Immigration Detention Ombudsman's office had been reduced by 85 and 91 percent, respectively. In the same article, Rebekah Tosado, a two-decade CRCL employee laid off in March 2025, said that to her knowledge CRCL had only two full-time staff members left, not counting its political-appointee acting head. A February 13, 2026 sworn declaration DHS filed in the lawsuit likewise counted two full-time federal employees at CRCL, while saying 25 to 30 contractors and several attorneys also work for the office and that its staffing is appropriate -- indicating the May 2025 reversal kept the offices nominally open without restoring their federal staffing. The staffing cuts leave ICE's rapidly expanding detention and enforcement operations -- documented elsewhere in this tracker, including a separate AP review of ICE employee misconduct -- with substantially diminished internal capacity to receive, investigate, and act on civil-rights and detention-condition complaints. On March 27, 2026, U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes denied the plaintiffs' motion for partial reconsideration of her July 2025 order denying their preliminary-injunction motion as moot; accepting the plaintiffs' clarification, she denied the injunction for lack of a showing of irreparable harm. In a May 12, 2026 court filing, DHS said the FY2026 appropriations law signed April 30, 2026 had completely defunded the Immigration Detention Ombudsman's office and that the office was being wound down, and argued the case was effectively moot; the plaintiffs responded that the zero funding was what DHS itself had requested and did not repeal the office's statutory duties. On July 1, 2026, Reyes heard the parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, took them under advisement, and directed the parties to settlement talks; after a July 21 meeting at DHS headquarters the parties asked for more time, and on July 31 the court stayed the case, with a joint status report due September 29, 2026. No ruling on the merits, and no independent audit restoring functional staffing levels, has been identified.

offense_category: Use of Administrative Subpoena Power to Unmask Anonymous Political Speech and Retaliate Against Critics -- distinct from this tracker's existing DOJ/Pirro entry, since here the acting agency is DHS itself using administrative (not grand jury) subpoena authority, at far larger reported scale
incident_summary:
By October 2025, DHS was publicly calling the filming of ICE agents "doxing," beyond the term's traditional meaning (publishing someone's private identifying information to enable harassment), while deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller placed "organized doxing" on a "continuum" with violence and a Trump national security directive tied doxing to domestic terrorism. That framing accompanied a subpoena program already under way: DHS issued hundreds of administrative subpoenas to major tech companies -- including Google, Meta, Reddit, Discord, and X -- demanding names, email addresses, phone numbers, and other identifying data for accounts that criticized ICE, reported ICE agents' locations, or attended protests against immigration enforcement, including operators of anonymous Instagram accounts documenting ICE raids. In one specific instance reported by The New Republic, DHS subpoenaed Google for account data tied to a 67-year-old U.S. citizen after he sent an email criticizing a DHS prosecutor over an immigration deportation matter. A DOJ attorney defended the subpoenas as within DHS's power to investigate "threats to its own officers or impediments to their officers." The Electronic Frontier Foundation sued DHS and ICE in April 2026 after the agencies ignored a FOIA request seeking records of the subpoena program; separately, when specific subpoena targets challenged them in court, DHS withdrew some of those subpoenas before a judge could rule, though no comprehensive public accounting of the program's total scope has been provided by DHS. Separately, The New York Times reported that Reddit, Meta, and Google voluntarily complied with at least some of the subpoenas rather than contesting them, though at least one of the companies said it notifies users and gives them a 14-day window to challenge a subpoena in court before complying.

EFF's April 14, 2026 complaints to the California and New York Attorneys General allege Google engaged in deceptive trade practices -- Google disclosed Cornell Ph.D. candidate Amandla Thomas-Johnson's data to ICE on May 8, 2025 and notified him only the same day, breaking its own long-standing advance-notice policy with none of that policy's stated exceptions (gag order, threat, child safety, hijacked account) applying. Neither AG's office had publicly announced a formal investigation. EFF's August 2026 commentary on tech companies' private pushback documents Meta pushing back on September 11, 2025 ICE subpoenas targeting a Pennsylvania ICE-documentation account by telling ICE it lacked statutory authority, and ICE withdrawing those subpoenas in January 2026 after the account's operators challenged them in court with ACLU help; it also cites Reddit's July-December 2025 transparency report disclosing three DHS subpoenas covering 11 users, all withdrawn after Reddit's objection.

A Wall Street Journal investigation, reported in August 2026, found ICE runs a round-the-clock contractor operation scouring the public internet, from Facebook to Instagram to X, for criticism, paying private firms millions to flag posts as threats; contractors (working under an $8 million contract between ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility, Amivero, and subcontractor Guidehouse) compile daily dossiers on flagged posters including name, location, date of birth, workplace, Social Security number, vehicle registration, and criminal history where available. ICE's surveillance-technology and consultant spending rose 57% year over year to $258 million in Trump's first full year back in office. DHS has since escalated beyond administrative subpoenas to grand jury subpoenas, which are harder for targets to fight, and has sent agents to question people in person over their posts; attorneys note most unmasked posters are never charged, leaving the tactic to function as intimidation even when it doesn't lead to prosecution. Per the same reporting, ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility describes the underlying monitoring as investigating at least 131 incidents of doxxing and threats toward agency personnel between January 2025 and March 2026. Of roughly 10 individuals identified as having formally challenged their subpoenas, judges upheld 4 grand jury subpoenas, DHS abandoned 3 cases, and 3 remained pending as of the WSJ's reporting -- no charges have been filed in any case where a subpoena was upheld; outcomes for challenged subpoenas were mixed, not uniform withdrawal, though the no-charges-filed pattern persists across every outcome. The WSJ also described what appears to be the same Reddit episode, in which Reddit objected on First Amendment grounds to DHS subpoenas targeting 11 accounts for "content critical of federal actions."

Members of Congress pressed the companies in two letters -- a February 25, 2026 House Homeland Security Committee Democrats' letter (Thompson/Correa/Thanedar) and a March 2, 2026 letter from Reps. Kelly and Jayapal plus 26 colleagues, both to major tech/telecom CEOs, neither of which any source reviewed shows as having received a public company response. A newer, September 1, 2026 letter from Sen. Wyden and Rep. Jayapal to Chief Justice Roberts and the GAO asks for an audit of DHS/DOJ nondisclosure demands on subpoena recipients, citing a documented case (DHS's Harvard subpoenas) where the agency asked the recipient to keep its subpoenas secret and then publicized the same enforcement action itself. Separately, EFF's own August 26, 2026 case list documents the program's target types extending beyond tech/social platforms: a March 2026 PayPal/Venmo subpoena for a Minnesota racial-justice organization, which PayPal/Venmo answered with data on March 20, 2026, and an April 12, 2026 T-Mobile summons for journalist Georgia Fort's phone records, issued under 19 U.S.C. 1509, a customs law, after a federal magistrate judge had twice rejected prosecutors' warrant applications for her YouTube account data. EFF's list shows the same customs-law authority behind several of the social-media demands, including those to Meta, Reddit and X, but in Fort's case it followed a judge's refusal to approve warrants.

On September 15, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras granted a preliminary injunction barring DHS from taking any action against David Streever, a Rochester, New York man, based on a warning notice DHS had issued him over an email in which Streever called then-acting ICE Director Todd Lyons a "monstrous human being" and compared him to Nazi official Reinhard Heydrich. Federal agents later tried to track Streever down at his home, an airport and a hotel to confront him about the email and serve the warning notice; the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) sued DHS and ICE on his behalf. Contreras found the warning notice likely violated Streever's First Amendment rights, writing that "the threat of such an investigation or prosecution looms over him like the sword of Damocles, and he is forced to self-censor under that threat." The injunction also bars DHS from issuing similar warnings suggesting Streever cannot engage in non-threatening criticism of the government.

incident_summary: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' detention facility, built by Gov. Ron DeSantis's administration and opened in the Everglades in July 2025, held immigration detainees under a 287(g) agreement authorizing Florida officers to help enforce federal immigration law alongside ICE. A DHS Office of Inspector General report, released September 2026, found the facility **confined at least 79 detainees in outdoor metal enclosures roughly 4-by-4 feet (16 square feet) -- and indoor cages of 18 square feet -- well below ICE's own minimum standard of 37 square feet for single-occupancy rooms**. Records showed detainees held in these enclosures between July 17, 2025 and January 18, 2026, for an average of just under an hour and a maximum of about two hours. Facility staff and posted signage described the enclosures as 'calming areas' where detainees could 'reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress and practice self-directed behavior,' and staff claimed detainees were not locked in despite visible locking mechanisms on the cages. Detainees separately complained of inadequate clean drinking water and being permitted to shower only three times weekly in bug-infested facilities, against ICE's own daily-shower standard. The Inspector General concluded that 'the use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment.' DHS disputed federal responsibility for the conditions, asserting ICE held no contract to operate the facility and that the 287(g) agreement did not grant the federal government authority over its physical operations -- a position the report itself undercuts by noting ICE personnel were on-site and detainees were issued ICE handbooks identifying the facility as an ICE facility. The facility permanently closed in June 2026; all 10 of the report's corrective recommendations were administratively closed after the closure rather than implemented, and the Inspector General separately warned that similar unchecked conditions remain a concern at other Florida state-run immigration facilities still operating.

incident_summary: In late January 2025, a longtime DHS staffer -- who had worked at the department in various roles since the George W. Bush administration, including through Trump's first term -- accidentally added a journalist to a group email containing unclassified but sensitive details (timing and possible target-home addresses) about an upcoming ICE operation in the Denver area. She caught the error immediately, contacted the journalist, who agreed not to publish, and the operation proceeded without incident. Despite causing no operational harm, DHS **placed her on administrative leave, opened an internal investigation, asked her to take a polygraph and surrender her cellphone (she declined both), and moved to revoke her security clearance -- a step that could end her career -- giving her 30 days to appeal**. NBC News reported the story March 27, 2025, explicitly framing it as raising questions about unequal punishment for inadvertent leakers under the Trump administration. The same week, CNN reported that an unnamed defense official said of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's Signal chat disclosure of live Yemen strike-timing details to a group that inadvertently included a journalist: 'It is safe to say that anybody in uniform would be court-martialed for this.' Hegseth faced no discipline, criminal charge, or removal; the Pentagon Inspector General's December 2025 report (covered in a related entry in this database) found that he broke DoD Instruction 8170.01 and federal records-retention rules in that chat, but recommended no action against him and made no referral for prosecution.

offense_category: Due Process Violation -- Mass Termination of International Students' Legal Status Based on Unverified Law-Enforcement Database Entries, Without Notice or Judicial Review -- contested by DHS as a lawful national-security screening measure; a federal court has allowed the underlying due-process claims to proceed past a motion to dismiss
incident_summary: Starting around April 2025, DHS quietly launched what advocates and reporting termed a 'Student Criminal Alien Initiative': running roughly 1.3 million international students' names through the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database and terminating their SEVIS (Student and Exchange Visitor Information System) records -- effectively ending their lawful F-1 student status -- based on database hits, including for individuals who had never been charged with or convicted of a crime, only dismissed charges or minor police encounters. **More than 4,700 students had their SEVIS records terminated in spring 2025 with no advance notice, no opportunity to respond, and no judicial review before the termination took effect**, throwing their ability to remain enrolled, work, or stay in the country into immediate jeopardy. The Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, later joined by the American Association of University Professors and the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts (AICUM), filed a federal lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on April 24, 2025 challenging the mass terminations as unlawful. Facing mounting litigation, DHS reactivated many terminated SEVIS records by late April 2025, restoring status for numerous affected students -- but did not concede the underlying policy was unlawful. On March 20, 2026, a federal judge largely denied the government's motion to dismiss the amended complaint, ruling the plaintiffs' due-process claims were not moot despite the reactivations because the challenged policy could reasonably recur, and that key issues -- including the legality of the mass revocations themselves -- remained unresolved. The case proceeded to discovery and merits litigation.

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: Publishing and Promoting an Inaccurate Public 'Worst of the Worst' Immigrant Database to Justify Enforcement Operations -- misrepresents the actual severity of arrestees' records to the public
incident_summary:
DHS created a public website in December 2025 branding a list of arrested immigrants -- roughly 25,000 people by mid-February 2026 -- as the "worst of the worst," which Secretary Noem, DHS, and the White House heavily promoted on social media to justify the administration's aggressive immigration enforcement operations. A CNN analysis found that while thousands of those listed were described as arrested for or convicted of serious charges such as sex crimes or homicide, hundreds more branded the "worst of the worst" were listed only for far less serious offenses, including single charges of traffic offenses, marijuana possession or illegal reentry. CNN also found that some of the cities with the most listed arrests were relatively small cities with large prisons or detention centers, a possible sign that many of those listed were already in custody rather than arrested in the community. John Sandweg, who served as acting ICE director under the Obama administration, said "the vast majority of so-called criminal aliens are individuals charged with or convicted of traffic offenses, DUIs and immigration-related offenses," adding of the serious-criminal population the administration describes: "That population is not out there."

After receiving CNN's questions, a DHS spokesperson admitted on February 17, 2026 that the charges against hundreds of listed immigrants had been described incorrectly, calling it "a glitch on the WOW website" that affected about 5% of entries and saying many of those listed with single minor offenses had additional crimes; on February 18 the spokesperson said the glitch had been "resolved." On February 20, DHS announced it had added another 5,000 people to the site, bringing the total to over 30,000. On March 4, ABC News reported that the site had listed Minnesota home renovator Telesforo Cerero-Palacios under "dangerous drugs" although a DHS record showed no criminal history; an ICE spokesperson pointed to an FBI number linked to multiple aliases, DHS appeared to remove him days after ABC began asking questions, and it did not answer whether he had been listed in error. Local outlet KTTC, which tracked the site's Minnesota listings, reported on March 16 that the count went from 486 in early February to 487 after the February 19 revision, rose to 505 by March 9, then dropped by 12 a week later; KTTC also found that roughly 44% of the Minnesota listings came from cities with federal or state prisons, and DHS responded that it "never claimed everyone on the website or every arrest in Operation Metro Surge was made at large in the community." DHS kept expanding the site, to more than 35,000 people by June 1, 2026 and more than 40,000 by July 28, 2026; no independent review of the accuracy of the added entries has been identified.

offense_category: Whistleblower Retaliation / Due-Process and First Amendment Violations -- a federal immigration judge alleges she was fired without notice or a hearing two days after formally raising concerns that ICE had unlawfully detained an unaccompanied minor in her own courtroom -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: Chloe Dillon, a San Francisco immigration judge for three years with 'excellent reviews' and thousands of resolved cases, presided over the case of an 18-year-old unaccompanied minor asylum seeker who arrived alone at the Montgomery Street courthouse on August 20, 2025. An ICE attorney asked Dillon to dismiss the case so the government could pursue expedited removal; Dillon instead granted the young man time to find an attorney before ruling on ICE's request, and separately emailed her supervisor raising concerns that ICE had unlawfully detained the minor. **Roughly 48 hours later, Dillon was fired by email from Sirce Owen, the Executive Office for Immigration Review's acting director, without notice or an opportunity to challenge the decision.** Dillon says a supervising assistant chief immigration judge had previously warned her, 'The White House is watching this issue. Like, do you really want to push this?' -- though she says she never learned which White House officials were involved. On September 10, 2026, Dillon filed a federal whistleblower lawsuit against DOJ, EOIR, Owen, and Attorney General Todd Blanche (named in his official capacity as DOJ's current head), seeking reinstatement, back pay, damages, and a declaration that the firing was unlawful, alleging violations of her First and Fifth Amendment rights and federal whistleblower-protection law. DOJ called the allegations 'patently false.' Dillon is one of more than 120 immigration judges removed during the administration's immigration-court turnover, according to the union representing immigration judges.

official: Elon Musk, former DOGE leader / Special Government Employee
offense_category: Granting Sensitive Federal-System Access to an Unvetted Individual With a Documented History of Data-Leak and Cybercrime-Adjacent Conduct -- an institutional-accountability and vetting-failure claim, not a criminal charge against Musk or Coristine personally
incident_summary:
Edward Coristine, a 19-year-old known online as "Big Balls," was given access to sensitive U.S. government systems in early February 2025 as part of DOGE, despite a documented history that included being fired from a cybersecurity-adjacent internship over an alleged data leak to a rival firm, and providing network services (via DiamondCDN, a company he ran while in high school) later used by a cybercriminal group that cyberstalked an FBI agent. Wired reported in February 2025 that he was listed in Office of Personnel Management records as an "expert," and security specialists quoted by Wired questioned whether he could pass the background check typically required for such access, one citing his limited real work experience. A recording from a 2022 dispute at Path Network, reported by CNN on February 21, 2025, captured Path executives debating whether then-17-year-old Coristine should be allowed to keep working there given suspicions he had leaked proprietary data -- the company's CEO chose to retain him temporarily under restricted conditions, and Path terminated him once it had determined what he had leaked, according to a Path subsidiary executive.

By May 2025 Coristine had become a full-time federal employee at the GS-15 level, one of the highest career civil-service pay grades. He resigned from DOGE in June 2025 but was almost immediately hired by the Social Security Administration as a special government employee -- a category with fewer disclosure obligations -- continuing his access to sensitive federal systems. Chief Data Officer Charles Borges's August 26, 2025 whistleblower disclosure, which named Coristine among four DOGE personnel, alleged that in June 2025 DOGE personnel had a live copy of the agency's NUMIDENT database -- names, birth data, citizenship, addresses, parents' names and Social Security numbers covering more than 300 million Americans -- placed in a cloud environment that circumvented oversight.

In a January 16, 2026 "Notice of Corrections to the Record" filed by the Justice Department in AFSCME v. SSA, the lawsuit over DOGE's access to SSA data, SSA disclosed DOGE Team actions it had found potentially outside SSA policy and/or noncompliant with the court's March 20, 2025 temporary restraining order, including sharing data through the unapproved third-party server Cloudflare and one team member's signing of a "Voter Data Agreement" with a political advocacy group; the notice did not name individual team members. Senator Gary Peters, ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, wrote SSA Commissioner Frank Bisignano on February 25, 2026 seeking records of any request involving Coristine, John Solly, Aram Moghaddassi or Mike Russo to transfer NUMIDENT data to a new cloud environment. House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia asked Coristine on March 9, 2026 to schedule a transcribed interview, and House Ways and Means Democrats pressed Bisignano in a March 12, 2026 letter. On April 10, 2026 the full Fourth Circuit vacated the case's preliminary injunction while calling the government's admissions "alarming"; the district court then lifted its stay and authorized limited discovery, and on June 26, 2026 refused to rescind that order.

offense_category: Public Exposure of Controlled National-Reconnaissance-Office Data Through DOGE's Own Website, Compounded by Independently Documented Vulnerabilities in That Website's Infrastructure -- an institutional-accountability claim about handling of sensitive national-security information, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: In mid-February 2025, DOGE's public website, updated to display federal workforce information across agencies, published **headcount and budget details for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) -- the intelligence agency that designs and operates U.S. spy satellites**. Multiple intelligence-community sources told ABC News this likely constituted a significant security breach, since both figures are treated as controlled information specifically because foreign adversaries could use them to infer how heavily the U.S. prioritizes particular intelligence-collection activities. Separately, two independent web-development specialists found the DOGE.gov website itself was vulnerable due to its reliance on an unsecured external database, which they said allowed unauthorized access and editing of the site's published content -- meaning the site's own infrastructure, not just what an authorized DOGE staffer chose to post, was a documented security weakness. On February 27, 2025, Senators Elizabeth Warren, Gerry Connolly, and Melanie Stansbury led a group of Democratic lawmakers in opening a formal investigation into DOGE's handling of sensitive national-security information, sending Musk a formal letter of inquiry.

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (served 2025-2026, removed April 2026) / DOJ leadership
offense_category: DOJ Moving to Erase a Political Ally's Criminal Conviction for Defying Congressional Oversight -- a discretionary prosecutorial decision benefiting a Trump ally, analogous in kind to this tracker's pardon-power entry (trump-kidan-donor-pardon-2026.json) though pursued through a motion to dismiss rather than clemency
incident_summary:
A jury had convicted Bannon on two counts in July 2022 of criminal contempt of Congress for defying a lawful subpoena from the House January 6 committee; he served prison time and paid a $6,500 fine. Bannon, a former senior Trump adviser and ally, had been one of the most prominent defendants prosecuted for defying the House's Jan. 6 investigation. On February 9, 2026, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro filed an unopposed motion in D.C. federal district court to dismiss Bannon's indictment, stating only that the government "has determined in its prosecutorial discretion that dismissal of this criminal case is in the interests of justice." The same day, Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the Supreme Court, where Bannon's petition challenging the D.C. Circuit's affirmance of his conviction was pending, to vacate that ruling and send the case back so the district court could grant the motion; his filing described the Jan. 6 committee as "a putative congressional committee." On April 6, 2026, the Supreme Court vacated the D.C. Circuit's ruling and remanded the case to that court "for further consideration in light of the pending motion to dismiss" -- clearing a path toward dismissal without itself dismissing the conviction. On July 16, 2026, the D.C. Circuit directed the parties to file motions to govern further proceedings; Bannon and the government jointly asked it to send the case back so the district court could address the pending, unopposed motion and terminate the prosecution, and on August 12, 2026 the D.C. Circuit remanded the case with instructions to address the motion to dismiss the indictment with prejudice under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 48(a).

U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols denied DOJ's motion to dismiss on August 26, 2026, finding that the motion did not explain DOJ's motivations for seeking dismissal and that its single sentence of explanation was the kind of "conclusory statement by the prosecutor" that D.C. Circuit precedent holds insufficient under Rule 48(a), which requires a statement of reasons. The denial was without prejudice -- DOJ is free to submit a renewed motion that complies with Rule 48(a) -- but Nichols directed any renewed motion to address whether the D.C. Circuit's 2025 decision in United States v. Thorpe, which held that the government may dismiss a prosecution only while it is pending, bars dismissal here, noting that his own judgment of conviction has not been vacated. As of late September 2026, no renewed motion appears on the court docket, and the district court's judgment of conviction remains in place.
elements_required: DOJ affirmatively sought to dismiss a completed, jury-convicted criminal case (conviction affirmed on appeal and sentence served) rather than merely declining to bring a similar future case
The conviction was for defying a lawful congressional subpoena -- itself a mechanism for enforcing legislative oversight -- which dismissal would effectively nullify as a deterrent
The beneficiary, Steve Bannon, is a prominent ally of President Trump, distinguishing this from a case-specific legal-merits reassessment unconnected to political relationships

DOJ's district-court motion gave only a one-sentence 'interests of justice' rationale, which the judge found conclusory; the Solicitor General's parallel Supreme Court filing called the Jan. 6 committee 'a putative congressional committee,' but the motion itself identified no specific defect in the conviction

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General (DOJ's Supreme Court litigation strategy)
offense_category: Reviving Historically Racist Legal Arguments in Official U.S. Government Supreme Court Briefing -- a legal-strategy and characterization dispute; not a criminal charge
incident_summary:
The Washington Post reported that Trump administration lawyers, defending the administration's effort to end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented immigrants and temporary visa holders, cited historical legal arguments originally made by Alexander Porter Morse -- a Confederate officer and Louisiana attorney who argued for legalized segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) and who was, over a century ago, part of a trio of legal advocates who spearheaded a failed, explicitly anti-Black and anti-Chinese effort to narrow the 14th Amendment's citizenship guarantee. The government's January 20, 2026 merits brief in Trump v. Barbara, like its September 26, 2025 petition for certiorari, quoted Morse's 1881 Treatise on Citizenship for the proposition that the Citizenship Clause "exclude[s] the children of foreigners transiently within the United States." A friend-of-the-court brief from the Chinese American Legal Defense Alliance called the arguments "built on a racist foundation," and a historian and a law professor quoted by the Post said the government's arguments echoed that first push to end birthright citizenship, while another law professor, Ilan Wurman, called the racism charge "a classic logical fallacy." The Post reported that if the Supreme Court adopted the administration's interpretation and reversed the long-settled reading of the Citizenship Clause, it could render hundreds of thousands of children born to immigrant parents stateless.

The Supreme Court decided Trump v. Barbara on June 30, 2026, with Chief Justice Roberts' majority opinion rejecting the administration's historical argument for narrowing 14th Amendment birthright citizenship as resting on "scant evidence," and holding (in practical effect 6-3, counting Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence in the judgment) that children born in the U.S. to undocumented or temporarily-present parents remain citizens at birth. The majority opinion itself traced the parental-domicile theory to commentators of the 1880s, citing Francis Wharton and Morse's 1881 Treatise on Citizenship, and noted that Wong Kim Ark (1898) had rejected that view; Justice Thomas's principal dissent relied on the same Morse passage. The interpretation DOJ was defending did not prevail, and the feared mass-statelessness outcome did not occur.

On August 6, 2026, Trump signed a new Executive Order 14418, "Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship," again restricting birthright citizenship. Where neither parent is a citizen, it bars agencies from recognizing the citizenship of children whose parent is an "alien enemy" (defined to include members of designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists); whose parent is a foreign-government employee (including ambassadors, foreign embassy or consulate staff who are nationals of that country, and immunity-holding international-organization staff); or whose parent engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship (including paid travel to give birth here or a paid surrogate) or in fraud to obtain citizenship; and of children born in U.S. territories where federal statute does not confer citizenship. The order says these categories fall outside the rule of birthright citizenship the Court announced in Trump v. Barbara, and directs agency heads to issue implementing guidance within 30 days, by September 5, 2026. It is a new executive action, distinct from the 2025 order (EO 14160) DOJ defended in Trump v. Barbara, but continues the same policy dispute after the Court ruled against the administration. On August 11, 2026, the ACLU-led Barbara plaintiffs asked the New Hampshire federal court to clarify or modify its existing injunction, arguing the new order tried to strip citizenship from members of the certified class. Trump, Judge Deborah Boardman on September 2, 2026 preliminarily enjoined enforcement of EO 14418 against the certified class, which her order describes as identical to the Barbara class, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed because the Supreme Court had held those children citizens at birth; she left the territory provision and the issuance of agency guidance unenjoined. DOJ moved on September 8 to dissolve that injunction or stay it pending appeal. In New Hampshire, after Judge Joseph Laplante indicated at a September 22 status conference that the supplemental complaint effectively represented a new case, the Barbara plaintiffs withdrew their pending motions on September 23, saying the new plaintiffs would refile elsewhere.

offense_category: Executive nullification of a federal civil-rights protection statute (the FACE Act, 18 U.S.C. §248) via pardon and enforcement-policy directive, effectively decriminalizing most future clinic-blockade/harassment conduct the statute was written to punish
incident_summary: On January 23, 2025, Trump granted full pardons to 23 people convicted under the FACE Act (Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act) for blockading, invading, or harassing patients at reproductive-health clinics. Among them: Lauren Handy, sentenced to nearly five years for directing a clinic blockade in which protesters chained themselves to clinic doors -- Handy separately made national news in 2022 after D.C. police found five fetuses in her apartment during the same investigation. The next day, January 24, 2025, Chad Mizelle -- chief of staff to the Attorney General's office, more than a week before Pam Bondi was confirmed as Attorney General on February 4, 2025 -- issued a DOJ memorandum directing that future abortion-related FACE Act prosecutions and civil actions 'will be permitted only in extraordinary circumstances' or cases with 'significant aggravating factors, such as death, serious bodily harm, or serious property damage,' and that no new abortion-related FACE Act action of any kind could proceed without sign-off from the Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division. In practice, this pairs a mass clemency for past violations with a policy directive sharply curtailing prosecution of future ones -- addressing both ends of enforcement in the same 24-hour window. **Since the pardons, at least two of the pardoned individuals have been separately charged with trespassing at a Pennsylvania abortion clinic, and at least three have been rearrested multiple times for clinic blockades**, according to reporting reviewed by the Center for Reproductive Rights.

incident_summary: In late September 2025, the New York Times reported that **federal prosecutors had subpoenaed travel records belonging to Fani Willis, the Fulton County, Georgia District Attorney who brought a 41-count racketeering indictment against Trump and 18 co-defendants over alleged 2020 election interference.** The subpoena, issued via a federal grand jury, sought records concerning Willis's travel in the fall of 2024, around the time of the presidential election, and was led by Theodore Hertzberg, the Trump-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Georgia. It was not publicly disclosed whether Willis herself was a formal target of the investigation, and her spokesperson said the office had 'no knowledge of any investigation.' The subpoena followed years of separate, parallel congressional scrutiny of Willis -- House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan had subpoenaed her for records related to her office's use of DOJ grant funds beginning in 2024, and Senators Chuck Grassley and Ron Johnson opened a related Senate inquiry -- but the September 2025 grand jury subpoena marked the first known instance of the Trump administration's own DOJ directly investigating Willis using federal compulsory process, rather than Congress. As of the most recent reporting reviewed, no charges had been filed against Willis and the investigation's scope and findings remained undisclosed, consistent with grand jury secrecy requirements.

offense_category: Federal Law Enforcement Resources Redirected to Re-litigate a Settled, Court-Confirmed 2020 Election Result -- expands a documented pattern with the earlier Fulton County, Georgia ballot seizure (and the later Fulton County poll-worker subpoena)
incident_summary:
A federal grand jury subpoena, confirmed by Arizona Senate President Warren Petersen, sought records related to the Arizona Senate's 2020 partisan "audit" of Maricopa County's presidential election results -- an audit conducted by Cyber Ninjas and its subcontractor Cyfir that was widely discredited by election experts and produced results confirming Joe Biden's victory despite the audit's methodology. The subpoena follows and expands a broader federal pattern of using DOJ and FBI resources to re-examine 2020 election administration more than five years after the election, after multiple independent audits, recounts, and court rulings in Arizona and nationally confirmed Biden's victory and found no evidence of the fraud the audit was commissioned to find; it follows the January 2026 FBI seizure of Fulton County, Georgia's 2020 ballots and precedes the April 2026 Fulton County poll-worker-data subpoena, both documented in this tracker's separate Fulton County entry, indicating a multi-state pattern rather than an isolated action.

Reporting based on emails obtained by American Oversight shows that Maricopa County Recorder Justin Heap -- an elected Republican official -- wrote to the county manager after, by his account, learning in mid-August 2025 that county elections and IT staff planned to delete certain 2020 and 2022 election records, had a meeting arranged with U.S. Attorney Timothy Courchaine for Aug. 27, 2025, and in September 2025 wrote to DOJ Civil Rights Division head Harmeet Dhillon that his office was "committed to full cooperation with the Department of Justice as it conducts its investigation" -- months before the March 2026 subpoena became public.

On the morning of March 7, 2026, an FBI agent took more than three dozen hard drives and servers containing audit-related data and Cyfir subcontractor material from the Arizona Senate building, according to a property receipt obtained by ProPublica; a copy of the subpoena later obtained by Votebeat confirmed that a federal grand jury was conducting a criminal investigation. Petersen said he complied with the subpoena "late last week." The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors and Recorder's Office, who jointly administer the county's actual election operations, said they had not received subpoenas as of this reporting, though the Board said it would cooperate if one arrived. ProPublica reported election-security experts warned the seized audit records could be "fatally flawed" as evidentiary material given the audit's own documented chain-of-custody and methodological problems.

On the morning of March 9, before Petersen's announcement, President Trump shared a Just the News article claiming the FBI had used a grand jury subpoena to obtain 2020 election data from Maricopa County itself (not just the Senate); the county's Elections Department said no records had been seized by the FBI, and Petersen, sharing a screenshot of Trump's post, said the subpoena was to the Senate for its audit records. In April 2026, Votebeat reported that Courchaine's office issued the Senate subpoena and is overseeing a grand jury impaneled in Phoenix.

A copy of the subpoena released under Arizona's public records law showed it sought virtually all of the audit's records, including Cyber Ninjas' forensic reports, clones of the county's election equipment software and data, and the Senate's communications with county election officials; KJZZ reported that, according to an FBI property receipt, Petersen turned over servers, USB drives and other devices holding more than 200 terabytes of data, and that a letter from Courchaine let him hand over the documents instead of testifying before the grand jury. Attorney General Kris Mayes said what the administration appeared to be pursuing was "not a legitimate law enforcement inquiry" but "the weaponization of federal law enforcement in service of crackpots and lies"; she and Secretary of State Adrian Fontes urged county recorders not to give confidential voter data to federal investigators even under a grand jury subpoena, and Mayes's office asked Petersen what exactly he gave the FBI. Petersen did not answer that letter and instead referred Mayes and Fontes to Courchaine for "obstruction of justice and tampering with a witness"; Courchaine replied that his office was "carefully reviewing the facts," and Mayes called Courchaine's letter "all nonsense."

In September 2026, CNN reported that Kurt Olsen, who as the White House's presidentially appointed Director of Election Security and Integrity made the referral behind the FBI's Fulton County ballot seizure, also "played a role" in the Justice Department's move to subpoena the Maricopa 2020 election records, and CBS News, citing a single source with direct knowledge, reported that Olsen had made several other 2020 election-related referrals to the Justice Department, including one in Arizona. In October 2026, Reuters reported, citing three people familiar with his work, that Olsen "oversaw the Justice Department's acquisition of Maricopa records through a subpoena to the Arizona Senate," records that included voter rolls, 2.1 million ballot images and signature-verification data; it reported that Olsen's wider search found no evidence of foreign manipulation of the 2020 election. The Justice Department has not publicly described Olsen's role.

The Heap material is included as context rather than integrated into `elements_required` or `cause`, since it plausibly describes a distinct accountability story (a county official's own coordination with federal investigators) rather than extending this entry's thesis about federally-directed re-litigation of settled results; Heap's later dispute with the Board of Supervisors is a separate local matter. official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General / Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Non-Compliance With a Statutory Deadline for Epstein-File Disclosure, Alongside FBI Compilation of Unverified Allegations Against Other Prominent Figures -- raises accountability concerns distinct from any single named individual's conduct within the files themselves
incident_summary:
The Epstein Files Transparency Act required DOJ to produce its Epstein/Maxwell-related files by December 19, 2025; DOJ said the process was delayed by the volume of material and the need to redact survivors' personal information. Following the broadly-criticized rollout of a partial release ("The Epstein Files: Part 1") on February 27, 2025, Attorney General Bondi directed the FBI to deliver the complete files within 24 hours and ordered FBI Director Kash Patel to produce a comprehensive report within 14 days; as of the reporting reviewed, 74 days had passed since that directive without the report's release.

On July 9, 2025, FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino -- himself a former prominent Epstein-conspiracy podcaster before joining the administration -- had a heated clash with Bondi at the White House after Bondi publicly stated evidence confirmed Epstein died by suicide and that DOJ found no incriminating "client list," triggering backlash from both Democrats and Bongino's own MAGA-aligned base who felt they had been overpromised disclosures. Bongino told colleagues he was considering resigning and did not report to work the following Friday; Bondi separately accused him of leaking stories that blamed her for the public backlash. The Daily Beast reported Bongino left a subsequent West Wing meeting abruptly amid the tension. Reporting on Vice President JD Vance's role was less specific than other aspects of the episode -- Vance, along with Bongino and Patel, had each separately hinted at forthcoming disclosures that never materialized, but no sourcing reviewed confirmed Vance directly mediated between Bongino and Bondi. Bongino ultimately remained in his post through this episode.

On July 18, 2025, Sen. Dick Durbin, ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, said his office had received a protected FBI whistleblower disclosure alleging Bondi had roughly 1,000 FBI personnel placed on 24-hour shifts starting in March 2025 to comb through approximately 100,000 Epstein-related documents and flag any mention of Trump. Independent journalist Allison Gill separately reported anonymous FBI sources corroborating the account, saying they were directed to log Trump mentions in an Excel spreadsheet. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said on July 21, 2025 that she was not aware of any effort to flag Trump's name and directed inquiries to the FBI. Durbin sent formal letters to DOJ leadership demanding an explanation, characterizing the deployment as a potential effort to identify and manage information about Trump within the files rather than the neutral, comprehensive review the department had publicly described; no source reviewed confirmed DOJ's or FBI's on-the-record response to the specific whistleblower allegation itself, distinct from the general denial reported through Leavitt.

In the run-up to the Transparency Act's December 19, 2025 deadline, Trump directed Bondi to open a new DOJ investigation into several of his political opponents' own links to Epstein; Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) publicly warned on November 15-18, 2025 that the new probe could function as a "smokescreen" and "last-ditch effort to prevent the release of the Epstein files," explaining the underlying mechanism: "If they have ongoing investigations in certain areas, those documents can't be released." Former U.S. Attorney Barbara McQuade confirmed the legal basis for that concern, telling reporters that with a pending investigation, DOJ "can assert executive privilege and try to prevent any more documents from being released."

As pressure mounted for full disclosure, CNN reported that FBI employees assembled a 21-slide internal presentation compiling what one employee described as "salacious statements" about 13 prominent men in Epstein's orbit -- including Donald Trump, Bill Clinton, Prince Andrew (Mountbatten-Windsor), Leon Black, and Harvey Weinstein -- drawn from unverified allegations in the investigative files. DOJ ultimately released more than 3 million pages of documents and photos, including the 21-slide presentation itself, as part of the broader disclosure; DOJ subsequently removed a photo showing Commerce Secretary Lutnick with Epstein from its own Epstein files website after the photo had already been part of the public release.

On March 17, 2026, a bipartisan House oversight committee subpoenaed Attorney General Bondi to testify about DOJ's handling of the Epstein files. Lawmakers from both parties alleged DOJ improperly redacted key information, failed to fully comply with the Epstein Files Transparency Act's disclosure requirements, and exposed sensitive details about survivors in the process. On April 2, 2026, Trump removed Bondi as Attorney General after a 14-month tenure, with sources citing her Epstein-files handling as one of several frustrations; Todd Blanche became acting Attorney General. Days before Bondi's scheduled April 14, 2026 deposition, DOJ told the committee the subpoena "no longer obligates" her testimony now that she is out of office -- a position bipartisan committee members rejected, with Democrats moving toward a contempt-of-Congress resolution.

Rather than face a contempt vote, Bondi agreed to a transcribed interview -- not a sworn, videotaped deposition, and one that let her decline individual questions -- held May 29, 2026. She defended DOJ's handling, calling the release process "an enormously complicated and labor-intensive process" and saying "justice and transparency in this matter have been delivered at the direction of President Trump," while acknowledging redaction errors occurred. Committee Chair James Comer said she could face prosecution if she lied to Congress and that a transcript would be released publicly. The House Oversight Committee released the full 111-page transcript on June 4, 2026. It shows AAG Harmeet Dhillon repeatedly invoking executive privilege to block questions about Bondi's own White House conversations, Bondi declining to say whether Trump directed DOJ's handling of the files or what he knew before the files' release, and Bondi attributing the release and redaction decisions to Todd Blanche by name more than 30 times. No outcome of the underlying files-compliance dispute, and no further public developments beyond the transcript's release itself, have been identified.

As of September 10, 2026, four European law-enforcement bodies (Poland, Norway, Latvia, Britain) say DOJ has not responded to their own formal evidence requests tied to their domestic Epstein-linked investigations -- a related but legally distinct compliance gap from the domestic statutory-deadline dispute this entry otherwise documents, since these are foreign mutual-legal-assistance requests rather than the Transparency Act's own release mechanism. DOJ says it has "not refused to assist any jurisdiction."
