official: Kristi Noem, Secretary of Homeland Security
offense_category: DOJ Criminal Subpoenas and FEMA/DHS Grant-Condition Demands Targeting Migrant Shelters and Their Funders Nationwide, Struck Down by a Federal Court as Unlawfully Coerced Immigration Enforcement
incident_summary: In March 2025, federal prosecutors served criminal subpoenas on at least three New York City hotels used as migrant shelters -- the Roosevelt Hotel, the Row NYC (Stewart Hotel), and the Hotel Chandler -- demanding the names, birth dates, and nationalities of residents, as well as the identities of the entities and individuals funding the shelter programs. In parallel, FEMA required recipients of its Shelter and Services Program grants nationwide to submit, within 30 days, lists of names and contact information for every migrant they had assisted, and **required each recipient organization's executive officers to personally sign sworn affidavits attesting they had no knowledge or suspicion that anyone in their organization had violated federal human-smuggling law -- effectively conditioning continued disaster/shelter funding on self-incriminating attestations and mass data handover with no individualized suspicion**. A coalition ultimately growing to roughly 20 states and the District of Columbia, led by Illinois, sued DHS, FEMA, and Secretary Kristi Noem in the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island (Illinois v. FEMA and the related Illinois v. Noem), arguing the administration was withholding congressionally appropriated emergency-preparedness funds unless states diverted resources to federal civil immigration enforcement. On September 24, 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge William E. Smith granted the states summary judgment and permanently enjoined DHS and FEMA from enforcing the immigration-related conditions across 40 separate federal grant programs, finding the conditions unlawful.
elements_required: Federal agencies (DOJ, FEMA/DHS) demanded personal identifying data on migrants and shelter funders without individualized suspicion of wrongdoing
Grant recipients were required to sign sworn, potentially self-incriminating affidavits as a condition of receiving already-appropriated emergency-preparedness funding
A large multi-state coalition formally challenged the conditions in federal court as unlawful coercion
A federal judge agreed and issued a permanent injunction, rather than the conditions being upheld or the case being dismissed

official: Aakash Singh, Associate Deputy Attorney General (reported by the New York Times in June 2026, and named in a July 15, 2026 Senate letter, as the official who expressed concern about the investigation in a phone call with U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. shortly before career prosecutors were told to abandon it, by May 2026; DOJ has not itself confirmed this account)
offense_category: Halting a Criminal Investigation Into Alleged Improper Payments Connected to a Presidential Clemency Grant -- no charges have been filed against anyone involved, and the investigation itself was shut down before reaching a conclusion
incident_summary:
Federal prosecutors in Brooklyn opened a criminal inquiry into how David Gentile -- founder of GPB Capital, convicted in 2024 of defrauding more than 10,000 investors in a roughly $1.6 billion fraud scheme -- received a presidential commutation of his seven-year sentence less than two weeks after reporting to prison. The same November 26, 2025 clemency grant also eliminated Gentile's court-ordered $15.5 million restitution obligation to the more than 10,000 defrauded investors, as Politico reported December 3, 2025; the sentencing court had received thousands of victim-impact statements, many from elderly retirees who described losing their entire life savings. Investigators reportedly gathered information about jailhouse communications in which Gentile discussed paying $2.5 million or more to people or companies to help secure clemency, and the inquiry examined whether the commutation involved improper payments or communications that could support federal charges. Reporting ties Frank Mann, a retired Catholic priest from Queens, to alleged payments linked to the commutation effort; Mann denied any involvement in an email to the New York Times, though people with knowledge of the prison communications said he corresponded with Gentile about lobbying the president on his behalf. The inquiry was halted before it reached a conclusion: by May 2026, Associate Deputy Attorney General Aakash Singh expressed concern about the investigation in a phone call with Joseph Nocella Jr., the U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of New York, and shortly afterward the career prosecutors were told to abandon their efforts, the New York Times reported June 21, 2026, citing two people with an understanding of the sequence of events.

At Blanche's July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing, Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked whether he had any involvement in the commutation or in stopping the investigation. Blanche said the president had not discussed the commutation with him, called the reporting the product of leaks containing "falsehoods," and declined to say whether an investigation had existed. The same day, Blumenthal and Sen. Ruben Gallego wrote to the Justice Department's acting Inspector General asking for an investigation into the closure, citing the reported Singh call to Nocella. DOJ has not confirmed or denied the reported Singh call. Singh was promoted to Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General by Attorney General Todd Blanche in late August 2026, giving him a broader portfolio overseeing operations at DOJ field offices and the litigating divisions at headquarters -- reported by Bloomberg Law (September 3, 2026) and relayed by Talking Points Memo the next day; Bloomberg noted that past officials in this role have wielded significant law-enforcement power behind the scenes. The promotion does not resolve the unanswered congressional referral to the DOJ Inspector General regarding Singh's reported role in halting the Gentile investigation.
elements_required: A federal criminal inquiry was opened specifically into whether payments were made to secure a presidential commutation -- not a routine clemency review, but an investigation into potential public corruption connected to the president's own clemency power

Investigators had reportedly gathered information about jailhouse communications in which the commutation's beneficiary himself discussed paying $2.5 million or more to help secure clemency, evidence sufficient to warrant continued investigation rather than an obviously baseless inquiry

The investigation was halted by DOJ political appointees rather than career prosecutors closing it for lack of evidence -- a decision reported as coming from political leadership rather than the line prosecutors handling the case

The commutation itself is publicly unusual on its face regardless of the payments question: releasing a defendant convicted of defrauding 10,000+ investors in a $1.6 billion scheme less than two weeks into a seven-year sentence

evidence.description: Politico reported December 3, 2025 that the same clemency grant also erased Gentile's court-ordered $15.5 million restitution obligation to the more than 10,000 defrauded investors, and that the sentencing court had received thousands of victim-impact statements, many from elderly retirees describing losing their life savings
evidence.maps_to_element: Establishes that the commutation's financial cost fell on victims, not just an early prison release, sharpening the accountability concern the halted-investigation angle already documents

status: No charges have been filed against Gentile, Mann, or any other individual; the congressional referral to the DOJ Inspector General regarding Singh's reported role remains pending with no IG outcome identified.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ could argue that public corruption cases tied to clemency decisions are legally complex, require proof of an explicit quid-pro-quo, and that the investigation may have been halted for genuine evidentiary reasons rather than to protect anyone connected to the president's clemency power.
comeback: The 'insufficient evidence' framing is undercut by the reported timeline: prosecutors had reportedly gathered information about the beneficiary's own jailhouse communications discussing a specific $2.5 million payment figure before the inquiry was shut down by political appointees rather than allowed to run its course through career prosecutors -- the halt itself, not just the final evidentiary picture, is what raises the concern.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The reported mechanism here -- a call from the Deputy Attorney General's office to a U.S. attorney, followed by career prosecutors standing down -- is the same channel this tracker documents in other cases where Main Justice leadership steered an individual U.S. attorney's office on a matter touching the president's interests: the Adams dismissal entry, where that office ordered charges dropped, and the SPLC indictment entry, where a whistleblower alleges the same official, Aakash Singh, ordered a case rushed forward. Those are different acts, and Singh's role in the Gentile and SPLC matters rests on reported or whistleblower accounts DOJ has not confirmed. The commutation at the center of the halted inquiry also belongs to the fraud-clemency pattern documented in the fraudster pardons entry, which counts Gentile's erased restitution among its examples.

official: Harmeet Dhillon, Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights
offense_category: DOJ Civil Rights Investigation Leveraging an Individual Tragedy Into a Broader Political Campaign Against Local School Policy -- an institutional-accountability claim about DOJ's use of investigative authority, not a criminal charge against any named official
incident_summary: The Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, led by Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, notified the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) in a March 2026 letter that it was opening an investigation into the district's 2019 policy directing staff not to disclose a student's gender identity to parents without the student's consent. The letter cited a lawsuit filed by parents Kathleen Mulligan and Andrew Parke, **who allege that LAUSD's non-disclosure of their child's social transition isolated them from their child and contributed to the child's suicide two years after graduating from Palisades Charter High School**. The investigation also referenced a separate complaint from a female student who alleged the district ignored her warnings about an unrelated perpetrator. Dhillon issued a public statement confirming and criticizing the policy. The LAUSD investigation is part of a broader DOJ pattern of civil rights inquiries into California and other school districts' gender-identity and parental-notification policies, including at least four Northern California districts and a separate Michigan gender-curriculum probe opened around the same period.
elements_required: LAUSD's 2019 policy directs staff not to disclose a student's gender identity to parents without the student's consent
A specific, tragic case -- parents alleging the policy contributed to their child's suicide -- is the stated trigger for DOJ's investigation, per DOJ's own letter

DOJ's Civil Rights Division, under a named Assistant Attorney General, opened a formal investigation and issued a public statement criticizing the underlying policy rather than confining itself to the specific case cited

The LAUSD investigation is one of multiple, similarly-framed DOJ investigations into school districts' gender-identity policies opened in the same period, consistent with a broader civil-rights-enforcement campaign rather than an isolated case-driven inquiry

evidence.description: Fox News reporting confirms DOJ's Civil Rights Division sent LAUSD a March 2026 letter opening the investigation, citing the Mulligan/Parke lawsuit over their child's suicide and a separate student complaint about an unaddressed perpetrator warning
evidence.maps_to_element: DOJ's investigation, its stated trigger, and its formal notification to LAUSD

evidence.description: LGBTQ Nation's reporting on the underlying parent lawsuit and the specific allegation that LAUSD's non-disclosure of the student's gender identity and social transition contributed to isolation from the family and the student's eventual suicide
evidence.maps_to_element: The specific tragic case DOJ's letter cited as its trigger

evidence.description: Reporting confirms Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon publicly confirmed and issued a statement criticizing LAUSD's policy, and that DOJ opened similar investigations into at least four Northern California school districts and a Michigan gender-curriculum probe around the same period
evidence.maps_to_element: The broader, multi-district pattern and the named official's public statement

status: Ongoing as of the reporting reviewed -- DOJ's investigation had not resulted in a public finding, settlement, or enforcement action against LAUSD as of this entry's addition; the underlying parent lawsuit and a separate California state-court challenge to a related non-disclosure policy were proceeding in parallel litigation tracks.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: a parent's allegation that a school policy contributed to their child's death is a legitimate basis for federal civil-rights scrutiny regardless of the policy's origin or purpose, DOJ has statutory authority to investigate potential parental-rights violations in federally-funded school districts, and opening an investigation is not itself a finding of wrongdoing against LAUSD.
comeback: The specific concern is not that DOJ investigated a tragic case, but that it used that single case to publicly criticize and target a broader district-wide (and now multi-district, multi-state) policy on parental notification of gender identity -- a politically contested issue predating this investigation -- rather than confining its inquiry to the individual allegations; the pattern of similarly-framed investigations opened against multiple California districts and at least one other state in the same period is more consistent with a coordinated policy campaign than case-by-case civil-rights enforcement.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of DOJ under this administration using investigative and subpoena authority to pursue politically-favored outcomes on gender-identity policy (see also the NYU Langone and Rhode Island Hospital transgender-care subpoena entries), applied here to K-12 school parental-notification policy rather than medical care.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts -- DOJ's investigation, its March 2026 letter, the cited triggering lawsuit, and Dhillon's public statement are corroborated across Fox News, LGBTQ Nation, and CBS San Francisco reporting on the parallel Northern California investigations. MODERATE confidence on characterizing DOJ's motive as primarily political rather than case-driven, since DOJ has not itself confirmed a broader policy objective beyond the individual cases cited -- the multi-district pattern is circumstantial support for that characterization, not a DOJ admission. incident_summary: Task Force Vulcan, a DOJ-led interagency effort launched in 2019, spent years building a case against MS-13's top leadership, indicting 14 gang leaders in 2020 on terrorism, drug-trafficking, and conspiracy charges. ProPublica's June 2025 investigation reported that several of the indicted leaders possessed direct knowledge of a secret deal between Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele's government and MS-13 -- favorable prison conditions, judicial protections, and territorial autonomy for the gang in exchange for electoral support for Bukele's party -- which contradicted Bukele's public image as the architect of a hardline anti-gang crackdown and was itself the subject of federal prosecutorial interest, including suspected diversion of USAID funds. **On March 11, 2025, DOJ dismissed all charges against MS-13 leader César Humberto López Larios; he was repatriated to El Salvador four days later.** A DOJ prosecutor identified in reporting by surname, Durham, sought to dismiss charges against and secretly deport a second gang leader, arguing in a court filing that public disclosure before the operation was complete 'could cause harm to the government's relationship with a foreign ally.' The dismissals and repatriations coincided with the Trump administration's broader deportation partnership with Bukele, under which El Salvador agreed to detain deportees (including at CECOT) in exchange for U.S. payments and diplomatic goodwill. House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Rep. Robert Garcia sent a formal letter to DOJ, State, and DHS on August 18, 2025 demanding an accounting of the case dismissals, characterizing the administration's actions as apparently designed to undercut Task Force Vulcan by returning key witnesses to Bukele's custody before their knowledge of his MS-13 dealings could be used.

incident_summary:
On May 7, 2026, NYU Langone Health received a federal grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas, demanding information on all patients under 18 who received gender-affirming care at the hospital system between 2020 and 2026, along with the names of the medical providers and others involved in offering that care. The hospital had already ended its Transgender Youth Health Program in February 2026. The hospital's notice indicated several other institutions had received similar subpoenas as part of the same investigation. On June 2, 2026, three families of transgender youth and two transgender young adults, represented by the ACLU, the New York Civil Liberties Union and Lambda Legal, filed a class action (Coe v. Blanche) in the Southern District of New York against DOJ and NYU Langone. On June 9, New York, California and 18 other states, plus the District of Columbia, moved to file an amicus brief supporting the plaintiffs.

Judge Katherine Polk Failla granted a temporary restraining order blocking disclosure of the requested medical information on June 24, 2026. A preliminary injunction issued July 6, 2026, with the court explicitly finding plaintiffs likely to succeed on the merits of their Fourth and Fifth Amendment claims. DOJ noticed an appeal to the Second Circuit on July 10, 2026; the district court denied DOJ's motion to stay the injunction pending appeal on July 17, 2026. DOJ then sought a stay from the Second Circuit, which denied it on August 26, 2026 -- the preliminary injunction remains in effect while DOJ's merits appeal (No. 26-1886) proceeds.

On September 18, 2026, DOJ announced an agreement with NYU Langone Hospitals resolving its investigations: NYU agreed to pay $8.5 million and to stop providing puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgical procedures to minors, and DOJ credited NYU for cooperation, including in DOJ's investigation of other entities. DOJ said the agreement followed similar ones with Mount Sinai Health System, another New York City provider, on September 4, and with Texas Children's Hospital, the Cleveland Clinic and Connecticut Children's. NYU denied any wrongdoing or liability and said the agreement removed the threat that it would have to turn over the patient information DOJ had demanded. Plaintiffs' counsel said no patient information had been disclosed to DOJ as part of the settlement and that the injunction remained in full effect. No criminal charges have been filed against any institution, provider, or patient.

The subpoena was issued from a district (Northern District of Texas) with no apparent jurisdictional connection to the New York hospital system it targeted
Multiple institutions beyond NYU Langone received similar subpoenas, indicating a coordinated campaign rather than an isolated, case-specific investigation
A federal court found sufficient grounds to block disclosure on an emergency basis pending further review, rather than allowing immediate compliance

District courts have repeatedly blocked these record demands, with one divided Ninth Circuit reversal. Yet NYU Langone, like Mount Sinai and other providers, settled on terms requiring it to end the care for minors while denying wrongdoing, without any charge being brought or any court upholding the subpoena to it -- an outcome consistent with the investigations serving as leverage to end lawful care rather than to pursue a specific, individualized criminal allegation.

incident_summary:
On July 4, 2025, a demonstration against Trump's mass-deportation push outside the Prairieland ICE detention center in Alvarado, Texas turned violent when former Marine reservist Benjamin Song shot and wounded a police officer who had just arrived at the scene. Nine defendants were tried together in a 12-day proceeding featuring testimony from more than 45 witnesses and over 210 exhibits; on March 13, 2026, a federal jury convicted all nine. Song was convicted of attempted murder of the officer and firearm counts; he and seven others were convicted of rioting, providing material support to terrorists, and explosives offenses (the explosives being fireworks), though four of those seven were acquitted of aiding-and-abetting attempted-murder and firearm charges. The ninth, Daniel Sanchez Estrada, was not at the protest and was convicted only of concealing documents and conspiracy to conceal them. Seven additional defendants, including Susan Kent, had pleaded guilty in November 2025 to one count of providing material support to terrorists. DOJ's own press releases branded the group "Antifa Cell Members." Sentences ranged widely: Song received 100 years; the other trial defendants received 30 to 70 years; those who pleaded guilty to the material-support count received 22 months to 15 years, including Kent, sentenced July 6, 2026 to 6 years for helping Song escape and hide after the shooting -- her sentencing concluded all federal district-court proceedings in the case. The Intercept reported that Sanchez Estrada received 30 years for moving a box of antifascist zines after the protest, with terrorism-linked sentencing guidelines applied to all the defendants, and Just Security separately analyzed how the terrorism statute used in the case is broadly enough defined that it could sweep in ordinary protest-adjacent conduct not involving violence.

At least four convicted defendants (Sanchez Estrada, Batten, Evetts, Elizabeth Soto) filed notices of appeal to the Fifth Circuit within a week of their June 23, 2026 sentencing, KERA News reported June 30, 2026; by July 6, 2026, court records showed all nine trial defendants, including Song, had filed notices of appeal. Southern Coalition for Social Justice and the Texas Civil Rights Project are representing Batten on appeal, describing her 50-year sentence as punishment "for attending a protest and running a book club." As of September 27, 2026, The Intercept reported, the Fifth Circuit had not yet issued a briefing notice. The same report detailed an argument Song's lawyers raised in an April 2026 new-trial motion: that the late disclosure of evidence of bullet strikes in the pavement, revealed only mid-trial, deprived them of the chance to make their case that Song, who they contend fired at the ground, never intended to shoot the officer.

incident_summary:
Erez Reuveni, a 15-year DOJ veteran immigration attorney fired in 2025 after refusing to comply with directives he believed violated court orders and his ethical obligations, filed an initial protected whistleblower disclosure in June 2025 alleging a pattern of senior DOJ and White House officials deliberately defying federal court rulings on immigration enforcement -- including knowingly violating court injunctions to carry out deportations under the Alien Enemies Act -- and retaliating against him for objecting.

DOJ later gave Reuveni's own complaint an on-record response: a short, unsigned OIG letter declining to investigate was sent one day after Reuveni asked OIG to probe former DOJ official Emil Bove and current leadership over the court-order-defiance allegations, and in January 2026 OIG told Reuveni it would refer his claims to DOJ's own Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) instead, separately citing pending litigation as a reason not to proceed. Reuveni's lawyers call both justifications pretextual: OPR itself "showed no interest" in taking up the claims, and the administration had already fired the attorney who ran OPR, which the lawyers describe as having "decapitated" that office. This response addressed Reuveni's own complaint specifically -- it does not extend to the broader set of 20+ allegations, including those raised independently by members of Congress, which remained without any confirmed OIG investigation.

In March 2026, Reuveni's lawyers told Congress that DOJ's own Office of the Inspector General had not investigated any of at least 20 serious misconduct allegations raised over the preceding 15 months, including complaints separately made by members of Congress, and that the OIG's inaction was occurring as the department's internal watchdog offices were being hollowed out, with leadership posts left vacant and internal oversight stalling department-wide.

incident_summary:
Attorney General Bondi issued a DOJ-wide memorandum on April 22, 2025 directing five enforcement priorities against pediatric gender-affirming care, including "Enforcement of Laws Outlawing Female Genital Mutilation," False Claims Act/FDCA investigations, and establishing a "Federal and State Coalition Against Child Mutilation." On July 9, 2025, DOJ announced it had issued more than 20 subpoenas to doctors and clinics providing gender-affirming care to minors nationwide, without naming the recipients or their locations. NBC News later identified the first named recipient in that wave -- Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP) had received a subpoena dated June 11, 2025 (due July 9), demanding patient names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, addresses, and parent/guardian information for minors prescribed puberty blockers or hormone therapy, plus staff personnel files, patient intake procedures, and insurance billing codes for gender-affirming care; GLAD Law's Jennifer Levi called it turning "doctor-patient confidentiality into government surveillance." Neither DOJ nor CHOP responded to NBC's request for comment. The same week, the FTC held a workshop critical of pediatric trans healthcare featuring detransitioners and anti-trans activists; former FTC staff told NBC News the event was politically organized and exceeded the agency's normal jurisdiction, a parallel but institutionally separate action from DOJ's own subpoena campaign.

U.S. District Judge Myong Joun's September 9, 2025 ruling quashed DOJ's subpoena to Boston Children's Hospital, one of the Massachusetts blocks in this nationwide campaign, which had sought patient records including Social Security numbers and home addresses, billing codes, communications with pharmaceutical manufacturers about puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones, and personnel files for all 2,000 of the hospital's employees. Judge Joun found the subpoena "motivated only by bad faith," writing that "the Administration has been explicit about its disapproval of the transgender community and its aim to end GAC [gender-affirming care]" and that its true purpose was "to interfere with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts' right to protect GAC within its borders, to harass and intimidate BCH to stop providing such care, and to dissuade patients from seeking such care."

DOJ subpoenaed Rhode Island Hospital (part of Brown University Health/Lifespan) for the birth dates, Social Security numbers, and addresses of every patient who received transgender care there over the prior five years, plus all documentation of adverse side effects in minor patients, assessments for puberty blockers or hormone therapy, patient intake forms, and guardian authorizations. On May 13-14, 2026, U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy (D.R.I.) blocked the subpoena, writing that DOJ had "proven unworthy" of the trust ordinarily extended to federal prosecutors. McElroy wrote that the administration "has publicly characterized gender-affirming care for minors as abuse, directed the justice department to bring its practice to an end, and celebrated when hospitals curtailed such programs as a result of this subpoena campaign" -- tying the subpoena to a stated political goal rather than a neutral investigative need. This is one of at least seven federal districts, including Massachusetts, where judges have blocked DOJ subpoenas seeking hospitals' transgender-care patient records as part of the same nationwide campaign, including a separate subpoena issued out of the Northern District of Texas to NYU Langone, tracked in a related entry in this database.

DOJ appealed McElroy's ruling to the First Circuit on May 14, 2026 (No. 26-1568), the day after the ruling. Rhode Island's Child Advocate separately sought an emergency injunction from the First Circuit to block record production pending that appeal; the First Circuit denied it around May 19-20, 2026 on irreparable-harm grounds -- a ruling against the Child Advocate's emergency motion, not a ruling on DOJ's appeal or against the underlying injunction. The District of Rhode Island's order quashing the subpoena remains in full force. On June 5, 2026, Judge McElroy referred DOJ attorneys -- centered on Enforcement and Affirmative Litigation Branch acting director Lisa Hsiao -- for possible disciplinary proceedings, finding a sworn declaration to the court "clearly misleading, if not utterly false" and citing an undisclosed side agreement with other hospitals in the same campaign; no proceedings have been scheduled.

DOJ's broader subpoena campaign against other hospitals continues in other districts, and on August 14, 2026 won its first appellate reversal of a similar district-court block (Ninth Circuit, QueerDoc/Seattle, 2-1, on the bad-faith finding specifically, remanded for further proceedings on overbreadth) -- the pattern is no longer one of uniform DOJ losses nationwide, though the Rhode Island ruling itself stands unaffected.

official: Donald Trump, President; Yaakov M. Roth, Acting Assistant Attorney General, DOJ Civil Division
offense_category: DOJ Intervening in a State Criminal Prosecution to Advocate for a Political Ally's Early Release, Citing Alleged Political Motives Without New Evidence -- addressed here as a rule-of-law/prosecutorial-independence question rather than a criminal charge
incident_summary:
Tina Peters, the former Mesa County, Colorado clerk, was convicted in August 2024 on four felony counts for orchestrating unauthorized access to Mesa County's secured election system in 2021 as part of an effort to find evidence supporting Trump's false claims of 2020 election fraud, and was sentenced in October 2024 to nine years in state prison. On March 3, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice, in a filing in Peters's federal habeas case signed by Acting Assistant Attorney General Yaakov Roth, announced it would "review" Peters's state conviction, questioning both the length of her sentence and Colorado's denial of bail pending her appeal as potentially "arbitrary or unreasonable" -- without identifying any new evidence or legal defect in the state proceedings. Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, in a March 2025 court filing, called the intervention a "grotesque attempt to weaponize the rule of law." At an April 22, 2025 federal hearing on Peters's bid for release, Justice Department lawyer Abigail Stout told Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak she was not authorized to discuss any ongoing review and had no knowledge of any evidence, leaving the department's actual reason for intervening in a completed state prosecution unexplained on the record.

Trump personally escalated the matter on May 5, 2025 in a Truth Social post directing DOJ to "take all necessary action to help secure the release" of Peters, describing her as an "innocent Political Prisoner" held "hostage ... by the Democrats, for political reasons" and subjected to "Cruel and Unusual Punishment," and criticizing Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser by name for jailing her. Trump escalated the pressure further on August 21, 2025, threatening on social media, "If she is not released, I am going to take harsh measures!!!" The Federal Bureau of Prisons went further in a letter the Colorado Department of Corrections received on November 12, 2025, seeking Peters's transfer into federal custody, and Michael Flynn, national security adviser during Trump's first term, has said she should be moved into federal custody because she could be a witness in an investigation of the 2020 election; the Department of Corrections said on November 26 that it was "not currently seeking a transfer," noting state law permits transfers to federal prison only when initiated by the state. On December 8, 2025, U.S. Magistrate Judge Scott Varholak dismissed Peters's federal bid for release on bond, ruling that her pending state appeal had to play out first, and she remained in state prison. Trump announced on December 11, 2025 that he was pardoning Peters; the document her attorney shared, which appears to be dated December 5, has no legal effect on her state conviction. A December 15, 2025 email from White House staffer Emily Underwood to officials at five federal agencies, including the Energy, Transportation and Interior departments, seeking a call "to discuss immediate actions that your department or agency can take with respect to Colorado," later surfaced in Colorado's lawsuit alleging federal retaliation over how the state runs its elections; CPR News reported it was sent a month after Colorado refused to move Peters to federal custody and days after the state ignored Trump's clemency declaration, and Colorado's Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper said it showed the administration targeting the state. The email, as reported, does not mention Peters.

On April 2, 2026, the Colorado Court of Appeals -- in a unanimous, 78-page opinion by Judge Ted Tow, reached independently of DOJ's intervention -- upheld Peters's underlying conviction but ordered her resentenced, finding the trial court's nine-year sentence was based "in part on improper consideration of her exercise of her right to free speech" (the panel found the sentencing judge's comments suggested the term was meant partly to stop Peters from continuing to espouse views the court deemed "damaging"). The same opinion rejected Peters's separate argument that a hypothetical presidential pardon could nullify her state conviction, holding the President has no pardon power over state offenses. The appeals court declined to rehear the case on April 23, 2026.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis commuted Peters's sentence on May 15, 2026 -- cutting her original nearly-nine-year term roughly in half, to four and a half years, and making her parole-eligible June 1, 2026. PBS NewsHour and ABC7 reported the commutation followed a sustained Trump pressure campaign on Polis (public attacks, exclusion from a White House governors' meeting, and administration moves against Colorado-based NCAR and U.S. Space Command); Polis had earlier said Peters would need to show "appropriate contrition, apology"; his commutation letter said her application "demonstrates taking responsibility for your crimes," though Peters has not publicly confirmed the admission Polis described. The commutation preempted the court-ordered resentencing before it occurred. Polis characterized the move as a commutation, not a pardon, and grounded it in the same disproportionate-sentencing/free-speech concern the Court of Appeals had already identified, not in the political-motive concern DOJ raised in its March 2025 filing. Peters was released June 1, 2026.

By August 2026, Peters was being considered for an elections-consultant role in Shasta County, California, with no parole condition identified that would bar it. The role did not materialize: after public backlash and a county Board of Supervisors censure of Registrar Curtis, Peters said in a September 1, 2026 statement released through her attorney, Peter Ticktin, "I have not accepted any position with the Shasta County Elections Office," only that "discussions" had occurred; Curtis offered a differing account (she declined due to travel commitments) that doesn't reconcile cleanly with his own earlier public statements that he believed she had accepted.

In a decision reported September 21, 2026, the Colorado Supreme Court declined to hear Peters's appeal of the Court of Appeals' rejection of her challenges, including her Supremacy Clause immunity and juror-misconduct claims, leaving the conviction intact.

offense_category: Weaponization of Federal Litigation Authority -- DOJ has sued 29 states and D.C. for sensitive voter registration data (addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers, partial Social Security numbers) under a legal theory federal courts have repeatedly rejected, then escalated to records-preservation letters threatening election officials with civil and criminal sanctions -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: Since 2025, **DOJ's Civil Rights Division has filed federal lawsuits against 29 states and D.C. seeking each state's full voter registration database, including sensitive personal data (home addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and partial Social Security numbers)**, asserting authority under the Civil Rights Act of 1960, the National Voter Registration Act, and the Help America Vote Act. Federal district courts have dismissed 23 of these lawsuits as of this entry, including rulings against DOJ in California, Oregon, Michigan, New Mexico, West Virginia, and New Jersey; U.S. District Judge Hala Jarbou (Michigan) held the federal voting laws DOJ cited do not require states to turn over this information, and U.S. District Judge Judith C. Herrera reached a similar conclusion dismissing the New Mexico suit. DOJ has appealed all three of its first losses and sought expedited review of the Michigan case at the Sixth Circuit, with a decision possible before the November 2026 midterms. On September 10, 2026, notwithstanding this string of losses, Eric Neff, acting chief of the Civil Rights Division's Voting Section, sent letters to election officials in the same 29 states and D.C. instructing them not to destroy 2024 election records, warning that failure to preserve the data 'may constitute spoliation of evidence' that could subject officials to 'civil and criminal sanctions.' Dhillon publicly characterized the letters as 'standard litigation practice, not a "threat,"' while Attorney General Todd Blanche has suggested DOJ may seek Supreme Court review if its appeals fail.

The pattern -- pursuing sensitive individual voter data at national scale via a legal theory courts have repeatedly rejected, then threatening the same officials with sanctions -- raises separation-of-powers and voter-privacy concerns beyond the merits of any single case

official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (DOJ issued these subpoenas January 20, 2026, during her tenure; no specific prosecutor named in reporting reviewed as personally directing them) -- immigration-enforcement obstruction investigation
offense_category: Grand Jury Subpoenas Quashed as Harassment/Retaliation for Constitutionally Protected Conduct -- a federal judge found the subpoenas served no legitimate investigative purpose
incident_summary:
On January 20, 2026, federal prosecutors served six grand jury subpoenas on the records custodians for Minnesota Governor Tim Walz's office, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey's office, St. Paul Mayor Kaohly Her's office, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison's office, and the Hennepin and Ramsey County Boards of Commissioners, demanding broad categories of records on federal immigration enforcement going back to January 1, 2025, as part of a stated investigation into obstruction of federal immigration enforcement. The subpoenas came during Operation Metro Surge, the administration's aggressive immigration surge in Minnesota, which had drawn widespread protests, and four days after news first leaked that DOJ was investigating Walz and Frey. The New York Times reported the same day that the subpoenas significantly expanded an inquiry first said to focus on Walz and Frey and said to center on whether Minnesota officials had conspired to impede federal agents, and that they came as the Justice Department had all but announced it would not charge the ICE agent who fatally shot Renee Good in Minneapolis (tracked separately in this database). NBC News placed the subpoenas within a growing number of DOJ investigations of people Trump had publicly targeted -- including then-Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, Democratic lawmakers, former CNN anchor Don Lemon, and protesters, each tracked elsewhere in this database.

In an order signed June 17, 2026, and unsealed June 22, Chief U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz quashed all six subpoenas, writing that "the Department has struggled -- without success -- to identify a single plausible investigatory justification for the subpoenas," calling the requests "extraordinarily broad" and finding they sought materials "that largely if not entirely relate to constitutionally protected conduct." Resting the ruling on the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering rule, the judge found that the subpoenas' "dominant purpose" was "to coerce Minnesota officials into assisting the federal government with enforcing civil immigration law and to harass and retaliate against them for failing to do so." ABC News noted that it is almost unheard of for federal judges to quash criminal subpoenas from Justice Department prosecutors. DOJ did not say whether it would appeal, and no appeal appears on the court's docket.
elements_required: DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas -- a coercive criminal-investigative tool -- to the offices of a sitting governor, two mayors and a state attorney general, and to the boards of the state's two largest counties, an unusually broad and high-profile set of targets
A federal judge found, after DOJ's own attempt to justify the subpoenas in court, that the Department could not identify any plausible investigatory purpose for them

The court found the material sought largely or entirely related to constitutionally protected conduct (public officials' policy positions and statements), not conduct ordinarily subject to grand jury investigation

The judge made an explicit judicial finding -- not just an inference invited by advocates -- that the subpoenas were issued 'to harass and retaliate against' the targeted officials for failing to assist federal enforcement of civil immigration law, alongside a finding that the subpoenas aimed to coerce that assistance

incident_summary: On September 29, 2025, CNN reported the Justice Department -- through prosecutors in the Western District of Virginia -- had opened a national-security investigation into FBI leadership during Christopher Wray's tenure (2020-2024) over alleged mishandling of documents connected to the Durham special counsel investigation, including questions about materials stored in 'burn bags' typically used to dispose of classified paper records. Investigators sought interviews with staff who worked on the FBI's seventh-floor leadership suite during Wray's directorship. The probe came in the wake of, and was reported alongside, Trump's public comments suggesting DOJ was investigating Wray following the recent indictment of former FBI Director James Comey. About a month later, on October 30, 2025, **Trump escalated by publicly demanding the prosecution of former Attorney General Merrick Garland, former FBI Director Christopher Wray, former Special Counsel Jack Smith, and former White House Chief of Staff/Homeland Security Advisor Lisa Monaco, accusing them of 'illegal' conduct for authorizing an FBI review of Republican lawmakers' phone data connected to the 2020 election-interference investigation**. Trump's public demand followed the same pattern already documented elsewhere in this tracker: his indictments of Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James, both of which Trump had also personally pushed Attorney General Bondi to pursue.
elements_required: DOJ opened a national-security investigation into the document-handling practices of the prior FBI leadership specifically, rather than a broader or institution-neutral review, following the administration's public campaign against Wray

Trump publicly and personally demanded criminal prosecution of four specifically named former officials (Garland, Wray, Smith, Monaco) for a specific investigative act (the 2020 phone-data review), rather than allowing DOJ to reach an independent charging decision

This public demand followed an already-documented pattern in this tracker (the Comey and James prosecutions) of Trump personally pressuring Bondi's DOJ to pursue charges against individuals he named publicly

official: Pam Bondi, Attorney General
offense_category: DOJ Criminal Prosecution of a Sitting State Judge for an Official Judicial Act -- Judicial-Independence Concern -- contested; DOJ maintains the prosecution targets obstruction conduct, not judicial decision-making itself, and a federal judge has allowed the case to proceed past a judicial-immunity challenge
incident_summary: On April 18, 2025, ICE agents, FBI agents, and DEA agents entered Milwaukee County Circuit Judge Hannah Dugan's courtroom to serve an administrative arrest warrant on Eduardo Flores-Ruiz, a noncitizen facing misdemeanor domestic-violence-related battery charges. Dugan allegedly directed Flores-Ruiz to leave through a back door normally reserved for jurors, allowing him to evade the agents. **Dugan was arrested in late April 2025 and indicted by a federal grand jury on May 13, 2025, on one felony count of obstructing or impeding a federal proceeding and one misdemeanor count of concealing a person to prevent arrest.** Dugan pleaded not guilty. Her defense moved to dismiss the case on judicial-immunity grounds, arguing that a judge's in-courtroom conduct is an official judicial act immune from criminal prosecution and that immunity should bar the case at the outset rather than being litigated later at trial. A magistrate judge recommended the case proceed, and U.S. District Judge Lynn Adelman upheld that recommendation, rejecting the immunity argument and allowing the prosecution to continue. More than 150 former state and federal judges signed a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi criticizing the prosecution as an attempt to intimidate the judiciary.
elements_required: DOJ brought federal criminal charges against a sitting state judge for conduct occurring in her own courtroom during a judicial proceeding
The judge's defense raised judicial immunity as a threshold bar to prosecution, not merely a trial defense
A federal district judge specifically considered and rejected that immunity argument, allowing the prosecution to proceed

A substantial bipartisan group of over 150 former judges publicly characterized the prosecution as judiciary-intimidation, a significant institutional pushback signal distinct from ordinary case commentary

official: Ed Martin, former DOJ Pardon Attorney (until August 2026; earlier head of DOJ's Weaponization Working Group)
offense_category: Improper Disclosure of Grand Jury Material (Rule 6(e) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which strictly limits who may access secret grand jury material and to whom it may be disclosed) -- compounded by a reported initial false denial to DOJ leadership
incident_summary:
A Justice Department internal review, overseen by Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche's office, examined whether grand jury material gathered in DOJ's mortgage-fraud investigations of Sen. Adam Schiff and New York Attorney General Letitia James -- both perceived political opponents of President Trump -- had been shared with people not authorized to possess it. At least two sources familiar with the review told CNN it found Ed Martin improperly handled grand jury material; one of them said the department found he had shared the secret grand jury material in the Schiff case. The same source said that when department leaders first asked Martin whether he had shared the material, he denied doing so; emails soon surfaced showing he had in fact shared it. CNN's sources did not say who received the material or why Martin shared it. The finding was at least part of the reason Martin was pushed out of DOJ headquarters: he was removed as head of DOJ's Weaponization Working Group on the first day of 2026 and relocated to a building across town housing the Office of the Pardon Attorney, his one remaining role. A person close to Martin said he and the Working Group "followed DOJ standards and procedures at all times." Martin has not been charged with a crime, and DOJ had not determined whether any law was broken.

In the same story that broke the internal review's finding, Deputy AG Blanche said in a statement to CNN: "there are no misconduct investigations into Ed Martin. Ed is doing a great job as Pardon Attorney" -- a present-tense denial at odds with the finding the review reportedly reached. The statement did not address whether there had ever been a review of Martin's handling of grand jury material. Martin remained active in the Pardon Attorney role as of an August 14, 2026 official Pardon Attorney announcement.

Trump announced August 21, 2026 that Martin is leaving the Pardon Attorney post entirely, to work outside DOJ on election-related legal battles for the 2026 midterms and 2028 presidential race. No outlet reviewed ties the departure to the grand jury disclosure finding; Trump presented it as a move to election legal work, though CNN's February report on the review had already said Martin was expected to leave the department within weeks. No organization or formal title for the election legal work Trump described was identified; by September 9, 2026, Martin had instead launched Firearm Rights for Americans, a group offering people barred from owning guns help in seeking restoration of their firearm rights, which he said he hoped would turn out Second Amendment voters in the midterms. The underlying accountability gap -- no termination, no referral, an on-record denial of any misconduct investigation -- stood as of his last day in the role.

incident_summary:
In August 2024, before taking office, Ed Martin -- a "Stop the Steal" organizer who had falsely denied Trump lost the 2020 election -- had given Timothy Hale-Cusanelli, a January 6 rioter federal prosecutors themselves had described as a "Nazi sympathizer" (he had worn a Hitler mustache to work at a naval weapons station and recorded an antisemitic rant comparing Orthodox Jews to a "plague of locusts"), an award for embodying "God, family, and country" at a ceremony at Trump National Golf Club, calling him an "extraordinary man" and "extraordinary leader."

After becoming interim/acting U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia in January 2025, Martin oversaw the dismissal of roughly 30 federal prosecutors who had worked on January 6 Capitol riot cases (via a memo signed by Acting Deputy AG Emil Bove) and, separately, demoted at least eight senior prosecutors who had handled those same cases to entry-level positions, conduct The Washington Post, CNN, and NPR all characterized as intended to pressure the prosecutors into resigning. Martin was also reported to have represented January 6 defendants in his own prior legal practice while simultaneously serving as the office's top federal prosecutor, an apparent conflict of interest.

When the Hale-Cusanelli award resurfaced in reporting during his 2025 confirmation fight, Martin issued a statement saying he was unaware of Hale-Cusanelli's antisemitic history and condemning those views "in the strongest terms possible." A group of former January 6 prosecutors formally asked DOJ's attorney disciplinary board to investigate Martin's conduct, and more than 100 veterans of the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. signed a letter calling him "an affront to the singular pursuit of justice for which this Office has stood for more than two centuries." Martin also failed to initially disclose over 150 paid appearances on Russian state-funded RT and Sputnik networks before taking office, only including them in a later follow-up disclosure letter. Facing opposition from Senate Republicans -- including Sen. offense_category: Evidence-Handling Irregularities and Persistent Uncorrected False Public Claims in a Border Patrol Shooting of a U.S. Citizen (Operation Midway Blitz)
incident_summary: On October 4, 2025, **U.S. Border Patrol Agent Charles Exum shot U.S. citizen Marimar Martinez five times in Chicago's Brighton Park neighborhood during Operation Midway Blitz**, a large-scale immigration-enforcement surge. DHS's same-day press release branded Martinez and a co-defendant, Anthony Ian Santos Ruiz, "domestic terrorists," stated Martinez "was armed with a semi-automatic weapon and has a history of doxxing federal agents," and said agents "were ambushed by domestic terrorists that rammed federal agents with their vehicles." Martinez and Ruiz were federally charged over the alleged ramming. Between October 8 and 10, 2025, Exum drove the vehicle involved -- key physical evidence -- more than 1,000 miles back to his Border Patrol station in Maine rather than it being held for examination; his supervisor subsequently had scuff marks on the vehicle buffed out. Exum was separately quoted bragging, "I fired 5 rounds and she had 7 holes. Put that in your book boys." On November 20, 2025, federal prosecutors moved to dismiss the indictment with prejudice, citing "new facts and information" -- barring any future refiling. In February 2026, a federal judge ordered the release of bodycam and other evidence, finding it would "counter the government's public narrative" of Martinez; the footage showed Exum appeared to turn his own vehicle's steering wheel toward Martinez immediately before the collision, after another agent in the vehicle said "it's time to get aggressive," directly contradicting the original ramming claim. As of this entry's research (Sept. 2026), DHS's October 2025 press release -- including the "domestic terrorist," armed, and ramming characterizations -- remains published on DHS's own website without a public correction or retraction, confirmed by direct review of that page during this entry's sourcing.

official: Gordon D. Kromberg, Assistant U.S. Attorney, Eastern District of Virginia
offense_category: First Federal Raid of a Journalist's Home in a National-Security Leak Investigation -- Judges Later Barred DOJ From Searching the Seized Materials Under the Privacy Protection Act
incident_summary: On Wednesday, January 14, 2026, the FBI executed a search warrant -- sought by Assistant U.S. Attorney Gordon D. Kromberg of the Eastern District of Virginia -- at the Virginia home of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson, seizing six electronic devices, including her phone, work computer, personal laptop, and smart watch, in an early-morning raid. Agents told Natanson she was not the target of the underlying investigation, which concerned government contractor Aurelio Perez-Lugones, a Maryland systems administrator with top-secret clearance charged under the Espionage Act with illegally retaining classified national defense materials and indicted on January 22, 2026 on five counts of transmitting national defense information (according to the FBI's affidavit, agents searching his home and car found a SECRET-marked document in his lunchbox and more SECRET-marked materials in his basement). Trump publicly indicated the leaked information concerned a U.S. military operation in Venezuela (this database's entry on Secretary Rubio and the Maduro raid documents that operation), though court documents reviewed did not confirm the connection. Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press President Bruce D. Brown called the search 'a tremendous escalation in the administration's intrusions into the independence of the press,' and Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray called it an 'extraordinary, aggressive action' raising 'profound questions and concern around the constitutional protections for our work.' This was the first time the Justice Department had raided a journalist's home specifically in connection with a national-security leak investigation. The court quickly issued a standstill order blocking the government from reviewing the seized devices' contents pending litigation; Magistrate Judge William B. Porter subsequently ruled that the court itself, not DOJ, would conduct any review, stating this prevented 'the equivalent of leaving the government's fox in charge of the Washington Post's henhouse.' On May 4, 2026, District Judge Anthony J. Trenga sided with Natanson and The Post, affirming the magistrate's ruling and **holding that the Privacy Protection Act 'bars the Government from searching in this particular case the PPA-protected materials that were seized,'** citing 'the harassing and chilling effects such a seizure could have on a reporter.' Between February 6-9, 2026, the Freedom of the Press Foundation filed a bar complaint against Kromberg with the Virginia State Bar, alleging he 'failed to disclose key provisions of the Privacy Protection Act when seeking' the warrant; the bar declined to investigate that complaint, but in March told Kromberg it was conducting a preliminary investigation, pointing to Judge Porter's opinion, then dismissed the matter in a July 2026 letter finding the evidence did not show a rules violation 'under the required evidentiary standard of clear and convincing evidence.'

offense_category: Directing an Intelligence-Community-Wide Anti-Leak Campaign, Including Expanded Polygraph Screening on Contact With the Press, That Press Freedom Advocates Warn Chills Journalism and Whistleblowing
incident_summary: Beginning early in her tenure as Director of National Intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard pursued a sustained campaign against leaks to the press across the intelligence community. On March 14, 2025, she announced an investigation into intelligence-agency leaks, citing reporting by HuffPost, The Washington Post, NBC News, and The Record as examples of what she called 'politically motivated leaks' that 'undermine our national security.' On April 23, 2025, she announced referrals of two individuals to the Department of Justice for allegedly leaking classified information, stating 'these deep-state criminals leaked classified information for partisan political purposes to undermine POTUS' agenda.' Bruce Brown, president of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, warned at the time that such investigations 'threaten the free flow of information that the public needs to hold the government accountable, especially in the national security context.' The campaign escalated in September 2025 when Gabbard sent a memo to intelligence agency leaders asking whether it would be feasible to conduct random polygraph examinations of both employees and contractors, with **the directive specifically emphasizing that polygraph questioning should include whether an individual had leaked information to members of the press as part of the standard security-clearance adjudication process**; an ODNI official told CBS News the memo reinforced existing regulations rather than creating new policy. CBS News reported on the directive October 10, 2025 after two sources -- at least one working under Gabbard at ODNI -- leaked details of it to reporters on condition of anonymity, fearing reprisal for speaking publicly. ODNI spokesperson Olivia Coleman responded to the irony directly, saying 'the fact that deep state actors leaked information about DNI Gabbard's directive, aimed at preventing leaks and protecting classified information, to the media is both deeply ironic and a powerful reminder of why her efforts to identify and deter leakers is urgently necessary.'

incident_summary: In March 2025 congressional testimony, DNI Tulsi Gabbard told Congress the intelligence community assessed Iran was not building a nuclear weapon and that Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei had not authorized resuming the program he suspended in 2003. Around June 11, 2025, amid rising Israel-Iran tensions, Gabbard posted an unauthorized three-minute video (filmed on a Hiroshima visit tacked onto an official trip) warning that 'warmongers' had brought the world 'closer to the brink of nuclear annihilation than ever before'; Trump was reportedly furious, questioned the relevance of the Hiroshima stop, and reportedly told her that if she wanted to run for president she shouldn't be in his administration. The Washington Post reported June 18-19, 2025, in the same pre-strike window, that Hegseth was ALSO effectively outside Trump's core Iran-strike decision-making circle despite his prominent public role -- officials and advisers described Trump as relying instead on a tighter, more experienced group for the actual decision: Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Rubio, CIA Director Ratcliffe, and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Caine, with both Hegseth and Gabbard better known at that point for their Fox News profiles and 'deep state' rhetoric than for standing inside that inner circle -- a distinction between who advised the actual strike decision and who later fronted the public/congressional messaging around it (see below). Around June 17-20, 2025, as Trump prepared to strike Iran's nuclear sites, he publicly said Gabbard was 'wrong' and told reporters 'I don't care what she said' -- a direct public rebuke of his own DNI's sworn congressional testimony, days before the June 21-22 'Midnight Hammer' strikes. Gabbard reversed course on social media, saying her testimony had been taken out of context by 'dishonest media' and that she and Trump were 'on the same page,' but was reportedly left out of the Situation Room photos documenting the strikes. After a leaked preliminary Defense Intelligence Agency assessment -- produced under DIA Director Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse -- suggested the strikes had only set Iran's program back by months rather than 'obliterating' it as Trump and Hegseth publicly claimed, the White House moved to limit classified intelligence-sharing with Congress and excluded Gabbard from a June 25, 2025 Senate Iran briefing, conducted instead by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Hegseth, Secretary of State Rubio, and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine; Sen. Chris Murphy said Gabbard was likely disinvited because officials knew she would not endorse the 'obliterated' characterization. On August 22, 2025, **Hegseth fired Kruse himself -- along with two other senior officers, Navy Reserve chief Vice Adm. Nancy Lacore and Naval Special Warfare Command's Rear Adm. Milton Sands -- with Bloomberg reporting the firing followed directly from the DIA's contradictory assessment**, tying Kruse's removal to the same dispute that had sidelined Gabbard two months earlier. The pattern extended into 2026: per Washington Post (Jan. 7) and Bloomberg (Jan. 8) reporting, Gabbard was excluded from months of administration planning for Operation Absolute Resolve, the operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, reportedly because her past non-interventionist record raised doubts about her support for military action, with Secretary of State Rubio said to prefer keeping her out; some White House aides joked DNI stood for 'Do Not Invite.' Gabbard's office and Vice President Vance both directly denied she had been excluded, calling the reporting false.

offense_category: ODNI Reorganization Used to Eliminate Election-Interference and Russia-Analysis Functions, Paired With a Clearance-Revocation Memo That Publicly Disclosed a Covert CIA Officer's Identity -- clearance decisions and agency reorganization are lawful executive functions; the accountability claim concerns the pattern's explicit political framing, its targeting of Russia/election-analysis personnel specifically, and the reckless handling of an undercover officer's identity
incident_summary:
On August 20, 2025, Gabbard announced "ODNI 2.0," a reorganization she said would cut her office's workforce by more than 40%, with affected positions ending September 23, and save more than $700 million annually -- billed as the largest ODNI restructuring since its post-9/11 creation. The plan dissolved the Foreign Malign Influence Center (which tracked foreign election interference), the National Counterproliferation and Biosecurity Center, and the Cyber Threat Intelligence Integration Center, folding their functions into other directorates, while merging the National Intelligence University into the National Defense University and eliminating the External Research Council and Strategic Futures Group. The New York Times reported that Gabbard framed the changes as part of her campaign to crush "the deep state," and in a social media post she said the plan would help in "rooting out deep state actors."

The day before, on August 19, 2025, Gabbard revoked the security clearances of 37 current and former officials -- including CIA deputies and Democratic congressional staffers -- whom she linked to the intelligence community's 2016 Russia-election-interference assessments, acting on what she said was a Trump directive; the Guardian, citing three people familiar with the matter, reported that Gabbard did not inform the White House before the revocations, frustrating several of Trump's top advisers and deepening animosity with the CIA; a senior intelligence official disputed that account, saying Trump had told Gabbard to remove such officials and that the list was emailed to the White House. In publicly naming individuals in the clearance-revocation memo, Gabbard identified a senior CIA officer who was working undercover -- a Russia expert with nearly 30 years of experience, according to the Washington Post, who had helped prepare Trump's briefing ahead of his Alaska summit with Vladimir Putin and who had an overseas posting already approved by CIA Director John Ratcliffe. Losing her clearance effectively ended her career. A U.S. official told NBC News that ODNI "didn't meaningfully consult with the agency" before the clearances were revoked; ODNI's spokesperson said it had coordinated with all agencies and that the memo listed names, not agency affiliations. The episode visibly deepened tension between Gabbard and Ratcliffe over declassification decisions and Russia policy. The same clearance-revocation action also cost the NSA its chief data scientist, Vinh Nguyen, a leading government expert on AI, cryptology, and advanced mathematics who focused on using AI to scrutinize foreign communications and improve the intelligence community's quantum-computing work. In the days before the revocation, the NSA's acting director, Lt. Gen. William Hartman, called Gabbard and asked to see the evidence that Nguyen had done anything to merit losing his clearance, the New York Times reported; Gabbard rebuffed the request and proceeded with the revocation. The Times reported that many, though not all, of the 37 had tangential connections to the intelligence agencies' review of Russian efforts to meddle in the 2016 election.

In late October 2025, the FBI submitted a sharply worded unclassified letter to Congress opposing a House bill that would have made ODNI the federal government's lead counterintelligence agency -- a proposal that would have significantly expanded Gabbard's institutional authority. The FBI wrote the change "would cause serious and long-lasting damage" to national security, citing its own decades of counterintelligence experience and 53-field-office network against a proposal it said would create bureaucracy and shift authority to officials without comparable expertise; reporting indicated the CIA shared many of the FBI's concerns.

On May 22, 2026, Gabbard told Trump she would step down to support her husband after his diagnosis with a rare form of bone cancer, effective June 30, 2026. ODNI's downsizing continued under acting DNI Bill Pulte, leaving the office at roughly half its early-2025 size by July 2026; Jay Clayton was confirmed as DNI on July 28, 2026.

official: Tulsi Gabbard, then-Director of National Intelligence (February 2025-June 2026; resigned and was followed by acting DNI Bill Pulte, then by Jay Clayton)
offense_category: Withholding a Whistleblower Complaint and Underlying Intelligence from Congress -- potential violation of statutory whistleblower-disclosure and congressional-notification obligations governing the intelligence community
incident_summary:
In spring 2025, the NSA intercepted a call in which two foreign nationals (described by the whistleblower's attorney as members of foreign intelligence) discussed a person close to President Trump (later reporting from The New York Times and Wall Street Journal reported that the conversation referenced Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, which Warner and Himes said they could not confirm, and indicated the discussion involved Iran). According to the whistleblower's attorney, Andrew Bakaj, rather than allow the NSA to publish its own intelligence report through normal channels, Gabbard personally carried a paper copy of the intelligence to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, then instructed the NSA not to publish the report and to transmit details directly to her office instead. A whistleblower, represented by Whistleblower Aid, first contacted the Intelligence Community Inspector General (ICIG) about this handling in spring 2025 (April 17, according to Bakaj's account to the Guardian), filing the complaint on May 21, 2025, and in June 2025 requested the disclosure be transmitted to Congress. The complaint alleges that a highly classified report was deliberately limited in distribution for political reasons, and that an intelligence agency's legal office failed to refer a potential crime to the Department of Justice, again for political reasons. Then-Acting ICIG Tamara Johnson initially determined that the complaint met the statutory definition of an "urgent concern" if true but could not determine whether it was credible -- a determination that gave the whistleblower the right to take the complaint to Congress; three days later, a follow-up memo concluded the first allegation was not credible and that she still could not assess the second, and the complaint was administratively closed in June 2025.

The complaint was not provided to the congressional intelligence committees until the evening of February 2, 2026 -- nearly eight months later -- when ICIG Christopher Fox hand-carried it to the Gang of Eight, whose members and staff reviewed it on a read-and-return basis because of its classified contents. Fox's February 2 letter to the intelligence committees' leaders gave a specific, dated breakdown of the delay: ongoing "complexity in the classification"; the 43-day government shutdown starting October 1, 2025; ODNI leadership changes, including the confirmation of a new general counsel, Jack Dever, whom clearance issues kept from viewing the complaint until December 1, 2025; a December 4 meeting at which Gabbard said she had not previously been told that clearance to share the complaint with Congress was pending; and a subsequent White House Counsel review for a potential executive-privilege assertion, with Gabbard's final approval to share the material granted only January 30, 2026. When the complaint was finally transmitted, it also arrived heavily redacted under executive-privilege claims, further limiting congressional oversight of the underlying allegation. When Gang of Eight members then asked to see the underlying intelligence report, ODNI told them the intelligence community could not provide it unredacted "due to the assertion of executive privilege."

Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chair Mark Warner and other Democrats publicly questioned the delay. Gabbard denied any wrongdoing, calling claims that she or ODNI "hid" the complaint "a blatant lie"; her office said both inspectors general "did not find the complaint credible," while Fox wrote that he would likely determine the allegations did not meet the statutory "urgent concern" definition; Whistleblower Aid countered that the ICIG had simply been unable to make a determination in the 14-day window. Congressional Republicans on the relevant committees rejected the complaint's substance, while Democrats continued to press over the length of the delay itself, a separate question from the complaint's underlying merits. The Guardian's February 7, 2026 reporting, citing Bakaj, detailed the handling described above -- the whistleblower's underlying allegation concerns Gabbard's handling of the intercepted call, not merely an administrative delay. Gabbard's office has said every action taken was fully within her legal and statutory authority. In a February 24, 2026 letter, Warner and House Intelligence Committee Ranking Member Jim Himes called the privilege assertion over an intelligence report "unprecedented," asked whether the President had asserted it, and said they understood Gabbard still had not given the complainant the security guidance the law requires for contacting the intelligence committees.

Whether the ICIG's itemized explanation adequately justifies the eight-month gap remains genuinely disputed; no independent body (e.g., a DOJ IG or bipartisan committee finding) has ruled on that adequacy question.

status: Unresolved: no independent body has ruled on whether the ICIG's itemized account justifies the eight-month delay. Gabbard denies wrongdoing; a former acting ICIG found one allegation not credible. ODNI withheld the unredacted underlying report from the Gang of Eight, citing executive privilege.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the complaint and underlying report were highly classified, requiring careful handling before transmission to Congress, the Inspector General's own office -- an independent overseer, not ODNI itself -- gave an itemized account of the delay, a former acting IG found the first allegation not credible, and the current IG said he would likely find the allegations did not meet the 'urgent concern' standard; Republican committee members reviewing the same material agreed the complaint lacked substance.
comeback: The IG's explanation for the delay and its conclusion about the complaint's credibility are two separate questions -- even accepting that one allegation was found not credible, an eight-month gap between a whistleblower's June 2025 request for congressional transmission and the material actually reaching the Gang of Eight in February 2026 is a long delay for a statutory notification process designed to keep congressional overseers informed in something close to real time. ICIG Christopher Fox did give Congress an itemized account of the delay (classification complexity, a 43-day shutdown, an ODNI general-counsel confirmation and clearance gap, and a subsequent White House Counsel executive-privilege review), so the live accountability question is not whether any account exists, but whether that account's specific causes -- several of them (a government shutdown, an internal confirmation process, a privilege review White House Counsel controlled) were substantially within the executive branch's own control -- justify an eight-month gap for a statutory process meant to keep Congress informed promptly, especially given the underlying intelligence itself concerned a matter that, according to the whistleblower's attorney, Gabbard personally routed to the White House Chief of Staff rather than through normal NSA publication channels.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] The pattern here is executive-branch control over what congressional intelligence overseers see: a statutory whistleblower-transmission process that stretched to roughly eight months, with its final steps running through a White House Counsel privilege review and Gabbard's own approval, followed by an executive-privilege assertion over the underlying intelligence report that Warner and Himes called unprecedented. Whether the delay was unlawful is unresolved; no court or independent body has ruled. It is a different kind of dispute from the personnel and analytic-politicization matters documented in the ODNI Pulte staff-purge and CIA politicization entries, and should not be read as the same conduct.
pull_quote: Gabbard called claims that she or ODNI “hid” the complaint “a blatant lie” -- but the complaint was not given to Congress for nearly eight months, and the unredacted underlying intelligence report was then withheld under a claim of executive privilege.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the underlying timeline (complaint filed, June 2025 transmission request, February 2, 2026 delivery to the Gang of Eight) -- corroborated by the whistleblower's counsel, the ICIG's February 2 letter as reported by CBS News, Warner and Himes's February 24 letter, and NBC News reporting including Gabbard's on-record response. The Guardian's Feb. 7, 2026 reporting on the intercept's substance (routed to Wiles, publication blocked) is attributed to the whistleblower's attorney and is HIGH confidence as to what the whistleblower alleges, though Gabbard's office disputes any characterization of wrongdoing and maintains her actions were within her statutory authority. The ICIG's itemized delay account is HIGH confidence, sourced directly to Fox's own letter to the House and Senate intelligence committees as reported by CBS News; whether that account's causes justify the delay's length, rather than merely explain it, remains a genuinely contested judgment call this entry does not resolve.
