official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (with President Trump as the removing authority)
offense_category: Politicized Removal of the Joint Chiefs Chairman, Chief of Naval Operations, and the Service Judge Advocates General Without Stated Cause -- the JAG removals specifically raise a contested statutory concern under the law protecting judge advocates' independent legal advice function
incident_summary:
On the night of Friday, February 21, 2025, the Trump administration fired Gen. CQ Brown Jr., Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and only the second Black officer to hold the post; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, Chief of Naval Operations and the first woman to hold that role; and Gen. Jim Slife, Air Force Vice Chief of Staff -- the first time in U.S. history two sitting members of the Joint Chiefs of Staff had been removed simultaneously. The same night, Hegseth announced he was removing the Judge Advocates General (the top uniformed lawyers) of the Army, Navy, and Air Force and requesting nominations for all three posts. That fired Lt. Gen. Joseph Berger (Army) and Lt. Gen. Charles Plummer (Air Force); the Navy post was already vacant after Vice Adm. Christopher French's resignation, and its acting JAG, Rear Adm. Lia Reynolds, stayed on pending a replacement -- a set of removals legal commentators dubbed the "Friday Night Massacre of Judge Advocates General." No public, on-record reason was given for any of the removals when they were announced. Hegseth announced Trump intended to nominate retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Dan Caine as the new Joint Chiefs chairman. Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), ranking member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, characterized the firings as "part of a broader, premeditated campaign by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth to purge talented officers for politically charged reasons," a characterization widely connected in contemporaneous and later reporting -- including The Guardian's March 15, 2025 retrospective on Hegseth's broader reshaping of the Pentagon -- to the administration's stated opposition to diversity, equity, and inclusion policies and to Hegseth's public, pre-confirmation criticism of Brown's and Franchetti's selection. This entry documents the origin point of a pattern this tracker separately documents continuing into 2026 through the removal of Vice Adm. Fred Kacher as Director of the Joint Staff, the forced retirement of Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George, and Hegseth's later interventions blocking promotions of Black and female officers -- each tracked in this database's own entries.

The pattern of removing senior women extended in July 2025 when the Pentagon reassigned Vice Adm. Yvette Davids, the first woman to lead the U.S. Naval Academy, out of that post roughly 18 months into her tenure, replacing her with Marine Corps Lt. Gen. Michael J. Borgschulte (the Academy's first Marine superintendent) and moving Davids to a deputy CNO role. The Hill reported Davids' reassignment made her at least the fifth senior female service member moved out of a leadership role since January 2025, alongside Franchetti, and cited experts warning the pattern -- combined with Hegseth's pre-confirmation record of statements opposing women in combat roles -- could have a "chilling effect" on women's enlistment and career advancement in the armed forces.

The Senate confirmed replacements for the Army JAG post (Maj. Gen. Bobby Christine) on June 29, 2025 and the Navy JAG post (Marine Maj. Gen. David Bligh) on July 31, 2025. The Air Force post stayed vacant longer. Defense One reported October 23, 2025 -- eight months after Plummer's ouster -- that acting Air Force JAG Maj. Gen. Rebecca Vernon, who had taken the role after the purge, had herself stepped down, with no one yet nominated to fill the post permanently; Hegseth had said he removed the Army and Air Force JAGs because they were "roadblocks to orders that are given by a commander in chief." Trump nominated Brig. Gen. Christopher Eason for the Air Force post in December 2025, and the Senate confirmed him on January 30, 2026.

Dan Caine was confirmed as Joint Chiefs chairman in April 2025, and the removals stand finalized with no court challenge specific to them identified -- distinguish from the separately litigated 2025 inspectors general firings, tracked elsewhere in this database, which produced an actual court finding. Brown himself has since become a public critic: in a July 3, 2026 Foreign Affairs essay co-authored with Duke political scientist Peter Feaver and attorney Andrew Kragie, Brown and his co-authors wrote that when presidents use the armed forces for "politically contentious missions, such as addressing domestic crime in cities," the military's work "becomes more fraught," and that "if you ask too much of the military, you risk the entire enterprise"; at the Aspen Ideas Festival the previous week, Brown said the pattern of Pentagon personnel firings is "not about merit," questioning whether remaining officers "are going to have a fair opportunity to advance in their career going forth."
elements_required: 10 U.S.C. provisions governing the Judge Advocates General prohibit any DoD officer or employee from interfering with a TJAG's ability to give independent legal advice to the service Secretary or Chief of Staff, or with any judge advocate's ability to give independent legal advice to commanders -- [contested application, not adjudicated] removing the service JAGs simultaneously (the Army and Air Force JAGs fired, the acting Navy JAG slated for replacement), without stated cause, is argued by legal commentators (Lawfare, Justia/Verdict) to functionally undermine this independent-advice protection, though the statute does not clearly specify removal procedure and the administration's Article II removal authority over these positions is itself a live legal question, not settled

The Joint Chiefs Chairman and service-chief removals themselves fall within the President's broad Article II authority to remove senior military leadership and are not, on their own, alleged to violate a specific statute -- the accountability concern here is the documented pattern and stated politicized motive, not an established legal violation for those two removals specifically

Multiple independent, on-record sources (Sen. Jack Reed, legal scholars writing in Lawfare and Verdict/Justia) characterized the same-night, first-ever-simultaneous scope of the removals as evidence of a coordinated, politically motivated purge rather than case-by-case performance-based personnel decisions

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Command Negligence / Public Misrepresentation of a Combat Incident -- Hegseth publicly described a facility soldiers say was essentially undefended against drones as 'fortified,' while survivors allege commanders ignored specific warnings and left soldiers to rescue and treat the wounded themselves -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary:
On March 1, 2026, an Iranian one-way attack drone struck a tactical operations center at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait, killing six soldiers of the U.S. Army's 103rd Sustainment Command and wounding more than 30 others. Soldiers told The Washington Post, which interviewed 17 people including survivors and other firsthand witnesses, that the unit's commander, Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, and his superior, Maj. Gen. John Hinson, had been briefed that Port Shuaiba was on an Iranian target list and that the unit's own force-protection assessments advised against the move, but sent the troops there anyway; soldiers also said Army Central did not fulfill the unit's request for a truck-mounted EAGLS counter-drone system, and one said it "was denied because of lack of assets." Survivors told CBS News the facility's defenses -- T-walls designed to stop mortar and rocket fragments, not aerial drone strikes, with vertical blast barricades but no overhead protection -- were essentially nonexistent against the actual threat: one survivor rated the position's drone-specific defense as "none." CBS News reported that most other troops in Kuwait had been relocated farther from Iranian range while the unit was moved to Port Shuaiba, and survivors described a chaotic aftermath with severe injuries (perforated eardrums, heavy bleeding, head wounds) in which soldiers triaged one another with makeshift bandages and drove the wounded to Kuwaiti hospitals in commandeered civilian vehicles. A soldier ordered to flee with Barnes later told The Washington Post that the general ran to a protective bunker after the blast while dozens under his command remained behind, and none of the troops the Post interviewed recalled seeing Barnes or Hinson help carry out the dead or tend the wounded; Army Central said leadership assisted with the evacuation before being medically evacuated for their own injuries. Secretary Hegseth publicly described the attacking drone as a "squirter" that penetrated the defenses of a "fortified" position -- a characterization survivors directly dispute, with one soldier stating: "Painting a picture that 'one squeaked through' is a falsehood. I want people to know the unit ... was unprepared to provide any defense for itself." Soldiers who were present say they fear no one will be held accountable for the command decisions that left them exposed.

At an April 29, 2026 House Armed Services Committee hearing, Rep. Pat Ryan asked Hegseth whether the survivors who contradicted his account were lying; Hegseth asked whether Ryan was "just going to monologue falsehoods all over the place" and said the Pentagon had moved 7,000 troops "off of the X" based on intelligence. The Army completed its more than 350-page investigation in early July 2026, and Army officials briefed the families of the six soldiers killed privately on July 9; according to sources and officials cited by CBS News and The Washington Post, the review assigned no fault and did not address punitive action, and it has not been released publicly. An Army official told The Post that Hinson initially appointed a mid-career officer under his own command to conduct the review before Army Central took it over under a more senior officer, a choice lawmakers later questioned. At a July 21, 2026 Senate Appropriations Committee hearing, asked by Sen. Tammy Baldwin about the denial of counter-drone systems to the unit, Hegseth claimed "there was not a single drone or defense request denied at any level," according to Baldwin's later letter, which says soldiers' accounts to The Post contradict him; he also said he would coordinate with CENTCOM to provide more information to Congress. A 13-lawmaker bicameral letter led by Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ryan, dated July 29 and released July 30, 2026, followed up on an April 2026 inquiry whose questions, the lawmakers said, Hegseth had not fully answered; it asked 23 questions, including why the investigation was first assigned to an officer under a commander's own chain of command, and set an August 12, 2026 deadline. On August 5, 2026, Baldwin wrote to CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper asking him, by August 18, to release the investigation's findings publicly and to give Congress the full unredacted report, its underlying documents and the classified Army Central review of pre-strike intelligence warnings and the post's defenses. No Pentagon response to either the August 12 or August 18 deadline, and no public release of the Army Central report, has been identified. In September 2026, CBS News reported, citing multiple sources, that Barnes had rejected at least two scouted relocation options in Saudi Arabia despite Army intelligence briefings from January onward that Port Shuaiba was a potential target, and more than 20 congressional Democrats asked the chairmen of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees to hold public hearings on the strike.

incident_summary: The Washington Post reported September 29, 2025 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's rollout of a new National Defense Strategy, publicly branded 'America First, Peace Through Strength,' represented a substantial departure from the two prior National Defense Strategies (2018 and 2022), both of which centered on deterring China as the pacing threat. **The new strategy instead emphasized homeland security and framed domestic threats -- what Hegseth and administration officials have called 'the enemy within' -- as a priority alongside or ahead of great-power deterrence, while pulling resources from Ukraine and Europe even as Russia continued its invasion**. According to the Post, Gen. Dan 'Razin' Caine, the Trump-appointed Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and a figure the administration has otherwise treated as a loyalist, personally pushed back on the strategy in private before its release, giving Hegseth what one source described as 'very frank feedback' and specifically urging him to keep the department focused on being able to 'deter and, if necessary, defeat China in a conflict.' The same source questioned whether Hegseth grasped the strategy's stakes: 'I don't know if Hegseth even understands the magnitude of the NDS, which is why I think Caine tried so hard.' The Post reported that Caine's objection was not isolated -- other career military officials described 'serious unease' with the pivot, and Hegseth's broader move away from longtime U.S. allies has alienated Pentagon seniors. This reporting emerged the same week CSIS had already begun publicly asking (September 25, 2025) why Hegseth was summoning generals and admirals to Washington, and one day before Hegseth's September 30, 2025 Quantico summit of nearly 800 senior commanders -- a separate event, documented in this tracker's hegseth-trump-quantico-generals-summit-2025.json, whose own content (fitness/grooming standards, hazing rules, Trump's 'training grounds' remarks) was about internal culture and domestic force-use policy rather than the strategic document's China/homeland prioritization shift described here.

offense_category: Politicization of a Merit-Based Military Promotion Process -- no criminal charge; this is an accountability claim about breaking longstanding norms insulating officer promotions from political interference, with a disparate-impact pattern along race and gender lines
incident_summary:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth personally removed officers from the Navy's slate of captains selected for promotion to one-star admiral by a board of senior Navy admirals. The New York Times reported on June 1, 2026, citing four current and former defense officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, that he had blocked at least seven of the selected officers, including at least two women, two Black men and three white men; a defense official later told Spectrum News that the board had selected 31 officers and Hegseth struck nine, including three women and two Black men. The resulting 22-nominee list, released publicly in late May 2026, includes no women, although women make up about 21% of the active-duty Navy, and appears to include only two nonwhite officers, although racial minorities make up about 38% of the active-duty Navy. The officials called the removals highly unusual: under Pentagon rules, the defense secretary is supposed to pull officers from a list only for moral, mental, physical or professional failings that raise questions about their fitness to lead. Current and former Navy officials said the officers struck appear to have been targeted for taking part in diversity-related events years or even decades earlier, and ABC News's sources said reasons included participation or involvement in military Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion initiatives. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell declined to say why the officers were removed, saying the department "will never consider the color of a service member's skin or their gender as a factor in promotions." No reversal or restoration of the removed officers has been identified.

Earlier, on March 27, 2026, The New York Times reported that Hegseth had removed four Army colonels (two Black men, two women) from a one-star general promotion list over the repeated objections of Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, who cited what the Times called the colonels' "decadeslong records of exemplary service." A March 31 Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace and Security analysis noted that senior military officials could not recall a defense secretary selectively removing individual officers from a vetted promotion slate. Military officials also told the Times that Hegseth's chief of staff, Lt. Col. Ricky Buria, had told Driscoll during a heated exchange the previous summer, over the promotion of a different officer, that Trump would not want to stand next to a Black female officer; Buria called that account "completely false." NBC News reported April 2, 2026, citing nine U.S. officials, that Hegseth had blocked or delayed promotions for more than a dozen Black and female senior officers across all four military branches; one of the officials said no service had been immune. Appearing before the House Armed Services Committee later that spring, Hegseth acknowledged pulling names from the Army one-star list but declined to give the specific grounds, speaking instead of a need to correct years of "gender and demographic engineering."

Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), the Senate Armed Services Committee's ranking member, has issued repeated public statements condemning the pattern and asserting that governing law reserves promotion-list removal authority to the President alone, not the Secretary of Defense -- a statutory-authority theory distinct from the disparate-impact framing above -- and cited a disparity in which women and minorities are under 20% of the general officer corps but nearly 60% of those Hegseth has fired or sidelined. Seven Democratic senators sent Hegseth a written demand for explanation on July 6, 2026, with an August 30, 2026 response deadline. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell publicly rejected the senators' letter around July 8, 2026, calling it a partisan push to "re-politicize military promotions" and stating decisions are "driven solely by merit"; no confirmation has been found either way of a separate formal written response by the August 30 deadline. On July 15, 2026, Sens. Cory Booker (D-NJ) and Brian Schatz (D-HI) asked the Defense Department's Inspector General to review Hegseth's removal of officers from promotion selection boards' lists.

The removal pattern itself continued escalating: The New York Times reported (August 28, 2026) four more Army officers selected for one-star rank blocked, in a move that appeared to target officers who had worked for generals Hegseth does not like, and a cumulative total of at least 45 officers removed from promotion lists this year, more than half female or Black -- a figure markedly larger than previously documented counts, not independently reconciled against them. NBC News reported (September 1, 2026) that Hegseth had removed at least six more Army officers from a list of 18 one-star generals selected for promotion to two-star rank.

incident_summary: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA), Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, had a long-scheduled, weeks-in-the-making classified oversight visit to the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) headquarters in Springfield, Virginia planned for Friday, September 5, 2025 -- a routine visit of the kind Warner said he had conducted regularly under both Democratic and Republican administrations. In the days before, far-right activist Laura Loomer posted a series of social-media attacks calling Warner a 'rabid Trump hater' who had attacked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, criticized NGA Director Vice Adm. Frank 'Trey' Whitworth (a Biden appointee), and demanded both the meeting be scrapped and Whitworth fired. Warner said Trump administration political appointees then canceled the visit, and in a September 2, 2025 statement called it a 'nakedly political decision' that 'undermines the dedicated, nonpartisan staff at NGA and threatens the principle of civilian oversight,' warning the administration appeared 'desperate to please Loomer.' **Loomer publicly took credit, posting that Whitworth's 'scheduled September 5th fireside love fest...has been CANCELED!' and renewed her call for Hegseth to fire him**. The Pentagon disputed Warner's characterization, telling reporters the visit was 'rescheduled, not canceled...to accommodate bipartisan participation in the town hall event'; no reporting reviewed confirms the visit was ever actually held on a later date. On September 18, 2025, Warner escalated the episode into a Senate floor speech warning more broadly of intelligence politicization, citing this NGA visit alongside the already-documented Loomer-driven firings of NSA Director Gen. Timothy Haugh and NSC staff (see the related entries below) as part of the same pattern, and stating: 'If we let politics dictate what intelligence is acceptable, we are effectively flying blind.' He also renewed the episode in a subsequent press statement titled 'Trump Administration Blocking Congressional Intelligence Oversight.' Whitworth left the NGA director post in November 2025, roughly two months after Loomer's public campaign to have him fired; no sourcing found ties his departure to that campaign specifically, and he moved to a private-sector role (Satellogic) in 2026 without any reporting characterizing his NGA exit as a forced removal.

offense_category: Potential Establishment Clause Violation -- Government-Backed Religious Services at the Pentagon -- an advocacy group's allegation, not an adjudicated constitutional violation; the filed suits seek records under FOIA
incident_summary: This pattern had an earlier, documented origin. The Guardian reported August 14, 2025 that Hegseth's Pentagon had rolled out recruitment advertisements built around biblical imagery and themes, and that Hegseth had personally amplified self-described Christian nationalist pastor Doug Wilson -- who wants to repeal women's suffrage, has defended slavery, and believes homosexuality should be criminalized -- reposting a CNN segment about Wilson in which Wilson said, 'I would like to see this nation being a Christian nation, and I would like this world to be a Christian world,' with the caption 'All of Christ for All of Life,' as the Guardian reported August 9, 2025; a Pentagon spokesman told the Guardian that Hegseth 'very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings.' That earlier online amplification preceded Hegseth's formal decision, roughly six months later, to invite Wilson to preach in person at a Pentagon worship service in February 2026, which CNN, the Washington Post, and Military Times each reported. Wilson, who CNN reported has advocated that the US adopt a Christian theocracy, preached on February 17, 2026 in the Pentagon auditorium in a sermon broadcast on the department's internal TV network, and the Pentagon said Hegseth 'was glad to welcome Pastor Wilson.' On March 25, 2026, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth led a monthly Christian worship service at the Pentagon, livestreamed to Defense Department personnel, at which he read a prayer he said was first offered by a military chaplain, **asking God to 'let every round find its mark against the enemies of righteousness and our great nation,' and to give 'unbreakable unity, and overwhelming violence of action against those who deserve no mercy.'** The service was part of the monthly Christian worship services Hegseth began hosting at the Pentagon in May 2025, at which, according to the Associated Press, only evangelicals had presided and pastors from his own denomination, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches, had appeared at least three times. On March 23, 2026, Americans United for Separation of Church and State filed suit in federal district court in Washington, D.C. against the Defense Department, with a parallel suit against the Department of Labor, seeking under the Freedom of Information Act the production of internal Pentagon communications about the recurring worship services -- including their cost, guests, any recordings, and any employee complaints received -- a request AU had first made in December 2025 that the Pentagon had not fully answered. The Defense Department answered the complaint on May 27, 2026, and Judge Trevor N. official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (policy drafted with the guidance of his personal attorney Tim Parlatore, a Navy Reserve officer then serving concurrently on Hegseth's staff and by 2026 a senior adviser to Hegseth)
offense_category: Imposing Pentagon Press-Credentialing Rules a Federal Judge Later Found Violated the First and Fifth Amendments, Drafted With the Guidance of the Secretary's Own Personal Attorney
incident_summary: In September 2025, the Pentagon distributed a new 21-page press-credentialing policy requiring journalists to sign a pledge agreeing that seeking to obtain unapproved information gathered at the Pentagon -- even unclassified information -- could be treated as 'soliciting' the disclosure of protected information, and warning that credentials could be revoked or denied if a journalist was 'reasonably determined to pose a security or safety risk.' The Washington Post reported October 15, 2025 that the policy had been drafted with the guidance of Tim Parlatore, Hegseth's longtime personal attorney -- who had previously represented Hegseth against sexual-assault allegations and separately represented Donald Trump and, per reporting, individuals connected to organized crime -- after Parlatore joined Hegseth's staff in March 2025 as a Navy Reserve officer while continuing to serve as a private attorney with outside clients, an arrangement that reportedly troubled some Defense Department legal officials. Journalists had until October 14, 2025 to sign the new rules; more than 30 news organizations, including The New York Times, The Washington Post, CNN, and Fox News, refused. On October 15, 2025, roughly 40 to 50 journalists turned in their Pentagon access badges together and exited the building rather than accept the restrictions, an action widely described as unprecedented in scale and near-unanimous across the ideological spectrum of outlets covering the Pentagon. In December 2025, The New York Times sued the Defense Department, Hegseth, and chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell over the policy; **a federal judge subsequently ruled that the provisions governing when press credentials could be revoked violated the First and Fifth Amendments**. Update 2026-09-29: The ruling came on March 20, 2026, from U.S. District Judge Paul L. Friedman, who vacated the challenged provisions and ordered the Pentagon to reinstate the credentials of seven Times reporters. The next business day, the Department issued an interim policy that closed the Correspondents' Corridor, the in-building press workspace reporters had used since the 1970s, and let credentialed journalists into the Pentagon only for five approved purposes and only with an escort at all times; Parlatore, by then a senior adviser to Hegseth, told The Times the new version used "more words to say the same thing." On April 9, 2026, Judge Friedman found the new restrictions violated his order and ordered The Times's reporters' access restored. On April 27, a divided D.C. Circuit motions panel stayed that order only to the extent it entitled journalists to unescorted access, finding the government likely to show the escort requirement fell outside the original ruling. The Times filed a second lawsuit on May 18, 2026, naming Parlatore among the defendants, and on June 30 Judge Friedman preliminarily enjoined the escort requirement as likely First Amendment retaliation; on July 16 another divided D.C. Circuit panel stayed that injunction, finding the government likely to show that a generally applicable escort rule is not retaliation. The government's appeals of both sets of rulings are set for oral argument on November 16, 2026, and the escort requirement remains in effect in the meantime.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Failure to Warn U.S.-Flagged Vessels and American Personnel of an Imminent War Zone Before Ordering Strikes -- an institutional-accountability claim about operational conduct endangering U.S. lives, not a criminal charge against a named official
incident_summary: When the U.S. began bombing Iran on February 28, 2026, five privately-owned, U.S.-flagged vessels that work closely with the U.S. military were in the Persian Gulf, and roughly half a dozen U.S. Merchant Marine Academy cadets were aboard two of them as part of their required sea-training program. The Department of Defense broke with precedent by giving no advance warning of the strikes to the vessels, the Merchant Marine Academy, or the Department of Transportation, which oversees the academy. Three sources close to the situation told NOTUS there was no warning; one said, 'Nobody told them. They were caught unawares,' and that officials 'weren't even given a whiff, weren't even given an indication' that strikes were imminent. Without advance notice, two people familiar with the situation said, there was no clear way to evacuate the cadets or the ships. **On March 2, 2026, the U.S.-flagged Crowley tanker Stena Imperative was hit in an Iranian attack while berthed at the Port of Bahrain, and a dockworker was killed shoreside;** two sources told NOTUS that another U.S.-flagged vessel was nearly hit by a projectile. More than 800 vessels became trapped trying to exit the Persian Gulf; one of the five U.S.-flagged ships, loaded with cargo, was losing money every day it could not leave. The crews found safe harbors in the region and kept the cadets aboard for weeks; the cadets were evacuated about a month after the war started, though as of NOTUS's April 9, 2026 report it was unclear whether all had returned to the United States. The Defense Department did not respond to requests for comment on the lack of warning. On March 20, 2026, Sen. Richard Blumenthal wrote CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper that the U.S.-flagged vessels 'appear to have received no warning or direction to reposition prior to the onset of hostilities,' requesting prioritized resupply and port access, a port call plan, a communications framework, and an explanation of what steps, if any, were taken to notify or reposition the vessels, with a response requested by March 26, 2026; no public CENTCOM reply has been identified. In an interview for NOTUS's April 9, 2026 report, Blumenthal criticized the administration for failing to alert the vessels, describing his concerns as 'sky high' and saying, 'The idea that these ships would be stranded was absolutely foreseeable ...' On April 26, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, Blumenthal, and Mark Kelly wrote Hegseth about a distinct incident, the March 1, 2026 Iranian drone strike on a U.S. post at Shuaiba port in Kuwait that killed six service members and injured more than 30 (tracked as its own entry in this database); the letter cited the failure to warn the U.S.-flagged vessels as part of 'a larger pattern' of failing to protect Americans in the region from Iranian retaliation, and asked what criteria DoD used to decide who needed a warning before the strikes. DoD replied to Warren on May 11, 2026, but in a September 21, 2026 letter urging the Armed Services chairmen to hold hearings on the Port Shuaiba attack, the lawmakers wrote that in its response DoD 'failed to directly answer our questions.'

The lack of warning left no clear way to evacuate, and at least one U.S.-flagged vessel was subsequently hit in an Iranian attack that killed a dockworker

A U.S. Senator with relevant oversight responsibility has called the vessels' stranding foreseeable and said warnings could have been issued, not merely an unfortunate consequence of fast-moving military operations

rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: operational security around the timing of military strikes is a legitimate and standard practice to protect mission success and force safety, advance warning to numerous private vessels risks the information reaching adversaries, and the strikes' timing was driven by broader strategic considerations rather than indifference to the cadets' or crews' safety.
comeback: Operational security concerns do not fully explain a complete absence of any warning to the Department of Transportation or the Merchant Marine Academy itself -- both part of the U.S. government -- which sourcing indicates broke with established precedent; the month-long stranding of American cadets in an active war zone, with no clear way to evacuate them, is a concrete, documented consequence of that specific gap, and the attack that hit a U.S.-flagged tanker and killed a dockworker shows the danger was real, not hypothetical.

Here the gap was coordination: by NOTUS's account, neither the Transportation Department nor its academy was told in advance, breaking with past practice. offense_category: Personal Intervention to Block Senior Military Promotions Along Racial and Gender Lines -- based on nine officials' accounts to NBC News; DoD has not confirmed the specific race/gender-motive characterization on the record
incident_summary: A named instance of Defense Secretary Hegseth's broader pattern of promotion blocking: in the spring of 2025, Hegseth declined to promote Lt. Gen. Douglas Sims over suspicions, held without evidence, that Sims had leaked sensitive information; after Sims was cleared, Hegseth briefly agreed to promote him, then reversed course again in early July 2025, maintaining that Sims was too close to former Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Mark Milley, the New York Times reported July 26, 2025. The move drew rare, direct pushback from Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine -- a break from the pattern, since most of this entry's other documented blockages did not draw comparable internal pushback from the Joint Chiefs' own chairman. On March 27, 2026, the New York Times reported, as The Hill relayed and NPR confirmed through a U.S. official, that Hegseth had struck two Black and two female Army officers from a one-star general promotion list after Army Secretary Driscoll repeatedly refused to remove them; NPR, citing a U.S. official, added that a Black colonel and a female colonel from another branch had also been taken off a promotion list. NBC News then reported on April 2, 2026, based on accounts from nine U.S. officials, that **Defense Secretary Hegseth had taken steps to block or delay promotions for more than a dozen Black and female senior officers across the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marines**. Officials told NBC some of the affected officers were seen as having been targeted because of their race, gender, or perceived affiliation with Biden-administration policies or officials; two officials said the attributes Hegseth cited for removing officers included past support for Covid vaccines or mask mandates for troops and affiliation with diversity, equity, and inclusion programs, and a second U.S. official told NPR that Hegseth has been weeding out senior officers deemed ideologically incompatible. The interventions raised concerns among officials within the affected service branches and, per NBC's reporting, within the White House itself. This entry extends the pattern of senior removals documented separately in this tracker's Army Chief of Staff purge entry to the promotion pipeline for the next generation of military leadership. One specific named instance did not succeed: Hegseth chief of staff Ricky Buria reportedly objected to Maj. Gen. Antoinette Gant's assignment to lead the Military District of Washington on the stated basis that Trump would not want to stand next to a Black female officer at public events -- Buria denies the account, and Army Secretary Driscoll pushed back at the time -- but Gant's assignment proceeded regardless, a nuance not captured uniformly by the pattern's general 'blocked or delayed' framing. Sens. Cory Booker and Brian Schatz sent a July 15, 2026 letter (released July 17) to the Defense Department Inspector General demanding an independent investigation of Hegseth's alleged intervention to block nearly 40 officers, half of them women or members of minority groups, from approved promotion lists, alleging he used personal views on race and gender to override the selection boards' merit-based process. On September 1, 2026, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had fired or blocked the promotions of more than 80 generals and admirals -- about 10% of the military's top officers -- including seven Army officers recently selected for two-star rank, two of them Black and two female, and that more than half of the officers affected by his dismissals were Black or female; Driscoll, who had complained to Trump about the firings and blocked promotions, had submitted his resignation. Days later, Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.) said on CBS that Hegseth had purged over 80 generals and admirals. On September 10, 2026, Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) urged Armed Services leaders to keep promotion-oversight provisions in the draft FY2027 NDAA and require written, justified notice within seven days to officers whose promotions are withheld or removed, citing at least 40 officers removed from one- and two-star lists since January 2025. In a September 14, 2026 report putting the figure at as many as 80, the Times reported that many current and former military leaders said Hegseth had targeted the military's most combat-tested leaders, "hollowing out an institution at war," with key leadership positions unfilled for months while the Iran war strained the force and shortfalls of critical missile interceptors raised questions about its staying power.
elements_required: Hegseth fired or blocked the promotions of more than 80 generals and admirals -- about 10% of the military's top officers -- including promotion-list removals across all four service branches, not a single isolated case
The affected officers include specifically identified Black and female officers, per named reporting

Multiple officials (nine, per NBC's sourcing) independently characterized the pattern as connected to race, gender, or perceived political/ideological association rather than performance or readiness concerns
The pattern is consistent with, and extends, an already-documented broader pattern of Hegseth's personnel interventions across the senior military leadership

status: Ongoing and escalating: Hegseth struck seven more officers from the Army two-star promotion list in late August 2026, the New York Times reported, with no reversal or on-record DoD confirmation of the motive characterization; the requested Inspector General investigation remains pending.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: the Secretary of Defense has legitimate authority to scrutinize promotion recommendations for any reason within his discretion, including concerns about an officer's judgment or public statements while serving, and characterizing race or gender as the operative factor -- rather than genuinely assessed performance, readiness, or judgment concerns -- is the officials' interpretation, not a confirmed fact. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell has called the reporting "fake news from anonymous sources," saying that under Hegseth, "military promotions are given to those who have earned them."
comeback: The specific concern is the consistency and scale of the pattern -- more than 80 generals and admirals fired or blocked, and promotions of more than a dozen Black and female officers blocked or delayed across all four branches, as described by nine officials (not a single disgruntled source) as connected to race, gender, or perceived political association rather than case-by-case performance review, and specifically tied by officials to Hegseth's public, sustained criticism of diversity and inclusion programs, distinguishing this from isolated, individually justified promotion holds.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of the broader pattern this tracker documents of Hegseth personnel decisions that officials describe as driven by ideological and loyalty considerations rather than conventional merit review (see also the Army chief-of-staff purge entry, the Navy one-star promotion-list entry, and the Butler removal entry, where reporting likewise ties Hegseth's objection to a Milley association).
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the scale and cross-branch scope of the promotion interventions, corroborated across NBC News, NPR, The Hill, and the New York Times, with NBC's account sourced to nine officials and the Times' early-September 2026 figure of more than 80 generals and admirals fired or blocked matched by Rep. Jason Crow's public statement (the Times' September 14 report put it at as many as 80). MODERATE confidence on the race/gender-motive characterization across the pattern as a whole, since it rests on officials' interpretation rather than an on-record DoD or Hegseth admission -- marked `contested: true` accordingly. HIGH confidence that the New York Times reported the Buria/Gant exchange, which its March 27, 2026 account sources to three current and former officials, including Driscoll's reported pushback; the motive itself remains disputed, since Buria denies the exchange took place. The Booker/Schatz Inspector General demand is confirmed by the senators' own July 17, 2026 press release -- an on-record statement from the administration's political opponents, not an independent finding. Army Secretary Driscoll's resignation is documented in the separate Army chief-of-staff purge entry, which covers the officer-removal mechanism rather than promotion blocking.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (ordered a pause in offensive cyber operations against Russia, which DoD's official channel then publicly denied had occurred)
offense_category: Public misrepresentation of a national-security decision to Congress and the public -- not itself a prosecutable act, but a documented false denial issued through DoD's official channel, later contradicted by a Republican committee chairman's on-the-record confirmation
status: Bacon (R-NE), the House Armed Services subcommittee chairman, publicly confirmed a one-day pause occurred; DoD's March 4, 2025 official denial that any such pause or stand-down order occurred was never formally corrected or retracted as of this entry's last verification
incident_summary: The Washington Post, Axios, Defense News, and Nextgov/FCW independently reported starting March 1, 2025 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had ordered U.S. Cyber Command to suspend offensive cyber and information-operations planning against Russia, apparently to support Trump's push to negotiate an end to the Russia-Ukraine war. On March 4, 2025, the Defense Department's official Rapid Response Twitter account publicly denied the reports, stating Hegseth 'has neither canceled nor delayed any cyber operations directed against malicious Russian targets and there has been no stand-down order whatsoever.' At a House Armed Services subcommittee hearing on May 15-16, 2025, Rep. Eugene Vindman (D-VA) confronted DoD witness Laurie Buckhout with the discrepancy between the March denial and the original reporting; Buckhout responded that she 'was not here at that time' and was 'not aware of any stand-down operations ordered' -- declining to dispute Vindman's characterization rather than defending the March denial. Subcommittee Chairman Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) then **confirmed on the record that U.S. cyber operations against Russia were in fact paused for one day in February 2025 during Trump's negotiating push**, describing it as 'typical for negotiations.' Vindman characterized the DoD Twitter account's March 4 statement as 'an outright lie,' saying 'this is not what the American people deserve.'
elements_required: DoD's official public statement (the March 4, 2025 Rapid Response Twitter account post) explicitly denied any cyber-operations pause or stand-down order had occurred
A named member of Congress from the President's own party (Bacon) confirmed on the record that a pause did in fact occur
No DoD official at the subsequent hearing disputed that a pause occurred, only disclaiming personal knowledge of it

Eugene Vindman confronted DoD witness Laurie Buckhout with the March denial; she did not dispute that a pause occurred, only that she lacked personal knowledge of it. Chairman Don Bacon confirmed a one-day pause occurred in February 2025.

rebuttal_anticipated: DoD could argue its March 4 statement was narrowly accurate depending on definitions -- e.g., distinguishing a brief 'planning pause' from actually 'canceling or delaying operations,' or arguing no live offensive operations were underway during the one-day window regardless of any planning halt, making the categorical denial technically defensible.
comeback: The original reporting from four independent outlets (Washington Post, Axios, Defense News, Nextgov/FCW) specifically described a halt to offensive cyber and information-operations planning, not a mere rhetorical distinction, and Bacon's on-the-record confirmation came from a Republican committee chairman with direct oversight access -- not a partisan opponent -- corroborating that a real pause occurred as reported and undercutting a 'technically true' defense of the DoD denial.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a pattern of this administration issuing categorical public denials of reported policy decisions that are later substantiated by on-the-record confirmation from within the administration's own party -- a pattern with echoes elsewhere in this tracker's coverage of contested public statements by Cabinet officials.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the original pause was independently reported by four separate national-security outlets in early March 2025; DoD's denial is preserved on its own official Twitter account and cited by Bloomberg and Stars and Stripes; the May 2025 hearing exchange and Bacon's confirmation are documented via CBS News reporting and Vindman's own office. The characterization of the denial as a deliberate 'lie' versus an imprecise or narrowly-framed statement is Vindman's own assessment, presented as his characterization rather than an adjudicated fact.

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (later 'Secretary of War')
offense_category: Policy/Regulatory Violation — DoD Instruction 8170.01 (mishandling of nonpublic DoD information) and a Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention policy violation (failure to preserve official communications), per the Pentagon Inspector General's December 2025 final report; closest criminal analogue: 18 U.S.C. §793(f), gross negligence in handling national defense information — NOT charged, included for reference only
incident_summary: On March 15, 2025, Hegseth **shared sensitive operational details (aircraft quantities, strike timing) about an imminent strike on Houthi targets in Yemen via Signal on his personal phone, in a chat that inadvertently included a journalist**. He also reportedly shared similar information in a separate personal Signal chat with his wife, brother, and personal attorney, Tim Parlatore.
elements_required: DoD Instr. 8170.01: use of personal device for official business (administrative, not criminal)
DoD Instr. 8170.01: use of non-approved commercial messaging app for nonpublic DoD information

Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention policy: failure to preserve official communications sent via Signal, an unapproved and non-archiving channel — the Pentagon IG's December 2025 final report found this violation in addition to the 8170.01 issues

[Reference only, not charged] 18 U.S.C. §793(f): lawful possession of national defense information; gross negligence permitting it to be removed from proper custody or disclosed; failure to report loss

evidence.description: Der Spiegel reported March 26, 2025 that its reporters, using a commercial contact-data provider and hacked customer data published online, found a mobile phone number and a Gmail address for Hegseth; the email address, and in some cases its password, appeared in more than 20 publicly accessible leaks, and the number led to a WhatsApp account Hegseth had apparently deleted only recently. Der Spiegel did not publish the data or test whether the passwords still worked, and said hostile intelligence services could use such data to try to install spyware on officials' devices. The Defense Department did not respond to its request for comment.
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on the exposure of Hegseth's personal contact data during the same period, not an element of any offense; Der Spiegel did not establish that the Signal chat ran on the exposed number

evidence.description: The New York Times reported March 27, 2025 that a dozen current and former Air Force and Navy fighter pilots said the mistaken inclusion of The Atlantic's editor in the chat, and Hegseth's insistence that he did nothing wrong by disclosing the plans, upended decades of military doctrine on operational security; the chat had carried the flight schedules for the F/A-18 Hornets targeting the Houthis in Yemen on March 15. The pilots said they could no longer be certain the Pentagon was focused on their safety when they strapped into their cockpits.
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on the operational-security concerns raised by current and former military pilots, not an element of any offense

evidence.description: The Wall Street Journal reported April 3, 2025 that the Pentagon Inspector General had announced that day a review of Hegseth's sharing of military plans in the Signal chat ahead of the Yemen strikes -- the review that produced the December 2025 report below
evidence.maps_to_element: Establishes when the IG review began

evidence.description: The New York Times reported April 20, 2025, citing four people with knowledge of the chat, that on March 15 Hegseth also shared details of the forthcoming Yemen strikes, including flight schedules for the F/A-18 Hornets, in a private Signal group chat called 'Defense | Team Huddle' that he had created in January and accessed on his private phone. The chat included his wife, Jennifer, who is not a Defense Department employee; his brother Phil and his personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore, who both had Pentagon jobs but no apparent need to know about the strikes; and about a dozen others from his inner circle.
evidence.maps_to_element: DoD Instr. 8170.01 violations (both elements, second instance, as reported; the IG could not verify this chat's contents)

evidence.description: On April 21, 2025, Sen. Adam Schiff wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio in his role as acting Archivist of the United States, urging the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) to take immediate action to preserve records from Trump administration officials' use of Signal and other commercial messaging apps, and to investigate whether cabinet members and other senior officials had adequately preserved such communications. The letter cited both the original 'Houthi PC small group' chat and The New York Times's report of Hegseth's second 'Defense | Team Huddle' chat with his wife, brother and personal lawyer. Because Rubio had been in the 'Houthi PC small group' chat, Schiff wrote that he should not oversee an investigation of activity he was involved in and asked whether NARA would appoint a senior career official to oversee it, and, citing Rubio's 'evident conflict of interest', whether NARA would contact the Justice Department or appropriate inspectors general for help. The letter posed eight questions with a May 5, 2025 response deadline.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention policy element -- documents contemporaneous congressional pressure for preservation; also adds the oversight-response landscape (Rubio's dual role as both a chat participant and acting NARA head) not previously captured in this entry

evidence.description: On April 21, 2025, the watchdog group American Oversight filed an amended complaint in its Federal Records Act suit against Hegseth, the other agency heads in the Yemen-strike chat and the National Archives (American Oversight v. Hegseth, D.D.C. No. 25-cv-883), adding Hegseth's 'Defense | Team Huddle' chat, which it said, citing The New York Times, included his wife, brother, personal lawyer, aides and advisors. The complaint noted that on March 27, 2025 the court had directed the defendants to preserve the Signal messages from March 11 through 15, and alleged, on information and belief, that none of them had preserved the Yemen-strike chat in its entirety.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element -- civil litigation over preservation of the chats, including the second chat (allegations, not findings)

evidence.description: CBS News reported April 25, 2025, citing sources familiar with the matter, that a computer monitor had been installed in Hegseth's Pentagon office giving him remote access to Signal and text messages on his personal cellphone, a setup two sources said bypassed standard Defense Department security protocols; Marine Col. Ricky Buria, an aide, had some oversight of the work, two sources said. CBS noted that the Associated Press had earlier reported his use of an unsecured 'dirty' internet line. A Defense Department spokesperson denied there was a 'dirty line' or any current Signal use in the office, describing a one-way line that alerts him to messages on the phone, which is kept outside the office.
evidence.maps_to_element: DoD Instr. 8170.01 violations (personal-device and unapproved-app elements); context on the scale of the security lapse

evidence.description: The Wall Street Journal reported May 5, 2025, citing people familiar with his management practices, that Hegseth had used Signal more extensively for official Pentagon business than previously disclosed, engaging in at least a dozen separate chats. In one case he told aides on the app to inform foreign governments about an unfolding military operation, and, two of the people said, he also used it to discuss media appearances, foreign travel, his schedule and other unclassified but sensitive information.
evidence.maps_to_element: DoD Instr. 8170.01 violations (both elements) -- establishes the pattern's scale (a dozen+ chats) beyond the two specific instances already documented; TAP analysis, not sourced: consistent with habitual use rather than an isolated error

evidence.description: The Associated Press reported June 6, 2025, citing two people familiar with the investigation and documents it reviewed, that the Pentagon Inspector General was looking into whether any of Hegseth's aides were asked to delete Signal messages about the March 15 strikes, and was asking past and current staffers who were with Hegseth that day who posted the information and who had access to his phone.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act element (question of message deletion, distinct from the IG's failure-to-retain finding below)

evidence.description: At a House Armed Services Committee hearing on the Defense Department's 2026 budget, Rep. Seth Moulton pressed Hegseth about his texts in a Signal group chat that may have included sensitive and classified information about the operation against the Houthis in Yemen.
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on congressional oversight, not an element of any offense

evidence.description: On June 20, 2025, Chief Judge James E. Boasberg granted American Oversight's preliminary-injunction motion only in part: he ordered the agency heads, including Hegseth, to promptly notify acting Archivist Rubio of the impending deletion of any Signal chats containing federal records, and Rubio to ask the Attorney General to act to preserve them. He found American Oversight had not shown that the agencies' recordkeeping programs were inadequate or that the court could provide redress for messages already deleted. The opinion recounts a Defense Department declaration that screenshots of the existing Signal messages at issue had been preserved in a recordkeeping system in the Secretary's office.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element -- court-ordered preservation duties for chats not yet deleted; no finding on already-deleted messages

evidence.description: Politico reported July 14, 2025, citing three people familiar with the probes, that investigators were looking at two close Hegseth aides: Ricky Buria, a senior Hegseth aide, and Tim Parlatore, Hegseth's personal attorney who also served as a top Pentagon adviser (“Ricky and Tim are some of the folks that they’re zeroing in on,” one said). In the Inspector General's probe, investigators were asking whether Buria helped set up the unsecured internet line that let Hegseth access Signal; in a separate Air Force Office of Special Investigations inquiry into leaks, they were asking whether Buria could have been a source for leaks and whether Parlatore attended meetings beyond his clearance level. The IG and OSI also asked witnesses whether they had been asked to delete Signal messages; one person said OSI investigators asked by name whether Buria or Parlatore had made such requests. Buria did not respond and Parlatore declined to comment.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act element (message-deletion questions); DoD Instr. 8170.01 elements (origin of the unsecured internet line)

evidence.description: The Pentagon Inspector General's report (DODIG-2026-021, dated December 2, 2025 and released December 4), prepared at the March 26, 2025 request of the Senate Armed Services Committee's chairman and ranking member, found that Hegseth sent sensitive, nonpublic operational information, the quantity and strike times of manned U.S. aircraft, over Signal on his personal cell phone about 2 to 4 hours before the strikes; that some of it matched a U.S. Central Command email classified SECRET//NOFORN; and that this did not comply with DoD Instruction 8170.01. It also found that Hegseth and his office did not retain the messages as federal records, as 44 U.S.C. 2911 and DoD Instruction 5015.02 require; some had auto-deleted. These findings cover the chat that included the journalist. An official told the IG of a 'Defense Team Huddle' chat that included non-DoD personnel, and one official said Hegseth posted the same strike information there; the IG said it could not verify whether that chat or his other Signal chats contained sensitive or nonpublic information because, a senior official in his office said, Hegseth would not provide access to his personal phone.
evidence.maps_to_element: DoD Instr. 8170.01 violations (both elements); Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element (failure to retain)

evidence.description: PBS NewsHour reported December 3, 2025, ahead of the report's public release, that Hegseth "declined an interview with the inspector general and he informed the inspector general that he considers this investigation completely partisan"; chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the review "a total exoneration of Secretary Hegseth"
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on cooperation with investigation and the administration's response, not an element of any offense

evidence.description: Fox News reported December 4, 2025 that the IG report affirms Hegseth, as the Pentagon's top classification authority, has broad authority to classify or declassify military information, while noting that policy still prohibits using nonsecure, nonofficial channels to send it.
evidence.maps_to_element: [Reference only] 18 U.S.C. §793(f) analogue (TAP analysis: weighs against it); does not affect the DoD Instr. 8170.01 violations

evidence.description: Lawfare reported December 5, 2025, citing the IG report, that Hegseth declined an interview request from the inspector general's office during the investigation and sent a written statement on July 25, 2025 instead
evidence.maps_to_element: Context on cooperation with investigation, not an element of any offense

evidence.description: In a declaration dated March 26, 2026 and filed in the American Oversight case on April 30, 2026, Timothy Parlatore, as Special Advisor to the Secretary of War, said the Secretary's office had confirmed through counsel in a June 27, 2025 status report that it knew of no Signal chats of Hegseth's containing federal records at risk of impending or automatic deletion. He stated that when he spoke to Hegseth on April 26, 2025, Hegseth searched his personal phone and found no such chats, and that Parlatore himself searched the phone on July 23, 2025 and verified that it then contained none.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element -- the Defense Department's sworn account of Hegseth's phone; it covers only records at risk of deletion when searched, not messages already deleted

evidence.description: On April 30, 2026, American Oversight and the government defendants, including Hegseth in his official capacity, jointly stipulated to dismiss the Signal records suit with prejudice, each party bearing its own fees and costs.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element -- how the preservation suit ended (no court finding on the merits)

evidence.description: The Atlantic reported June 29, 2026 that Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Gen. Dan Caine were in a Signal group chat with auto-deleting messages. The report draws on records the State Department produced on June 22, 2026 in a Freedom of Information Act case brought by Democracy Forward Foundation, whose motion in that case (ECF 37-1) describes the production as undated screenshots of the 'chat settings' of 16 Signal threads, including one named 'SS/APNSA,SD,CJCS' with messages set to auto-delete in '8 hours' and Rubio as a member; Mediaite, reporting on the same records, said that chat was administered by Caine and included Hegseth and Rubio. The screenshots show no message contents, so they do not establish that the Parlatore declaration above was false.
evidence.maps_to_element: Federal Records Act / DoD records-retention element -- later-disclosed auto-delete setting on a chat reportedly including Hegseth; it does not show when the chat existed or what it held

evidence.description: A June 30, 2026 federal court opinion in The New York Times's second lawsuit over Pentagon press access (New York Times Co. v. Department of Defense, D.D.C. No. 26-1690) recounts The Times's reporting that Hegseth shared details of the planned Yemen strikes in a second private Signal group chat that included Timothy Parlatore, whom the opinion describes as a Senior Advisor to Hegseth, as well as Hegseth's wife and brother
evidence.maps_to_element: DoD Instr. 8170.01 violations (second instance) -- court record naming Parlatore as a member of the second chat

status: Investigated; a December 2025 Pentagon IG report found Hegseth broke DoD Instruction 8170.01 by sending strike details over Signal on his personal phone, and he and his office failed to keep the messages. It could not verify his other chats, including the reported family-and-lawyer chat. No charges.
rebuttal_anticipated: Hegseth/administration position: no classified information was shared, he had authority to declassify, and the investigation is partisan. Spokesman called the report 'a total exoneration.'
comeback: The 'exoneration' framing answers a question that wasn't the actual finding. The IG report addressed two separate questions: (1) was classified information disclosed, and (2) were DoD's own communication-security rules followed. He may have prevailed on the first, but the report found he violated DoD Instruction 8170.01 by using a personal device and unapproved app for nonpublic operational information. Declassification authority is not the same as operational security authority -- he had the legal right to decide what was classified, not the right to send strike timing over his personal phone outside secure channels. Citing a win on one question to dismiss a loss on the other is the kind of sleight-of-hand a genuinely strong position shouldn't need.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] A Secretary of Defense brought in from a media background without the secure-communications discipline typically built over a career in uniformed or career-civil-service positions, combined with a rapid operational pace that incentivized speed over protocol. This is a structural appointment-quality issue as much as an individual-judgment failure: the IG found a DoD Instruction violation, not a one-time lapse of someone who otherwise operates within the system's norms -- Hegseth reportedly sent the same information in a second, separate personal Signal chat with family members (the IG could not verify it), which suggests habitual use of personal channels for operational content, not an isolated error. See also the Rubio Signal auto-delete entry, which covers a later-disclosed auto-deleting chat that included Hegseth, Rubio and Caine, in a separate court dispute.

The second, family-and-lawyer chat rests on The New York Times's April 2025 reporting (four sources), later recounted in a June 2026 court opinion; the IG could not verify its contents. The Wall Street Journal's dozen-plus-chats finding and the aide-focused probes rest on anonymous-source reporting from single outlets. On severity, this reads as a real but narrow process violation, not evidence of a prosecutable crime: 'leaked classified information' would overstate the findings; 'circumvented secure communication requirements for operational planning' is better supported. official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense; Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Recalling Nearly 800 Senior Commanders From Global Posts on Short Notice for a Politicized Address, Including a Presidential Proposal to Use U.S. Cities as Military 'Training Grounds' That Raises Posse Comitatus Act Concerns
incident_summary: On September 30, 2025, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth summoned nearly 800 generals, admirals, and senior enlisted leaders -- virtually the entire senior command structure of the U.S. armed forces -- from posts around the world to Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia on short notice, for an unprecedented, in-person mandatory address. Hegseth used the address to declare 'today we end the war on warriors' and 'the era of the Department of Defense is over,' announcing new physical-fitness and grooming standards ('no more fat generals,' 'no more beardos') raised to a uniform 'male level' regardless of service member sex, the elimination of racial hiring/promotion quotas, the loosening of restrictions on boot-camp hazing, and looser rules of engagement for combat operations. President Trump also addressed the assembled commanders, telling them 'we're under invasion from within' and **proposing American cities be used as military 'training grounds,' naming Chicago specifically, and stating he had ordered the creation of military 'quick reaction forces' to 'help quell civil disturbances.'** Deploying the U.S. military for domestic civilian law enforcement is generally prohibited by the Posse Comitatus Act of 1878, absent a specific statutory exception (such as the Insurrection Act). Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI), the Senate Armed Services Committee's ranking Democrat and a former 82nd Airborne officer, called the speech 'divisive and corrosive.' Defense analysts and a former senior defense official criticized the summit's substance and cost: one former official said 'I cannot believe 800 generals and flag officers were brought into that building to hear a pep-speech that would be better delivered by a captain to a bunch of enlisted and lieutenants out in the field somewhere,' and analysts noted the event cost taxpayers millions of dollars to transport senior officers worldwide on short notice, pulling critical leadership away from active operational commands during the trip. Experts also warned the event's repeated references to recent senior-officer firings (part of Hegseth's broader pattern of dismissals, tracked elsewhere in this database) signaled that dissent could end careers, creating an atmosphere that could make commanders hesitant to offer honest counsel during an actual crisis. The Pentagon subsequently issued a memo requiring all service members to complete a 'Warrior Ethos Tasking' -- watching the speech video and reviewing the new policy memoranda -- by the end of October 2025. Marine Col. Doug Krugman's last day in uniform, ending a 24-year career, was September 30, 2025 -- the same day as the Quantico summit. In a Washington Post op-ed published October 16, 2025, Krugman wrote that he had already decided to resign his commission before the summit took place, but cited Trump's remarks there -- 'if you don't like what I'm saying, you can leave the room -- of course, there goes your rank, there goes your future' -- as illustrating exactly the climate that drove his decision, writing: 'I continued to serve despite all that because I believed the Constitution brought the country more success than failure, and I believed our presidents took their oaths to it seriously. With President Trump, I no longer believe that.'

official: Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense
offense_category: Withholding Combat Casualty Information From the Public -- the Pentagon did not disclose three Iranian strikes on U.S. forces in Jordan, which injured dozens of troops and damaged helicopters, in the week before a publicly disclosed strike killed three soldiers -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: The New York Times reported on July 20, 2026, citing several U.S. officials who spoke on condition of anonymity, that Iranian forces struck U.S. forces in Jordan three separate times in the week before the July 17, 2026 attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base that **killed two U.S. soldiers (1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan and Pvt. Isabella Gonzales) and left a third (Sgt. Angel S. Rampersad) missing; the Pentagon confirmed Rampersad's death on July 25**. The three earlier strikes injured dozens of U.S. service members and damaged several helicopters, according to the Times, but the Pentagon did not disclose the strikes, the casualties or the damage. One U.S. military official told the Times that Central Command is not required to release information about injured troops, especially when they quickly return to duty; another asked why the Pentagon would divulge information that could help Iran zero in on its ballistic-missile and drone attacks on Jordan and other bases in the Middle East, where thousands of U.S. troops are stationed. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell rejected the report on the record as "baseless and malicious accusations" and "fabrications," then said that nearly 100 service members had been "deemed to have some degree of injury since July 7, 2026," 96% of whom had returned to duty; the Times said it stood by its reporting. On July 23, 2026, all 12 Democrats on the Senate Armed Services Committee, led by Sen. Mazie Hirono, wrote to Hegseth asking for total casualty figures, an explanation of gaps in the Pentagon's casualty database, and details on the three earlier Iranian attacks in Jordan, including who authorized not disclosing them, noting that as of July 21 the database listed 14 service members killed despite wide reporting of 18; they asked for answers by July 30, and no reply has been identified. House Oversight Committee Democrats Garcia and Subramanyam opened a formal inquiry on August 4, 2026 into separate changes the Pentagon made to its own casualty-tracking database, alleging four soldiers' deaths were briefly removed from the public Iran-war casualty count before being reclassified into a newly created 'Overseas Operations' category (acting Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez had attributed the earlier drops in the totals to "temporary data disruptions" on the database website and said the "site anomalies are currently being resolved") -- a distinct allegation from the undisclosed-earlier-strikes reporting above, though both concern the same broader casualty-transparency pattern. The lawmakers asked for a response by August 18, 2026; the Pentagon declined to comment on the letter, and no response has been identified. On August 6, 2026, Sen. Tammy Duckworth introduced S. 5300, the Honoring the Sacrifice of Troops in War Act of 2026, with 17 Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Bennet, Hickenlooper, and Rosen; the bill, referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee, would require DoD to combine all Iran War casualty records into one accurate count and notify next-of-kin of any resulting corrections -- a direct legislative response to the database-reclassification pattern. The bill has seen no action since its referral. On September 18, 2026, The Washington Post reported that five U.S. officials said **at least 22 U.S. service members had died in the Middle East since the war began on February 28 -- four more than the 18 then listed in the Pentagon's public casualty database** -- and that a sixth official put the toll at 23; the Post reported that not all of the additional deaths were directly tied to the Iran conflict, but all involved U.S. personnel in the region during the hostilities. Hegseth called the report "DISGUSTING and FAKE. A complete LIE" in a post on X. By September 22, the database total had risen to 19 after an Army officer suffered a fatal medical emergency while flying to the Middle East, but the Post reported that the gap with officials' count remained unresolved; it also noted that the Pentagon had separately announced, in news releases, the deaths of two service members at bases Iranian forces had attacked, on missions it described as unrelated to the Iran war, and that neither appears by name in the database. Hegseth, who did not address whether every death had been tallied under the Pentagon's long-standing practices, told a reporter, "Even if we wanted to attempt to hide a combat death, we never would and we never could." On September 25, the Post reported that the Pentagon had quietly added 37 wounded troops (29 sailors and eight Marines) to the database, bringing the war's wounded total to 861, without saying when or how they were hurt; Central Command declined to comment.

rebuttal_anticipated: The strongest rebuttal combines the Pentagon's on-record position -- that casualty data is posted publicly on its casualty database and that most injuries since July 7 were minor concussions, with 96% of those injured back on duty -- with the rationale unnamed U.S. military officials gave the Times: operational security concerns about giving an active adversary detailed targeting feedback are a legitimate wartime consideration, and routine, real-time public disclosure of every strike and casualty is not standard practice in any active conflict.
comeback: The operational-security rationale explains withholding tactical detail, but does not fully explain withholding the basic fact that U.S. personnel had already been injured and equipment damaged in multiple incidents -- particularly once Congress and the public were separately being asked to weigh a war-funding request (see this tracker's context on requested Iran war funding) without full knowledge of the human cost already incurred.

In each, the Pentagon's on-record response was denial or a technical explanation; for the undisclosed strikes, the operational-security rationale came only from officials speaking anonymously -- a rationale that can justify withholding tactical detail but not, on its own, the basic fact that troops were hurt. Related information-restriction concerns appear in this tracker's entries on the Minab school strike and the Kuwait drone-strike command-negligence allegations, which involve different incidents and are not the same act.

official: Tom Homan, White House Border Czar (the recorded conduct predates his current role, while he was a private citizen expected to join the incoming Trump administration); Todd Blanche, Deputy Attorney General; Emil Bove, former Acting Deputy Attorney General (opposed continuing the investigation)
offense_category: Alleged Bribery/Anticipatory Influence-Peddling Tied to a Promised Future Government Role, and the Trump DOJ's Subsequent Closure of Its Own Predecessor Investigation Into a Sitting Senior Official — Contested, Not Independently Adjudicated
incident_summary: In summer 2024, before the presidential election, the FBI opened an undercover investigation in the Western District of Texas -- a joint effort with that U.S. Attorney's office and DOJ's Public Integrity Section -- after a separate investigation's subject alleged Tom Homan was soliciting payments in exchange for helping steer future government contracts if Trump returned to office and Homan rejoined the administration. On September 20, 2024, undercover FBI agents posing as business contractors met Homan in Texas; according to MSNBC's reporting of internal case summaries and multiple sources, hidden cameras recorded Homan accepting $50,000 in cash, delivered in a paper bag from the restaurant chain Cava, after indicating he could help facilitate contracts once in office. Public Integrity Section supervisors initially supported continuing the investigation. After Trump's January 2025 inauguration and Homan's appointment as White House border czar, then-Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove opposed continuing the probe; a DOJ appointee characterized it as a 'deep state' investigation in early 2025. FBI Director Kash Patel later requested a status update, after which Trump-appointed DOJ officials **closed the case without publicly disclosing a reason, with the administration later saying a review found 'no credible evidence of any criminal wrongdoing.'** MSNBC's investigative report became public September 20, 2025 -- one year to the day after the recorded meeting. Homan's own public response shifted over time: he initially told reporters he 'did nothing criminal' without denying he received money, then at a NewsNation town hall explicitly denied taking '$50,000 from anybody.' The White House, through Deputy Press Secretary Abigail Jackson, denied the allegations and characterized the reporting and subsequent inquiry as politically motivated. House and Senate Democrats (led by Rep. Jamie Raskin and joined by multiple senators, including a letter to AG Pam Bondi) formally demanded DOJ and the FBI release the recordings and case file; without subpoena power in the House minority, their inquiry has been unable to compel disclosure. No recordings or case file have been made public as of this entry. Independent fact-checkers, including Snopes, were unable to assign a truth rating to the core cash-acceptance claim because the original reporting relied on anonymous sources and firsthand confirmation could not be independently obtained; The New York Times separately reported that its own anonymous sources disagreed internally on whether the evidence was sufficient to charge Homan with bribery at all.
