official: Pam Bondi, then-Attorney General (directed by presidential memorandum)
offense_category: DOJ Investigation of the Opposing Party's Fundraising Infrastructure, Directed by Presidential Memorandum and Escalated by a Parallel Congressional Contempt Threat -- an institutional-accountability claim about coordinated multi-branch pressure on a single-party target, not a criminal charge against any named official
incident_summary: The congressional side of this effort began well before the DOJ probe: House Administration Chair Bryan Steil opened an inquiry into ActBlue's donor-verification practices in October 2023 and subpoenaed the platform in October 2024. By late March 2025, Republican lawmakers were asking the Treasury Department for 'suspicious activity reports' mentioning ActBlue and pressing for Treasury and FBI probes, while Elon Musk sought, without evidence, to tie ActBlue to protests and vandalism against Tesla. In April 2025, President Trump signed a memorandum directing then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate online political fundraising platforms for alleged straw-donor and foreign-contribution violations; although the memo's directive covered online fundraising platforms generally (the White House fact sheet cited 'ActBlue and other online fundraising platforms'), **ActBlue -- the Democratic Party's dominant fundraising platform, which has processed nearly $17 billion in donations since 2004 -- was the only platform named**. ActBlue called the memo a 'brazen attack on democracy in America.' In parallel, House Republicans led by Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan, Oversight Chair James Comer, and House Administration Chair Bryan Steil pursued their own year-plus congressional investigation into ActBlue's foreign-donation vetting practices. On May 7, 2025, the three chairmen wrote to Bondi, citing Trump's memorandum, sharing their ActBlue findings and saying they would like to 'work collaboratively with DOJ.' An April 2, 2026 New York Times report cited internal ActBlue documents describing the resignation of interim general counsel Aaron Ting and an internal message from former legal counsel Zain Ahmad alleging retaliation after he reported misconduct internally -- documents the House committees said ActBlue had not produced despite subpoenas. On April 14, 2026, the chairmen demanded full compliance with their subpoenas; a House Republican aide told CBS News that a contempt vote was among the options. On June 10, 2026, ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones invoked her Fifth Amendment right more than 20 times during a House Administration Committee hearing, declining to answer questions including on ActBlue's donation-verification procedures and whether it had given Congress false information. In a June 18, 2026 letter, made public on June 22 in a House Judiciary press release that called it a threat to hold ActBlue in contempt of Congress, the three chairmen called it implausible that all 422 documents on ActBlue's privilege log -- including Ting's resignation letter and Ahmad's message -- were entirely privileged, rejected the privilege claims over those two documents and over documents circulated among non-lawyers, and demanded them by June 26, 2026, saying the committees remained prepared to enforce their subpoenas 'through all available mechanisms.' The letter itself does not mention the DOJ investigation. Separately, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton had sued ActBlue in Texas state court on April 20, 2026; after ActBlue sued him in federal court in Massachusetts alleging retaliation, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns on June 11 preliminarily barred Paxton from pursuing the Texas case, writing that the lawsuit 'was filed in retaliation,' and Paxton appealed to the First Circuit. In September 2026, Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway opened a state consumer-protection investigation of ActBlue, saying the House Administration Committee had referred its findings to her office; ActBlue called it part of a 'coordinated campaign.'

official: Donald Trump, President; Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (contradicted by Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao's own public statement)
offense_category: Public Misrepresentation of a Foreign Military Sale Decision -- Trump's administration publicly characterized the pause differently than its own Acting Navy Secretary's on-record explanation; NOT charged, a characterization/transparency dispute
incident_summary: At a May 21, 2026 Senate Appropriations defense subcommittee hearing, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, answering Sen. Mitch McConnell, disclosed that the Trump administration had paused a $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan to conserve munitions for U.S. operations against Iran: 'Right now we're doing a pause in order to make sure we have the munitions we need for Epic Fury -- which we have plenty. But we're just making sure we have everything, but then the foreign military sales will continue when the administration deems necessary.' He said any decision to proceed would be up to Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Cao's explanation cut against Hegseth's own assurance to lawmakers earlier that month that 'the munitions issue has been foolishly and unhelpfully overstated. . . . We have plenty of what we need.' Cao said at the hearing that he had not 'spoken to the Taiwanese' about the decision, and on May 22 Taiwan's presidential office said it had no information about any U.S. adjustment to the sale; a Pentagon spokesman said the details 'remain predecisional until finalized by the President' and that Taiwan policy was unchanged. On May 25 Taiwan's foreign minister told lawmakers that Cao was 'not the final policymaker' on foreign arms sales, and its defense minister said there had been no formal notice of a delay -- moves the Maritime Executive described as an attempt to row back Cao's comments. Six days before Cao's testimony, Trump had given a different account: asked in a May 15 Fox News interview with Bret Baier, during his trip to Beijing for talks with Xi Jinping, whether he would move forward with the package, he said, 'I'm holding that in abeyance, and it depends on China. It's a very good negotiating chip for us, frankly' -- tying the hold to leverage with China rather than to munitions supply. On May 30, at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, Hegseth said there had been 'no change' in the U.S. position on Taiwan and, asked about Cao's remarks, said, 'Hung Cao is fantastic, but I would not couple the two in any way at all,' adding that U.S. stockpiles were 'more than suited' and that any decision on future Taiwan arms sales 'will rest with' the president. In June the State Department reiterated that arms sales to Taiwan were not dependent on Beijing's consent. On July 15, 2026 the House passed a fiscal 2027 appropriations bill (H.R. 8595) with $500 million in Foreign Military Financing for Taiwan, a separate program that does not commit money to the paused package; the Senate had not passed it as of late September. Trump and Xi ended a three-day summit in Washington on September 25, 2026, after which Trump had made no public comment on the $14 billion package, which still awaited his decision.
elements_required: A senior on-record U.S. official (the Acting Navy Secretary) publicly gave a specific, substantive reason for the arms-sale pause -- conserving munitions for the Iran war -- that differs from the administration's separate public characterization of stockpile adequacy
The affected ally (Taiwan) was not notified before the pause became public through Cao's own statement, an accountability/transparency gap distinct from the substance of the contradiction itself

Taiwan's own government publicly and specifically disputed Cao's authority to characterize the policy, itself evidence that the administration's messaging on this decision was not coordinated or consistent
The $14 billion dollar figure and the pause itself are not disputed by any party -- only the stated reason and its policy implications are contested

rebuttal_anticipated: The administration could argue that a temporary munitions-review pause during an active conflict is ordinary military-logistics prudence, that Cao's remarks reflect his own view rather than a coordinated administration statement, and that Taiwan's arms sale was only paused, not cancelled.
comeback: The specific problem isn't that a pause happened -- it's that a sitting Acting Navy Secretary gave a specific, substantive reason (conserving munitions for the Iran war) in direct tension with the administration's own separate public assurances that stockpiles remained adequate, and that a treaty-adjacent security partner learned of a $14 billion sale's pause without direct notification. That gap between what officials say privately drives policy and what they say publicly to allies and the press is the accountability issue, independent of whether the pause itself is defensible on the merits. Trump's own 'negotiating chip'/'in abeyance' framing outranks a subordinate's account of the same pause -- if the President himself describes withholding the sale as China leverage, that is a materially different and more consequential explanation than Cao's stated munitions-logistics rationale, and sharpens rather than resolves the contradiction this entry documents.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of senior officials' public accounts of military and foreign-policy decisions being contradicted by their own department's officials, personnel or records -- here, the President, the Defense Secretary and the Acting Navy Secretary gave different on-record explanations for the same paused sale, and none was reconciled (see also this tracker's Hegseth Kuwait entry, where Hegseth's description of a base's defenses was contradicted by survivors' accounts).

incident_summary: DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari launched a formal audit of DHS privacy practices, focused first on ICE and the Office of Biometric Identity Management (OBIM), examining how the agencies collect, share, and secure personally identifiable and biometric data used in immigration enforcement -- explicitly including whether the practices violate federal law or privacy/unlawful-search protections. The audit's initial scope covers DHS's contracts with Palantir, facial-recognition tools, a face-scanning mobile app, and DHS's use of government biometric databases. **Internal footage obtained by 404 Media showed ICE officers using facial-recognition apps to determine the citizenship status of teenagers who were not carrying identification**; one app, Mobile Fortify, draws from a combined pool of more than 200 million images stored across DHS, FBI, and State Department databases. Senators had separately urged DHS's watchdog to investigate the expanding use of biometric and surveillance data by ICE and CBP. Auditors indicated the probe's scope could expand to other parts of DHS as it examines the agency's growing reliance on biometric markers in immigration enforcement.

offense_category: Institutional Prioritization of Arrest Quotas Over Lawful, Safe Operations, With Documented Sharp Rise in Non-Criminal Arrests -- an institutional-accountability claim about operational policy and its documented consequences, not a criminal charge against any named official
incident_summary: A New York Times Magazine investigation published April 14, 2026, drawing on interviews with more than 80 current and former DHS employees plus Justice Department officials, reported that Stephen Miller, Trump's homeland security adviser, had set a target of 3,000 arrests a day and one million deportations a year, and that many of those interviewed, while supporting increased enforcement, criticized the administration's execution, aspects of which they characterized as chaotic, dangerous and ineffective. **Citing ICE data, the Times reported that arrests of people with no conviction of any kind had risen 770% under Trump, against a 37% rise in arrests of people with violent convictions.** The same 770% figure had been published on April 7, 2026 by the UC Berkeley-based Deportation Data Project, from ICE records released through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit; DHS called that analysis "cherry picked" and said it had not verified its accuracy. Current and former officials interviewed said the pressure to hit numerical targets, rather than to prioritize public-safety threats, drove increasingly aggressive interior-enforcement tactics and strained agency operations, with some officials describing the approach as prioritizing quotas and political messaging over lawful, careful casework. This reporting is distinct from, but consistent with, this tracker's separately-documented finding (per a Wall Street Journal investigation) that Noem and adviser Corey Lewandowski had fired or demoted roughly 80% of the career ICE field leadership in place when they started, while sidelining rivals and dissenters and carrying out operations over the objections of longtime immigration officials -- creating conditions in which internal pushback against unsafe or overly aggressive quota-driven tactics would have been institutionally discouraged. Noem was fired as DHS Secretary in March 2026 and reassigned to a newly created envoy role, tracked as its own entry in this database. Former Sen. Markwayne Mullin succeeded her in March 2026, and Lyons left the acting director post at the end of May 2026. The arrest pace did not slow after Noem's removal: ABC News reported August 4, 2026, citing sources familiar with the data, that ICE arrested 51,000 people in July 2026, the largest single-month total in DHS history. DHS's own September 2, 2026 press release then put June 2026 arrests at 43,900, July at 50,208 and August at 50,925 -- three straight monthly records and the second consecutive month above 50,000. DHS's official July count is about 800 below the figure ABC News had from unnamed sources; either count shows record arrests continuing under Mullin.

offense_category: Mass, Indefinite DNA Collection From Non-Convicted Immigrants and Children, Permanently Expanding a Criminal Database -- distinct from this tracker's biometric-surveillance entry, which concerns facial-recognition/image databases rather than genetic material
incident_summary: The "detainee" index of the FBI's Combined DNA Index System (CODIS) -- the sub-index where DHS-collected profiles are stored -- grew by roughly 995,000 profiles in 2025 alone, reaching 3,345,692 by December 2025, per FBI records analyzed by Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology and reported by WIRED. Subtracting the roughly 75,000 people whose DNA CBP sent to the FBI in 2025, Georgetown estimates ICE alone may have added as many as roughly 920,000 profiles, which by Georgetown's estimate makes DHS the single largest source of new genetic profiles in the national criminal DNA system; ICE has refused to release its own totals. The vast majority of people in ICE custody have no criminal conviction; DNA is taken from nearly everyone in immigration custody under a 2020 policy change, then retained indefinitely and made searchable by law enforcement nationwide against unsolved-crime evidence. **DHS documents describe routine collection as starting at age 14, but CBP records identify 492 children under 14 whose DNA CBP sent to the FBI between January 2025 and January 2026, including thirty-three 7-year-olds, thirty-two 6-year-olds, twenty-one 5-year-olds, and a 4-year-old processed in El Paso on January 7, 2026**. By 2025, federal prosecutors were charging people in immigration custody who refused to provide a DNA sample. WIRED identified two such prosecutions: Hugo Moreno-Mendez, arrested by ICE at a March 13, 2025 probation check-in in Waco, Texas, was found guilty by a magistrate judge on August 18, 2025 and sentenced to time served; Ronald Genao-Diaz, who refused CBP officers at the airport in Carolina, Puerto Rico, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to time served and a fine. A 2021 ICE training presentation had stated the agency was unaware of a single refusal case ever accepted for prosecution. Georgetown and two immigrant-rights groups are also pursuing the records in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit -- Georgetown Law Center on Privacy & Technology, et al. v. CBP, et al., No. 1:25-cv-01732 (D.D.C.), filed June 2, 2025 by the Center on Privacy and Technology, the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, and Americans for Immigrant Justice after ICE and CBP failed to make a determination on the groups' August 1, 2024 FOIA requests for records on DNA collection policy and practice; Georgetown's research draws on ICE training materials and CBP records it has since obtained. During a May 26, 2026 oversight visit to the Dilley Immigration Processing Center in Texas, Reps. Joaquin Castro, Greg Stanton, and Nanette Barragán learned that ICE was collecting DNA from detained parents and children; the lawmakers told WIRED officials gave conflicting explanations of why the samples were taken, where they were sent, and how long they would be kept. In a letter made public June 13, 2026, they pressed DHS Secretary Mullin and ICE's leadership for ICE's DNA-collection policies, sharing and retention practices, and any privacy or civil-rights assessments. In July 2026 correspondence, DHS told them ICE may collect DNA from children as young as 14 and confirmed that samples collected under the program are sent to the FBI for entry into CODIS; ICE said it was unaware of any privacy or civil-rights assessment of the practice. DHS has not explained why CBP records show submissions for 492 children under 14.
elements_required: DHS/ICE collected DNA from immigration detainees, most of whom had not been convicted of any crime, and entered it into CODIS, a database designed for convicted-offender and crime-scene evidence

DHS's own stated minimum age of 14 was not followed in at least 492 cases documented in CBP records, involving children as young as 4, a specific documented gap between policy and practice

offense_category: Warrantless Federal Agent Visits to Legal Aid Organizations Seeking Client and Financial Records -- no warrant, subpoena, or other legal instrument was presented; no criminal charge has been identified against any organization or individual
incident_summary: During a roughly 48-hour sweep around June 11-12, 2026, agents from ICE's Homeland Security Investigations and the HHS Office of Inspector General showed up in person at the Washington, D.C.-area offices of at least three nonprofit legal aid organizations that represent unaccompanied migrant children -- the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, Kids in Need of Defense (KIND), and Ayuda -- **seeking client files, financial records, and information about the children the organizations serve. The agents presented no warrant, no subpoena, and cited no legal authority for the requests**. All three organizations refused access, and the agents left empty-handed. Amica executive director Michael Lukens called the visits 'a blatant abuse of power to try to intimidate child advocates,' and KIND president Wendy Young said the pattern reflects 'an overarching approach which is to harass and intimidate those organizations that are set up to provide services to this very vulnerable population.' No public record -- no warrant, no OIG report, no agency statement -- has explained what specific misconduct HSI or HHS OIG believed they were investigating.
elements_required: Federal agents from two different agencies (ICE HSI and HHS OIG) visited multiple legal aid nonprofits in a coordinated, near-simultaneous sweep, indicating a planned operation rather than isolated, unrelated inquiries
Agents sought client files and financial records -- categories of sensitive information a warrant or subpoena would ordinarily be required to compel -- without presenting any such legal instrument

No public agency statement, warrant application, or OIG report has articulated a specific factual basis or legal theory for the visits, despite all three organizations declining and the agents departing without incident

The targeted organizations share a common, narrow function -- providing legal representation to unaccompanied migrant children -- establishing a viewpoint/mission-based pattern rather than a neutral fraud or compliance sweep untethered to the organizations' advocacy role

offense_category: Defending and litigating to preserve ICE agents' face-masking and unmarked-vehicle anonymity after the FBI's own bulletin documented resulting criminal impersonation -- a policy choice, not itself unlawful, but one DHS/DOJ have affirmatively maintained and expanded litigation to protect even after the safety harm it enables became a matter of federal law-enforcement record
incident_summary: Since early 2025, ICE agents have routinely worn masks and used unmarked vehicles during immigration enforcement operations nationwide. Kristi Noem, DHS Secretary until March 2026, publicly defended the practice, saying it protects agents' personal safety and their ability to continue investigative work. The Guardian reported June 28, 2025 on a spate of arrests of people accused of impersonating immigration officers, from California to North Carolina, including a North Carolina man accused of posing as an ICE officer to sexually assault a woman -- documenting the impersonation-crime pattern months before the FBI's own October 2025 bulletin, first reported in early November, made it a matter of formal federal warning. Critics -- including New York Attorney General Letitia James, who led a multistate coalition urging Congress to act, and the Democratic lawmakers who introduced the federal VISIBLE Act in July 2025 to require agents to display identification and limit mask use -- warned the practice made it impossible for the public to distinguish real agents from impersonators. **In October 2025, the FBI issued a bulletin -- an advisory prepared by its Office of Partner Engagement and New York field office, first reported by Wired on November 4 -- warning that criminals were posing as ICE officers to carry out robberies, kidnappings, and sexual assaults across several states, and urging law enforcement to identify themselves and help the public verify agents' identities.** House Homeland Security Committee Democrats then demanded a briefing from DHS and the FBI (letter of Nov. 12-13, 2025), tying the crimes to ICE's masked, unidentified agents; DHS said its agents verbally identify themselves. In September 2025, California enacted SB 627, the 'No Secret Police Act,' banning extreme masking by law enforcement including federal agents statewide, effective January 1, 2026. The Justice Department sued California over SB 627 and a companion identification law, SB 805, on November 17, 2025. In February 2026 a federal district judge preliminarily enjoined the mask ban as applied to federal officers, finding that it unlawfully discriminated against the federal government, and on April 22, 2026 a Ninth Circuit panel barred California, pending appeal, from enforcing SB 805's requirement that non-uniformed federal officers visibly display identification, finding the administration likely to succeed on its Supremacy Clause claim. Philadelphia's City Council passed a similar ordinance, part of its 'ICE Out' package, on April 23, 2026; adopted May 8 without Mayor Cherelle Parker's signature, it barred law enforcement, including federal agents, from concealing their identity or using unmarked vehicles within the city. Rather than adopting mandatory identification measures in response to the FBI's own warning, the Justice Department sued Philadelphia on June 18, 2026, calling the ordinance unconstitutional; on July 2, 2026, days before it was to take effect, Trump-appointed U.S. District Judge Chad Kenney preliminarily enjoined it on Supremacy Clause grounds, holding that no state has the power to impede or burden federal agents carrying out federal law. On August 24, 2026, DOJ expanded its lawsuit against Philadelphia to challenge a second 'ICE Out' ordinance, one barring city agencies from honoring ICE immigration detainers.

offense_category: Noncompliance with Federal Court Orders -- ICE violated 210 release and bond-hearing orders in 143 Minnesota habeas cases, as tallied by the district's chief judge; no contempt finding against any ICE official, and DOJ disputes the characterization
incident_summary:
During Operation Metro Surge, the immigration enforcement operation that ran from December 2025 until February 12, 2026, federal judges in Minnesota were flooded with habeas corpus petitions from people challenging their detention: Patrick Schiltz, then Chief Judge of the District of Minnesota, later told FOX 9 the court had 12 such cases in all of 2024, 130 in 2025 and 1,111 in the first three months of 2026. Judges repeatedly ordered detainees released or given bond hearings, and ICE repeatedly failed to comply.

In one case, Schiltz on January 14, 2026 ordered ICE to give a detained man a bond hearing within seven days or release him; neither happened. On January 26 he ordered Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons to appear in person and show cause why he should not be held in contempt, writing that this was "one of dozens of court orders with which respondents have failed to comply in recent weeks" and that the practical consequence had almost always been significant hardship: **a detention was extended, a person who should have stayed in Minnesota was flown to Texas, or a person flown to Texas was released there and told to figure out a way to get home.** ICE released the man, and on January 28 Schiltz canceled the hearing but attached an appendix identifying 96 court orders issued since January 1 that ICE had violated in 74 cases, warning that the list was hurriedly compiled and that "ICE has likely violated more court orders in January 2026 than some federal agencies have violated in their entire existence."

In a February 9 email to Schiltz, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen accused the court of wildly overstating ICE's noncompliance, based on a review of the first 12 listed cases. Days later, U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino held a Justice Department attorney in civil contempt, with $500 daily fines, after the government released a man in Texas without his identification documents despite her order to release him in Minnesota with his property; the documents were returned the next day and no fines were imposed. The judges rechecked every case on Schiltz's list, and in a February 26 supplemental order Schiltz found that ICE had violated 97 orders in 66 of the originally listed cases, plus 113 more orders in 77 additional cases, most of them violated after January 28: 210 violated orders in 143 cases in all. He wrote that the administration had sent 3,000 ICE agents to Minnesota "to detain people without making any provision for handling the hundreds of lawsuits that were sure to follow," and that the court was "not aware of another occasion in the history of the United States in which a federal court has had to threaten contempt -- again and again and again -- to force the United States government to comply with court orders," and that it would move to criminal contempt if necessary: "One way or another, ICE will comply with this Court's orders." The same day, Judge Jeffrey Bryan ordered Rosen and an ICE representative to a contempt hearing over property not returned to released detainees; at that March 3 hearing Bryan said he had not "ruled out the consequence of imprisonment," then took the matter under advisement without acting.

In a September 2026 interview with The New York Times, Schiltz, by then a senior judge after stepping down as chief judge in June, said the government's conduct during the surge had created "a grave threat to the rule of law," while saying most of the failures appeared to be due to incompetence rather than conscious defiance. The Times put ICE's violations at nearly 100 orders, the size of the January tally; the 210 figure is the February total. A Justice Department spokesperson said the administration "will continue to fully comply with court orders" and had generally satisfied the substance of the orders, and a DHS spokesperson said the department operates in line with the Constitution and federal law.

offense_category: Weakened Oversight and 'Absolute Immunity' Claims Enabling ICE Employee Misconduct at Elevated Risk as the Agency Rapidly Expands -- documents the administration's stated legal posture and oversight choices, not an allegation that officials personally committed the underlying crimes
incident_summary:
**An Associated Press review found at least two dozen ICE employees and contractors have been charged with crimes since 2020, involving patterns of physical and sexual abuse, corruption, and other misuse of authority.** Specific documented cases include a former top official at a Texas ICE contract facility sentenced to probation in February 2026 after admitting he grabbed a handcuffed detainee by the neck and slammed him into a wall; an ICE contractor who pleaded guilty in December 2025 to sexually abusing a detainee over a five-month period at a Louisiana facility; and two Minnesota ICE employees who faced federal sexual-misconduct charges involving underage girls, including an ICE investigator who pleaded guilty to sending images and videos of himself having sex with a 17-year-old. While AP found most documented cases predated Congress's recent $75 billion appropriation to expand ICE hiring and detention capacity, the review reports that legal experts warn such misconduct could accelerate given the volume of new hires and their empowerment to use aggressive tactics. The Trump administration has argued ICE agents have 'absolute immunity' for on-duty actions and has weakened independent oversight mechanisms.

Concrete evidence of the hiring-surge vetting risk legal experts warned about was already documented as early as October 22, 2025 -- NBC News reporting, citing a current and two former DHS officials and former ICE Baltimore field office director Darius Reeves, found ICE had shortened academy training from 13 weeks to eight, and later to six, waived age limits, and sent recruits to training before completing standard background checks, fingerprinting, and drug testing, in pursuit of the administration's target of expanding ICE to 10,000 agents by year's end. Since the hiring surge began in summer 2025, ICE dismissed over 200 recruits during training -- most for failing physical-fitness or written exams (nearly half of recent arrivals failed the written exam) -- but fewer than 10 were dismissed specifically after training staff discovered pending criminal charges, failed drug tests, or safety concerns, including one recruit charged with strong-arm robbery and domestic-violence-related battery. A current DHS official told NBC News: 'There is absolutely concern that some people are slipping through the cracks.' DHS told NBC the figures were 'not accurate' and said most new hires were experienced law enforcement officers.

A direct, concrete instance of the administration weakening independent oversight mechanisms: in December 2025, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb blocked DHS Secretary Noem's policy requiring members of Congress to give seven days' advance notice before inspecting ICE facilities, finding it likely violated a 2019 appropriations law permitting unannounced congressional inspections. After an ICE officer fatally shot a U.S. citizen in Minneapolis, Noem issued a new memorandum on January 8, 2026 reinstating the same notice requirement; on January 10, 2026, Reps. Ilhan Omar, Angie Craig and Kelly Morrison were denied an oversight visit to ICE detainees at the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building at Fort Snelling. Noem's stated justification was that the facility was funded through the 'One Big Beautiful Bill' Act rather than DHS's own appropriations bill, exempting it from the law Judge Cobb had cited. The twelve House Democrats who had brought the original July 2025 suit (Reps. Neguse, Espaillat, Raskin, Garcia, Correa, Crow, Escobar, Goldman, Gomez, Ruiz, Thompson, and Torres) sought emergency relief; on January 19, 2026, Judge Cobb denied that request on procedural grounds, writing 'the court emphasizes that it denies plaintiffs' motion only because it is not the proper avenue to challenge defendants' January 8, 2026, memorandum and the policy stated therein, rather than based on any kind of finding that the policy is lawful.' After the lawmakers amended their complaint, Cobb temporarily blocked the January 8 policy on February 2, 2026, and on March 2, 2026 stayed it for the rest of the case, finding significant evidence it had been issued and enforced with the annually appropriated funds the law restricts. The administration appealed; on May 8, 2026, a three-judge D.C. Circuit panel unanimously refused to pause Cobb's ruling during the appeal, saying only that the administration had not met the stringent requirements for a stay; Judge Neomi Rao, concurring, wrote that the record did not show unannounced visits caused harms beyond administrative inconvenience, but that the administration was very likely to win its appeal because the lawmakers lack standing. The appeal itself remained pending, with the main briefs filed in June and July 2026. Limits on access continued in practice: on September 10, 2026, Rep. Escobar, one of the suit's plaintiffs, made an oversight visit to Camp East Montana, the ICE tent camp at Fort Bliss in El Paso that can hold up to 5,000 people and is the country's largest immigration detention facility, after DHS reported two detainee disturbances there on September 1 and 7. She told the Guardian she was not allowed to speak with any of the detained immigrants, and that she had requested surveillance footage of the incidents but had not received it. A DHS spokesperson disputed her account, saying 'any member of Congress can still request to speak with any illegal alien in ICE custody' and that ICE will facilitate a meeting if both sides agree, and denied that there had been an official request for data and footage; lawmakers have said ICE limits such visits by requiring them to submit, in advance, the names and personal information of detainees they want to speak with. At least three people detained at the camp have died in ICE custody, including a 55-year-old man whose January 2026 death was ruled a homicide after security guards beat him, according to the Guardian.

Subsequent reporting has substantiated the accelerating-risk mechanism experts warned about: internal ICE academy syllabi obtained by CBS News showed the deportation-officer academy course cut from 72 days (July 2025) to 42 days (February 2026); a CNN analysis found deportation officers, previously required to complete about 20 weeks (roughly 100 days) of training, now get less academy training than almost any other federal law enforcement role; and former ICE instructor Ryan Schwank told a forum held by congressional Democrats that 240 hours of a 584-hour program had been cut, including firearms and constitutional-law classes, which DHS denied. An internal ICE email reviewed by Reuters warned that the 'high volume of new hires' and stalled background checks could create uncertainty when misconduct allegations arise, and a former official told Reuters background checks were not being completed before recruits reached the academy, with two recruits flagged as suspected MS-13 members and at least five trainees fired over active arrest warrants; DHS denied any vetting problem. Separately, on February 25, 2026, a Cameron County, Texas, grand jury declined to indict the HSI agent who fatally shot U.S. citizen Ruben Ray Martinez in March 2025, amid disputed DHS claims and conflicting agency statements, prompting a formal House Oversight Democrats investigation demand -- a fatal shooting that has produced no criminal charge. In May 2026, two DHS officials said ICE would scrap the 42-day course and return to 72 days of academy instruction for classes starting July 1, 2026, though DHS did not confirm it at the time (The Washington Post, republished by the Boston Globe); in June 2026 an internal ICE memo, which DHS confirmed, extended the core course from 42 days to roughly 71 days starting in July and required officers trained under the 42-day course to take an additional follow-on program (CBS News). That is still shorter than the roughly five-month (about 20-21-week) total training deportation officers previously received, which included about five weeks of Spanish-language instruction cut in 2025 (PolitiFact, citing ICE's careers page and AP; CNN: '20 weeks, or roughly 100 days'); no source reviewed says the Spanish-language portion was restored. No broader accountability or vetting reform beyond these training changes has been identified.

House Oversight Democrats' March 2026 letter demanding a DHS Inspector General probe into Martinez's death and the concealment of its circumstances situates the case within a broader count: 23 people shot by DHS personnel over the preceding 14 months, with Martinez one of three U.S. citizen fatalities in that period -- the other two, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both in Minneapolis in January 2026, are documented in this tracker's own separate entries or context rather than this one. That broader count is cited here as scale context, not as evidence that the same weakened-oversight mechanism documented above caused all three deaths; no source ties Good's or Pretti's cases to this entry's specific claims about ICE training cuts, vetting failures, or the Martinez grand jury outcome. No further public accountability finding, and no update to the House Oversight investigation's status, has been identified. Joshua Orta, a passenger-witness who disputed DHS's account of the Martinez shooting -- saying the vehicle was moving slowly and agents fired without warning -- died in a car accident on February 21, 2026, hours after a friend texted him a news story reporting that ICE was responsible for Martinez's death -- news his family believes may have contributed to the crash (Texas Tribune, May 4, 2026). Noted here as context on the case's human toll, not as further evidence of misconduct or oversight-weakening in itself.

A second named-victim shooting occurred September 20, 2026, when an ICE officer shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, a Venezuelan man working as a DoorDash driver in Austin. His lawyer says he entered the U.S. in 2024 through the CBP One app to seek asylum and received a removal order after missing a hearing whose notice went to the wrong address; a senior administration official told NBC News he had no criminal history beyond being in the country illegally, and DHS said he had a final order of removal and that the shooting followed a 'dangerous attempt to evade arrest.' Garcés Pérez says an ICE SUV struck his car and an officer refused his request to pull over somewhere safer before he was shot. The officer, a recent hire who had previously worked for another federal law enforcement agency and completed ICE training in August 2025, was not wearing a body camera, CNN reported, citing sources. Garcés Pérez was taken from the hospital to an ICE detention center in Pearsall with a bullet lodged near his spine; a federal judge temporarily blocked his deportation. Federal prosecutors then charged him with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer, alleging he struck an officer with his side mirror while fleeing the initial stop; the defense called the charge retaliation. On September 30, U.S. Magistrate Judge Dustin Howell found probable cause and denied bond as a flight risk, keeping him in federal custody (AP; WOAI). The ICE officer who did wear a body camera, driving a separate car, turned it off during the pursuit (AP). The shooting drew protests in Austin.

comeback: The specific accountability concern this entry documents is prospective and structural, not solely retrospective: the administration's own stated 'absolute immunity' legal position and its weakening of independent oversight mechanisms are contemporaneous policy choices layered on top of a documented historical misconduct pattern and a rapid, unprecedented workforce expansion -- a combination outside experts specifically warn increases future risk, independent of how any single past case was resolved.

incident_summary: ICE agents attempted to pull over a van in Newark, New Jersey on February 25, 2026; when the driver fled, agents pursued, and the chase ended in a multi-vehicle crash at Clinton Avenue and 10th Street. **Three children -- two 15-year-olds and a 12-year-old -- were among those injured and taken to University Hospital for evaluation; the fleeing driver was also injured and hospitalized.** Newark police were not involved in the pursuit and responded only to the resulting crash. Newark Mayor Ras Baraka publicly said ICE failed to follow New Jersey's vehicle pursuit guidelines and called for accountability. In response, Baraka signed an executive order barring immigration enforcement operations in Newark city buildings without a judicial warrant and directing city employees to report suspected unauthorized federal enforcement activity.

offense_category: Sustained Public Mischaracterization of ICE Enforcement as Targeting 'Criminal Aliens'/'The Worst of the Worst,' Contradicted by the Administration's Own Internal and Reported Data -- an institutional-accountability and public-transparency claim, not a criminal charge against Noem or Mullin personally; attributed to them as DHS Secretary with operational oversight of ICE, per this tracker's institutional-attribution standard
incident_summary: Beginning within Trump's first two weeks back in office, reporting repeatedly found that ICE's actual enforcement and detention activity did not match the administration's public framing that enforcement prioritized 'criminal aliens' and 'the worst of the worst.' On January 31, 2025, HuffPost compiled early reporting showing the gap: NBC News, citing an unnamed government source, reported that 48% of the 1,179 people immigration agents arrested on the first Sunday after the inauguration had no criminal history apart from possible unauthorized border crossing; Colombian officials said none of the 200 people deported to Colombia on two flights were criminals, and the Washington Post reported that those flights carried more than 20 children and two pregnant women. HuffPost tied the pattern to Trump's reversal of the prior, narrower enforcement priorities and to a quota of 75 arrests per day for ICE field offices. **On June 16, 2025, CNN reported that internal ICE data it had obtained showed fewer than 1 in 10 of the roughly 185,000 immigrants booked into ICE custody from October 2024 through May 2025 had been convicted of serious crimes like murder, assault, robbery or rape, with more than 75% having no criminal conviction other than an immigration or traffic-related offense.** That period covers the last months of the Biden administration and the first months of Trump's. On June 30, 2025, a CBS News analysis of ICE data released to the Deportation Data Project found that after White House adviser Stephen Miller announced a target of 3,000 arrests a day in late May, new ICE detentions of people facing only civil immigration charges rose more than 250% from the first week of May to the first week of June, and that only about 8% of everyone detained since January 20 had a violent-crime conviction. This pattern predates and is distinct from a later, separate entry in this database documenting a specific December 2025 DHS 'worst of the worst' public website found to contain factual errors overstating individual arrestees' offense severity. The pattern continued into FY2026. In November 2025 the Cato Institute reported that leaked nonpublic ICE data showed nearly three in four (73%) people booked into ICE custody so far that fiscal year had no criminal conviction, and only 5% had a violent one. In January 2026, immigration researcher Austin Kocher's analysis of ICE's published detention statistics found that people without criminal convictions accounted for 92% of the growth in the ICE-arrested detained population between September 21, 2025 and January 7, 2026: 72% had no criminal charges or convictions and 20% had at most pending charges, while 8% had convictions. Kristi Noem, who publicly defended the 'criminal aliens' framing throughout 2025, was fired as DHS Secretary in March 2026. The Senate confirmed Markwayne Mullin as her successor 54-45 on March 23, 2026, and he was sworn in the next day. The pattern continued and deepened into July 2026: CBS News reported that July was the first month of the second Trump administration in which people with only civil immigration violations -- no criminal convictions or pending charges -- made up more than half of ICE arrestees, and that people with violent-crime convictions made up about 4% of those taken into custody that month. The Associated Press, in a report carried by PBS NewsHour, counted a monthly arrest total of 49,571, the highest of the second Trump administration, up 15% from June and up 70% from February 2026 (DHS's own September release later put July at 50,208). In August 2026, at a conference of state governors, Mullin used the same framing while urging more local cooperation with ICE: "let's work to get the worst of the worst off the streets and then you won't see me in your cities and states like you do as much," CBS News reported.

status: Ongoing -- the no-criminal-record enforcement pattern has continued and deepened through mid-2026, with people who have only civil immigration violations now making up a majority of ICE arrestees as of July 2026; Noem's successor, Mullin, has used the same 'worst of the worst' framing.

comeback: This entry does not dispute that immigration violations are themselves unlawful -- the accountability question is the specific, repeated public framing of enforcement as targeting 'criminal aliens' and 'the worst of the worst' (implying convictions for serious crimes like murder or assault) when the administration's own internal data, independently obtained by CNN, showed fewer than 1 in 10 detainees met that description, a gap documented consistently across three separate reporting periods spanning five months.

Two related matters are documented separately: a DHS 'worst of the worst' website that overstated individual arrestees' offenses, and the number of deaths in ICE custody in 2025, the most in more than two decades.

The `contested: true` flag reflects that the administration disputes the characterization (not the underlying arrest/conviction figures themselves, which are sourced to its own data). The underlying institutional-pattern claim is unaffected; it continued to hold, and by a wider margin, through the FY2026 data now added above. official: Mike Johnson, Speaker of the House
offense_category: Obstruction of a Duly-Elected Member's Seating to Block a Discharge-Petition Vote -- a constitutional-representation and cover-up-motive claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: Adelita Grijalva won a special election on September 23, 2025 to fill Arizona's 7th Congressional District seat, left vacant by her late father's death. **Speaker Mike Johnson kept the House in an extended shutdown recess -- eventually a fourth straight week, per an October 13, 2025 AP report -- and refused Democrats' requests to swear Grijalva in immediately**, saying she would be sworn in once the House returned to regular session (which he tied to the government shutdown ending). Grijalva had publicly committed to signing a discharge petition seeking a floor vote to compel release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein; her signature would have been the petition's 218th and final one needed to force the vote. House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia said on October 15, 2025 that 'Speaker Johnson is keeping the House in recess and holding the American people hostage so Adelita is blocked from being the 218th signature on the discharge petition to release the Epstein files,' calling it a 'White House cover-up.' Johnson repeatedly and explicitly denied any connection between the delay and the Epstein petition. Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes sent Johnson a demand letter on October 14, 2025 and, when he did not act, filed suit on October 21, 2025 seeking a declaratory judgment compelling him to administer the oath, arguing the delay disenfranchised Arizona's 7th District voters ('taxation without representation'); Johnson called the suit 'patently absurd' and said Mayes 'has no jurisdiction.' Grijalva was sworn in, and signed the discharge petition as its 218th signature, on the same day -- more than seven weeks after her election win.
elements_required: An elected member-elect was not seated for an unusually extended period (over seven weeks) relative to normal House practice
The delayed member had publicly committed to providing the decisive signature on a specific, high-profile discharge petition opposed by the Speaker's own party leadership and the President

The Speaker's stated reason for the delay (waiting for the House to return to regular session) was itself substantially within the Speaker's own control, since he set the House's recess schedule during the shutdown

A state attorney general -- an independent, differently-motivated actor -- concluded the delay was legally objectionable enough to sue, on a constitutional-representation theory distinct from the Epstein-cover-up allegation

rebuttal_anticipated: Johnson could argue -- and did, on the record -- that swearing in new members while the House is in a shutdown recess (with no floor votes scheduled at all) is not standard practice regardless of the member's party or any pending petition, and that the timing coincidence with the Epstein petition does not itself establish intent.

Garcia's allegation and circumstantial timing, not a document or admission from Johnson himself, who explicitly denied it on the record -- present as contested, not established fact.

official: Jim Jordan, Chairman, House Judiciary Committee (with Rep. Scott Fitzgerald)
offense_category: Congressional Investigative Power Used to Pressure Politically-Targeted Universities -- contested; House Judiciary frames this as a legitimate antitrust inquiry into tuition price coordination, not retaliation
incident_summary: In April 2025, House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, joined by Senate Judiciary Chairman Charles Grassley and others, sent letters to all eight Ivy League schools seeking documents and communications related to alleged collusion in setting tuition and financial aid. On June 26, 2025, **Jordan and Rep. Scott Fitzgerald issued a formal subpoena to Harvard specifically, demanding internal communications about its tuition-setting and financial-aid process, with a July 17 compliance deadline**. Harvard called the subpoena 'unwarranted, unfair, and unnecessary,' stating it had already produced thousands of pages of documents and that there was no basis for a collusion allegation; the committee nonetheless deemed Harvard's roughly 400-document response, delivered after 79 days, inadequate. The investigation expanded on July 1, 2025 when the committee issued mirroring subpoenas to Brown University and the University of Pennsylvania, with a July 22 compliance deadline, as part of the same Ivy League tuition-pricing antitrust probe. The subpoenas arrived amid a broader, well-documented pattern of the administration and allied congressional committees targeting Harvard specifically over unrelated disputes (SEVP revocation, research funding freezes), raising the contested question of whether the antitrust rationale is the subpoena's genuine driver or a vehicle for continued pressure on an institution already targeted on other fronts.

Harvard's response, though substantial (thousands of pages, ~400 documents in the specific subpoena response), was deemed inadequate by the committee
The subpoena and probe arrived during a period of well-documented, separately-tracked administration pressure on Harvard over unrelated matters

The investigation subsequently expanded to other Ivy League schools (Brown, Penn) using mirrored subpoena language, suggesting an institution-wide antitrust theory rather than Harvard-specific targeting alone

official: Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Chairman, House Judiciary Committee
offense_category: Potential weaponization of congressional oversight and criminal-referral power against a former prosecutor over contested closed-door testimony -- not itself an executive-branch action, but a pattern of using investigative/referral power to pursue a perceived political adversary; the underlying perjury allegation, if pursued, would be a genuine false-statements matter under 18 U.S.C. Sec. 1001, the statute the referral cites, but no charge has been filed
incident_summary: **On December 7, 2025, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan subpoenaed former Special Counsel Jack Smith for a closed-door deposition on December 17, 2025, seeking documents and testimony about Smith's prosecutions of Trump over the 2020 election and classified-documents cases**. Smith's team said he would comply but noted he had previously (in October 2025) offered to testify publicly so lawmakers' questions and his answers would be visible to everyone; Jordan chose the closed-door format instead, telling Fox News it gave lawmakers and committee lawyers more time to question Smith. Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin criticized the closed-door format at the time, saying Republicans would 'spin, distort, and cherry-pick his remarks through press leaks.' The December 17 deposition proceeded in one-hour increments alternating between the two parties. In a letter dated July 22, 2026 and made public July 23 -- roughly seven months later -- Jordan issued a formal criminal referral asking DOJ to investigate Smith for 'willfully and intentionally false statements' made under oath at that deposition (the letter cites the federal false-statements law, 18 U.S.C. § 1001), specifically over Smith's testimony that neither he nor his team sought the contents of lawmakers' text messages, only toll (metadata) records. Records DOJ later produced showed Smith's team had obtained message content for communications involving 44 lawmakers -- but per Raskin's rebuttal, those came from a National Archives production of White House staff communications, not from a subpoena directed at the lawmakers' own phones or messages, a factual distinction Raskin says Jordan's referral elides. At his July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing, the week before the referral, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, asked by Sen. Josh Hawley whether he had thought about investigating Smith for perjury, said 'We take testimony in front of this body very seriously, yes,' and replied 'Yes, senator' when Hawley said he hoped Blanche would investigate and possibly prosecute Smith; a criminal referral is a recommendation, not a charge. Smith's counsel called the referral evidence of 'a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system' against 'a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.' Raskin called the referral 'baseless' and predicted it would be 'laughed out of court.' Update 2026-09-30: On September 29, 2026, Smith testified publicly before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley. In prepared remarks he said, 'I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the President or others,' said he stood by his decision to charge Trump, and said he would prosecute a former president on the same facts 'regardless of whether that President was a Republican or a Democrat.' Grassley called Smith's operation 'a partisan weapon that broke the rules.' Smith defended the toll-records subpoenas, saying the records show who a call was to and from and its length, and that nondisclosure orders were sought because he had 'strong reason to believe that Donald Trump would destroy evidence.' ABC News reported that Blanche had said in July testimony that the department was investigating the Republicans' referral; no charge against Smith has been reported.
elements_required: Jordan chose a closed-door deposition format over Smith's own stated preference for public testimony, a format choice Democrats characterized as enabling selective leaks rather than transparent oversight

The specific perjury allegation turns on whether Smith's testimony that he sought only 'toll records,' not message contents, from lawmakers was knowingly false -- versus Raskin's competing account that the message contents Jordan cites came from a National Archives production of White House staff communications, a different legal mechanism than a subpoena directed at lawmakers themselves

No DOJ charge or indictment has been reported -- the referral is a request; at his July confirmation hearing Blanche signaled DOJ might investigate Smith for perjury, and ABC News later reported Blanche had said in July the department was investigating the referral, but no charging decision has been announced

The roughly seven-month gap between the December 2025 deposition and the July 2026 referral, combined with the referral's timing well after the deposition's content was known, is presented here as a fact pattern without asserting a specific political motive beyond what Smith's counsel and Raskin have publicly alleged

Combined with the roughly seven-month gap between the deposition and the referral, and Smith's own prior public offer to testify openly (which Jordan declined), the sequence is consistent with a referral built to generate a prosecutable-sounding allegation against a political adversary rather than one arising from a clear-cut factual contradiction.

MODERATE-LOW confidence on the underlying perjury allegation's merits, which is a direct factual dispute between Jordan's and Raskin's competing characterizations of where the 44 lawmakers' message content actually came from -- this entry presents both accounts rather than adopting either, consistent with this tracker's treatment of similarly disputed factual claims elsewhere. incident_summary.base: **On December 7, 2025, House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan subpoenaed former Special Counsel Jack Smith for a closed-door deposition on December 17, 2025, seeking documents and testimony about Smith's prosecutions of Trump over the 2020 election and classified-documents cases**. Smith's team said he would comply but noted he had previously (in October 2025) offered to testify publicly so lawmakers' questions and his answers would be visible to everyone; Jordan chose the closed-door format instead, telling Fox News it gave lawmakers and committee lawyers more time to question Smith. Ranking Member Rep. Jamie Raskin criticized the closed-door format at the time, saying Republicans would 'spin, distort, and cherry-pick his remarks through press leaks.' The December 17 deposition proceeded in one-hour increments alternating between the two parties. In a letter dated July 22, 2026 and made public July 23 -- roughly seven months later -- Jordan issued a formal criminal referral asking DOJ to investigate Smith for 'willfully and intentionally false statements' made under oath at that deposition (the letter cites the federal false-statements law, 18 U.S.C. § 1001), specifically over Smith's testimony that neither he nor his team sought the contents of lawmakers' text messages, only toll (metadata) records. Records DOJ later produced showed Smith's team had obtained message content for communications involving 44 lawmakers -- but per Raskin's rebuttal, those came from a National Archives production of White House staff communications, not from a subpoena directed at the lawmakers' own phones or messages, a factual distinction Raskin says Jordan's referral elides. At his July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing, the week before the referral, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, asked by Sen. Josh Hawley whether he had thought about investigating Smith for perjury, said 'We take testimony in front of this body very seriously, yes,' and replied 'Yes, senator' when Hawley said he hoped Blanche would investigate and possibly prosecute Smith; a criminal referral is a recommendation, not a charge. Smith's counsel called the referral evidence of 'a chilling eagerness to weaponize the justice system' against 'a career, nonpartisan public servant who faithfully and fearlessly performed his duties by following the facts and the law.' Raskin called the referral 'baseless' and predicted it would be 'laughed out of court.'

updates.label: Update
updates.text: Update 2026-09-30: On September 29, 2026, Smith testified publicly before the Senate Judiciary Committee, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley. In prepared remarks he said, 'I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the President or others,' said he stood by his decision to charge Trump, and said he would prosecute a former president on the same facts 'regardless of whether that President was a Republican or a Democrat.' Grassley called Smith's operation 'a partisan weapon that broke the rules.' Smith defended the toll-records subpoenas, saying the records show who a call was to and from and its length, and that nondisclosure orders were sought because he had 'strong reason to believe that Donald Trump would destroy evidence.' ABC News reported that Blanche had said in July testimony that the department was investigating the Republicans' referral; no charge against Smith has been reported.

confidence_note.base: HIGH confidence on the sequence of dated events -- the December 7, 2025 subpoena, the December 17, 2025 closed-door deposition, and the criminal referral (letter dated July 22, 2026, made public July 23) -- corroborated across CBS News, PBS NewsHour, ABC News, Axios, and NBC News, and by the committee's referral letter itself. MODERATE-LOW confidence on the underlying perjury allegation's merits, which is a direct factual dispute between Jordan's and Raskin's competing characterizations of where the 44 lawmakers' message content actually came from -- this entry presents both accounts rather than adopting either, consistent with this tracker's treatment of similarly disputed factual claims elsewhere.

incident_summary: Vice Adm. official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Whistleblower Protection Act / First Amendment Retaliation Against Federal Employees -- NOT charged criminally; challenged via a federal civil lawsuit and Office of Special Counsel complaints, not criminal prosecution
incident_summary: On September 4, 2025, two former senior NIH officials -- Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID, the position Dr. Anthony Fauci previously held), and Dr. Kathleen Neuzil, former director of NIH's Fogarty International Center -- filed a joint whistleblower complaint with the U.S. Office of Special Counsel alleging they were forced out of their positions in retaliation for objecting to the cancellation of research grants and clinical trials, the politicization of scientific decisions, and what they described as baseless hostility toward vaccines from newly installed NIH leadership. Marrazzo, who had been placed on indefinite leave in March 2025, alleged Principal Deputy NIAID Director Dr. Matthew Memoli made statements mirroring Kennedy's views that 'vaccines are unnecessary if populations are healthy' and that NIH 'should not focus on vaccines.' Neuzil, placed on administrative leave April 12, 2025 before involuntarily resigning, separately objected to NIH canceling grants based on what she called 'anti-South Africa hostility' and an incorrect belief that certain grants advanced diversity, equity, and inclusion goals. Both officials' complaint also alleged that a $500 million universal-flu-vaccine program NIH awarded in May 2025 bypassed normal scientific peer review despite relying on technology multiple scientists described as badly outdated. **Twenty-two days after filing the OSC complaint, on September 26, 2025, Secretary Kennedy fired Marrazzo outright.** Marrazzo subsequently sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, naming Kennedy, NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, Memoli, and NIH as defendants, alleging the termination violated the Fifth Amendment's due process guarantee, the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978, the Administrative Procedure Act, the First Amendment, and the Whistleblower Protection Act.
elements_required: A federal employee engaged in protected whistleblowing activity (filing an OSC complaint alleging agency wrongdoing)
The employee's supervising official had knowledge of the protected activity
An adverse employment action (termination) followed the protected activity within a timeframe supporting an inference of retaliation
The stated agency rationale for the action does not independently account for the timing or the specific retaliatory statements alleged

evidence.description: Marrazzo and Neuzil's joint September 4, 2025 whistleblower disclosure to the U.S. Office of Special Counsel, alleging retaliation for objecting to grant/clinical-trial cancellations, vaccine-hostile statements from NIH leadership including Dr. Matthew Memoli, and a $500 million flu-vaccine program that bypassed normal peer review

Neuzil's OSC complaint remains a separate, non-litigated administrative filing as of the same date. No criminal charges, as this is a civil whistleblower-retaliation and employment matter.
rebuttal_anticipated: The administration would likely argue Kennedy retains independent management authority over NIH leadership appointments and removals, that Marrazzo's and Memoli's underlying policy disagreement over vaccine research priorities reflects a legitimate difference in scientific judgment rather than retaliation, and that the termination timing, while proximate to the OSC filing, does not by itself establish retaliatory intent.

The underlying policy dispute over vaccine research priorities is genuinely contested and outside this entry's scope; this entry documents the retaliation claim's factual timeline and legal posture, not a judgment on the vaccine-policy merits themselves. official: Scott Kupor, Director of the Office of Personnel Management
offense_category: Likely Administrative Procedure Act and First Amendment Violation -- Politicizing Nonpartisan Civil Service Hiring
incident_summary: In May 2025, OPM under Director Scott Kupor issued a "Merit Hiring Plan" that added an essay question to federal job postings across the government, asking applicants to "[i]dentify one or two relevant Executive Orders or policy initiatives that are significant to [the applicant], and explain how [the applicant] would help implement them if hired." The question appeared on more than 70,000 federal job postings for nonpartisan civil service positions. Kupor publicly defended the plan as reinforcing "the nonpartisan character of the federal workforce," and OPM guidance described the question as non-mandatory, non-scored, and not a "political litmus test." Three federal employee unions sued OPM and Kupor in November 2025, arguing the question amounted to a de facto political loyalty test that pressured applicants to signal support for Trump's agenda to be considered for hire. On September 11, 2026, U.S. District Judge George O'Toole (D. Mass.) **sided with the unions, finding they were likely to succeed in showing "there is no legitimate governmental interest in inquiring into the political beliefs of applicants to federal civil service vacancies," and that the question likely violated the Administrative Procedure Act by infringing First Amendment speech rights**. O'Toole ordered OPM to notify agencies by the end of that week that the question should be removed from active job postings.
elements_required: OPM, under Kupor, added an essay question to 70,000+ nonpartisan federal job postings asking applicants how they would help implement the President's executive orders and policy priorities

OPM publicly described the civil service positions involved as nonpartisan and the question as non-scored, while court filings and union plaintiffs presented evidence applicants could not skip the question despite OPM's claim it was optional
A federal judge found plaintiffs likely to succeed in showing the government had no legitimate interest in probing job applicants' political beliefs for nonpartisan civil service roles
The court found the question likely violated the Administrative Procedure Act by infringing applicants' First Amendment rights
The court ordered removal of the question from active postings, which OPM had not done voluntarily prior to the ruling

rebuttal_anticipated: OPM characterized the question as optional, non-scored, and merely intended to gauge an applicant's understanding of and interest in the administration's priorities -- a legitimate, nonpartisan hiring consideration comparable to asking about familiarity with an agency's mission, not a political loyalty test, and no applicant's answer was shown to have actually affected a hiring decision.

Directing every federal job applicant nationwide to write about implementing the President's specific executive orders, on over 70,000 postings, goes well beyond gauging general mission familiarity.

official: Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law and former (2017-2021) senior White House adviser; private investor via his firm Affinity Partners
offense_category: Foreign Self-Dealing -- a president's family member profiting from a foreign government's favorable treatment of his private business while that same government simultaneously seeks better relations with the president's own administration; not itself a charged offense, but a documented conflict-of-interest and foreign-influence concern
incident_summary: Affinity Partners, the investment firm Jared Kushner founded after leaving his White House post, partnered with Dubai billionaire Mohamed Alabbar to develop a roughly $500 million Trump Tower hotel and apartment complex in Belgrade, Serbia, on the site of the former Yugoslav army headquarters -- a building bombed by NATO in 1999 and protected as a cultural monument. The Serbian government, led by President Aleksandar Vučić, agreed to grant Affinity Partners a 99-year lease to the site at no cost and, in November 2025, passed legislation to fast-track the project's approval; Vučić's government publicly framed the deal as a way to strengthen ties with the Trump administration at a time when the U.S. had imposed 35% tariffs on Serbian imports and sanctioned NIS, Serbia's Russian-controlled oil monopoly. Removing the site's historic-monument protection required an expert opinion from Serbia's Republic Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments; **Serbian organized-crime prosecutors found that opinion had been forged, and on December 15, 2025 indicted Serbian Culture Minister Nikola Selaković -- a close Vučić ally -- along with three other officials on charges of abuse of office and document falsification for their roles in stripping that protection to clear the way for the project**. Hours after the indictments were announced, Affinity Partners withdrew its application, stating it was 'stepping aside... out of respect for the people of Serbia and the City of Belgrade' -- withdrawing only once the underlying corruption became a criminal matter, not before, despite sustained public protests against the project throughout 2025.

The host government (Serbia) explicitly linked the project to improving relations with the Trump administration, at a time when the U.S. was applying economic pressure (tariffs, sanctions) on that same government

Serbian prosecutors found the specific legal step needed to enable the project -- removing the site's cultural-monument protection -- rested on a forged official document, leading to criminal indictments of the country's culture minister and three others
Kushner's firm withdrew only after the indictments were announced, not in response to the year-long public controversy and protests that preceded them

official: Corey Lewandowski, former senior adviser to DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, serving as an unpaid 'Special Government Employee'
offense_category: Federal Procurement Authority Violation -- exercising contracting authority he did not legally hold as a Special Government Employee, potentially implicating federal procurement regulations governing who may bind the government to a contract; DHS OIG (Inspector General Joseph Cuffari) was reported in July 2026 to be weighing a criminal referral, but none has been reported as made as of September 2026
incident_summary: Corey Lewandowski, a former Trump campaign manager who served as an unpaid Special Government Employee and senior adviser to then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem until both left DHS in March 2026, is under investigation by the DHS Office of Inspector General for allegedly improperly participating in the award of DHS contracts -- a function he had no legal authority to perform in his SGE capacity. In early 2026, scrutiny centered on a $220 million no-bid DHS advertising campaign featuring Noem. On March 6, 2026, Sens. Peter Welch and Richard Blumenthal wrote to the three firms involved -- Safe America Media, which signed a $143 million no-bid contract; People Who Think, which received a $77 million no-bid contract; and subcontractor the Strategy Group -- asking whether Noem, Lewandowski, or any DHS employee financially benefited. On March 10, NBC News reported that Trump had personally questioned aides about whether Lewandowski profited from the campaign. On March 23, **House Oversight Committee Ranking Member Robert Garcia expanded Oversight Democrats' investigation after NBC News reported that Lewandowski allegedly demanded kickbacks from private-prison contractor GEO Group tied to the value of its DHS contracts, then, after rejecting the company's counteroffer to put him on retainer, allegedly told a senior DHS official not to award it more contracts**. On March 25, House Judiciary Democrats asked Chairman Jim Jordan to subpoena Lewandowski over the ad spending, citing internal records reviewed by ProPublica indicating he approved major contracts and noting that $143 million was routed to a newly formed LLC created days before the award; no subpoena has been reported. On March 26, CNN reported that the DHS inspector general had launched a sprawling investigation into how DHS contracts were solicited and handled, including Noem's and Lewandowski's involvement; which specific contracts it covers is not public. At a June 17, 2026 confirmation hearing, DHS management nominee Brian Cavanaugh told Sen. Maggie Hassan that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin had begun reviewing contracts Lewandowski might have approved. On July 10, 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported that investigators led by Inspector General Joseph Cuffari had found evidence Lewandowski may have been involved in improperly awarding contracts, that people who reviewed the documents or had knowledge of the approvals said he personally signed specific contracts despite not being a full-time federal official, and that investigators were weighing a criminal referral to the Justice Department that was not imminent; DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and White House officials have been briefed on the inquiry. On September 7, 2026, the Journal reported that Lewandowski had operated as a de facto "shadow secretary" at DHS, citing an episode in which a proposed $2.7 billion Palantir agreement sat unsigned while he sought a one-on-one meeting with CEO Alex Karp and was later cut to $1 billion. The same report said he pitched officials of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates on retaining him for outside work, offering help with matters within DHS's remit such as visas; both rebuffed him. Lewandowski, through a spokesperson, has denied issuing contracts at DHS and said he has not been contacted by investigators. He called the September report "anonymous-source, politically driven reporting."
