offense_category: Misuse of Administrative Subpoena Power to Target Protected Speech -- no criminal charge; this is a First Amendment/investigative-power-abuse accountability claim, distinguished from a judicial subpoena because administrative subpoenas require no judge's approval
incident_summary: A Washington Post investigation found **DHS used administrative subpoenas -- which, unlike grand jury or judicial subpoenas, require no judge's sign-off -- to seek personal data on government critics and people engaged in constitutionally protected speech**, including at least one case in which DHS sought to identify a person who had emailed a DHS attorney criticizing the agency's handling of an asylum seeker's case. That person, a 67-year-old Philadelphia-area retiree identified in court filings as Jon Doe, sent the email on October 30, 2025; about four hours later DHS issued an administrative subpoena to Google for information about him and his Gmail account, and about two and a half weeks later two DHS agents and a local police officer came to his home to question him about the email. Google did not hand over the data. Represented by the ACLU, Doe moved in federal court in the Northern District of California on February 2, 2026 to quash the subpoena as retaliation for protected speech; on February 5, DHS told Google it wanted the subpoena retracted and told Doe's lawyers the investigation was closed, without explaining why he had been investigated, and Doe dismissed his motion on February 10. The Post and the ACLU also reported earlier DHS subpoenas seeking to unmask Instagram users who posted about ICE raids in Los Angeles and the people behind an Instagram and Facebook account that tracked ICE raids in Pennsylvania; DHS abandoned both after the ACLU challenged them. The same unsigned-administrative-subpoena mechanism was also used starting around July 2025 against a different target: landlords, pressured to turn over tenant records for immigration enforcement, tracked as a companion entry in this database. On March 2, 2026, Reps. Robin Kelly and Pramila Jayapal and 26 other House Democrats wrote to ten tech and telecom CEOs asking how they handle DHS administrative subpoenas; no Republicans signed the letter. Following the Post's reporting, a bipartisan group of three Democratic and three Republican lawmakers, led by Sen. Ron Wyden and Rep. Adriano Espaillat, introduced the Subpoena Abuse Prevention Act (S. 4594, May 20, 2026, with Sen. Cynthia Lummis; H.R. 8966, May 21, 2026, with Reps. Thomas Massie, Robin Kelly and Eric Burlison), which would require government officials to certify under penalty of perjury that they are not using subpoenas to monitor or retaliate against people exercising free-speech or other constitutionally protected activity, and would separately limit the government's ability to obtain phone records without a judge's order.

The response to this pattern was bipartisan, not partisan criticism -- three Republican and three Democratic members of Congress co-sponsored corrective legislation specifically citing this conduct

Secretary Noem, as the DHS official ultimately accountable for the department's use of its subpoena authority, is the accountable official, whether or not she personally authorized each individual subpoena

offense_category: Retaliatory Personnel Practices and Contracting Centralization Producing Documented Dysfunction Across a Cabinet Department -- distinct from this tracker's other DHS entries (subpoena abuse, surveillance audit), which concern specific external-facing actions rather than internal management conduct
incident_summary: A Wall Street Journal investigation found significant infighting, dysfunction, and self-promotion-driven decision-making at the top of DHS under Secretary Kristi Noem. **Noem and adviser Corey Lewandowski fired or demoted roughly 80% of the career ICE field leadership that was in place when they started, and, in Reason's summary of the Journal's reporting, career immigration-enforcement staff were let go or demoted for questioning or objecting to Noem's decisions** -- the Journal itself detailed individual episodes, such as a top ICE lawyer placed on administrative leave and later demoted after declining to sign off on Lewandowski's request for a law-enforcement badge and gun (DHS said the leave was for unrelated reasons) -- creating what multiple sources described as a culture of fear across DHS's 23 sub-agencies as the pair fired, reassigned, and demoted personnel. The Journal also reported Noem tracked border czar Tom Homan's television appearances to ensure she received more airtime than him, despite the two rarely speaking directly. Separately, Noem and Lewandowski centralized control over DHS contracting, which the Journal reported led to delays, higher prices, and potential conflicts of interest. Trump announced Noem's ouster as DHS Secretary on March 5, 2026, and reassigned her to a newly created envoy role. On March 18, 2026, the top Democrats on the House Oversight, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Homeland Security committees (Reps. Robert Garcia, Rick Larsen and Bennie Thompson) asked the DHS Inspector General to investigate Lewandowski's influence over DHS contracting. On March 26, CNN reported, citing two people familiar with it, that Inspector General Joseph Cuffari had opened a sprawling investigation into how DHS contracts were solicited and handled, including Noem's and Lewandowski's involvement; the IG's office said it does not confirm or deny the existence of investigations. On April 1, The New York Times reported that the inquiry was scrutinizing Lewandowski's interactions with companies seeking DHS business, among them Palantir, which reportedly complained to administration officials about its dealings with him. NBC News had reported on March 23 that the IG was investigating the award of $220 million in advertising contracts without full and open competition, and separately reported allegations that Lewandowski sought payments from contractor GEO Group in exchange for favorable contract decisions, which he denies. In July 2026 the Journal reported that investigators had found evidence Lewandowski may have been involved in improperly awarding contracts and were weighing a criminal referral to the Justice Department that was not imminent; a representative for Lewandowski denied he issued contracts and said he had not been contacted by investigators. No referral, charges, or findings have been publicly reported; the inquiry remains open.

The scale is substantial and specific: roughly 80% of the career ICE field leadership in place when Noem and Lewandowski started fired or demoted, not an isolated personnel dispute

Contracting authority was centralized in a manner the Journal's reporting connects to concrete negative outcomes (delays, higher prices, potential conflicts of interest), not merely a management-style preference

offense_category: Public Accusation of Criminal Assault via Official Social Media Without Charges or Convictions -- disproportionately targeting U.S. citizens; not a criminal charge against Noem herself, a due-process/accountability claim regarding DHS's public communications practices
incident_summary: A Wall Street Journal investigation reviewed more than 100,000 posts made over roughly a year by accounts linked to DHS, ICE, CBP, and senior administration officials during Kristi Noem's tenure as Secretary -- the Journal's graphic of government posts includes two from her own X account -- as part of the administration's social-media campaign defending aggressive immigration enforcement. **The Journal identified 279 people publicly accused by name or identifying detail of assaulting federal immigration or Border Patrol agents. Of those 279, 181 -- about 65% -- were U.S. citizens, not the undocumented immigrants the enforcement campaign is officially aimed at.** The Journal, publishing its findings in March 2026, tracked each identified case through the legal system: close to half of the 181 citizens accused were never charged with assault, and none of them had been convicted at trial. Fifteen people named in government posts had pleaded guilty before trial, ten of them to lesser offenses than the government first charged. The Journal's team separately reviewed more than 200 videos tied to the assault allegations, using both agency body-camera footage and bystander recordings, and found many of the videos cast doubt on the government's own claims that agents had been assaulted. Independent DOJ referral data, published February 24, 2026 -- predating this entry's underlying WSJ investigation -- corroborates the charging-failure pattern from a second, official-statistics angle: a record 274 DHS referrals to federal prosecutors in FY2025 with Section 111 (assaulting, resisting or impeding a federal officer) as the lead charge (126 from ICE alone, up from 28 in FY2024), with at least two dozen already dismissed, resulting in acquittal, or rejected by grand juries. By then, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller had posted on X that failed cases in Los Angeles were the result of 'mass judge and jury nullification, deep in blue territory, of slam-dunk assault cases against federal law enforcement.' A separate New York Times review published July 18, 2026, of close to 550 arrests for alleged assaults during encounters with immigration agents found that of 459 resolved cases, 246 ended in guilty pleas, only four trials ended in convictions, and 213 ended in jury acquittals, charges thrown out by judges, or cases withdrawn by prosecutors.

offense_category: Federal Records Act Compliance Failure and Contradictory Public Statements Over DHS's Preservation of Text Messages
incident_summary: In July 2025, watchdog group American Oversight submitted a FOIA request seeking text, Signal, and email communications of Secretary Kristi Noem and other top DHS officials related to the National Guard's deployment to Los Angeles and Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' migrant detention facility. On July 23, 2025, **DHS responded that 'text message data generated after April 9, 2025, is no longer maintained' -- meaning DHS had stopped preserving senior officials' text messages for roughly three and a half months by the time of the request**. The New York Times first reported this response on August 22, 2025; DHS subsequently gave contradictory public assurances that it did continue to preserve text-message records, without explaining the discrepancy with its own written FOIA response. American Oversight said a failure to preserve records as described would violate the Federal Records Act and urged Noem to immediately recover any missing records and notify the National Archives of any unlawful destruction, as the statute requires. On October 20, 2025, American Oversight sued DHS, Noem, the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), and Acting Archivist Marco Rubio over the agency's failure to produce the requested records and the unresolved preservation question. A November 21-22, 2025 joint status report revealed DHS had issued a notice directing officials to preserve records relevant to the litigation, spurred by the lawsuit itself. In early April 2026, DHS admitted in a court filing that its original 'no longer maintained' assertion had been 'erroneous,' attributing it to a 'misunderstanding' tied to technology changes -- an explanation that, as of this entry's sourcing, had not been independently confirmed to demonstrate DHS actually complied with its Federal Records Act preservation obligations throughout the disputed period.

DHS later admitted in the litigation that its original non-preservation statement was 'erroneous,' without independently confirming full compliance during the disputed period

official: Kristi Noem, then-Secretary of Homeland Security (served 2025-2026, replaced by Markwayne Mullin in 2026)
offense_category: Retaliation against protected federal whistleblowers -- potential violation of the Whistleblower Protection Act and First Amendment
incident_summary: On August 25, 2025, 14 FEMA employees sent Congress a formal dissent letter, later called the 'Katrina Declaration,' describing 'gross waste and mismanagement, abuses of authority, dangers to public health and safety' at the agency and warning that Trump administration and DHS Secretary Kristi Noem's policies were 'gutting critical reforms to FEMA's ability to respond to emergencies' put in place after Hurricane Katrina. The next day, August 26, 2025, DHS placed the public signers on indefinite administrative leave, ordered them to stop working, and imposed a communication blackout; at least one employee was terminated outright on a charge of 'Conduct Unbecoming a Federal Employee.' The employees, represented by the Government Accountability Project, filed for whistleblower protection. On December 1, 2025, **FEMA management reinstated the employees after its own legal counsel determined their conduct was protected under the Whistleblower Protection Act and the First Amendment** -- a resolution GAP's press release characterized as full reinstatement with no disciplinary action. Within hours of CNN reporting the reinstatement publicly, DHS reversed it, placing the workers back on administrative leave; a DHS spokesperson said they had been 'wrongly and without authorization reinstated by bureaucrats acting outside of their authority,' and the administration stated it 'will not tolerate rogue conduct, unauthorized actions, or entrenched bureaucrats resisting change.' Rep. Frank Pallone called the reversal 'retaliation in plain sight' and said Trump and Noem were 'tearing down the agency that protects Americans,' naming risk to coastal states including New Jersey. The employees filed a complaint with the Office of Special Counsel, with a further appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board possible if unresolved there. The dispute remained unresolved through the following months; on April 30, 2026, under new DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin -- who was simultaneously rolling back several other Noem-era FEMA policies (including a $100,000 spending-approval threshold) ahead of the 2026 hurricane season and the FIFA World Cup -- DHS offered all employees associated with the matter a return to duty, effectively ending the roughly eight-month saga with full reinstatement.

DHS placed the signers on administrative leave and terminated at least one employee within a day of the letter becoming public, a timing sequence supporting an inference of retaliation for the protected disclosure rather than an independently-arising personnel action

FEMA's own legal counsel -- not an outside party -- determined in December 2025 that the employees' conduct was legally protected, before DHS leadership overrode that determination hours after it became public
DHS's own public statement characterized the reinstatement as unauthorized 'rogue conduct' by 'bureaucrats,' rather than disputing the legal merits of the protected-whistleblower determination itself

The dispute was not resolved through litigation or an OSC/MSPB ruling on the merits; it ended via a discretionary reinstatement offer under new DHS leadership eight months later, so no formal adjudicated finding of unlawful retaliation exists in sourcing reviewed

incident_summary: On April 16, 2025, then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem sent Harvard University a letter demanding extensive records on international students, including alleged criminality and misconduct, as part of a broader administration campaign targeting the university over campus protests, admissions, and hiring practices. When Harvard did not fully comply to DHS's satisfaction, Noem ordered the revocation of Harvard's Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) certification on May 22, 2025 -- the authorization every U.S. school needs to enroll international students on F-1, J-1, and M-1 visas. **Losing SEVP certification would have immediately stripped Harvard's roughly 7,000 international students and scholars of legal status to study or work in the U.S., forcing many to transfer schools or leave the country mid-degree.** Harvard sued DHS the next day, May 23, 2025, alleging the revocation violated the First Amendment (retaliation for protected activity), the Administrative Procedure Act, and due process; U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs granted a temporary restraining order that same day, then a preliminary injunction on June 20, 2025, finding Harvard was likely to succeed on the merits. DHS did not relent: on July 9, 2025, it escalated with administrative subpoenas demanding Harvard turn over records, communications, and other documents on immigration-law-enforcement compliance dating back to January 1, 2020, publicly accusing the university of enabling visa abuse and 'advocating violence.' Jamie Raskin, the Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, formally referred Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem to the Department of Justice for investigation into potential perjury and knowingly false statements to Congress, based on her testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee on March 3, 2026 and the House Judiciary Committee on March 4, 2026. The referral letter was addressed to Attorney General Pam Bondi. The referral identified four categories of allegedly false statements: (1) Noem testified that DHS complies with federal court orders, while the referral, citing federal court findings including Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz's February 26, 2026 finding of 210 ICE violations of court orders in Minnesota alone, says **DHS had repeatedly defied court orders to release individuals from ICE detention, in some cases failing to release people for days or weeks after a court-ordered release date**; (2) she made claims about the bidding process for a $220 million DHS television ad campaign contract that the referral disputes, and denied that adviser Corey Lewandowski had a role in approving DHS contracts; (3) she made claims about the detention of U.S. citizens by immigration agents, despite ProPublica having separately documented more than 170 U.S. citizens held by immigration agents; and (4) she made claims about detention conditions. Richard Blumenthal asked whether Lewandowski had 'a role in approving contracts' at DHS, Noem answered 'No,' but internal DHS records reviewed by ProPublica showed Lewandowski personally approved a multimillion-dollar equipment contract, and current and former DHS officials said he had approved numerous contracts and was typically the last sign-off before Noem on contracts above $100,000. A DHS spokesperson responded that 'any claim that Secretary Noem committed perjury is categorically FALSE,' and a DOJ spokesperson said the department 'has received the latest political stunt from the Democrats.' official: Donald Trump, President (reportedly at activist Laura Loomer's urging)
offense_category: Firing the Nation's Top Signals-Intelligence and Military Cyber Officials Reportedly at an Outside Activist's Urging on Loyalty Grounds, Leaving the NSA and Cyber Command Without Senate-Confirmed Leadership for Nearly a Year
incident_summary: On April 3, 2025, President Trump fired Gen. Timothy Haugh, the Senate-confirmed director of the National Security Agency and head of U.S. Cyber Command, and removed his civilian deputy, Wendy Noble, who was reportedly reassigned to the office of the under secretary of defense for intelligence -- roughly a year into what is traditionally a three-year term, and with no public explanation of an official reason. CNN and ABC News, citing sources, reported the firings followed a private April 2 Oval Office meeting in which far-right activist Laura Loomer presented Trump research on officials she deemed disloyal (CNN described a list of roughly a dozen names) and urged Haugh's removal; CNN's sources said she also urged Noble's. Loomer publicly took credit overnight, posting that Haugh and Noble 'have been disloyal to President Trump. That is why they have been fired,' and that Haugh had been 'HAND PICKED by General Milley, who was accused of committing treason by President Trump.' Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One on the afternoon of April 3, before Haugh's removal was reported, Trump called Loomer 'a very good patriot' who 'makes recommendations of things and people, and sometimes I listen to those recommendations,' said he makes the decisions, and denied she was involved in that week's National Security Council firings; asked about her posts on Haugh, the White House referred reporters back to those comments. Lt. Gen. William Hartman, Haugh's deputy at Cyber Command, was designated acting commander of Cyber Command and acting NSA director, and Sheila Thomas acting NSA deputy director. **The agency then went without a permanent, Senate-confirmed director for nearly a year: by November 2025, Nextgov/FCW (in a story republished by Defense One) reported that a leadership vacuum had produced sustained morale problems ('the morale inside the organization is rather depressed... that's what happens when your boss disappears'), a wave of additional senior departures -- including NSA's top lawyer, April Falcon Doss, reportedly also let go on Loomer's advice -- and a pause in recruiting for the NSA's Legal Honors Program, a key pipeline for the agency's legal talent.** The White House had reportedly considered elevating Hartman to the permanent post but backed off those plans. On August 21, 2025, the NSA announced that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard had designated Joe Francescon -- a former NSA analyst who held senior National Security Council roles in Trump's first term -- as the agency's next deputy director, with Trump's approval. official: Kurt Olsen, former White House Director of Election Security and Integrity (October 2025-May 2026); now senior counsel, U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida
offense_category: Abuse of Federal Investigative Power to Re-litigate the Settled 2020 Election, by an Official With a Court-Sanctioned Record of False Election Claims -- no criminal charge or court finding of wrongdoing against Olsen for his government work; making referrals was within his office. The concern rests on two courts' sanctions, an attorney-discipline finding, and a federal judge's criticism of the affidavit his referral produced
incident_summary:
Kurt Olsen, a Washington lawyer who spent much of his career in securities and product-liability litigation, entered election work after Trump's 2020 loss. According to congressional testimony by a top Justice Department official from Trump's first term, Olsen pressed the department to file a Supreme Court lawsuit challenging the results in battleground states, and he helped Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's bid to get the Supreme Court to overturn Joe Biden's win.

His later election litigation drew sanctions. Representing Kari Lake and Mark Finchem in a 2022 federal suit to ban electronic vote-counting in Arizona, Olsen and co-counsel Andrew Parker were sanctioned under Rule 11 and 28 U.S.C. 1927 and held jointly liable for $122,200 in fees; on March 14, 2025 a divided Ninth Circuit panel affirmed, finding they **made false, misleading, and unsupported factual assertions** and did not make a reasonable pre-filing inquiry. On May 4, 2023 the Arizona Supreme Court separately fined Olsen and co-counsel Bryan Blehm $2,000 for calling it an "undisputed fact" that 35,563 ballots were added at a vendor, a representation it called "unequivocally false." In 2024 Arizona's Presiding Disciplinary Judge ruled that Olsen had violated rules against false statements to a tribunal and dishonest conduct; in October a hearing panel found he had acted knowingly but admonished him, citing his clean record and remorse. In fairness, other reviews went his way: an Arizona disciplinary panel dismissed a separate complaint over the voting-machine suit (affirmed by the Arizona Supreme Court in May 2025, one justice dissenting in part), and six Ninth Circuit judges dissented from denial of rehearing, calling the sanctions a weaponization against disfavored litigation. Parker's petition to the U.S. Supreme Court is pending.

In 2025 Olsen moved inside the government. Reuters reported that, while still holding no government post, he steered a June 2025 intelligence-agency inspection of a Dominion voting machine in Puerto Rico toward proving foreign vote manipulation; the inspection found no evidence of hacking or altered votes, and by late summer Olsen told Trump the contractor was secretly funded by George Soros, which the firm denied. In late October 2025 Trump appointed him White House Director of Election Security and Integrity, a temporary special-government-employee post.

On January 28, 2026, FBI agents seized about 650 boxes of Fulton County, Georgia's 2020 ballots and records. The FBI's sworn warrant affidavit, unsealed February 10, 2026, states: **"The FBI criminal investigation originated from a referral sent by Kurt Olsen, Presidentially appointed Director of Election Security and Integrity."** Judge Boulee's later order records that Olsen formally referred the matter to the FBI by 9:03 a.m. on January 5, 2026, and that Thomas Albus, U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Missouri and Special Attorney to the Attorney General, received it that day. The affidavit was sworn by FBI Special Agent Hugh Raymond Evans, drafted from his witness interviews, and does not describe the referral's contents. On May 6, 2026, U.S. District Judge J.P. Boulee let DOJ keep the ballots, finding Fulton County had not shown "callous disregard" of its rights and that Olsen's referral came before the county clerk's motion that the county said the criminal case was a pretext to get around, a timing he said "cuts against" that claim. He found the affidavit "defective in some respects," one statement in it "misleading" and others "troubling," and called the seizure "certainly not perfect," but said this was not a case "where an officer intentionally lied." Reuters, citing three people familiar with his work, reported that in March 2026 Olsen oversaw DOJ's subpoena of the Arizona Senate for Maricopa County 2020 records; Reuters found his investigation turned up no evidence that foreign actors manipulated the 2020 election.

On May 18, 2026, eleven senators led by Democrat Alex Padilla demanded his removal, arguing he had exceeded the 130-day limit for special government employees; Olsen told Reuters he left the White House in May because "my 130 days were up." He then joined the Southern District of Florida as senior counsel on the "grand conspiracy" investigation of Trump's critics, where, according to a court declaration by John Brennan's lawyer, he told Brennan's team in September that Brennan was a "target" of a narrower investigation. On September 28, 2026 Olsen emailed that he was leaving that case. CNN and CBS first reported, citing sources, that he had quit DOJ; both later reported that DOJ officials had misread the email, and a DOJ official told CBS he remains senior counsel but is off the investigation. CBS also reported, citing two sources, that his security clearance had run into a problem before he stepped away.

official: Sean Parnell, Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs; Steve Feinberg, Deputy Secretary of Defense; Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Defense (Parnell announced the overhaul, his office issued the repeal rule and the ombudsman's removal notice, and his principal deputy Andrew Brey signed the journalists' separation notices; Feinberg issued the March 2026 memo; Hegseth is a defendant only in his official capacity as department head, and no source reviewed shows him personally directing the firings)
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation Against Government-Employed Journalists (alleged; Pickering v. Board of Education / Garcetti v. Ceballos public-employee speech doctrine, under which a federal judge found the claim unlikely to succeed at the preliminary stage) and Administrative Procedure Act Notice-and-Comment Violation (alleged) in removing the regulations that guaranteed Stars and Stripes' editorial independence -- civil litigation, not criminal
incident_summary: Stars and Stripes, the Defense Department-owned news organization that serves U.S. troops, military families and veterans and gets about half its budget from the department, had operated since 1994 under federal regulations (32 C.F.R. Part 246) requiring "a free flow of news and information to its readership without news management or censorship," adopted after a congressionally ordered GAO study of allegations of military censorship at the paper. On January 15, 2026, Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell, the Assistant to the Secretary of Defense for Public Affairs, posted on X that the department would "refocus [Stripes'] content away from woke distractions that syphon morale," with "no more Associated Press reprints." The same day, the department published a final rule (91 Fed. Reg. 1706) removing those regulations without notice and comment, on the ground that they covered internal procedures and their removal would not have "an impact or burden to the public." On March 9, Deputy Secretary of Defense Steve Feinberg issued a "modernization" memo, effective immediately, that affirmed the paper's editorial independence while limiting wire-service content, barring comics and other syndicated features unless Parnell approved an exception, banning publication of "controlled unclassified information," requiring content to be consistent with "good order and discipline," routing the ombudsman's information for Congress through the department, and moving Parnell's office into an oversight role. The paper's congressionally created ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, who had criticized the changes in her columns, was then notified that her last day would be April 28; she wrote that the notice came from Parnell's office and gave no reason, and she sued in June. On June 3, two subscribers who sit on the paper's publisher's advisory board sued (Dardarian v. Department of Defense) to vacate the repeal and the memo under the Administrative Procedure Act; two veterans later joined them. On July 5, CBS Sunday Morning aired a segment on the dispute in which editor-in-chief Erik Slavin, who had his supervisor's approval for the interview, said that being told to drop "a perfectly accurate story" for one "written by the Pentagon" would be a red line, and Middle East reporter Lara Korte said she worked "for Stars and Stripes... not for the Pentagon." According to the journalists' later lawsuit, a July 28 performance review of publisher Max Lederer, approved by Parnell as his rater, faulted him because his "editor and another reporter participated in a network story they know was meant to criticize the DoW efforts with Stripes." The suit alleges that on August 12, the day after Stars and Stripes published a story on hardships aboard the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, Parnell's principal deputy, Andrew Brey, ordered Lederer to deliver separation notices to Slavin and Korte over their CBS remarks; the department says the notices were completed on August 6, before that story ran. Lederer refused and announced his retirement. **On August 21, the department issued notices of proposed separation to all three**: Slavin and Korte over their CBS remarks, citing a lack of authorization from Parnell's office even though their supervisors had approved the interview, and Lederer for refusing to deliver their notices and for his interview with his own paper about his retirement. The same day, it issued a revised DoD Instruction 5122.11 that carried forward most of the March memo's content restrictions. The three sued Parnell, Brey, Hegseth and the department on August 27 (Slavin v. Parnell), and the department agreed to hold off on the firings while the court considered their motion. On September 4, U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden denied a preliminary injunction, finding that Slavin and Korte likely spoke as part of their official duties, and so without First Amendment protection under Garcetti v. Ceballos, and that Lederer's refusal to deliver the notices was likely enough on its own to justify firing him. He wrote that the plaintiffs' "real complaint seems to be that they were victims of a cruel bait-and-switch," fired "for giving pre-approved interviews on their paper's behalf in which they largely toed the company line," and that whatever else that might violate, "it does not clearly offend the First Amendment." CBS News reported that all three were placed on administrative leave after the notices, and news coverage since the ruling has described all three as fired; the sources reviewed do not state the effective separation dates. In a statement he posted on X the day after the ruling, and later provided to the Ethics and Journalism Initiative, Parnell said the department has the authority and responsibility to keep the paper focused on the force "rather than becoming a platform for airing employee grievances." The journalists' lawyer said they would keep pursuing their procedural claims. In the subscribers' case, the plaintiffs added the new instruction to their suit and filed a consolidated summary-judgment motion on September 16, with briefing scheduled to run into December; in Smith's case, the government, citing Judge McFadden's ruling, argued she wrote as ombudsman and is unprotected, and a hearing on her preliminary-injunction motion before Judge Amit Mehta was set for September 24, at which she asked to present live testimony.

incident_summary: **Former FBI agents Jamie Garman, Blaire Toleman, and Michelle Ball -- who the lawsuit describes as having amassed 'exemplary' service records -- sued FBI Director Kash Patel, then-Attorney General Pam Bondi, the FBI, and DOJ, alleging they were illegally purged from the bureau for having worked on 'Arctic Frost,' the FBI's investigation (opened in April 2022, later brought under special counsel Jack Smith) into the alleged criminal conspiracy to overturn Trump's 2020 election loss, which led to Trump's August 2023 indictment on four charges.** The suit alleges Patel and Bondi violated the agents' First and Fifth Amendment rights by firing them based on perceived political affiliation tied to their Arctic Frost work, without evidence of individual misconduct or due process. The named plaintiffs seek to represent a proposed class of all FBI employees fired since January 2025 over perceived political affiliation without due process -- at least 50 people by the complaint's estimate, a group that CBS News reported reaches beyond Arctic Frost to employees fired for other alleged political reasons. It was the second suit that month over the Arctic Frost firings: on March 19, 2026, two anonymous former agents had filed Doe 1 v. Patel, a related but separate case, and the Garman complaint was formally noticed as related to it. The lawsuit additionally alleges that Patel or people acting at his direction, and then-Deputy Director Dan Bongino, gave Congress Arctic Frost material protected by grand jury secrecy rules without court authorization, and that Senate Judiciary Chair Chuck Grassley then published some of it, including material naming Garman; disclosing grand jury material without court permission is a crime, so this is a separate legal issue beyond the firings themselves. This lawsuit is a direct legal-accountability consequence of the staffing purges documented separately in this tracker's Government Services database. On June 18, 2026, the government moved to dismiss both suits, arguing the agents were at-will employees removed over how they performed their assigned duties rather than for their perceived politics. Between July 29 and August 3, 2026, five sets of outside parties sought leave to file amicus briefs supporting the plaintiffs -- the FBI Agents Association; First Amendment scholars represented by the Campaign Legal Center and Yale's Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic; Lawyers for the Rule of Law; Justice Connection with 38 former FBI personnel; and former senior DOJ officials -- and the court granted each request. Briefing on the motion to dismiss closed August 18, 2026, and Judge Jia M. Cobb set an in-person hearing on the motions in both cases for October 21, 2026.

offense_category: Waiving Standard Security-Clearance Polygraph Requirements for the FBI's Deputy Director and Two Personal Aides, Granting Top-Secret/SCI Access Despite Unresolved or Inconclusive Results
incident_summary: ProPublica reported on November 24, 2025 that **FBI Director Kash Patel granted unprecedented polygraph waivers to three of his closest aides -- Deputy Director Dan Bongino, congressional-affairs liaison Marshall Yates, and Patel's personal assistant Nicole Rucker -- allowing all three to obtain Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) clearances, the level required for access to the nation's most sensitive intelligence, including presidential briefings, despite polygraph results that did not clear under normal standards.** Sources told ProPublica that Yates and Rucker did not clear their polygraph exams; Bongino's specific results were not established in reporting. Former FBI officials said they could not recall any senior official ever receiving such a waiver, with one recalling only a single such waiver in seven years, granted to an outside subject-matter expert -- not a sitting senior FBI leader. The FBI's own employment guidelines require all employees to pass a polygraph as part of obtaining Top Secret clearance. An FBI Security Division employee filed a formal internal complaint with the division's director, Robert Turner, alleging the waivers violated agency policy, and separately shared the complaint with the Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General. An FBI spokesperson denied that any of the three had 'failed' their polygraphs -- a characterization that leaves open whether the results were instead deemed inconclusive -- but declined to specify what, if anything, in ProPublica's reporting the FBI considered false.
elements_required: The FBI Director personally waived a standard, employment-guideline-mandated security-clearance requirement for his own deputy and two personal aides
At least two of the three did not clear their polygraph exams under normal standards, per multiple sources
The waivers granted access to SCI-level intelligence, the most sensitive tier, despite that unresolved vetting result -- a departure former officials said had no real precedent for senior leadership

An FBI Security Division employee formally objected internally and escalated the complaint to DOJ's Inspector General, indicating the waivers were controversial within the agency's own security apparatus, not merely from outside critics

evidence.description: ProPublica's original investigative report identifies all three waiver recipients (Bongino, Yates, Rucker), the SCI clearance level granted, the polygraph-clearance shortfall for Yates and Rucker, former officials' statements that such a waiver for senior leadership was unprecedented, the internal complaint to Security Division director Robert Turner and DOJ's Inspector General, and the FBI's on-record denial that anyone 'failed' their polygraphs
evidence.maps_to_element: Full incident: waiver recipients, clearance level, unprecedented nature, internal complaint, and FBI's response

status: Unresolved as of this entry. An internal complaint has been referred to DOJ's Office of the Inspector General; no OIG findings, and no reversal of the waivers, were identified in reporting reviewed.
rebuttal_anticipated: The FBI's on-record position is that none of the three 'failed' their polygraphs, implying inconclusive rather than disqualifying results, and that the Director has discretion to grant waivers for trusted senior personnel he has direct, ongoing working knowledge of.
comeback: The FBI's own employment guidelines make polygraph clearance a requirement for Top Secret access, not a discretionary formality, and former officials -- not partisan critics -- said they could recall no precedent for waiving it at this level for sitting senior FBI leadership; a single-source report of one prior waiver, for an outside expert rather than an internal official, is a materially different situation than exempting the Bureau's own Deputy Director and the Director's personal staff. The FBI's denial that anyone 'failed' notably does not address whether the results were inconclusive -- itself normally grounds for further review, not an automatic waiver -- and the agency declined to specify what else in the reporting it considered inaccurate.

offense_category: Directing a Cross-Case Campaign to Manufacture Criminal Prosecutions Against Perceived Political Opponents, With Career Prosecutors Removed for Refusing to Proceed -- no criminal charge against Patel personally; this entry documents the pattern-level accountability claim underlying this tracker's separate, official-specific vindictive-prosecution entries for the Comey, Brennan, and James cases
incident_summary: New York Times reporting from June 2026 (syndicated by the Philadelphia Inquirer), based on interviews with multiple people with knowledge of the effort, describes FBI Director Kash Patel's pursuit of a "grand conspiracy case" against President Trump's perceived foes as the driving force behind a 2025-2026 effort to find prosecutors willing to charge them, despite evidence that career investigators found weak; the New Republic summarized that report. Patel said on Joe Rogan's podcast in June 2025 that he had found documents inside FBI headquarters confirming his suspicions; those documents, found in FBI "burn bags," underpinned his push to have James Comey and John Brennan investigated for lying to Congress. The same account describes pressure on the Comey case also coming through deputies of then-Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, and pressure to charge New York Attorney General Letitia James coming from the White House after Blanche told a July 2025 meeting that the evidence did not support a case against her; in September 2025 Trump publicly complained that Comey, James, and Sen. Adam Schiff had not been charged. **Prosecutors who examined the evidence and declined to proceed were removed or saw their investigations transferred to more compliant colleagues. Todd Gilbert, interim U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Virginia, whom Patel personally directed on his first day in July 2025 to pursue the burn-bag case, resisted pressure to impanel a grand jury because his team did not believe there was a sufficient factual basis, and was pushed out after 37 days; his office's later declination memo concluded no charges were warranted.** Eastern District of Virginia U.S. Attorney Erik Siebert, who did not believe the evidence supported charging Comey, was fired in September 2025, and the grand conspiracy case moved to the Miami U.S. Attorney's office. In the Brennan probe there, CNN reported in March 2026 that career prosecutors who viewed the case as relatively weak were resisting pressure from top Justice officials to bring charges; in April 2026 DOJ removed the senior career prosecutor overseeing the case after she raised concerns about the strength of the evidence and put Trump ally Joe DiGenova in charge, and CBS News reported that two FBI agents assigned to it had served on Patel's Director's Advisory Team, one of whom had worked on the Comey prosecution. This tracker separately documents four of the resulting individual cases in more detail: the original Comey case, brought via Lindsey Halligan, an unlawfully-appointed interim U.S. Attorney, and dismissed without prejudice in November 2025 when a federal judge found Halligan's appointment invalid; a second, separate Comey prosecution filed April 28, 2026 in the Eastern District of North Carolina over a since-deleted Instagram post of seashells arranged as "8647," charged as a threat against the President; the Brennan grand-jury investigation, in which Brennan has been told he is a target but has not been charged; and the James case, also indicted by Halligan and dismissed on the same appointment defect, after which two grand juries declined to re-indict her. After the original Halligan-based Comey indictment collapsed on the appointment defect, DOJ did not close the matter: it filed the entirely new Eastern District of North Carolina indictment against Comey five months later, under a different legal theory (an alleged threat, rather than false statements or obstruction) -- direct, concrete evidence for this entry's own core thesis, that resistance or procedural setbacks redirect rather than end the underlying campaign, and the clearest single documented instance of it; the Times account adds that career prosecutors and agents had rejected the seashell case in 2025, after the Secret Service interviewed Comey and saw no point in a full investigation. This entry documents the pattern-level claim that Patel's drive was central to the push across these cases, alongside pressure from Blanche's office and the White House, and that DOJ personnel who resisted were removed -- a distinct accountability claim from any single case's merits, since it concerns the process by which targets were selected and prosecutors were pressured, not any one prosecution's individual legal footing.
elements_required: Reporting based on current/former DOJ and FBI officials attributes a sustained, personal push to build criminal cases against Trump's perceived foes (the "grand conspiracy" case targeting Comey and Brennan) to Patel, alongside documented pressure from DOJ leadership and the White House on the Comey, James, and Schiff matters

At least one specific, named instance is documented of a prosecutor examining the evidence, finding an insufficient factual basis, and refusing to proceed (declining to impanel a grand jury) despite direct pressure to do so

The pattern spans at least four distinct targets across multiple DOJ components and time periods, and includes at least one instance (Comey) where an initial prosecution's dismissal on procedural grounds was followed by a new indictment of the same target via a different venue and legal theory rather than the matter being closed -- indicating a sustained campaign against specific individuals rather than four unrelated, one-off prosecutorial decisions

incident_summary: Erica Knight, Patel's personal publicist and crisis-communications specialist since before he became FBI Director -- the two met through a mutual friend after Patel left the first Trump administration in 2021 -- now works inside the FBI as a contractor, not a federal employee, hired earlier in 2025. CBS News and Yahoo News (republishing the same investigation) reported she is employed through Xpect Solutions, a technology and security services firm, with her compensation paid to that company out of the FBI Office of Public Affairs budget -- a budget that already funds an Office of Public Affairs staff of over 150 people. The FBI declined to disclose her salary or contract terms, and Knight declined to comment on her own compensation. **She works alongside FBI Assistant Director Ben Williamson to draft statements issued under Patel's name, develop his talking points for media interviews, and manage his prolific personal social-media presence on X, and reporters have nicknamed her the 'Kash whisperer' for her ability to channel his views and secure favorable coverage.** Patel has publicly credited her as 'the best captain and teammate' in his rise to FBI Director. Knight's other clients include Alina Habba, who served as acting U.S. Attorney for New Jersey before a federal court ruled her appointment unlawful. Rep. Jamie Raskin, the House Judiciary Committee's ranking Democrat, has demanded the FBI release Knight's contract, saying 'if there's nothing to hide, then the bureau should have no problem releasing Ms. Knight's contract.' Some FBI agents have separately questioned, per CBS's and Yahoo's reporting, whether taxpayer funding for a director's personal publicist is an appropriate use of Bureau resources given the Office of Public Affairs' existing size, and have noted Knight's social-media defenses extend to Patel's personal conduct, not only his official duties as Director.

offense_category: Removing Screening Safeguards for FBI Special Agent Applicants to Meet a Hiring Quota -- weakens a career-track vetting standard designed to assess judgment and communication skills, not itself a legal violation but an accountability-relevant standards rollback
incident_summary: **FBI Director Kash Patel is set to eliminate the requirement that existing FBI support staff applying to become special agents complete an in-person interview and a writing assessment -- two long-standing vetting steps.** Under the new process, internal candidates who pass a written exam through an online portal can proceed directly to new-agent training at the FBI Academy in Quantico. The change is part of Patel's internal push to hire 700 new special agents in a single year to bolster the bureau's roughly 10,000-agent workforce amid a documented staffing crunch (see also patel-fbi-field-office-purge-2025-2026.json, this tracker's separate entry on FBI staffing losses). FBI leadership maintains standards remain intact and that the change removes only duplicative steps for already-vetted internal employees. Critics, including retired supervisory special agent Jeff Crocker, argue the removed steps are key screening safeguards -- in-person interviews, Crocker told Reuters, are essential for evaluating a candidate's maturity, verbal communication, and analytical problem-solving skills that a written exam alone cannot assess.

offense_category: Misuse of federal law-enforcement resources and personnel for personal benefit -- no criminal charge; this is a resource-misuse/ethics accountability claim, distinguished from an ordinary personal-conduct story by the diversion of operational FBI staffing
incident_summary: Scrutiny of FBI Director Kash Patel's use of bureau resources for his girlfriend, country singer Alexis Wilkins, intensified in late October 2025, when public flight logs and Wilkins's own social-media posts showed that Patel had taken the FBI's $60 million Gulfstream jet on October 25, 2025 to watch Wilkins perform at a Penn State wrestling event, then flown with her to Nashville the next day. On November 17, 2025, MS NOW reported that Wilkins was being protected by SWAT agents from the FBI's Nashville field office, and on November 23, 2025 the New York Times reported that Patel had sent two SWAT agents from the FBI's Atlanta field office to guard Wilkins at the April 2025 National Rifle Association convention in Atlanta, where she performed the national anthem, and that current and former FBI officials called the use of SWAT agents to protect her 'highly unusual.' FBI spokesman Ben Williamson defended the arrangements to the Times, saying Wilkins had faced 'hundreds of credible death threats' tied to her relationship with Patel, stating that Patel's transportation spending was comparable to that of predecessors Christopher Wray and James Comey, and adding that 'bad faith criticisms of F.B.I. travel will not deter the bureau from our mission.' A New York Times investigation published May 15, 2026, and widely repeated by follow-on outlets, documented a pattern of Patel using federal jets, security resources, and FBI personnel for personal and leisure purposes involving Wilkins. On May 10, 2025, Patel and Wilkins flew from Washington, D.C. to Philadelphia on an FBI Gulfstream V jet to attend a Chris Stapleton/George Strait concert, watching from a private suite reported to cost between $35,000 and $50,000, while the FBI flight crew and Patel's security detail stayed on duty past 11 p.m. waiting for the concert to end, collecting overtime pay; through an FBI spokesperson, Patel declined to say who paid for the suite, and representatives for the performers did not confirm the FBI's claim that Wilkins was their invited guest. Separately, Wilkins -- who does not reside with Patel -- was assigned a full-time security detail made up of elite FBI agents previously assigned to the Nashville field office's SWAT team, reportedly the first time a senior FBI official's romantic partner (rather than spouse or dependent) has received a full FBI protective detail. The reporting also recalled the October 2025 Penn State jet trip. An earlier NYT report (Feb. 28, 2026) had already documented the security detail, additionally reporting that it was staffed by rotating FBI SWAT teams covering personal errands and events (not just concerts), and that FBI staffing in Nashville, where Wilkins lives, was increased around the same period -- former officials said this raised concerns about an unprecedented allocation of tactical resources. The May 15, 2026 NYT report also covered a 'VIP snorkel' excursion Patel joined at the USS Arizona Memorial around an official Hawaii trip, which the Associated Press had first reported on May 14, 2026 from government emails. Congressional scrutiny had begun earlier. On December 1, 2025, House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin and Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove wrote to Patel demanding FBI and Justice Department aircraft travel records; their letter cited the Penn State trip and the flight with Wilkins to Nashville, a golf trip to Scotland, a Texas hunting retreat, earlier Senate Democratic criticism of his flights to hockey matches and fight nights, and Patel's move to shield the FBI jet from public flight tracking after his travel drew scrutiny. Patel has responded publicly that he is 'entitled to a personal life just like my other agency counterparts.' In April 2026, the New York Times reported that **FBI agents opened an investigation into Times reporter Elizabeth Williamson beginning around March 2026, after she wrote the story documenting Patel's use of FBI personnel to protect and transport Wilkins -- agents interviewed Wilkins, queried law-enforcement databases for information on Williamson, and moved toward assessing whether she had violated federal stalking law.** Some Justice Department officials, according to a person briefed on the matter, saw the inquiry as retaliation for an article that Patel and Wilkins did not like and determined there was no legal basis to proceed. The FBI denied that Williamson was personally investigated, said agents had interviewed Wilkins about a death threat made against her after the article, and said investigators 'were concerned about how the aggressive reporting techniques crossed lines of stalking' but pursued no further action. The Times called the inquiry an attempt to criminalize routine reporting. In a July 8, 2026 letter announced the next day, Raskin and Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin launched a bicameral investigation into Patel's 'abuse of FBI jets and tax dollars,' following a private May 5, 2026 letter from Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley questioning his spending and travel; it cites other recreation on official trips, including the Hawaii snorkeling, helicopter tours in East Asia and a $100,000 trip to the 2026 Winter Olympics. Earlier, on February 24, 2026, Durbin had asked the Government Accountability Office to add whistleblower information to its ongoing review of Patel's aircraft use and asked the Justice Department's Inspector General to investigate.

official: Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: First Amendment Retaliation Under Color of Law (potential civil/criminal exposure: 18 U.S.C. §242, deprivation of rights under color of law; misuse of federal investigative authority; possible Antideficiency Act / misuse-of-government-resources issues for the underlying security detail and transportation) — NOT charged, no criminal referral identified in available reporting
incident_summary: After New York Times reporter Elizabeth Williamson wrote in late February 2026 about Patel's girlfriend, Alexis Wilkins, receiving FBI security and transportation, including SWAT teams escorting her on her travels, the FBI under Patel began investigating Williamson in March 2026, the Times reported on April 22: agents interviewed Wilkins, queried databases for information on the reporter, and recommended moving forward to determine whether she broke federal stalking laws. Some Justice Department officials saw the inquiry as retaliation for an article Patel and Wilkins did not like and determined there was no legal basis to proceed; the FBI said it was not pursuing a case. The FBI called the account false, and Patel adviser Erica Knight said Williamson was never personally investigated and that agents asked Wilkins about her only as part of a threat case against a man later charged with threatening Wilkins after reading the article. Separately, after The Atlantic's Sarah Fitzpatrick reported on Patel's conduct, MS NOW reported in May 2026 that the FBI had launched a criminal leak investigation focusing on her, which the FBI denied, and **Patel later ordered polygraph examinations of more than two dozen of his own staff to identify sources who spoke to reporters.** As of June 2026, Democracy Forward's FOIA lawsuit seeking records on Patel's conduct was active, filed after the agencies missed FOIA response deadlines (Democracy Forward's April 21, 2026 request had given the FBI 20 days to produce documents); Democracy Defenders Fund had filed a separate FOIA suit over a previously undocumented $75,000 taxpayer-funded Italy/Olympics trip in February 2026. In a separate storyline, Patel filed a $250 million defamation suit against The Atlantic and staff writer Sarah Fitzpatrick over her April 17, 2026 article "The FBI Director Is MIA," which reported allegations of excessive drinking and unexplained absences (Patel v. Atlantic Monthly Group LLC, 1:26-cv-01329, D.D.C., filed April 2026); the suit is now contested on the merits. The case is assigned to Judge Emmet G. Sullivan. The Atlantic moved to dismiss on July 27, 2026, arguing Patel's own record makes the underlying drinking allegations "inherently plausible"; Patel filed his opposition brief on the August 17, 2026 deadline, contending the court must draw all inferences in his favor at the motion-to-dismiss stage. The discovery dispute's substance is now on the record: The Atlantic seeks internal DOJ/FBI records on Patel's absences and unreachability -- material Patel's own complaint relies on -- while resisting discovery into its own newsgathering process; Patel's team calls this "discovery for me but not for thee" and argues The Atlantic hasn't shown good cause for a stay. Defendants filed their replies in support of the motions to dismiss and to stay discovery on August 31, 2026; no ruling appears on the docket.

incident_summary: On June 4, 2020, a group of FBI agents in Washington, D.C. knelt during a protest following George Floyd's murder, an act they say was intended to de-escalate tensions with a hostile crowd rather than to express political solidarity with the broader movement. An FBI internal review at the time concluded the kneeling was a de-escalation tactic, not a political statement, and a Justice Department Inspector General review separately found no misconduct and no Hatch Act violation. **Despite both clearances, FBI Director Kash Patel fired 12 of the agents in September 2025. Their termination letters cited 'unprofessional conduct and a lack of impartiality' and accused the agents of 'weaponisation' of the FBI** -- the same word Patel and the administration have used to describe the conduct they say justified purging Trump-investigation-linked personnel elsewhere in the Bureau (see this project's Government Services entry on Patel's FBI field-office purge). On December 8, 2025, the 12 fired agents sued Patel in U.S. District Court, alleging their termination was part of a 'campaign of retribution' and that 'defendants targeted plaintiffs in particular because of plaintiffs' use of deescalation with civilians that defendants perceived as opposed to, or otherwise not affiliated with, President Trump.' The lawsuit further alleges that immediately upon becoming FBI Director on February 21, 2025, Patel began working to fire the agents, and that FBI senior leaders who spoke to him early in his tenure believed he had already decided to terminate them and that the decision had originated from the White House -- an allegation that, if proven, would mean the firings carried out a White House decision rather than an independent judgment of the underlying conduct.

offense_category: Personal/Recreational Use of FBI Aircraft Allegedly Delaying Real Investigations, Including Mass-Shooting Responses -- expanded from an initial Olympics-trip controversy to whistleblower allegations of concrete investigative harm, disclosed to Senate Judiciary Ranking Member Durbin's staff and partly disputed by the FBI
incident_summary: FBI Director Kash Patel traveled to Milan, Italy on a government jet during the 2026 Winter Olympics and was recorded in a roughly 45-second video celebrating in the U.S. men's hockey team's locker room after their gold-medal win over Canada, drinking beer, singing along to a Toby Keith song, and having a gold medal draped around his neck. When questioned by media, Patel said he was "extremely humbled" that his "friends" on the team invited him to celebrate, and separately defended the trip as an official visit to meet with Italian law enforcement to help provide security for American athletes and fans. According to a person familiar with the matter cited by NBC News on February 27, 2026, President Trump told Patel directly that he was displeased both with the viral locker-room video and with Patel's use of a government jet for the trip, though that disapproval did not result in a reported personnel consequence. CNN's follow-up reporting examined the FBI jet-use controversy and the practical constraints (security, communications needs) that shape how FBI directors typically travel. On February 24, 2026, Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin released whistleblower disclosures made to his staff alleging that **Patel's handling of FBI aircraft delayed responses to at least two major investigations: after the December 13, 2025 Brown University mass shooting, the FBI's shooting reconstruction team could not fly from Richmond, Virginia because, per a whistleblower, Patel had ordered the Hostage Rescue Team on standby, a hold that froze the aircraft's use by any other FBI team, so the team drove overnight from Quantico, Virginia to Providence, Rhode Island during a winter storm, arriving at 9 a.m. the next morning; and the shooting reconstruction team's deployment to Utah after conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassination was delayed by at least a day by a plane and pilot shortage that Durbin attributed to Patel's personal flights, because the team could fly only after the pilots' mandated rest periods.** MS NOW, citing sources and the whistleblower's account, reported the same day that Patel had been flown on one of the FBI's two jets to south Florida and was there on the day of the Brown shooting. FBI spokesman Ben Williamson disputed the Brown account, saying it was initially a state-led homicide investigation with the FBI in an assisting role, that evidence response agents from the FBI's Boston field office reached the scene roughly two hours after the shooting, and that a plane to Rhode Island "wasn't needed." In the Feb. 24 letter that carried those disclosures, Durbin asked the DOJ Inspector General to investigate what he called Patel's "irresponsible joyriding" on DOJ and FBI aircraft and asked the Government Accountability Office to add the new information to its ongoing review of Patel's aircraft use, which Durbin first requested in May 2025; no outcome of either has been identified. A July 8, 2026 bicameral letter from House Judiciary's Raskin and Senate Judiciary's Durbin directly contradicts Patel's own official justification for the Olympics trip: Patel testified to the Senate Appropriations Committee on May 12, 2026 that the FBI "purposely planned" the trip around a wanted hacker's presence in Italian custody, but Patel had publicly announced his Olympics travel plans on July 3, 2025 -- the same date Italy took custody of that suspect, 218 days before the Olympics -- and DOJ's own records show the suspect was not extradited to the U.S. until April 27, 2026, over two months after the Olympics concluded. The letter also reveals Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, a Trump ally, separately raised similar spending and travel concerns in a private May 5, 2026 letter, and documents additional alleged incidents: a VIP snorkeling experience in Hawaii, a taxpayer-funded helicopter tour during a multi-country East Asia trip, and personnel demoted in Brussels for allegedly failing to keep Patel adequately entertained. At a September 15, 2026 Senate Judiciary Committee oversight hearing, Sen. Peter Welch questioned Patel about the locker-room celebration; Patel said the players, "who are my friends, invited me to the locker room," said no security incident occurred during the Games, and called the capture of "China's most prolific hacker" and his return to the United States the most important result of the trip.

official: Kash Patel, FBI Director
offense_category: Press Freedom / Politicization of Federal Law Enforcement -- FBI Director personally directing a criminal leak investigation from the White House at presidential direction, rather than through normal DOJ/FBI process insulated from political control
incident_summary: After the New York Times reported security concerns about President Trump's new Qatari-donated Air Force One (specifically, that Trump left a NATO summit in Turkey aboard the older presidential aircraft over Secret Service security concerns with the new plane), the White House directed FBI Director Kash Patel to personally oversee a leak investigation into the Times's sourcing. **Patel canceled a scheduled trip to Chicago and spent approximately eight hours at the White House itself -- not FBI headquarters -- personally running the investigation. On Friday, July 10, 2026, the investigation produced grand jury subpoenas, issued by Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton, to multiple New York Times reporters, with federal agents delivering some subpoenas directly to journalists' homes.** The Times's own reporting called Patel's running of the investigation from the White House rather than FBI headquarters a major departure from historical practice, and CNN described the White House's control over the probe as a significant breach of the Justice Department's historic independence. At his July 15, 2026 confirmation hearing to be Director of National Intelligence, Clayton testified that "we followed the procedures" and repeatedly called the subpoenas the "least intrusive" means possible, but declined to say whether the White House or top Justice Department officials ordered him to send the subpoenas. At his own confirmation hearing the same day, Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told the Senate Judiciary Committee that reporters were not targets but "material witnesses." At a July 23, 2026 hearing, U.S. District Judge Arun Subramanian repeatedly asked how subpoenas issued two days after the Times's first story could be the last resort that binding Second Circuit precedent and DOJ policy require, and said he would quash them if they were not withdrawn; prosecutors, who admitted "inadvertent errors" in their filings, withdrew them. A prosecutor also acknowledged, NBC News reported, that the government had mistakenly obtained phone records tied to reporters' relatives, including spouses and one reporter's mother, after a public-source database wrongly linked the numbers; The New York Times later described it as the administration having demanded that phone companies turn over the records of two of the reporters' wives and of one reporter's mother. A DOJ spokesperson attacked the judge's conduct and said the investigation "remains ongoing." On July 27, 2026, every Senate Judiciary Committee Democrat signed a letter to Blanche, who had acknowledged authorizing the subpoenas, demanding information on his and Clayton's roles. The Senate confirmed Clayton as Director of National Intelligence the next day, July 28, 2026, by a 51-47 vote.

The investigation was conducted from the White House itself rather than FBI headquarters, with the FBI Director present for an extended period
The investigation targeted journalists specifically over reporting that embarrassed or angered the president, not an investigation independent of the story's political content
The investigation produced subpoenas, including some delivered to journalists at their homes, within days of the triggering news report

comeback: The specific facts distinguishing this from a routine leak investigation are the White House's direct tasking of the FBI Director, the investigation being run from the White House building itself rather than FBI or DOJ facilities, and the speed and personal scale of the response (an eight-hour, director-led effort producing home-delivered subpoenas within days) -- all following a story that embarrassed rather than genuinely endangered the president, since the security concern being reported was itself the news, not a secret compromised by the reporting.

offense_category: Firing FBI Personnel Connected to a Biden-Era Investigation Into Patel's Own Phone Records -- raises a direct personal-conflict-of-interest concern, since the FBI Director used his removal authority against staff connected to an investigation of himself
incident_summary: **The FBI fired at least 10 agents and staff members who had been connected to obtaining 'toll records' (call timing and recipient logs, not call content) for phone numbers belonging to Kash Patel and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, sought in 2022-2023 as part of the Biden-era federal investigation into Trump's handling of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago.** Patel told Reuters the toll-record collection was 'outrageous and deeply alarming,' characterizing it as Biden-administration overreach. Legal observers noted that subpoenaing phone toll records -- which reveal only call metadata, not conversation content -- is a routine, unremarkable step in major federal investigations, including ones involving prominent officials' associates. It was not confirmed in sourcing reviewed whether the specific fired staff had personally sought, approved, or executed the toll-record request, or were terminated simply for having been assigned to the broader investigation.

Toll-record subpoenas are, per legal observers, a routine investigative step rather than an unusual or improper one, undercutting Patel's 'outrageous' characterization as the sole basis for termination

incident_summary: Terren Peizer, founder and former CEO of healthcare company Ontrak, was convicted by a federal jury in 2024 of insider trading and securities fraud -- the first criminal case built on the theory that a pre-arranged stock-selling plan (normally used to shield executives from insider-trading liability) could itself be used to commit the fraud, since Peizer sold more than $20 million of Ontrak stock in mid-2021 while possessing material non-public negative information about the company's largest customer. offense_category: Repeated Failure to Persuade D.C. Grand Juries to Indict in Cases Tied to Trump's Federal Policing Surge -- a pattern of prosecutorial overreach evidenced by citizen-juror rejection, not a single failed case
incident_summary: By early September 2025, D.C. federal grand juries had declined to indict at least six times in recent cases connected to Trump's federal policing surge and National Guard deployment in the city -- a pattern NBC News and other outlets characterized as a rebuke of prosecutors' charging decisions by ordinary D.C. citizens serving as jurors. Named examples include Nathalie Rose Jones, an Indiana woman whom a grand jury declined to indict over alleged threats against Trump (prosecutors said she had posted on Facebook about "disemboweling" the president; she allegedly called Trump a "terrorist" and a "Nazi" in a voluntary Secret Service interview on August 15, 2025, and was arrested on August 16 after joining a protest near the White House), and Sean Charles Dunn, whom prosecutors sought to charge with felony assault of a Customs and Border Protection officer for allegedly throwing a sandwich -- a case documented in more detail in this database's separate entry on his failed prosecution. A separate grand jury also declined to indict a second person accused of threatening to kill Trump, Edward Alexander Dana, who allegedly made the threat while being arrested on unrelated vandalism charges. The pattern extended to non-threat cases as well, including local residents accused of minor confrontations with federal agents during the crackdown. Prosecutors' office is led by Jeanine Pirro, whose office brought the underlying charges in these cases. A further named example: DC resident Sydney Lori Reid, arrested in late July 2025 while filming federal agents transferring detainees from DC jail to ICE custody, whom prosecutors accused of assaulting or impeding an immigration officer and an FBI agent. **A federal grand jury rejected the felony assault charge against Reid three separate times in the month after her arrest; on August 25, 2025, Pirro's office told the court it would charge her with a misdemeanor rather than drop the case, a charge that does not require grand jury approval.** Reid's public defenders said "three grand juries have now declined to indict Ms. Reid for felony assault on a law enforcement officer." Reid's arrest preceded the August federal takeover of D.C. policing, though outlets grouped her case with the surge-era refusals. Several of the named cases then collapsed: on September 4, 2025, prosecutors asked a magistrate judge to dismiss the federal case against Dana, recharging him with misdemeanors in D.C. Superior Court; on September 5, Pirro's office moved to dismiss the case against Jones "in the interests of justice" (by then, the Associated Press counted grand juries balking at least seven times in five cases since the surge began); on October 16, 2025, a jury acquitted Reid of the misdemeanor after less than two hours of deliberation; and on November 6, 2025, a jury acquitted Dunn of misdemeanor assault.

offense_category: Failed Attempt to Criminally Indict Sitting Members of Congress Over Protected Legislative/Political Speech -- a grand jury's own refusal to indict is itself strong evidence the underlying prosecution theory lacked merit
incident_summary: In November 2025, six Democratic lawmakers -- Sens. Elissa Slotkin and Mark Kelly, and Reps. Chris Deluzio, Chrissy Houlahan, Maggie Goodlander, and Jason Crow -- released a joint video urging U.S. military servicemembers and intelligence community personnel to refuse illegal orders, following the administration's deadly boat strikes in the Caribbean. President Trump publicly called their statements "seditious" and demanded the lawmakers be "arrested and put on trial." Trump's actual November 20, 2025 Truth Social post was considerably more severe than that summary suggests -- **he wrote, 'SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR, punishable by DEATH!' Asked about it the next day on Fox News Radio, Trump said, 'I'm not threatening them, but I think they're in serious trouble.'** A group of former military lawyers, the Former JAGs Working Group, said the video "simply described the law as it pertains to lawful versus unlawful orders" and "did not suborn mutiny or otherwise encourage military members to disregard or disobey lawful orders issued to them." (Secretary Hegseth's February 2025 "Friday Night Massacre" firings of the Army, Navy, and Air Force's top Judge Advocates General are tracked separately in this database.) U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office subsequently sought to indict the six lawmakers for allegedly violating a federal law barring interference with the loyalty, morale, or discipline of the armed forces. On February 10, 2026, a federal grand jury in Washington, D.C. declined to return an indictment, reportedly without a single juror voting to charge -- the latest in a series of grand jury rebukes of Pirro's office's prosecution attempts in the capital. Bloomberg Law reported Pirro's office staffed the case with two Pirro hires with minimal federal prosecution experience, including Steven Vandervelden, a dance photographer who had worked for Pirro decades ago and still ran an active photography studio. On February 19, 2026, Reps. Robert Garcia and Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary Committees, asked DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility to investigate the conduct of Pirro and the two prosecutors who presented the case. On February 23 and 24, 2026, NBC News and CBS News reported, citing sources, that Pirro's office had decided to stop pursuing the case against the six lawmakers in Washington. On August 25, 2026, the Legal Accountability Center said it filed bar complaints in New York (against Pirro and Vandervelden) and Virginia (against prosecutor Carlton Davis), asking bar officials to investigate whether they violated professional-conduct rules in seeking the indictment. House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin separately wrote to Pirro on August 26, 2026, describing her office as "one of the most significant and routine violators of basic legal and ethical standards" regarding candor to the court and compliance with judicial orders; that letter concerns the office's court conduct generally, not this case.
elements_required: The video's content -- reminding servicemembers of their existing legal duty to refuse illegal orders -- reflects established military law rather than incitement to disobey lawful orders

President Trump publicly and personally called for the lawmakers' arrest and prosecution before any indictment was sought, indicating the prosecution effort followed presidential direction rather than an independent prosecutorial judgment

A grand jury -- ordinary D.C. citizens, not a judge or the defendants' own attorneys -- independently declined to return an indictment despite hearing only the prosecution's evidence, the customary one-sided grand jury process

This was one of a documented series of grand jury rejections of Pirro's office's prosecution attempts in Washington, indicating a pattern rather than an isolated case of a good-faith theory that simply fell short
