offense_category: Use of Grand Jury Subpoena Power to Unmask Anonymous Political Speech -- no criminal charge has been identified against any of the targeted social media users; this is a First Amendment/investigative-power-abuse claim
incident_summary: In March 2026, Homeland Security Investigations sent administrative summonses, which need no judge's sign-off, to Reddit and X seeking to identify two anonymous users who had posted criticism of ICE; after each user's lawyers challenged the summons in federal court, DHS withdrew it. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, led by Jeanine Pirro, then **issued grand jury subpoenas to Reddit (on March 31, 2026, four days after the Reddit summons was withdrawn) and to X (by early May) seeking the names, addresses, and banking information of the two anonymous users**, directing the companies to deliver the records to an ICE office. The subpoenas were signed by prosecutor Brendan Horan; the users have not been told what offense is under investigation, and DOJ declined to comment. The Reddit user's attorney, Lauren Regan of the Civil Liberties Defense Center (CLDC), said some of her client's posts were as simple as "expletive ICE," but that she suspects the post that drew the government's attention was one referencing the ICE officer who shot Minnesota protester Renee Good and where he had lived; The Intercept reported that the user had shared widely circulating biographical details of that officer, Jonathan Ross, adding "Hopefully he moves up to Stillwater State Penitentiary." The X user's attorney, Joshua Koltun, said his client's post was a sarcastic comment about donating to the same ICE officer, with an address the user had seen elsewhere on social media attached, and said the post "does not contain a trace or an inkling that any violence was intended." Both users, who learned of the subpoenas from the platforms and were given a short window to challenge them before Reddit and X would have to comply, moved to quash the subpoenas and to unseal the proceedings before Chief Judge James Boasberg. Judge Boasberg denied CLDC's motion to quash the Reddit subpoena and its motion to unseal the proceedings, in a ruling CLDC announced on June 17, 2026. Per CLDC's own July 13, 2026 statement, CLDC immediately appealed Boasberg's ruling to the D.C. Circuit, and the district court granted a stay pausing disclosure of the Reddit user's identity pending that appeal.

incident_summary:
The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, under Jeanine Pirro, opened a criminal investigation in November 2025 into Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell over a roughly $2.5 billion headquarters renovation project, tied to Powell's June 2025 testimony about the project before the Senate Banking Committee. The Wall Street Journal reported that on Thursday, January 8, 2026, Trump confronted a group of dozens of U.S. attorneys gathered at the White House for what was meant to be a ceremonial photo event, calling them "weak" and complaining -- after Attorney General Pam Bondi introduced the group -- that they were moving too slowly to prosecute his chosen targets, including specifically that no case had yet been brought against Sen. Adam Schiff, part of the broader Patel-driven prosecution-campaign pattern tracked as its own entry in this database. The very next day, Friday, January 9, 2026, Pirro's office served the grand jury subpoenas on the Fed described below. Powell publicly called the investigation a pretext, saying it was not really about his testimony or the renovation but a consequence of the Fed setting interest rates independent of the president's preferences, amid Trump's escalating public pressure campaign for Powell to cut rates and eventually leave the Fed.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a swing vote on the Senate Banking Committee (split 13-11 Republican-Democrat), announced on January 12, 2026 that he would block all of Trump's Federal Reserve nominees -- including Kevin Warsh, Trump's reported pick to succeed Powell as chair -- until DOJ's criminal probe concluded, a position he reiterated in late January and again in February 2026 even as other Republicans sought an off-ramp. Separately, on January 13, 2026, central bank governors from the European Central Bank (Christine Lagarde), the Bank of England (Andrew Bailey), and the central banks of Canada, Brazil, Switzerland, Sweden, Denmark, South Korea, and Australia issued an unprecedented joint statement declaring they "stand in full solidarity" with Powell and the Federal Reserve, calling central bank independence "a cornerstone of price, financial and economic stability" that must be preserved "with full respect for the rule of law and democratic accountability."

In March 2026, Powell publicly stated he had "no intention of leaving" the Fed's Board of Governors until the DOJ investigation was "well and truly over with transparency and finality" -- signaling he would remain past his term as chair, set to expire May 15, 2026, specifically to see the investigation through, a stance PBS NewsHour reported could itself "backfire" on Trump by keeping Powell in a position of influence longer. Around the same time, on March 13, 2026, **Chief Judge James Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia quashed the subpoenas, finding the government had produced "essentially zero evidence" to suspect Powell of a crime and that the record supported the appearance of political pressure over rates rather than a genuine criminal predicate.**

In April 2026, Trump said he would "have to fire" Powell if he did not leave his post as the investigation continued. Around the same time, with the investigation reportedly "hitting roadblocks," three prosecutors from Pirro's office made an unannounced visit to the Fed's headquarters construction site seeking a "tour" to "check on progress" of the renovation; they were turned away. On April 24, 2026, Pirro announced on X that she was closing the criminal probe, with the Fed's own inspector general taking over review of the renovation cost overruns.

On May 3, 2026, however, appearing on CNN's "State of the Union," Pirro said her office was continuing to litigate the issue, confirmed she would appeal Boasberg's ruling, and stated that once the inspector general's report concluded, her office "will not hesitate to restart a criminal investigation should the facts warrant doing so." The same day, Trump publicly said the Powell probe should continue: "Take it to the end and see." Contrary to that statement, her office did not appeal Boasberg's ruling: with the Sunday, May 3, 2026 deadline to file a notice of appeal having passed, the U.S. Attorney's office announced Monday, May 4, 2026 that it would not pursue an appeal, reasoning that one was likely to be dismissed as moot given the investigation's own closure. Instead, prosecutors asked Boasberg to vacate his prior rulings in the case.

After his term as Fed chair ended on May 15, 2026, Powell announced he would remain on the Fed's Board of Governors -- a seat with its own separate term -- explicitly citing what he called "unprecedented" legal attacks on the central bank's independence by the administration, and in doing so blocked Trump from filling that board seat with a new appointee. On June 11, 2026, Boasberg denied the motion to vacate, writing that the government's brief "neither offers new evidence nor points to any material error" -- reaffirming, on reconsideration, his March 2026 finding that the government had produced "essentially zero evidence" to suspect Powell of a crime.

A separate, non-DOJ development: Judicial Watch, a conservative government-transparency watchdog group unaffiliated with Pirro's office, filed a Freedom of Information Act suit (No. 1:26-cv-01113, D.D.C.) on April 2, 2026 -- per Judicial Watch's own case page, cited as a primary source -- and in an August 17, 2026 filing asked the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia to compel the Federal Reserve to release the two grand jury subpoenas at issue in the underlying investigation, arguing the Fed is improperly withholding them from public view; the Fed has resisted disclosure, asserting the subpoenas are protected from release. This is a public-records/transparency dispute distinct from Pirro's own prosecutorial decision-making.

On September 30, 2026, the Federal Reserve's inspector general, Michael Horowitz, released its 120-page evaluation of the renovation, which Powell himself had requested in July 2025. The report found that the Fed's board had not effectively managed the project: its approved budget grew from $1.317 billion in February 2020 to $2.381 billion in December 2024, and more than four years after construction began the board still had not set a guaranteed maximum price with its construction manager. **But the inspector general wrote: "At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred requiring a referral to the U.S. Attorney General," and it identified no administrative misconduct.** Pirro said that day that her office would review the report. Trump, undeterred, wrote on Truth Social that Powell "should be forced to resign, IMMEDIATELY!" from the Fed's board and that if he did not, "he should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence," adding that he had asked Attorney General Todd Blanche to study the report. On Friday, October 2, 2026, Blanche told Bloomberg News, "We're not reopening a criminal investigation into him," while not ruling out Justice Department action if an independent audit the Fed has committed to uncovers evidence of criminal wrongdoing.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Inflating a Minor Protest Incident Into a Felony Prosecution That Failed at Every Stage -- a grand jury's refusal to indict and a subsequent jury acquittal are themselves strong evidence the felony theory lacked merit
incident_summary: In August 2025, Sean Dunn, a former DOJ paralegal, threw a Subway sandwich at a Customs and Border Patrol officer participating in Trump's federal law-enforcement surge in Washington, D.C. -- an incident he characterized as a protest. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office sought a felony assault charge carrying up to eight years in prison. **A D.C. grand jury refused to indict Dunn on the felony charge, a step described in reporting as a notable rebuke joining a string of failed prosecutions against protesters arrested by the administration's militarized federal deployment. Rather than dropping the matter, Pirro's office then filed a misdemeanor assault charge against Dunn, which proceeded to trial. On November 6, 2025, a federal jury in Washington, D.C. found Dunn not guilty after only several hours of deliberation.** This case was one of at least six D.C. grand jury refusals to indict in crackdown-related cases by early September 2025 -- including a woman a grand jury declined to indict over an alleged online threat against Trump -- tracked as part of a broader pattern in this database.
elements_required: A minor incident (a thrown sandwich, no injury alleged) was charged at the felony level, carrying a multi-year prison exposure disproportionate to the conduct
A D.C. grand jury declined to return the felony indictment -- grand juries rarely refuse prosecutors, making this itself significant evidence the felony theory was not supported by probable cause
Rather than accepting that outcome, the U.S. Attorney's office pursued a misdemeanor charge instead of declining to prosecute, which also failed at trial by jury acquittal

status: Concluded -- Dunn was acquitted by jury verdict on the misdemeanor charge, after the grand jury had already declined the felony charge; no further prosecution has been identified.
rebuttal_anticipated: Pirro's office would characterize the felony charge as a legitimate application of the law to an assault on a federal officer regardless of the object thrown, argue that grand jury and jury outcomes reflect normal prosecutorial risk rather than misconduct, and note that some charge is not inherently improper simply because it is ultimately unsuccessful.
comeback: A grand jury's outright refusal to indict is a rare and significant check -- grand juries indict in the overwhelming majority of cases prosecutors bring -- and pursuing a second, lesser charge after that refusal, which also failed at trial, indicates the office was determined to obtain some conviction from a minor incident rather than exercising ordinary prosecutorial discretion to decline charges altogether; reporting situates this within a broader pattern of the same office pursuing and losing multiple protester-related cases from the same federal deployment.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a pattern of using disproportionate criminal charges against protesters and critics of a federal law-enforcement deployment, with repeated failures at the grand jury and trial stages suggesting charging decisions driven by political messaging rather than the strength of the underlying case. This same grand-jury-refusal pattern is also cited, as one of several named examples, in the FBI street-policing entry in this database's government-services tracker, which documents FBI agents being diverted from fraud/corruption/counterintelligence casework to support the D.C. deployment itself -- a possible institutional-capacity contributor to the weak-case pattern this entry documents at the individual-prosecution level.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence -- the felony charge, the grand jury's refusal to indict, the subsequent misdemeanor charge, and the jury's not-guilty verdict are all independently corroborated across NBC News, NPR, PBS NewsHour, CBS News, and CNBC. The characterization of the prosecution as politically motivated or a 'circus' is an editorial framing from reporting and commentary, not an adjudicated finding, and is flagged as contested accordingly.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Use of a rarely-invoked 'special' grand jury -- a type empowered to publicly name individuals and allege wrongdoing even when there is not enough evidence to bring criminal charges -- convened in the immediate aftermath of a public presidential rebuke over a separate dismissed prosecution; convening a special grand jury is a lawful prosecutorial tool, not itself unlawful, but its low evidentiary bar for public accusation and its timing relative to political pressure on Pirro's own position are the accountability-relevant concern
status: Ongoing as of this entry's sourcing -- the special grand jury's actual subject was reported August 27, 2026 as an investigation into D.C. schools and the city's oversight of youth; no report has been issued and no charges have been announced as of this entry's last verification.
incident_summary: In early August 2026, Pirro's office moved to drop vandalism charges against several defendants -- including an Olympic canoeist -- accused of damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, after determining the damage stemmed from faulty contractor construction rushed ahead of America 250 celebration events, not vandalism. President Trump publicly and repeatedly criticized Pirro over the dismissals, saying she 'choked' and 'folded like an umbrella, and people get away with things,' and did not rule out firing her; Pirro subsequently met with Trump at the White House, after which her position was reported safe for the time being. Shortly after this public clash, **reporting revealed Pirro's office had convened a rarely used 'special' grand jury in Washington, D.C. -- a type that, unlike a standard grand jury, can issue a public report naming individuals and alleging misconduct even when prosecutors lack sufficient evidence to bring charges -- overseen by prosecutor Steven Vandervelden**, a Pirro ally previously assigned to the separate investigations of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell (tracked in this database's pirro-powell-vindictive-investigation entry) and D.C. police crime statistics. Later reporting (Washington Post, August 27, 2026) clarified the special grand jury's actual subject as an investigation into D.C. schools and the city's oversight of youth -- a distinct matter from both the Reflecting Pool dismissals and Vandervelden's earlier Powell assignment, which is otherwise unrelated to this entry beyond sharing the same overseeing prosecutor.
elements_required: Pirro's office dropped vandalism charges tied to the Reflecting Pool after concluding a contractor's faulty, rushed construction -- not vandalism -- caused the damage, a decision Trump publicly and repeatedly criticized, including raising the possibility of firing her.

Within days to weeks of that public pressure, Pirro's office sought and obtained a rarely used special grand jury -- a tool distinguished specifically by its ability to publicly name individuals and allege wrongdoing without meeting the evidentiary threshold required to charge them, unlike a standard grand jury.

The special grand jury is overseen by Steven Vandervelden, the same prosecutor separately assigned to the Powell investigation and D.C. police crime-statistics review, indicating a pattern of using this prosecutor for politically salient inquiries.

No public report has been issued and no charges have been announced as of this entry's sourcing; the grand jury's confirmed subject (D.C. schools/youth oversight) has not been shown in any source reviewed to be causally connected to the Reflecting Pool clash, only temporally proximate to it.

rebuttal_anticipated: Pirro's office could argue the timing is coincidental -- a special grand jury requires weeks of internal paperwork to convene, meaning the process plausibly began before or independent of the Reflecting Pool clash, and its actual subject (D.C. schools and youth oversight) has no apparent connection to Trump's criticism of her or to any of his perceived targets.
comeback: Even crediting that the paperwork process predated the public clash, the underlying accountability concern is not about the D.C.-schools subject matter's legitimacy -- it's that a U.S. Attorney facing an explicit, public threat to her job reached for one of the rarest tools in federal prosecution, one specifically distinguished by its ability to publicly brand people as wrongdoers without ever meeting a charging threshold or affording a criminal trial's procedural protections, at the exact moment her toughness on prosecution was being publicly questioned by the President who could fire her.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a broader pattern in this database of DOJ officials responding to presidential pressure over perceived leniency by reaching for more aggressive, lower-evidentiary-bar prosecutorial tools -- the same overseeing prosecutor's other assignment (the Powell investigation) reflects the same institutional pattern of high-profile, politically salient inquiries clustering around this office.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence for the sequence of events -- the Reflecting Pool dismissal, Trump's public criticism, and the special grand jury's existence and unusual public-report capability are independently corroborated by NBC News, NPR, and two separate Washington Post reports. MODERATE on whether the special grand jury's timing was actually caused by the Trump clash rather than coincidental prior planning -- no source reviewed shows internal DOJ deliberation establishing causation, only temporal proximity; the causal link is a reasonable inference from timing, not a proven fact.

official: Jeanine Pirro, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia
offense_category: Suspending Two Career Prosecutors Within Hours for Accurately Describing January 6 as a 'Mob of Rioters' in a Court Filing, Then Substituting a Sanitized Filing That Omitted the Defendant's Jan. 6 Involvement
incident_summary: On October 28, 2025, two career DOJ prosecutors, Carlos Valdivia and Samuel White, filed a sentencing memorandum in the case of Taylor Franklin Taranto -- a former January 6 defendant who received clemency from President Trump and was later separately convicted of weapons and hoax charges after being arrested near the Obamas' home in 2023 with firearms and ammunition in his van -- describing the events of January 6, 2021 factually: 'thousands of people comprising a mob of rioters attacked the U.S. Capitol while a joint session of Congress met to certify the results of the 2020 presidential election.' **Within hours of the filing, both Valdivia and White were placed on administrative leave and locked out of their DOJ accounts. The next morning, the filing was replaced with a nearly identical 12-page memo, this time signed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Travis Wolf on behalf of Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia -- the substitute version omitted any reference to Taranto's involvement in the January 6 riot itself**, describing only his separate 2023 crimes near the Obama residence. At Taranto's sentencing hearing that Thursday, he received time served and three months of supervised release.
elements_required: Two named career prosecutors were suspended and locked out of their systems within hours of filing a factually accurate court document describing January 6 as a riot carried out by a 'mob of rioters'
DOJ leadership, under U.S. Attorney Pirro, replaced that filing with a substantively altered version omitting the defendant's own January 6 conduct

The defendant whose sentencing memo was altered was a Trump-pardoned January 6 participant with a documented history of subsequent, separate violent-adjacent conduct (arrested near a former president's residence with firearms)
The altered filing's timing and content directly preceded and plausibly influenced a lenient sentencing outcome (time served) in a case involving weapons found near a former president's home

evidence.maps_to_element: The prosecutors' suspension and the timeline

evidence.maps_to_element: The exact original language and the substitute filing's specific omission

evidence.description: Forbes's reporting on Taranto's background (2023 arrest near the Obamas' home with firearms and ammunition, his prior Jan. 6 clemency) and the time-served sentencing outcome
evidence.maps_to_element: The defendant's background and the sentencing outcome

status: Taranto was sentenced to time served and three months of supervised release on October 30, 2025. No public reversal of Valdivia's and White's suspension, and no independent explanation for the specific factual omission in the substitute filing, was identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry.
rebuttal_anticipated: DOJ leadership could argue that characterizing a defendant's conduct is a matter of prosecutorial discretion and framing, that 'mob of rioters' was inflammatory language inappropriate for a formal sentencing memo regardless of its factual accuracy, and that career prosecutors are not entitled to file documents inconsistent with their supervisors' preferred characterization of a case.
comeback: The concern documented here is not a stylistic disagreement over tone, but that two career prosecutors were suspended and locked out of DOJ systems within hours specifically for including an accurate factual description of a defendant's own underlying conduct, and that the substitute filing did not merely soften the language -- it omitted the defendant's Jan. 6 involvement from his own sentencing memo entirely, in a case that concluded in a lenient time-served sentence for someone previously found with firearms near a former president's residence.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with a broader pattern this tracker documents of DOJ leadership under this administration suppressing or punishing career staff who describe January 6 in terms the administration finds politically unfavorable (see the Martin entry and the Bondi entry for related but factually distinct instances of Jan.-6-prosecution-staff discipline) -- this entry documents suppression of specific factual language in an active court filing rather than a personnel purge alone.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the timeline, the exact language of both filings, the named prosecutors' suspension, and the sentencing outcome, corroborated across CBS News, ABC News, MS NOW, and Forbes. This entry is related to but factually distinct from this tracker's other Jan.-6-prosecutor-discipline entries (Ed Martin's broader purge, the Govoni-case collateral-damage firing) -- cross-referenced, not duplicated.

official: Donald Trump, President (signed the memorandum)
offense_category: Executive Reversal of a Longstanding Prohibition on Private-Sector Offensive Cyberoperations, Adopted Without New Legislation and Criticized as Under-Developed by Named Cybersecurity Experts
status: In effect -- NSPM signed Aug. 12, 2026; detailed implementing guidance due within two months; no participating companies publicly identified as of this writing
incident_summary: The New York Times reported in January 2026 that draft versions of the administration's forthcoming National Cybersecurity Strategy discussed expanding private companies' role in offensive cyberoperations, including 'hack back' authorities or mechanisms resembling historical Letters of Marque, drawing early concern from former military and intelligence officials. The administration's National Cybersecurity Strategy, released March 6, 2026 (a brief, three-to-five-page document), included language that the government would 'unleash the private sector by creating incentives to identify and disrupt adversary networks and scale our national capabilities,' though it stopped short of explicitly authorizing private cyberattacks at that stage. On August 12, 2026, Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum (NSPM) that went further, **directing a Homeland Security Task Force National Coordination Center to vet and authorize 'Participating Companies' to conduct offensive cyber surveillance (including spyware deployment) and disruptive attacks aimed at destroying data or systems belonging to foreign transnational criminal organizations, under federal direction and control. This reverses decades of U.S. policy that had prohibited private companies from conducting 'hack back' operations**, which previously exposed firms to liability under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act regardless of the target's own conduct. The NSPM includes some oversight mechanisms: a two-month deadline for detailed implementing guidance, a $1 million escrow deposit from participating companies (forfeitable for non-compliance), a requirement that both the Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security sign off on operations before execution, procedures intended to prevent targeting of Americans or U.S.-based systems, and a mandatory notification requirement if a participating company discovers an imminent attack on critical infrastructure. Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy, a cybersecurity firm, publicly called the policy 'half-baked,' warning that American personnel conducting these operations 'could easily be classified as non-uniformed combatants while traveling overseas,' exposing them to foreign prosecution -- a legal-exposure risk the memorandum itself does not appear to resolve. As of this writing, no specific companies have been publicly confirmed as enrolled participants; the White House did not respond to questions about whether any firms were already active under the program.
elements_required: A longstanding, decades-old U.S. policy prohibited private companies from conducting offensive 'hack back' cyberoperations
The President signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum reversing that prohibition via executive action, not new legislation
The memorandum's own stated oversight mechanisms (DOJ/DHS sign-off, escrow deposit, guidance deadline) were publicly documented alongside the authorization itself

A named cybersecurity-industry expert publicly characterized the policy's legal and operational safeguards as inadequate ('half-baked'), specifically flagging combatant-status/foreign-prosecution exposure risk for American personnel
No specific participating company had been publicly confirmed as of this writing, meaning the program's real-world operation and oversight in practice remains untested

evidence.description: TechCrunch reported that on August 12, 2026, Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum directing a Homeland Security Task Force National Coordination Center to vet and authorize private 'Participating Companies' to conduct offensive cyber surveillance and disruptive/destructive operations against foreign transnational criminal organizations -- marking a shift in the government's longstanding position while stopping short of allowing companies to 'hack back' cyber threats; the memorandum requires a $1 million escrow deposit, a two-month guidance deadline, and DOJ/DHS sign-off before operations.

rebuttal_anticipated: The NSPM includes real, specific oversight mechanisms not typically present in a purely deregulatory action: a substantial escrow deposit, mandatory DOJ/DHS sign-off before any operation, an explicit prohibition on targeting Americans or U.S. systems, and a critical-infrastructure notification requirement -- the administration could argue this is a carefully bounded expansion of a legitimate national-security tool against foreign criminal networks, not a reckless deregulation of cyberwarfare, and that no harm has yet occurred since no operations or participating companies have been confirmed as active.
comeback: The oversight mechanisms are the administration's own stated safeguards, not yet independently tested against any actual operation, and a named cybersecurity-industry expert -- not a partisan critic -- has already identified a specific, unaddressed legal-exposure gap (combatant-status risk for American personnel operating abroad) that the memorandum's text does not appear to resolve. Reversing a decades-old prohibition via executive memorandum, without new legislation clarifying personnel liability or international-law status, shifts a significant policy question away from congressional deliberation and toward implementing guidance the administration itself has two months to write -- guidance not yet public as of this writing.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a pattern of authorizing a previously-prohibited, legally fraught activity (private offensive cyberoperations) via executive memorandum rather than legislation, with real but self-designed oversight mechanisms whose adequacy is disputed by outside technical experts before any operation has been publicly tested against them.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the sequence of documents (NYT's January 2026 draft-strategy report, the March 2026 strategy release, the August 2026 NSPM) and the NSPM's specific terms, corroborated across TechCrunch, Schneier on Security, RealClearDefense, IBTimes UK, Tech Times, and Lawfare's analysis. Jake Williams's criticism is a named, on-record expert quote, not an anonymous or reported characterization. No specific participating company has been confirmed, and the program's real-world operation has not yet been independently tested or audited as of this writing -- this entry documents the authorization and its criticized design, not yet a documented operational harm.

official: William (Bill) Pulte, Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency; Acting Director of National Intelligence (dual role, June-early August 2026)
offense_category: Potential Misuse of Federal Authority/Confidential Financial Data (relevant standards: 12 U.S.C. provisions governing FHFA's regulatory data access; potential 18 U.S.C. §1905, unauthorized disclosure of confidential information by a government employee; potential Privacy Act of 1974 violation); separately, potential unlawful disclosure of grand jury material (Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(e)) — NOT charged; GAO investigation formally opened and underway, federal grand jury reportedly investigating a related matter, no findings or charges confirmed
incident_summary: Beginning April 2025, as FHFA director, Pulte made a series of criminal referrals to DOJ against prominent Trump critics and political opponents -- including NY AG Letitia James, Sen. Adam Schiff, Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, and Rep. Eric Swalwell -- alleging mortgage fraud, using mortgage data accessible through his oversight of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. DOJ opened a formal grand jury investigation into James on August 8, 2025 following Pulte's referral, subpoenaing records tied to her civil fraud judgment against Trump and her NRA lawsuit, and assigned Weaponization Working Group director Ed Martin to oversee the James and Schiff probes; Martin urged James to resign "as an act of good faith" and, a week later, traveled to her Brooklyn home to pose for photos outside it, conduct her attorney called a violation of DOJ ethics rules. The referrals themselves bypassed FHFA's own inspector-general review process, with Pulte sending the accusations directly to Trump-aligned DOJ prosecutors instead -- a former DOJ inspector general called the approach "highly irregular." Public records showed Pulte paid fees to obtain Lisa Cook's mortgage documents in August 2025, the day before making a criminal referral against her. **Fannie Mae officials who internally investigated whether Pulte improperly obtained Democratic officials' mortgage records were themselves removed: chief ethics officer Suzanne Libby was removed, general counsel Danielle McCoy resigned under pressure, and FHFA's acting inspector general Joe Allen, who had forwarded the internal findings to prosecutors, was asked to step down.** Allen was removed in November 2025, reportedly after he also planned to tell Congress that the agency was not cooperating with inspector-general investigators. The office he had led was then cut back sharply: on August 31, 2026, FHFA's general counsel told it that its fiscal 2027 funding would be no more than $20 million, down from $51.7 million in fiscal 2026 and the $55 million in the President's own budget request. On September 30, James Hodge, the acting principal deputy inspector general performing the inspector general's duties, notified congressional oversight committees that **the cut would force the office to shed roughly 70-80% of its staff and end essentially all of its criminal investigations** of mortgage, bank, and other fraud involving Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Home Loan Banks, including support for ongoing cases in more than 30 U.S. Attorney's offices; by its count, its criminal program, staffed in recent years by roughly 40 special agents and three prosecutors, had produced more than 1,270 convictions and nearly $75 billion in monetary results since 2011. FHFA said the office's budget and staffing were far out of line with peer inspector-general offices and that it "fully supports the independence and mission" of the office. All eleven Senate Banking Committee Democrats wrote to Pulte on October 1 calling the cut unlawful and demanding he fully fund the office, and congressional Democratic leaders including Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries said he was "shutting down the independent watchdog that is responsible for investigating his misconduct" and should resign. Mother Jones wrote that the office is reportedly investigating Pulte's own alleged misconduct; the office's letter does not address that. On September 11, 2025, House Financial Services Committee ranking member Rep. Maxine Waters led House Democrats in a letter asking FHFA's own inspector general (distinct from the GAO investigation documented below) to review whether Pulte complied with applicable federal and agency rules in obtaining, reviewing, and publicly releasing Cook's mortgage records; in a CNBC interview around the same time, Pulte acknowledged he had received a "tip" prompting the referral but declined to disclose its source. On November 17, 2025, eight Senate Democrats led by Elizabeth Warren formally requested a GAO investigation; GAO confirmed on December 4, 2025 that it had accepted the request and opened a formal investigation into whether Pulte and FHFA employees misused federal authority and resources, and has stated it expects to complete the review in late 2026 or early 2027. Separately, Rep. Eric Swalwell filed a civil lawsuit against Pulte on November 25, 2025, alleging Pulte violated the Privacy Act of 1974 by accessing his mortgage records for political purposes; that suit was dismissed without prejudice on March 20, 2026 after DOJ never acted on the underlying referral -- Swalwell's team characterized this as "calling his bluff" rather than a vindication of Pulte's conduct, and the suit can be refiled. A federal grand jury in Maryland has also reportedly been used to scrutinize how the Schiff mortgage-fraud probe run by Pulte and DOJ official Ed Martin was handled: a witness subpoena asked about anyone "claiming to be working for or at the direction" of the Justice Department, Martin or Pulte, apparently examining whether the team improperly deputized outsiders to aid the Schiff investigation, and a related DOJ review examined whether grand jury material from the Schiff and James inquiries had been illegally shared with unauthorized people. In February 2026, at least two sources told CNN the review found Martin -- who worked with Pulte on the Schiff referral -- improperly handled grand jury material; one source said the department found he shared secret grand jury material in the Schiff case and initially denied it to department leaders before emails showed otherwise. CNN's sources said the finding was at least part of the reason Martin was pushed out of DOJ headquarters; he had been removed as head of DOJ's Weaponization Working Group on January 1, 2026. The Maryland probe's status as to Pulte remains unconfirmed, and Attorney General Bondi has publicly denied any investigation into Pulte. In September 2026, the Wall Street Journal reported, as relayed by Talking Points Memo and Deadline Detroit, that Pulte had also examined mortgage information of Todd Blanche, now attorney general, while Blanche was deputy attorney general and the two were clashing over the mortgage investigations; according to the Journal's account, some officials believed Pulte had been trying to collect information on Blanche and others to undermine them and pressure them to more quickly pursue the investigations. A lawyer for Pulte said "any statement that Director Pulte examined or reviewed" Blanche's mortgage files was false, FHFA and Justice Department representatives called the story an attempt to drive a wedge between the two men, and a Justice Department spokeswoman said Blanche has a single mortgage of his own and cosigned a loan on a home owned by his son. A Virginia grand jury declined on December 4, 2025 to return a new indictment against James after her October indictment was dismissed over Halligan's unlawful appointment -- a second, independent rejection of that referral. Reuters reported Pulte's own father and stepmother, Mark and Julie Pulte, had since 2020 claimed homestead tax exemptions -- the same category of exemption underlying his fraud accusation against Cook -- on residences in both Bloomfield Township, Michigan and Florida simultaneously; eight tax and real estate experts told Reuters such dual exemptions are typically permissible only in a narrow exception for spouses living entirely independent lives, which did not appear to apply here. After Reuters's inquiries, Bloomfield Township's director of assessing said the township would revoke the exemption on the Pultes' Michigan residence. No charges had been brought against Pulte, James, Schiff, or Cook as of that point, though a related case over Cook's attempted removal, Trump v. Cook, reached the Supreme Court, which ruled June 29, 2026 that she may remain in her position pending that litigation. Pulte's June 2026 appointment as Acting Director of National Intelligence, while retaining his FHFA role, was challenged as potentially violating the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, since the statute states the Principal Deputy DNI "shall" (not "may") act when the position is vacant, and a qualified, available person -- Aaron Lukas, a career intelligence officer -- held that position. The Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as DNI on July 28, 2026, ending the dual-role arrangement months earlier than the January 26, 2027 ceiling the FVRA's 210-day acting-service limit would otherwise have allowed. Clayton was not sworn in for roughly a week after confirmation, during which Pulte continued acting as DNI -- including ordering further ODNI staff terminations -- which the Cato Institute's legal analysis says exceeded his FVRA authority the moment Clayton was confirmed, exposing those actions, including the terminations, to legal challenge. Sen. Warner has introduced legislation requiring Senate-confirmed acting DNIs in response to the episode.

Documented sequence connecting data access to subsequent political/public referral action against specifically named political opponents

Separate, distinct legal question: whether grand jury material was unlawfully disclosed (Fed. R. Crim. P. 6(e) secrecy requirements)
Separate civil claim: whether accessing and using Swalwell's mortgage records for the referral violated the Privacy Act of 1974

Lowell called the resignation demand and the house visit 'outside the bounds of DOJ and ethics rules' and a 'truly bizarre, made-for-media stunt.'
evidence.maps_to_element: Additional evidence the referral process was conducted as public political pressure rather than routine law enforcement

evidence.maps_to_element: A second, independent evidentiary rejection of the James referral -- a grand jury, not just a court on a procedural ground, declined to indict on the merits presented

evidence.description: The Government Accountability Office formally confirmed on December 4, 2025 that it had accepted a request from eight Senate Democrats (led by Elizabeth Warren) and opened an investigation into whether Pulte 'potentially misused federal authority and resources to publicly accuse prominent Democrats and President Trump's perceived political enemies of mortgage fraud'; GAO stated it would first need to determine the full scope and methodology of the review, meaning no completion timeline is available
evidence.maps_to_element: Formal nonpartisan investigation opened into the misuse-of-authority question

Eric Swalwell filed a civil lawsuit against Pulte on November 25, 2025, alleging Pulte 'abused his position by scouring databases at Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac... for the private mortgage records of several prominent Democrats' and violated the Privacy Act of 1974, which Swalwell's complaint says 'was designed to bar federal officials from leveraging their access to citizens' private information as a tool for harming their political opponents'

evidence.description: Federal prosecutors assembled a grand jury in Maryland to review the mortgage fraud allegations made against Schiff, in a probe involving Pulte and Justice Department official Ed Martin; a subpoena for a witness in the matter asked whether they dealt with anyone 'claiming to be working for or at the direction' of the Justice Department, Martin, or Pulte, apparently reviewing whether the team improperly deputized two figures outside the Justice Department to aid the Schiff investigation

Eric Swalwell and FHFA filed a joint stipulation on March 20, 2026 dismissing his Privacy Act lawsuit against Pulte without prejudice; Swalwell's spokesperson said the suit was dropped because DOJ never acted on Pulte's referral against him -- 'We called his bluff... He never brought it' -- meaning the dismissal reflects the referral's practical failure to produce charges, not a court finding that Pulte's conduct was lawful, and the suit can be refiled

evidence.description: At least two sources familiar with a DOJ internal review told CNN on February 4, 2026 that it found Ed Martin -- the DOJ official who worked alongside Pulte on the Schiff referral -- improperly handled grand jury material; one source said the department found Martin shared the secret grand jury material in the Schiff case and initially denied doing so when asked by department leaders, before emails surfaced showing he had. Martin has not been charged, and DOJ had not determined whether any law was broken; Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche told CNN 'there are no misconduct investigations into Ed Martin,' a statement that did not address whether there was ever a review of Martin's handling of grand jury material. Attorney General Pam Bondi, responding to a social media post about the related Maryland probe, wrote on X, 'There is no investigation into Bill Pulte'

Cook, allowing Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook to remain in her position while litigation over her attempted removal continues; Pulte publicly renewed his mortgage fraud allegations against Cook after the ruling, and as of this update Cook has still not been charged or indicted on any of Pulte's referred allegations, which she has called 'baseless'

evidence.maps_to_element: Resolves this entry's prior open-ended FVRA timeline question -- Pulte's dual role ended via Clayton's confirmation, not by reaching the statutory 210-day ceiling

evidence.description: Clayton was not sworn in until roughly a week after his July 28, 2026 Senate confirmation, during which Pulte continued exercising Acting DNI authority -- including ordering a further round of ODNI staff terminations described as an approximately 30% reduction. Cato Institute legal analysis concludes the FVRA's plain text ended Pulte's acting authority the moment Clayton was confirmed, not when he was sworn in, making everything Pulte did as acting DNI during that week -- including the terminations -- legally vulnerable to challenge; affected employees would have a strong argument they were never lawfully terminated.
evidence.maps_to_element: Documents a new, more concrete FVRA violation than this entry's prior speculative framing -- not merely a structural question about who should be acting DNI, but a specific legal analysis that Pulte exercised authority (including firing staff) after that authority had already lapsed

evidence.description: Talking Points Memo and Deadline Detroit, relaying a September 2026 Wall Street Journal report based on people familiar with the matter: Pulte examined mortgage information of Todd Blanche while Blanche was deputy attorney general and the two were clashing over the mortgage investigations of Trump foes; some officials believed Pulte had been trying to collect information on Blanche and others to undermine them and pressure them to more quickly pursue the investigations. A lawyer for Pulte said 'any statement that Director Pulte examined or reviewed' Blanche's mortgage files was false; FHFA and Justice Department representatives called the story an attempt to drive a wedge between the two men, and a Justice Department spokeswoman said Blanche has a single mortgage of his own and cosigned a loan on a home owned by his son.
evidence.maps_to_element: Extends the documented sequence of mortgage-data access aimed at specific people beyond named political opponents to a senior DOJ official who questioned the referrals -- reported on anonymous sourcing and denied by Pulte's lawyer

evidence.description: Letter of September 30, 2026 from James Hodge, Acting Principal Deputy Inspector General performing the duties of the FHFA Inspector General, to the chairs and ranking members of the Senate and House oversight, banking and financial services committees: FHFA's general counsel told the office on August 31, 2026 that its fiscal 2027 funding would be no more than $20 million (a 61.3% cut from its $51.7 million fiscal 2026 operating budget and 63.6% below the $55 million in the President's budget); the office expects to reduce staffing by approximately 70-80%, which 'will result in the discontinuance of essentially all criminal investigations conducted by our Office of Investigations,' and will cease supporting ongoing criminal investigations in more than 30 U.S. Attorney's offices. The letter says its special agent cadre has numbered around 40 agents plus three Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys, with more than 1,270 convictions and nearly $75 billion in monetary results since 2011, and that before fiscal 2027 FHFA had always funded the office's requested amount.
evidence.maps_to_element: Extends the documented pattern of the officials and offices that scrutinized Pulte's records access being removed or weakened, here the inspector general's office whose earlier findings were forwarded to prosecutors

evidence.maps_to_element: Congressional oversight response to the inspector-general budget cut

evidence.description: Joint statement of October 1, 2026 by congressional Democratic leaders including Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, Dick Durbin, Elizabeth Warren and Maxine Waters: Pulte was 'shutting down the independent watchdog that is responsible for investigating his misconduct,' the cut would likely result in 'the firing of approximately 40 law enforcement personnel who protect families from mortgage fraud,' and he 'should resign.'
evidence.maps_to_element: Congressional leaders' response to the inspector-general budget cut; the link to Pulte's own conduct is the lawmakers' characterization, not a finding

Government Executive reported that the former acting FHFA inspector general was removed in 2025, reportedly after he shared information with the prosecutors investigating Letitia James and was planning to tell Congress the agency was not cooperating with inspector-general investigators.

Maxine Waters led a September 11, 2025 letter asking FHFA's own inspector general to review Pulte's compliance with agency rules in the Cook mortgage-records matter; Pulte separately acknowledged on CNBC he acted on an anonymous 'tip' he declined to identify
evidence.maps_to_element: A distinct, earlier oversight request (FHFA's own IG) preceding the GAO investigation already documented, plus Pulte's own on-record refusal to identify his source

status: Ongoing: GAO's probe of Pulte's referrals and the grand-jury-leak question remain open, with no findings or charges against him. FHFA cut its watchdog's budget 61% from fiscal 2026, which the office says ends nearly all its criminal probes. Pulte's lawyer denies he examined Blanche's mortgages.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: FHFA has legitimate regulatory authority to investigate mortgage fraud, the referrals were based on genuine documentary discrepancies in primary-residence declarations, and pursuing fraud regardless of the political prominence of the subject is appropriate regulatory diligence, not targeting. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung has separately defended Pulte publicly, calling him one of Trump's 'most loyal and important advisors' and dismissing scrutiny as a 'pathetic attempt to distract' from the administration's work. On the inspector general's budget, FHFA's defense is fiscal: it says the office's funding request equaled about 16% of the agency's operating budget, against roughly 2% for a typical inspector general, and that it "fully supports the independence and mission" of the office.
comeback: Legitimate fraud enforcement doesn't typically follow the specific pattern documented here: accessing a sitting Federal Reserve Governor's personal mortgage records the day before publicly announcing a referral against her, then removing the internal officials -- an ethics officer, a general counsel, an inspector general -- who scrutinized how those records were obtained. That last point strengthens the case considerably: it's one thing to defend the referrals themselves, but removing the people who raised internal questions about the process looks like consciousness of a problem worth suppressing, not confidence in a clean process. The outcome of the James referral closes the argument on evidentiary quality: indicted, then dismissed for an unlawful prosecutor appointment. And the pattern across James, Schiff, Cook, and Swalwell -- all named political opponents of the president -- is too consistent, and now the subject of a formal, nonpartisan GAO inquiry, to support a 'neutral enforcement' framing. The peer-ratio defense of the inspector-general cut ignores what the office says sets it apart: it is the main law-enforcement body for mortgage fraud in a market of more than $7.8 trillion in Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac assets, its budget method had been accepted since 2011, and the President's own budget had proposed $55 million for it. The office itself says the $20 million level ends essentially all of its criminal investigations, which sits badly with Pulte's own stated priority of fighting mortgage fraud.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] AP reporting ('How Bill Pulte Learned the Art of the Attack, From His Own Family to Letitia James') traces a consistent personal behavioral pattern from Pulte's family litigation (PulteGroup, 2021-2022) through the FHFA referrals, characterized as 'identify an adversary, deploy institutional authority as a weapon, publicize aggressively, and treat procedural and legal constraints as obstacles rather than rules.' What changed when he arrived at FHFA was the institutional power available -- and what changed again with his June 2026 appointment as Acting DNI, which formally ended with Jay Clayton's July 28, 2026 confirmation, was the scale of intelligence data accessible to someone operating with that documented pattern. The later record fits the same pattern: referrals sent around FHFA's own inspector-general process straight to Trump-aligned DOJ prosecutors, the Fannie Mae and FHFA officials who looked into his records access pushed out, the FHFA inspector general's office itself then funded at a level it says ends its criminal investigations (echoing the administration's wider removal of inspectors general), and roughly a week of continuing to act as DNI after Clayton's confirmation, including further ODNI staff terminations, that the Cato Institute's legal analysis says exceeded his FVRA authority. The referrals also fed the James prosecution and what CNN's sources describe as Ed Martin's grand-jury leak, and figured in the fight over Cook's attempted removal. The September 2026 report that he also examined Blanche's mortgages while the two clashed over the cases, which his lawyer denies, would extend the same method to a senior official inside the administration.

official: William (Bill) Pulte, Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency
offense_category: Installing an Unvetted Personal Loyalist With a Vacated Felony Sex-Offense Conviction and Pending Pardon-Bribery Allegations as a Consultant Inside Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
incident_summary: Mark Zarkin, a Michigan restaurateur (owner of Steven Lelli's On The Green in Farmington Hills) and prominent Detroit-area Trump fundraiser with no documented housing-finance experience, was appointed by FHFA Director Bill Pulte as a consultant to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac after Pulte took office in March 2025. Six sources confirmed the role to Reuters, and Reuters found Zarkin still held an active Freddie Mac email account identifying him as a 'consultant' as recently as the weeks before publication. **In 1999, Zarkin pleaded no contest to attempted third-degree sexual conduct in Macomb County, Michigan, after investigators recovered his DNA during a pelvic examination of a woman who was underage and 'mentally incapacitated' by alcohol and Valium; he was sentenced to eight months in jail, three years' probation, and mandatory sex-offender registration.** In 2009, a judge granted his attorney's petition to vacate that conviction, reasoning Zarkin had not understood the registry requirement when he accepted the plea -- even though court records show registration was explicitly part of the original plea agreement, and the judge's order gave no further explanation; legal experts told Reuters the vacatur was 'unusual.' Separately, an ongoing 2025 Wayne County, Michigan lawsuit alleges Zarkin discussed with Jamiel Altaheri, the recently resigned Hamtramck police chief, a scheme to pay Trump as much as $5 million for a pardon of an unnamed New York associate accused of financial crimes; two plaintiffs, a former city manager and a former police officer, allege they lost their jobs partly for disclosing the plan. Zarkin denied everything by text message to Reuters, stating 'I have never been employed by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. I also have no criminal record. Anything you say to the contrary is defamatory.' Pulte called Reuters' questions 'filled with completely false and defamatory statements' without elaborating, and FHFA's media office issued an unsigned statement calling 'nearly all' of Reuters' statements 'false, misleading, or defamatory,' also without specifics; Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
elements_required: The FHFA director installed a personal ally with no documented housing-finance credentials as a consultant inside the two federally regulated mortgage giants

That individual has a documented felony sex-offense conviction, later vacated under circumstances legal experts characterized as unusual, contradicting the individual's own denial of any criminal record
That same individual is separately named, in a pending lawsuit, in an alleged scheme to pay the president millions of dollars for a pardon -- a serious, though as-yet-unproven, allegation

The responsible official (Pulte) and the individual both issued blanket denials without addressing Reuters' specific documented findings (the Freddie Mac email, the court records, the vacatur circumstances)

evidence.description: Reuters' exclusive investigation, based on six sources and Zarkin's own active Freddie Mac email, documents his appointment, his 1999 conviction and its 2009 vacatur (with the court's own records showing registration was originally part of the plea, contradicting the vacatur's stated rationale), the Wayne County pardon-bribery lawsuit's specific allegations, and on-the-record denials from Zarkin, Pulte, and FHFA's media office

offense_category: Fifth Amendment due-process violation and agency-regulation noncompliance -- terminating federal officers without the internal appeal and reassignment process their own employment regulations require (a procedural/administrative-law claim, not itself an allegation that DEIA work was unlawful)
status: Blocked by courts -- the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed (2-1, July 2, 2026) a preliminary injunction requiring CIA and ODNI to give the 19 plaintiff-officers an internal appeal/reassignment process before any termination; the officers remain on paid administrative leave pending that process, and no final termination has taken effect as of this entry's last verification
incident_summary: Following Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order rolling back federal DEIA programs, CIA Director John Ratcliffe moved to terminate 51 career CIA officers who were on temporary rotational assignments to diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility (DEIA) programs, and ODNI under Director Tulsi Gabbard took parallel action against DEIA-assigned officers there. Ratcliffe publicly defended the move as building a 'colorblind meritocracy' focused solely on merit-based hiring and promotion; the New York Times reported May 13, 2025 that this was the first public clash between career intelligence officers and Trump's new spy-agency leadership over the DEIA rollback. Seventeen CIA officers and two ODNI officers (19 total) sued in February 2025, arguing the terminations violated their due-process rights and the agencies' own employment regulations, since the DEIA rotational assignments did not strip the officers of their permanent career positions or the reduction-in-force protections (appeal rights, consideration for other jobs) those positions carry. In late March 2025, Senior U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga (E.D. Va., a George W. Bush appointee) issued a preliminary injunction barring the government from implementing the terminations, finding what Ratcliffe attempted functioned as a reduction in force triggering the officers' regulatory appeal and reassignment rights, and ordered the plaintiffs kept on paid administrative leave pending further proceedings. The government appealed. **On July 2, 2026, a divided panel of the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed Trenga's injunction 2-1; writing for the majority, Judge Nicole Berner held that CIA and ODNI had to honor the officers' Fifth Amendment due-process protections and follow their own existing regulations -- providing an internal appeal process and an opportunity for reassignment -- before terminating them, regardless of the CIA Director's broader statutory hiring/firing authority.** Judge Paul Niemeyer dissented, arguing the ruling improperly constrained that authority. The panel's opinion also included pointed criticism of the government's legal arguments on appeal as beside the point.
elements_required: The affected officers held permanent career positions carrying Fifth Amendment due-process protections and/or agency reduction-in-force regulations (appeal rights, reassignment consideration), distinct from their temporary DEIA rotational assignments
The agencies attempted to terminate them without affording the internal appeal and reassignment process those protections/regulations require
A court (not just the plaintiffs) found the process afforded was legally deficient

Fired CDC Director Susan Monarez told senators in August 2025 that Kennedy had instructed her to meet with Siri, though she ultimately did not do so. Siri's law firm has pursued a specific-interest advocacy through vaccine-exemption litigation (partnering with West Virginia's governor in June 2024 on a religious-exemption lawsuit against the state's Board of Education, followed by HHS itself issuing reminders to states in September 2024 to respect religious exemptions), a December 2024 FDA petition to withdraw or suspend the standalone polio vaccine, multiple lawsuits against children's toothpaste makers over fluoride content, and a 12-page FDA petition demanding strengthened pregnancy warnings on Tylenol's label -- filed roughly two weeks before President Trump's September 22, 2025 address linking Tylenol use in pregnancy to autism, with Siri's firm having separately encouraged clients as early as 2023 to file Tylenol-autism litigation while related cases were pending. **Siri's nonprofit client, the Informed Consent Action Network (run by Del Bigtree, Kennedy's former campaign communications director), has funneled substantial funding to Siri's firm -- $6 million in 2023 alone and roughly $13 million total since 2018 -- meaning Siri has a direct financial stake in the same anti-vaccine legal and policy landscape he has helped shape from inside the department vetting process.** Legal-ethics expert Elizabeth Chamblee Burch said the arrangement raises 'insider influence' concerns about whether HHS decisions are 'backed by hard science and research' or shaped by Siri's outside interests. official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Administrative Procedure Act Violation — Arbitrary and Capricious Agency Action (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A)) — preliminary judicial finding (likelihood of success) actually obtained against the agency's vaccine-advisory decisions; this is civil administrative law, not a criminal matter; separately, the CDC director's firing raises whistleblower-retaliation-adjacent concerns not yet tested in litigation
incident_summary:
Kennedy fired all 17 sitting members of the CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) on June 9, 2025, replacing them with eight new appointees, several with anti-vaccine ties; one appointee withdrew before the panel's first meeting, leaving seven members ahead of a vote on thimerosal. Ousted members and outside groups warned the shake-up, combined with concurrent CDC staff cuts, would weaken U.S. immunization infrastructure; insurers largely stayed silent on whether they would keep covering vaccines the new panel might drop, with only one major insurer committing to continued coverage as of early July 2025. Kennedy's appointees included Vicky Pebsworth -- a nurse who has long claimed, contrary to scientific consensus, that vaccines caused her son's autism -- and the CDC separately hired Lyn Redwood, former head of Kennedy's own Children's Health Defense organization, to advise its vaccine safety office and present to the reconstituted ACIP. On July 23, 2025, HHS ended U.S. distribution of thimerosal-containing flu vaccines, citing decades-old, scientifically unsupported claims linking the preservative to autism despite FDA assurances to the contrary. On July 30, 2025, the panel's own ousted former members publicly condemned the purge in a New England Journal of Medicine commentary warning that Kennedy and his new panel were abandoning rigorous scientific review and open deliberation. The next day, federal health officials told major medical associations, including the AMA and American Academy of Pediatrics, by email that their experts were being removed from ACIP's vaccine-policy workgroups.

CDC Director Susan Monarez -- Senate-confirmed only weeks earlier -- was ousted on August 27, 2025; the White House said she was terminated after refusing to resign, and her lawyers said she had been targeted after she "refused to rubber-stamp unscientific, reckless directives and fire dedicated health experts." At least three other senior CDC leaders, including chief medical officer Debra Houry, resigned in protest, amid broader turmoil at an agency already hit by mass layoffs and by Kennedy's May 2025 rollback of COVID-19 vaccine guidance for healthy children and pregnant women; HHS's fiscal 2026 budget proposal would have left CDC's budget 42% below its fiscal 2024 level. Former Principal Deputy Director Anne Schuchat warned the loss of experienced leadership left the country "really at risk." Nine former CDC directors from both parties, in a New York Times op-ed, said Kennedy's actions were "endangering every American's health," and more than 20 medical organizations together with over 1,000 current and former HHS employees separately called for his resignation. Dr. Jeanne Marrazzo, former head of NIH's infectious disease institute, filed a whistleblower complaint with the Office of Special Counsel alleging she had been removed from her post in retaliation for objecting to the administration's hostility toward vaccines and its abrupt cancellation of grants and clinical trials. Even former Trump Surgeon General Jerome Adams called for Kennedy's firing. Sen. Bill Cassidy -- whose vote had been decisive in confirming Kennedy -- had said on August 28 that the panel's September meeting should not occur until significant oversight had been conducted and that, if it proceeded, any recommendations made should be rejected as lacking legitimacy. At a September 4, 2025 Senate Finance Committee hearing, where Kennedy was grilled by both Democrats and Republicans, Sen. Maria Cantwell called him a "charlatan" over his cancellation of $500 million in mRNA vaccine research. Acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill, installed after Monarez's ouster, told staff the agency needed to end "mission creep" and practice "radical transparency" -- language Kennedy had also used days earlier in his own Wall Street Journal op-ed arguing the CDC should be limited to infectious-disease work. Separately, HHS lawyers themselves objected, fearing a violation of the Federal Advisory Committee Act, when CDC rules gave MIT professor and vaccine critic Retsef Levi sweeping authority -- setting agendas, appointing members, shaping recommendations -- over a CDC COVID-vaccine workgroup. In a parallel purge at the FDA, vaccine expert and Kennedy critic Paul Offit was dropped from the FDA's Vaccines and Related Biological Products Advisory Committee (VRBPAC) in late August 2025 after HHS held up, and never approved, his paperwork for a further term through 2027 that a senior FDA official had asked him to serve; HHS said his term had expired. At a September 17, 2025 Senate HELP Committee hearing, Monarez testified that Kennedy had directed her to commit in advance to approving every ACIP recommendation regardless of the scientific evidence, and former CDC Chief Medical Officer Debra Houry testified that CDC's leaders had been expected to serve as "rubber stamps for the Secretary's decisions," amid what was then the worst measles outbreak in 30 years; Houry later told the Guardian that Kennedy's changes represented "a hostile takeover of the agency."

The reconstituted panel's own votes began in September 2025: on September 18, 2025 the panel voted 8-3 to drop the recommendation that children under four receive the combined MMRV vaccine rather than separate shots, and the next day voted to downgrade COVID-19 vaccination for adults and children from routine to "shared clinical decision-making." Through the fall, a new ACIP workgroup began examining vaccine timing and ingredients including aluminum, with Robert Malone and allies pushing to delay the newborn hepatitis B vaccine. In December 2025, Kennedy elevated Martin Kulldorff to a senior HHS science role and Kirk Milhoan, a pediatric cardiologist already on the panel, became ACIP's chair; after the panel's December meeting, at which it changed the universal newborn hepatitis B recommendation, Milhoan was heard comparing its members to "puppets on a string." In a podcast released January 22, 2026, Milhoan suggested the public might reconsider polio vaccines, pushed back on the assertion that vaccines have been proven to reduce the spread of polio and measles, and described the old schedule's approach as "heavy-handed, authoritarian" -- the immediate policy backdrop for the March 16, 2026 ruling below.

Medical and public-health organizations led by the American Academy of Pediatrics, joined by individual patients, had sued in federal court in Massachusetts in July 2025 and later expanded the case to challenge Kennedy's dismissal of ACIP's existing members and their replacement with appointees critical of or lacking expertise in vaccines; Judge Brian E. Murphy denied the government's motion to dismiss on January 6, 2026. On March 16, 2026, **a federal judge stayed the appointments of 13 Kennedy-appointed ACIP members and every vote the panel had taken, finding the government disregarded the scientific methods built into ACIP's procedures** -- a preliminary ruling that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their Administrative Procedure Act claims, and the strongest documented legal finding in this entry. The same ruling said the newly appointed members "appear distinctly unqualified" for a committee dedicated to vaccines. Monarez's August 2025 firing, described above, is not itself the subject of confirmed litigation. Internal HHS emails later released by Sen. Bernie Sanders showed Kennedy directly ordering the CDC to pull flu vaccine ad campaigns and restrict vaccine access. Separate reduction-in-force-related litigation over the broader CDC staff cuts is ongoing, and no criminal charges have been filed in connection with any of the conduct this entry documents.

As a direct consequence of the March 16, 2026 ruling, planned federal guidance for that fall's flu and COVID-19 vaccines was left in limbo; with CDC still lacking a Senate-confirmed director as of late March 2026 (a gap that ended with Erica Schwartz's August 5, 2026 confirmation; tracked separately in this database) and core ACIP advisory functions effectively frozen by the ruling, doctors quoted by NBC News warned that routine public health guidance-setting was grinding to a halt at a time when clear guidance for the upcoming respiratory-illness season was needed. HHS published notice of a revised ACIP charter on April 6, 2026 in response to the litigation. DOJ filed a notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on April 29, 2026 (No. 26-1503). On May 1, 2026, the district court denied defendants' April 23 motion to stay proceedings pending the appeal. In response to the ruling's preliminary finding that his ACIP appointees appeared unqualified and the panel was likely unlawfully reconstituted, Kennedy moved to rewrite ACIP's own membership charter, broadening the eligibility criteria for panel membership in a way that makes it easier to appoint members without traditional vaccine expertise -- addressing the court's specific finding by changing the rules governing who can qualify, rather than by appointing more conventionally credentialed members under the existing rules. The March 16, 2026 order stayed the January 2026 CDC memo that had cut back the childhood immunization schedule, putting the earlier schedule back in effect, and stayed every vote the reconstituted ACIP had taken since June 2025, including the thimerosal vote, the downgrade of COVID-19 vaccination to shared clinical decision-making and the removal of the universal hepatitis B birth-dose recommendation (the memo itself had cut routinely recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, limiting or downgrading shots including hepatitis A, meningococcal, rotavirus and influenza); it declined preliminary relief against Kennedy's May 2025 directive dropping COVID-19 vaccine recommendations for healthy children and pregnant women. CDC published a Federal Register notice on May 19, 2026 (announced May 18) withdrawing the April 6 notice, citing an administrative error in meeting the Federal Advisory Committee Act's revised public-notification timing requirements, and, because the charter had lapsed, formally re-establishing ACIP under the replacement charter dated May 14, with the revised charter expanding eligible member expertise and reorienting the committee's duties toward vaccine safety and evidence gaps. A related but legally distinct action, documented separately in this tracker: Trump's May 29, 2026 executive order directing CDC/ACIP toward a specific reduced vaccine count -- a presidential directive over policy content, not a claim about this ACIP panel's legal composition. The First Circuit granted the government's motion to expedite briefing on June 16, 2026.

Defendants' reply brief in the First Circuit appeal (No. 26-1503) was due July 27, 2026. Defendants had not initially requested oral argument, but on August 14, 2026 they asked the First Circuit to calendar argument at the earliest available date or decide the appeal on the briefs; the court ordered argument for the next available date, and it was set for October 6, 2026. In the district court, Judge Murphy heard defendants' second motion to stay proceedings on July 23, 2026 and granted a stay until September 3, 2026, canceling the August 18 hearing on plaintiffs' July 17 motion to complete the administrative records. Defendants moved on September 3 to extend the stay, and on September 11, 2026 the court stayed the case until the First Circuit issues its decision; the March 16 order remains in place in the meantime.

rebuttal_anticipated: [DRAFT] Likely defense: the Secretary has statutory authority to oversee and direct agency policy, including vaccine guidance and personnel decisions; disagreement with the science doesn't make the process unlawful, and the judge's ruling addressed a specific panel's composition/process, not Kennedy's broader authority to set department direction.
comeback: [DRAFT - needs your input] A federal judge didn't rule that Kennedy has the wrong opinion on vaccines -- that would be a policy disagreement, not a legal one. The ruling was specifically that the government had 'disregarded' the scientific, legally codified methods by which ACIP decisions had long been made 'and thereby undermined the integrity of its actions,' a procedural and evidentiary failure, which is exactly the kind of arbitrary-and-capricious finding APA exists to catch. The internal emails showing direct, paid-campaign-cancelling control over CDC messaging -- not high-level policy direction, but day-to-day operational control over specific public health communications -- is hard to characterize as ordinary secretarial oversight.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Reporting (NYT, cited via MS NOW) suggests Kennedy is largely disengaged from routine departmental management generally, while exercising unusually direct and granular control specifically over vaccine-related messaging and personnel -- suggesting the underlying cause isn't a coherent administrative philosophy but a narrow, personally-motivated override of the area where his pre-existing activist commitments conflict most directly with the agency's institutional expertise. The entry's own record fits that reading: Kennedy fired the CDC director after she resisted his efforts to control vaccine guidance (see the CDC leadership-vacancy entry), and answered the court's preliminary finding that his ACIP appointees appeared unqualified by broadening the charter's eligibility rules rather than appointing conventionally credentialed members. A related but legally distinct presidential directive over vaccine-schedule content is tracked in the Trump childhood-vaccine executive order entry.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence. This entry rests on actual federal court rulings, read directly on the docket (American Academy of Pediatrics v. Kennedy, D. Mass. No. 1:25-cv-11916): the January 6, 2026 denial of the government's motion to dismiss, and the March 16, 2026 preliminary ruling that plaintiffs were likely to succeed in showing the ACIP reconstitution and the January 2026 schedule changes violated the APA, which stayed the 13 appointments and all of the reconstituted panel's votes and described the new members as appearing "distinctly unqualified." These are preliminary findings, not a final judgment; the government's appeal is pending in the First Circuit (argument set for October 6, 2026). Internal HHS emails released by Sen. Sanders add direct evidence of ministerial control over CDC messaging. The June 2025-January 2026 antecedent chronology (the ACIP purge and replacement appointees, Redwood and Pebsworth, the thimerosal decision, the workgroup expulsions, the Monarez ouster and its fallout, the Levi and Offit personnel actions, the September 2025 votes, Kulldorff's move to HHS and Milhoan's elevation to chair) rests mainly on major-outlet reporting, some of it paywalled. HHS's own remedial charter notice was withdrawn for missing a basic procedural requirement (Federal Register, May 19, 2026), a second documented procedural failure in the same area.
