offense_category: Embedding a disciplined, non-credentialed conspiracy promoter in a federal vaccine-safety data role, combined with a broken transparency commitment to Congress -- no criminal charge; this is an accountability/transparency claim
incident_summary: HHS hired David Geier -- a longtime promoter of the debunked vaccine-autism link who was disciplined by Maryland regulators for practicing medicine without a license and has never held a medical license -- as a 'senior data analyst' with access to the CDC's Vaccine Safety Datalink. The hiring was first reported on March 25, 2025 by the Washington Post, followed by NBC News and the New York Times, which reported that he was brought on to work on a study reexamining the debunked vaccine-autism link. House Energy and Commerce Committee Democrats formally opened an inquiry into the hiring on April 10, 2025, and the Autistic Self Advocacy Network and other disability-rights and public-health groups condemned the appointment. At a May 14, 2025 Senate hearing, Kennedy said Geier had not been hired to run autism research but to review Vaccine Safety Datalink records, and that he had been hired by an independent contractor rather than as an HHS employee. **At a September 4, 2025 Senate Finance Committee hearing, Kennedy told Sen. Ben Ray Luján that Geier's study protocols 'are public,' but Luján's April 1, 2026 letter said that after a diligent search and a request to HHS staff, the protocols had not been produced or identified anywhere in the public domain.** On September 8, 2025, days after that hearing, Trump shared a decades-old video on Truth Social featuring David Geier and his father Mark Geier discussing their discredited vaccine-autism claims, amplifying the same figures at the presidential level while David Geier remained at HHS. At an April 22, 2026 Senate Finance Committee hearing, Kennedy said Geier is a contract employee reporting to the CDC, agreed to give senators Geier's contract and its scope by that Friday, and said he could not share the protocols governing Geier's work because they did not exist yet, promising them once the work was complete. In a May 21, 2026 Mother Jones report, a Luján spokesperson said HHS had still not provided the contract or anything related.

incident_summary:
Gavin de Becker, a celebrity security adviser, served as Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s security adviser during his 2024 presidential campaign and was a major donor to a super PAC backing that campaign, The Daily Beast reported. In 2025, the year Kennedy became Secretary of Health and Human Services, **de Becker gave him free flights to and from Fiji and Greece and the use of a vacation home in Washington, D.C., gifts that Kennedy's own annual financial disclosure valued at more than a quarter of a million dollars** -- nearly $97,000 for roundtrip flights to Fiji, where de Becker owns a compound, and almost $45,000 for a roundtrip to Greece, according to The Wall Street Journal's reporting on the 2025 gifts as relayed by Mediaite and MS NOW; the filing values use of the D.C. home at $126,500. De Becker also wrote a book, Forbidden Facts, published by Skyhorse Publishing, alleging government suppression of information about brain damage from childhood vaccines.

The same disclosure showed that Kennedy received two book advances of $2 million apiece from Skyhorse Publishing in the past year, while serving as secretary, against a secretary's salary of around $250,000. Skyhorse has published his earlier books and paid him $451,000 in consulting fees the year before he joined HHS; one of the new books will be called Unsettled Science, and the filing states that two of the three books in the Skyhorse agreement were completed before he entered government service. In his ethics agreement Kennedy had pledged not to engage in any writing, editing or promotional activities associated with his Skyhorse books while in office, yet in July 2026 he posted on X about his 2021 Skyhorse book, The Real Anthony Fauci, which NPR described as defying that agreement.

The filing itself was late: due May 15, 2026, it was filed August 13 after an extension, revised four times in September, and signed by an HHS ethics official on September 17. NPR reported that HHS ethics officials had approved it but the separate Office of Government Ethics had not yet signed off. The Wall Street Journal obtained the amended filing through a records request and reported the gifts in mid-September, and NPR reported on the filing on September 22 and 24.

HHS said Kennedy "complies with all applicable federal ethics laws, regulations, and financial disclosure requirements" and works with career HHS ethics officials to disclose his gifts and outside activities. De Becker told NPR that Kennedy is "my closest friend in the world for many years," that their families vacation together every year, that the gifts began "years before he was at HHS," and that "I have nothing whatsoever to do with HHS in any regard." Virginia Canter of Democracy Defenders Fund told NPR the gifts and advances were so large that they raise the question of a prohibited "supplementation of salary," and asked whether de Becker gives such gifts to all his friends or only to Kennedy; Washington University law professor Kathleen Clark called it "very weird" that Kennedy accepted $4 million in advances for two books he had promised not to write or edit while secretary.

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., HHS Secretary
offense_category: Announcing That a Presidential Commission Would Investigate the Childhood Vaccine Schedule Despite Prior Assurances Not to Undermine Vaccine Confidence -- an institutional-credibility and consistency claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: On February 13, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14212 creating the President's Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Commission, with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as its chair. On February 18, 2025, Kennedy told HHS staff in a closed-door meeting that the new commission would scrutinize the childhood vaccine schedule, along with electromagnetic radiation, glyphosate and other pesticides, ultra-processed foods, SSRIs and other psychiatric drugs, PFAS and microplastics, as possible causes of the country's chronic disease epidemic; 'nothing is going to be off limits,' he said, according to a video viewed by The Hill. The remarks drew scrutiny because they came despite assurances Kennedy had given during his confirmation process that he would not seek to undermine public confidence in existing, well-established vaccines. Kennedy's statement is the earliest-dated action in what became a documented, escalating chain of vaccine-policy actions this tracker follows separately in later entries -- including a January 2026 immunization-schedule overhaul and the May 2026 Executive Order 14407 realigning the childhood vaccine schedule based on a December 2025 HHS assessment. The commission's own first deliverable undercut its credibility on release. Its 'Make America Healthy Again' assessment report, published in late May 2025, **was found by NOTUS, which first reported the problems on May 29, 2025, to cite at least seven sources that do not appear to exist, plus other citations that misrepresented real studies' findings; ABC News, Rolling Stone and PolitiFact followed, and experts quoted by PolitiFact said the nonexistent titles were a hallmark of AI-generated citations. Dr. Katherine Keyes, cited as the first author of a paper on teen depression and anxiety during the pandemic, told NOTUS and ABC News she never wrote it; the American Academy of Pediatrics and JAMA Pediatrics both told ABC News they could not locate certain cited papers in their own publications.** White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt attributed the errors to 'some formatting issues' while stating the administration had 'complete confidence' in Kennedy's team. On June 2, 2025, Rep. Stephen Lynch, the House Oversight Committee's acting ranking Democrat, sent Kennedy a letter demanding information on how the report was drafted, reviewed, published and later amended, including whether AI was used. At a June 24, 2025 House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing, Kennedy called the fabricated citations 'wrong' and a 'mistake,' said he had not personally fact-checked the report, and maintained that its 'foundational assertions' were accurate.

incident_summary: On August 17, 2026, **according to people cited by The Washington Post, an Air Force-operated Gulfstream jet flew HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from the Washington, D.C. area to Des Moines, Iowa, arriving hours ahead of his first scheduled event. The Defense Department charges roughly $9,000 per hour to operate that aircraft, compared with approximately $250 for a commercial ticket on the same route under the government's own discount travel program.** During the trip, Kennedy appeared alongside Republican candidates in contested 2026 midterm races -- Rep. Internally, Chris Klomp, Trump's nominee for HHS deputy secretary, questioned whether military-jet use was necessary on at least one other occasion; Kennedy agreed with the concern and opted not to use a jet for that trip, indicating the department itself recognized the practice as discretionary rather than operationally required.

offense_category: False Statement to Congress (potential concern under 18 U.S.C. §1001 if made with knowledge of falsity; not charged, no criminal referral identified) -- misrepresenting a specific constituent's documented medical circumstances to deflect accountability for NIH staffing cuts
incident_summary: At a May 14, 2025 Senate hearing, Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA) confronted HHS Secretary Kennedy with the case of her constituent Natalie Phelps, a Bainbridge Island mother of two with stage IV colorectal cancer enrolled in an NIH Clinical Center immunotherapy trial. Murray said Phelps's own NIH doctors had told her twice that her treatment was being delayed roughly four weeks because of NIH staffing cuts from the reduction-in-force, and asked Kennedy for a personal update within 24 hours. Following a recess, **Kennedy told the committee Phelps had actually been found 'medically ineligible' for the trial and that her situation had nothing to do with the RIF, adding that NIH was trying to place her in a different trial instead. Murray immediately and directly disputed this on the record, stating Phelps was already enrolled in the trial -- eligibility was not in question** -- and that the delay was a care-delivery problem, not an eligibility determination, per Phelps's own doctors' statements to her twice.
elements_required: A specific, checkable factual claim was made to Congress by a Cabinet secretary (Phelps's 'medical ineligibility') that is capable of being true or false, not mere rhetorical spin
The claim directly contradicts a first-hand account -- the patient's own doctors, relayed by the senator who had spoken with the patient directly -- rather than only a policy disagreement
The claim served to deflect responsibility for a specific, documented harm (a cancer patient's treatment delay) attributable to the secretary's own department's staffing reduction
No public correction or retraction from Kennedy or HHS was identified in reporting reviewed

official: Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Secretary of Health and Human Services
offense_category: Personal Financial Conflict of Interest in Pursuing Policy That Could Weaken Vaccine Manufacturers' Legal Liability Shield -- no criminal charge; an accountability claim regarding undisclosed/documented conflicts shaping federal health policy
incident_summary: AP reported a specific, named instance of the conflict this entry documents: in June 2025, HHS awarded a **$150,000 contract** to an Arizona law firm for "expertise" on the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), whose attorney Andrew Downing had a leading role in product-liability lawsuits against Merck over its Gardasil HPV vaccine, including claims of a rare movement disorder; Downing was listed in HHS's own staff directory for a time. In a podcast the year before joining the effort, Downing had criticized the VICP for taking "a hard line" against such cases, pushing attorneys like himself toward civil lawsuits instead -- the same civil-liability exposure this entry's central conflict concerns. On July 28, 2025, Kennedy announced in a post on X that he would overhaul the VICP, saying it "has devolved into a morass of inefficiency, favoritism, and outright corruption," and that, working with Attorney General Pam Bondi, "we will steer the Vaccine Court back to its original congressional intent" -- an announcement Reuters noted came after Kennedy had fired all 17 members of the CDC's vaccine advisory committee in June 2025 and replaced them with members including known vaccine skeptics. Kennedy is pursuing changes to the VICP -- a federal system Congress created in the 1980s, after lawsuits drove vaccine manufacturers out of the U.S. market, to provide no-fault compensation for rare, serious vaccine side effects and, in exchange, shield manufacturers from direct liability litigation. In January 2026, STAT News reported that Kennedy's slashing of the federally recommended childhood vaccine schedule, documented separately in this tracker, created new uncertainty about manufacturers' legal protections; HHS said the liability shield remained in place, but STAT reported that Kennedy's allies were hopeful the move opens the door to stripping vaccine makers of their liability shields -- a longtime aim of Kennedy's, which he pursued for years before joining the administration, as an attorney who represented plaintiffs in vaccine-injury lawsuits and, per this tracker's separately-documented measles entry, personally collected referral fees from such litigation. On January 27, 2026, Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Richard Blumenthal, Ed Markey, and Angela Alsobrooks sent Kennedy a formal letter raising conflict-of-interest concerns about his role overseeing VICP policy given this financial history and his ties to vaccine-injury lawyers, including Downing, whose firm's HHS contract, the letter said, grew from $150,000 in June 2025 to $400,000 by September 2025; they asked for answers by February 10, 2026. In March 2026, ProPublica noted that the program covers only immunizations the CDC recommends for routine administration to children or pregnant women, leaving shots moved to other categories open to injury lawsuits. ProPublica warned that if the liability shield collapses, manufacturers could exit the U.S. market as they did in the 1980s -- a risk with heightened stakes given the CDC's March 2026 warning that polio was circulating in 28 additional countries, and a diphtheria outbreak that began in Western Europe in 2022, the largest rise in cases there in 70 years. Merck agreed in June 2026 to pay about $50 million to settle more than 200 Gardasil product-liability lawsuits, including cases in which Kennedy had been an attorney of record before joining HHS and cases brought by Wisner Baum, the firm to which he had referred Gardasil plaintiffs and where his son Conor works. Separately, on a distinct legal track, on June 30, 2026 HHS announced that Kennedy had signed determinations terminating the COVID-19 emergency use authorization (EUA) declarations first issued in 2020, for drugs and biological products (effective June 29, 2027) and for medical devices (effective December 26, 2026), with HHS saying the circumstances that justified those emergency authorities no longer exist. HHS's announcement concerned the EUA declarations and did not address the separate PREP Act declaration that gives makers of COVID-19 countermeasures liability immunity; either way, this is a different mechanism from the VICP shield that is this entry's central subject. In a letter dated July 28, 2026, Sens. Warren, Alsobrooks, Blumenthal, and Andy Kim wrote to Kennedy about the Merck settlement, asking by August 11, 2026 whether he played any role in it, how many of the settled Gardasil cases he had referred to Wisner Baum, whether his son received his share of the fees, and how much money he has received from vaccine-injury lawsuits while serving as Secretary. Wisner Baum managing partner Brent Wisner told Reuters that "at no time" will Kennedy or his son receive fees from a Gardasil settlement. During his confirmation, Kennedy had initially said he would keep a 10% fee from Gardasil cases he referred to Wisner Baum; after Warren and other lawmakers raised conflict concerns, his February 1, 2025 amended ethics agreement said he would assign that stake to a non-dependent adult family member, which he told the Senate Finance Committee would be his adult son, and on May 12, 2025 he certified that he had completed the divestitures in his ethics agreement. In an August 1, 2026 post on X, Kennedy said that neither he nor anyone in his family had "received a penny" from the settlement and that before taking office he had "relinquished any interest in potential Gardasil fees back to the Wisner Baum law firm." On August 24, 2026, Sens. Warren, Wyden, Blumenthal, and Alsobrooks wrote that this statement suggested he had either modified his ethics agreement or strayed from it, noting that their staff found no amendment to his public financial disclosures or ethics documents reflecting a change, and asked for answers by September 9, 2026. In an August 25, 2026 reply on Kennedy's behalf, HHS Assistant Secretary for Legislation Gary Andres wrote that on February 11, 2025 Kennedy had irrevocably assigned his outstanding Gardasil contingency-fee interests directly to Wisner Baum rather than to a non-dependent adult family member, and that HHS's ethics official had reported his compliance with his ethics agreement on May 14, 2025. On September 24, 2026, the same four senators, noting that Kennedy was confirmed on February 13, 2025, two days after the change, wrote that the reply was, to their knowledge, the first disclosure to Congress of the change, called his apparent failure to report it to ethics officials "deeply alarming," questioned whether any agreement with Wisner Baum about future payments accompanied the transfer, and requested answers by October 8, 2026. HHS spokeswoman Emily G. Hilliard told the AP that HHS had confirmed Kennedy's compliance with his ethics agreement in May 2025 and said, "Any claim that Secretary Kennedy maintained a financial interest in this litigation after taking office is false." Separately, NPR reported on September 24, 2026 that Kennedy's latest annual financial disclosure listed a payment of nearly $7,000 from Wisner Baum, described as "final payment at termination of agreement of Referral Fees On Contingency Fee Case"; the firm told NPR the payment was not related to the Gardasil case and said Kennedy and his family had not received any fees recovered from the Gardasil cases. This Gardasil-specific dispute concerns a different, though related, category of vaccine-litigation financial interest than the VICP liability-shield policy conflict that is this entry's central subject.

official: Brooke Rollins, Secretary of Agriculture
offense_category: Potential First Amendment Establishment Clause Violation (government endorsement/coercion of religion) and related APA claims — active federal civil litigation (not criminal); filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California
incident_summary: USDA employees filed a lawsuit against Rollins over a series of escalating religious messages sent department-wide, culminating in an April 2026 Easter email referencing "sin," being "destroyed," and Christ's resurrection as "the foundation of our faith." The formal complaint, National Federation of Federal Employees, et al. v. U.S. Department of Agriculture (No. 3:26-cv-04406, N.D. Cal., filed May 13, 2026), was brought by the National Federation of Federal Employees (representing more than 19,000 USDA employees) together with seven individual USDA employees from Jewish, Buddhist, Pagan, and atheist backgrounds. One of them, Adam Diamond, voluntarily dismissed his claims on May 19, 2026, leaving six individual plaintiffs. Plaintiffs allege the messages, which grew markedly more explicitly Christian over a roughly 10-month period beginning July 2025, were "unconstitutionally coercive" and left non-Christian or non-religious employees feeling "unwelcome, excluded and like outsiders," with one plaintiff, Lanette Dietrich, reporting that when she asked to be removed from the distribution lists used for religious messages she was told this was not possible and that elevating her request would "create trouble" for her, and another stating he felt the messaging conveyed he was "going to hell" for not sharing Rollins's beliefs. **The complaint notably cites USDA's own November 2025 internal memorandum, which explicitly forbids officials from using "official authority to pressure subordinates" regarding religious beliefs, arguing Rollins's own department policy contradicts her conduct.** Rollins has responded to the lawsuit publicly and unapologetically rather than disputing the underlying facts, and has continued sending agency-wide religious content (Memorial Day, Independence Day 2026) during the pendency of the suit. A separate ethics complaint is pending with the USDA Inspector General regarding unrelated conflict-of-interest allegations, which USDA disputes as frivolous. Plaintiffs filed a motion for a preliminary injunction and stay on July 22, 2026 seeking to bar further religious messaging while the case proceeds, first noticed for an August 27, 2026 hearing before Magistrate Judge Laurel Beeler. That hearing never took place. On July 27, 2026 Judge Beeler approved the parties' stipulation to brief the motion together with a government motion to dismiss and moved the hearing to October 29. On July 28 the case was randomly reassigned to U.S. District Judge Trina L. Thompson, and the hearing was reset for October 27, 2026 before her. On August 21, 2026 the government filed a combined motion to dismiss and opposition, arguing that the plaintiffs lack standing, that the emails are not agency action reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act, and that the emails fit the nation's history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse and coerce no one. Plaintiffs filed their opposition on September 21, 2026; the government's reply is due October 5.

In its August 21, 2026 filing, the government argued that the plaintiffs lack standing because offense at seeing religious messages is not a cognizable injury, that the emails are not "agency action" under the APA, that holiday emails with religious references fit the nation's history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse, and that the emails "do not request, much less coerce, anyone to do anything" and establish no denominational preference.

The complaint's citation of USDA's own November 2025 memo is significant: this isn't only an outside legal theory being applied to Rollins's conduct, it's an allegation that her own department's written rules were violated. An active federal lawsuit exists with specific named plaintiffs describing concrete fear of career retaliation -- the question of whether this crosses the Establishment Clause line is before a court, not yet settled in the administration's favor, and Rollins's public 'He is Risen' response to the lawsuit suggests no intention to change course pending that ruling.

incident_summary: Former CNN journalist Don Lemon, civil rights attorney Nekima Levy Armstrong, and seven others were federally charged over a January 18, 2026 incident in which anti-ICE protesters disrupted a service at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota. Lemon and eight co-defendants each face two federal charges, first brought in the original indictment: conspiracy to violate someone's constitutional rights, and violating the FACE Act (which prohibits force or threats interfering with someone's First Amendment religious-exercise rights). Lemon has said he was present to chronicle the protest as a journalist, not to participate in it. The grand jury indictment followed an earlier, failed DOJ attempt to secure charges via a federal magistrate judge, who found no probable cause to arrest Lemon. When Magistrate Judge Douglas Micko signed only three of the eight arrest warrants DOJ presented on January 20, U.S. Attorney Rosen personally called the court to demand district-court review of the other five. **Patrick Schiltz, then Chief Judge of the federal district court in Minnesota, wrote to the Eighth Circuit on January 23, 2026 that two of those five -- Lemon and his producer -- were "not protesters at all" and that "[t]here is no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior or conspired to do so."** A three-judge Eighth Circuit panel then denied DOJ's request to order the five warrants signed (one judge, L. Steven Grasz, wrote separately that he saw probable cause). DOJ turned to a grand jury, which indicted Lemon and eight others on January 29, 2026, and Lemon was arrested in Los Angeles while covering the Grammy Awards, according to his attorney. Schiltz's letter addressed the evidence DOJ offered for the warrants, not the later grand jury case, and he is not the judge presiding over the prosecution; the charges have not been dropped. Lemon, Levy Armstrong and three other defendants pleaded not guilty at a February 13, 2026 arraignment in St. Paul; journalist Georgia Fort, also charged, pleaded not guilty on February 17. On February 23, 2026, Magistrate Judge Micko refused the government's request to designate the case "complex" under the Speedy Trial Act, which would have excluded at least 90 days from the speedy-trial clock, finding that nine defendants charged with the same offenses from "the same discrete course of conduct" was "not particularly complex"; he did give the government 30 more days for discovery. A superseding indictment unsealed February 27, 2026 charged 30 more people with the same two counts, including Lemon's producer, Michael Beute, bringing the case to 39 defendants; on March 23, 2026 Judge Provinzino granted the government's motion to dismiss the charges against one of them, Heather Danae Lewis. Magistrate Judge Micko denied defense requests for grand jury materials on June 10, 2026. On August 7, 2026, Lemon's attorneys filed three motions to dismiss: one alleging vindictive prosecution, one arguing his newsgathering was protected by the First Amendment, and one arguing that the FACE Act's house-of-worship provision exceeds Congress's Commerce Clause power. Fort had filed three dismissal motions the day before, on First Amendment, vindictive-prosecution and failure-to-state-an-offense grounds. On objections from Lemon, Fort and 32 co-defendants (Lemon's team cited grand jury "irregularities"), U.S. District Judge Laura Provinzino, who presides over the case, ordered DOJ on August 18, 2026 to produce by August 25, for her own private (in camera) review, the transcripts and evidence of its January 29 and February 26, 2026 grand jury presentations; the government filed a notice of an in camera submission on August 21. On September 24, 2026, with 101 defense pretrial motions pending, including the dismissal motions, Micko gave the government until October 16 to respond and moved the motions hearings to November 3, 5, 9 and 10, 2026.

incident_summary: On June 16, 2026, U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen announced a federal indictment, filed under seal on June 11, against 15 people, described by prosecutors as members of two Minneapolis groups (Direct Action Minnesota and Black Cat Workers Collective) with alleged "antifa" ties, on charges including conspiracy to impede or injure a federal officer, assault on a federal officer, and destruction of government property, tied to protests at the Whipple federal building -- which houses the regional ICE field office and a detention facility -- on January 23 and March 1, 2026. **Among those charged is Erik Davis, chair of Macalester College's religious studies department; the indictment cites a Signal message in which he asked people with AFL-CIO connections to focus organizing on the Whipple building, and prosecutors say he moderated organizing meetings, described himself as an anarchist, and attended an anti-ICE rally where others wore "Antifa"-branded sweatshirts.** His attorney, Jordan Kushner, said the only thing Davis is accused of is participating in meetings, and Cato Institute analyst David Bier, reviewing the 94-page indictment, found only one documented, charged act of violence against an agent's person, by a different defendant. Rosen's announcement explicitly invoked NSPM-7 -- one of the first known instances of DOJ citing that presidential memorandum as a basis for arrests -- as part of a stated effort to prosecute perceived antifascist organizing as domestic terrorism-adjacent conduct. Davis faces up to six years in prison if convicted. The defendants were arraigned beginning July 1, 2026, and the court designated the case complex in August. On August 13, 2026, Kevin Riach, attorney for co-defendant Isaac Sant, filed a discovery motion with dozens of government exhibits showing how DOJ and DHS put NSPM-7 into practice, and asked the court to order the government to disclose more. The documents revealed HSI surveillance operations -- "Operation Puppet Master," opened January 28, four days after federal agents killed protester Alex Pretti, and "Project Whipple Shield," begun two weeks later, both launched under NSPM-7's authority according to the filing -- that used undercover infiltration of meetings, license-plate tracking, and administrative subpoenas for years of financial records from labor unions and nonprofits, none of which has been charged. The filing was reported by the Associated Press (carried by CBS Minnesota), KSTP, Democracy Now and The Hill. On August 25, Protect Democracy filed an amicus brief on behalf of the Cato Institute, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression and the Society for the Rule of Law, groups spanning the ideological spectrum, urging Magistrate Judge David T. Schultz to order the government to reveal more about how NSPM-7 was put into practice in Minnesota; Schultz granted leave to file it on August 26 and heard the discovery motion on August 27. Talking Points Memo reported on September 2 that emails produced in discovery show HSI agents using PATRIOT Act Section 314(a) -- which lets investigators learn which banks hold an entity's accounts without a warrant, subpoena, or grand jury -- though the target of the search is not clear and the search terms are not revealed, and a former prosecutor told TPM the government would now know which banks every group on HSI's "conspiracy" chart uses, a chart that prosecutors and HSI told the grand jury included public-sector unions, the Democratic Socialists of America, the AFL-CIO and SEIU. Also on September 2, Schultz allowed the government to file supplemental briefing describing "Operation Keyhole," another HSI initiative named in the case; the government filed it on September 10, and Sant's response was due September 25. No ruling on the discovery motion had been issued as of late September. Pretrial motions are due December 18, 2026, with a motions hearing set for January 8, 2027; no trial date appears on the docket.

incident_summary: **In April 2025, Sali Berisha -- Albania's indicted former president and prime minister, barred from the U.S. since 2021 under Section 7031(c) of the State Department's annual appropriations act over Biden-era State Department findings that he misappropriated public funds to enrich relatives -- signed a two-year, $6 million lobbying contract with Continental Strategy, a Republican consulting firm.** Continental's roster included Chris LaCivita (a co-manager of Trump's 2024 campaign), Alberto Martinez (a former chief of staff to then-Senator Rubio), and Katie Wiles (daughter of White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, though AP reporting specifically found she was not staffed on the Berisha account). The Associated Press reported the arrangement was funded in part through a New Jersey-based group called the 'Make Albania Great Again Foundation,' whose donors were not publicly disclosed at the time. A little over a year later, on June 12, 2026, the State Department confirmed it had issued a waiver lifting Berisha's Section 7031(c) 'persona non grata' designation following what it described as an in-depth case review, restoring his and his family's ability to travel to the U.S. Berisha, announcing the reversal himself, credited Secretary of State Rubio personally, telling Albania's parliament 'I am back.' No sourcing reviewed directly quotes Rubio or any other State Department official connecting the lobbying campaign to the waiver decision, and none of the outlets covering the June 2026 reversal itself mention Continental Strategy or the lobbying contract at all -- the connection here is a documented, well-sourced temporal and access relationship (a paid lobbying campaign built specifically around Trump-administration proximity, followed just over a year later by exactly the sanctions reversal it was hired to obtain), not a proven quid pro quo.
elements_required: Berisha was under a formal, named State Department sanction (Section 7031(c), imposed 2021) over specific corruption findings, not an informal or symbolic designation

Berisha personally financed a $6 million, multi-year lobbying contract specifically staffed with individuals holding direct personal/professional ties to Trump-administration decision-makers, including a former chief of staff to Rubio himself
The State Department, under Rubio, reversed the sanction via a formal waiver just over a year after the lobbying contract began, restoring exactly the travel access Berisha sought

No sourcing reviewed establishes a direct causal link between the lobbying campaign and the waiver decision -- the connection documented here is temporal proximity and access design, not proof of an explicit exchange

comeback: The concern this entry documents is the access design itself, not a claim of proven bribery: Berisha paid $6 million specifically to a firm staffed with a former Rubio chief of staff and a Trump campaign co-manager, seeking exactly the sanctions relief the State Department delivered a little over a year later, under the same Secretary Berisha himself credited by name. Whether or not the lobbying campaign was the actual cause, the pattern -- indicted foreign politician, large lobbying contract built around personal proximity to the decision-maker, subsequent reversal of the exact policy sought -- is precisely the appearance-of-access problem worth documenting regardless of whether explicit causation can be proven from public sourcing.

official: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State, and Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Misleading Congress About Military Intentions Toward Venezuela, Then Launching an Unauthorized Special-Forces Raid That Captured a Foreign Head of State Without Any Advance Congressional Notification -- a War Powers Resolution consultation-and-notification dispute; not itself criminally charged
incident_summary: On January 3, 2026, more than 200 U.S. special operations forces raided Fuerte Tiuna military base in Caracas (Operation Absolute Resolve), capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, after Maduro failed to reach a safe room; **Venezuela's Defense Ministry reported 83 deaths in the raid, including 47 Venezuelan troops and 32 Cuban soldiers.** Trump announced the capture from Mar-a-Lago. This was a dramatic escalation of the Caribbean/Pacific counter-narcotics boat-strike campaign already tracked in this database (see venezuela-war-powers-resolution-votes-2025.json for the preceding months' congressional votes on that campaign). Neither Trump nor Secretary of State Rubio notified any member of Congress in advance. In a November 2025 classified briefing to lawmakers, ahead of that month's Senate war-powers vote, Rubio -- per the Washington Post's and CNN's reporting on the briefing, as summarized in Reason's own analysis of the episode -- indicated the administration was not currently preparing to target Venezuela directly and did not believe it had a proper legal argument for doing so; CNN separately reported officials told lawmakers the U.S. was not currently planning to launch strikes inside Venezuela. After the raid, Democrats accused Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth of having lied in that briefing: Sen. Andy Kim said 'Secretaries Rubio and Hegseth looked every Senator in the eye a few weeks ago and said this wasn't about regime change. I didn't trust them then and we see now that they blatantly lied to Congress,' and Rep. Gregory Meeks told the Post 'Rubio said that there were not any intentions to invade Venezuela. He absolutely lied to Congress.' Rubio's own subsequent defense was inconsistent on its face: he characterized the raid as a 'law enforcement operation' not requiring congressional authorization, a characterization Trump's own public description of it as an 'extraordinary military operation' contradicted. Al Jazeera's post-raid fact-check of Trump's separate public justifications for the broader campaign found several did not hold up: his claim that each U.S. strike on suspected drug boats (32 strikes since September 2025, killing roughly 115 people) saves 25,000 American lives was contradicted by experts who note Venezuela plays a minor role in U.S. drug trafficking, with no drug evidence provided for the strikes; his claim that Maduro 'sent savage and murderous gangs' (Tren de Aragua) to terrorize American communities was contradicted by an April 2025 National Intelligence Council report finding the Maduro government 'probably does not have a policy of cooperating' with the gang; his claim Venezuela had 'stolen' U.S. oil ignored that Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in 1975; and his claim that Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, was 'willing' to cooperate was contradicted by her own public denunciation of the operation, on Venezuelan state television, as 'brutal aggression.' The raid prompted a further round of Senate action (following the Nov. 6, 2025 procedural vote on S.J.Res. 90 already documented in this database's companion entry venezuela-war-powers-resolution-votes-2025.json): per the Senate's own official roll call record, a motion to discharge a new joint resolution, S.J.Res. 98 -- like S.J.Res. 90, directing removal of U.S. armed forces from unauthorized hostilities against Venezuela, but introduced in the new (2nd) session of the 119th Congress -- succeeded 52-47 on January 8, 2026, with Sens. Rand Paul, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Todd Young, and Josh Hawley joining Democrats. On January 14, 2026, a subsequent procedural vote to advance toward final passage failed as Sens. Josh Hawley and Todd Young, who had joined Democrats on the January 8 vote, reversed course after Rubio personally assured Hawley 'point blank, we're not going to do ground troops' and gave Young a written commitment to seek congressional authorization in advance of any future 'major military operations,' 'circumstances permitting.' That vote ended in a 50-50 tie, broken by Vice President JD Vance against the resolution. On January 28, 2026, weeks after the raid, Rubio told the same Senate Foreign Relations Committee 'we are not postured to, nor do we intend or expect to have to take any military action in Venezuela at any time' regarding further action -- language nearly identical to his pre-raid assurances, this time as a forward-looking statement rather than one later proven false by an already-completed operation. Maduro and Flores were flown to the United States and held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center; on January 5, 2026 they were arraigned before U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in Manhattan on federal narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and weapons charges, pleading not guilty -- Maduro interrupted the proceedings to declare 'I am innocent... I am still president of my country' and separately said he had been 'kidnapped.'

offense_category: Institutional Accountability Failure in Prisoner-Swap Vetting -- including a convicted violent felon, who did not meet the swap's own "wrongfully detained" criterion, in a prisoner exchange with no public accounting of who made that call or why -- an institutional-accountability claim about process and transparency, not a criminal charge against any named individual

incident_summary: In 2016, Dahud Hanid Ortiz -- a U.S. military veteran and dual Venezuelan-American citizen -- killed two Cuban women and an Ecuadorian man at a law office in Madrid, Spain, and fled to Venezuela afterward. Spain convicted him in absentia and requested his extradition, but Venezuela's constitution bars extraditing its own citizens, so Venezuela prosecuted him itself: he was arrested in 2018 and sentenced by a Caracas court on January 9, 2024 to 30 years in prison. In 2023, the Biden administration, aware of Ortiz's criminal record, chose not to include him when it negotiated a different prisoner swap with Venezuela that year. On July 18, 2025, the Trump administration completed a three-way exchange: El Salvador returned roughly 250 Venezuelan migrants to Venezuela -- men the U.S. had deported under the Alien Enemies Act in March 2025 and paid El Salvador to hold at the CECOT mega-prison -- and in return Venezuela released 10 Americans (five citizens and five green-card holders), including Ortiz. Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly announced the released Americans were "on their way to freedom." **Of the 10 people released, 8 were officially classified by the U.S. government as "wrongfully detained" -- the stated criterion used to justify prioritizing Americans for return -- but Ortiz was not among them.** The New York Times reported that at least some people in the Trump administration knew of Ortiz's murder conviction before he was included in the swap, and Venezuela's Justice Minister, Diosdado Cabello, publicly confirmed U.S. officials were told of the conviction and still wanted him released. No U.S. official has since explained, on the record, why a convicted violent felon who did not meet the swap's own wrongful-detention criterion was included. Ortiz has been reported living freely in Orlando, Florida since his return.

No U.S. official has publicly identified who made the decision to include Ortiz or explained the reasoning, leaving the process by which a non-wrongfully-detained convicted felon was selected for release undisclosed

And even granting that Venezuela set the guest list, the administration still classified 8 of the 10 released Americans as "wrongfully detained" but not Ortiz -- meaning its own public justification for the swap does not explain why he was accepted, a gap no official has addressed on the record.

official: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
offense_category: Federal Records Act Compliance / Candor to the Court -- the State Department declared to a federal court, under penalty of perjury, that Rubio does not use Signal's auto-delete function; The Atlantic later reported, citing an anonymous source, that Rubio turned on disappearing messages in an official chat about two months after one of those declarations, and State's own court-ordered production showed him as a member of chats set to auto-delete -- NOT charged, contested facts, included for reference only
incident_summary: After The Atlantic revealed on March 24, 2025 that Rubio had participated in an auto-deleting Signal chat with other senior national-security officials discussing Yemen strike war plans (the chat at the center of this tracker's separate Hegseth Signal/Yemen entry), Democracy Forward filed a FOIA request two days later for Rubio's and then-chief of staff Mike Needham's Signal messages about the administration's El Salvador renditions, and for the names, participants and deletion timelines of the Signal groups they used for official business; it sued in May 2025 (Democracy Forward Foundation v. DOJ, D.D.C., Judge Amit Mehta). Separately, in June 2025, Judge James Boasberg, ruling in American Oversight's Federal Records Act suit over the Yemen chat, ordered the agency heads to notify Rubio, as acting archivist, of any Signal chats holding federal records at risk of deletion, and ordered Rubio to ask the Attorney General to start a recovery action for those records and to notify Congress. Opposing Democracy Forward's motion for a preservation order, State filed a July 22, 2025 declaration by Agency Records Officer Mallory Rogoff stating that, as of July 21, 2025, LeapXpert software on Rubio's government-issued phone archives "all messages sent and received, regardless of whether the sender configures a message to 'auto-delete,'" and that the Office of the Secretary had confirmed "Secretary Rubio does not use the auto-deletion functions in third party messaging applications when sending communications that may include federal records." State repeated that sentence under penalty of perjury in declarations by Susan Weetman (September 9, 2025) and Timothy Kootz (October 2025), filed under a stipulated preservation order. **About two months after the Weetman declaration, Rubio changed the settings in a Signal chat about administration matters with other senior officials so that messages would automatically delete, according to a person familiar with the exchange who spoke anonymously to The Atlantic; a State Department official contested the idea that Rubio made a practice of it but said he could not address the specific instance.** In April 30, 2026 declarations filed under a settlement with American Oversight, State did not repeat its claim that Rubio does not use disappearing messages, instead stating that an application on his device collected messages "even if those messages otherwise have a deletion timeline setting enabled." On June 22, 2026, under court order, State produced to Democracy Forward undated screenshots of the settings of 16 Signal chats, collected by August 2025, that show Rubio as a member of chats with disappearing messages enabled -- including a chat with Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Caine named "SS/APNSA,SD,CJCS" set to delete messages after eight hours, and a redacted-name chat set to one week; the newly disclosed chats date from the first half of 2025. On August 12, 2026, Democracy Forward asked the court to reinstate a hearing or allow limited discovery into State's candor and its compliance with the preservation order. On September 11, 2026, State opposed, reaffirmed that Rubio "does not use" the auto-deletion functions, noted that any member of a chat can set a deletion timeline, and cited a Deputy Assistant Secretary's review finding no preserved record showing Rubio enabling auto-delete in any thread. Democracy Forward replied on September 23, 2026; no ruling had been entered as of late September.

official: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State and, since September 2026, National Security Advisor (acting from May 2025); also served as Acting Archivist of the United States and Acting USAID Administrator in 2025
offense_category: Potential Federal Vacancies Reform Act (FVRA, 5 U.S.C. §3345 et seq.) compliance issues — concentration of multiple statutorily limited acting roles in one individual; NOT charged, no formal violation finding identified, but Rubio's exit from the Archivist role, which NARA says came at the Act's 300-day limit, indicates an internal recognition the statutory clock applied
incident_summary: Beginning in 2025, Rubio simultaneously held Secretary of State plus, at various points, Acting USAID Administrator (February to August 2025), Acting Archivist of the United States, and Acting National Security Advisor (from May 1, 2025). **Rubio became acting Archivist on February 16, 2025, after Trump fired Archivist Colleen Shogan on February 7. NARA and Rubio's staff say he gave up the role on December 4, 2025, just within the Vacancies Act's 300-day limit for vacancies early in a new administration (210 days is the usual limit), after delegating the Archivist's functions to senior adviser James Byron rather than to a Senate-confirmed successor.** The change was not made public until February 4, 2026, when a NARA spokesperson told Federal News Network that Rubio was no longer serving as acting Archivist. Trump nominated Bradford Wilson for the post on March 2, 2026. In late March 2026, Sen. Tammy Duckworth asked GAO to investigate whether Rubio overstayed the limit, raising the prospect that his departure had been backdated; NARA and GAO confirmed the vacancy had not been reported to GAO until January 23, 2026. Georgetown law professor David Super said the late report at a minimum violated the Act's reporting requirement; NARA called his conclusions inaccurate. The Senate confirmed Wilson on August 7, 2026, and NARA announced him as the 12th Archivist on August 21. On September 22, 2026, three administration officials told Fox News Digital that Trump had signed a commission formally making Rubio national security adviser, ending his acting status in a post that does not require Senate confirmation.
elements_required: FVRA generally limits acting service in a vacant Senate-confirmed position to 210 days (longer in specific circumstances), after which the position must be filled by nomination/confirmation or the acting designee must step back
Whether each of Rubio's concurrent acting roles independently complied with FVRA timing and eligibility requirements
Whether 'delegation of authority' to a non-Senate-confirmed senior advisor (as occurred with the Archivist role) is itself a permissible workaround or a separate compliance question

Whether actions taken by Rubio in any of these roles during a period of questionable FVRA compliance could be subject to legal challenge by affected parties (the typical real-world consequence of FVRA violations is that actions taken by an improperly-serving official can be invalidated)

NARA says Rubio left the acting Archivist post Dec. 4, 2025, at the 300-day limit; an Archivist was confirmed Aug. 2026. His security adviser role (no Senate confirmation) became permanent Sept. 2026.
rebuttal_anticipated: Likely defense: each acting designation independently complied with applicable statutes (FVRA or specific agency enabling legislation), and strategic sequencing of acting-role durations reflects responsible management of transition timelines, not circumvention of Senate confirmation.
comeback: Complying with a statutory deadline isn't the same as complying with the statute's purpose. By NARA's account, Rubio relinquished the Archivist role on the 300th day of the vacancy, exactly at the FVRA limit -- a precision that's harder to characterize as coincidental than as deliberate deadline management. And delegating the Archivist's functions to a non-Senate-confirmed adviser, while Rubio also served as Secretary of State and acting national security adviser, raises a distinct question: whether the practical effect of stacking acting designations on one confirmed official is to bypass Senate confirmation for multiple roles simultaneously, achieving through sequencing what the FVRA's confirmation requirements were designed to prevent through Senate oversight.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Consistent with the Sonderling entry's five acting and deputy roles, several held at once: a pattern of piling acting designations onto a few trusted officials, which lets them run agencies whose leaders need Senate confirmation without the Senate's participation and stretches one person's reach across several agencies beyond what any single confirmation authorized. Rubio's case shows the pattern at the National Archives, a Senate-confirmed post that went without a confirmed leader for about eighteen months after Colleen Shogan's firing; by NARA's account Rubio left it at the Vacancies Act's 300-day limit, delegating its functions to an adviser rather than to a nominee. The national security adviser post is different: it needs no confirmation, so its September 2026 conversion from acting to permanent raises no Vacancies Act question, though it keeps two full-time jobs in one person's hands.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the roles held and when they began. The Archivist end date rests on NARA's account (December 4, 2025, the 300th day of the vacancy); the change was not made public until February 4, 2026. LOW confidence on whether this constitutes an actual legal violation -- FVRA compliance involves technical questions (which exception applies to which role) not resolved in available reporting, and no court or oversight body has weighed in. This entry documents a pattern of concentrated acting authority, raising legitimate questions about institutional design and confirmation practices -- not that Rubio violated federal law, which isn't established. As of September 2026, no formal violation finding or legal challenge has been identified; Sen. Tammy Duckworth asked GAO in March 2026 to investigate whether Rubio overstayed, raising the prospect that his departure was backdated; no GAO response has been found. The national security adviser post is not Senate-confirmed and so is not FVRA-limited in the way the Archivist post is; Rubio held it on an acting basis from May 2025 until Trump formally made it permanent in September 2026. Rubio also took on an informal portfolio in January 2026 overseeing post-Maduro Venezuela transition planning, and Mike Needham, a longtime Rubio aide at the State Department, became Deputy National Security Advisor in May 2026 -- neither is itself a new FVRA-limited acting role.

official: David Sacks, White House AI and Crypto Czar (through March 2026) and Co-Chair, President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) thereafter
offense_category: Conflict of Interest in Policy Influence -- an administration adviser with personal financial holdings in the AI industry personally intervened to shelve federal AI-safety oversight; no criminal charge; the White House issued him conflict-of-interest waivers covering both his crypto holdings (March 2025) and his AI holdings (made public June 2025), whose adequacy ethics experts dispute
incident_summary: **White House adviser David Sacks personally called President Trump between the night of May 20 and the morning of May 21, 2026, ahead of a planned May 21 signing ceremony, and persuaded him to abruptly shelve a draft executive order that would have set up a voluntary framework for AI companies to submit their most advanced models to national-security agencies for testing up to 90 days before public release (industry had sought a 14-day window, according to reports cited by Seoul Economic Daily).** According to Politico's account, as relayed by Fortune, Sacks told Trump he feared the voluntary vetting would act as a de facto licensing regime; the Wall Street Journal reported he warned the order could slow the AI industry and put the U.S. at a disadvantage against China. Sacks, a venture capitalist whose firm holds AI-industry investments, had separately been the subject of a September 2025 letter from Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Rep. Melanie Stansbury and six other Democratic lawmakers questioning his ethics waivers and whether he had exceeded his 130-day limit, and of December 2025 reporting (NPR, following a New York Times investigation) on his "vast AI investments" while serving as a White House adviser on AI policy. Earlier in his tenure as the formal White House AI and Crypto Czar (a Special Government Employee position, subject to a 130-day time limit), Sacks received a blanket ethics waiver from White House Counsel David Warrington, issued in March 2025, covering conflicts of interest in matters "of general applicability concerning the digital asset industry" -- a waiver specific to crypto. A second, AI-specific ethics waiver from Warrington, undated but made public by the White House in June 2025, followed. Sacks stepped down from the formal AI/Crypto Czar role in March 2026 after reaching the 130-day SGE limit, moving on to co-chair PCAST, a post the council's January 2025 executive order had assigned to the Special Advisor for AI and Crypto and to which the White House announced his appointment in March 2026; he held it at the time of the May 2026 AI executive order intervention. The draft AI-safety executive order was shelved. On June 2, 2026, Trump signed a different order that asks AI companies, on a voluntary basis, to give the government access to covered frontier models up to 30 days before release, rather than the draft's 90 days. Warrington later left the administration for the private sector; Trump announced in August 2026 that Will Scharf would replace him as White House Counsel, effective September 1, 2026 (PBS NewsHour, August 10, 2026).

A formal conflict-of-interest waiver exists on the record for Sacks covering crypto-industry matters specifically -- documenting that the administration itself recognized his financial holdings created conflicts requiring formal waiver in an adjacent policy area he also worked on

A second, AI-specific conflict-of-interest waiver from White House Counsel David Warrington, made public in June 2025, exists on the record -- it states that Sacks had initiated divestment of his direct holdings in Meta, Amazon and Taiwan Semiconductor, and that the Craft Ventures funds had initiated or completed divestment of over 97% of their holdings that may be affected by his AI-policy work; the administration thus formally addressed the AI conflict, and the dispute is over whether the waiver adequately resolves it

incident_summary: Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old political appointee who began as senior adviser to DRL -- the State Department bureau that selects and distributes human-rights grants -- on Trump's second inauguration day, spent his first 18 months in the role courting far-right political movements in Europe, which he has publicly described the U.S. as sharing a 'common civilizational struggle' with, including in a State Department Substack post titled 'The Need for Civilizational Allies in Europe' criticizing Europe as a 'hotbed of digital censorship, mass migration, restrictions on religious freedom.' **Under Samson's direction, DRL staff were instructed to begin awarding funds to Lex Libertas, a South African organization founded by a prominent figure in the country's white Afrikaner movement -- occurring alongside the administration's separate, parallel policy fast-tracking refugee status for white South African Afrikaners.** DRL officials also traveled to Paris in support of Marine Le Pen after a French court barred her from office over a conviction the administration characterized as politically motivated 'lawfare' against conservatives; DRL subsequently excluded French organizations from a related grant program, citing foreign-interference concerns, even as the bureau's broader posture favored right-wing European causes. This redirection occurred concurrently with a much larger cut: State Department officials recommended eliminating roughly 80% of DRL's overall grant programs -- a total of roughly $1.3 billion -- preserving only two programs (covering China and Yemen), per Guardian reporting on an internal DRL white paper.

official: Donald Trump, President (public announcement); Karoline Leavitt, White House Press Secretary (confirmed a joint State Department/DHS review targeting Somali-Americans specifically)
offense_category: Threatened Denaturalization Targeted at One National-Origin Group, Raising Fifth/Fourteenth Amendment Equal-Protection and Due-Process Concerns
status: Threatened/under review -- State Department and DHS reviewing cases; no denaturalization proceeding against a Somali-American tied to this announcement had been filed as of this writing
incident_summary: On January 13, 2026, at a speech to the Detroit Economic Club, **Trump said his administration would revoke the citizenship of naturalized Americans 'from Somalia or anywhere else' convicted of defrauding U.S. citizens, attributing much of a large Minnesota public-benefits fraud scandal to people who 'came into the country illegally from Somalia' -- despite the fraud defendants being predominantly naturalized citizens or lawful residents, not people who entered illegally.** In earlier remarks (reported by Al Jazeera in late December 2025 and by The Hill), White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt confirmed the administration was 'looking at' revoking citizenship specifically for Somali-Americans caught up in the fraud scheme, and that DHS and the State Department were jointly reviewing what steps would be needed. Trump separately told reporters he would denaturalize citizens 'in a heartbeat' if they were 'dishonest,' and said of Somali immigrants specifically that 'many of the people that came in from Somalia, they hate our country.' The underlying Minnesota fraud scandal -- the Feeding Our Future child-nutrition-program scheme, the largest pandemic-relief fraud case charged in U.S. history at roughly $250 million, plus related autism-services and Housing Stabilization Program fraud bringing the total scope toward $822 million-$1 billion -- has produced 78 defendants charged and 56 convictions as of this writing; the U.S. Attorney's Office for Minnesota has stated approximately 89% of those charged are Somali-American. The administration's denaturalization threat invokes a real, pre-existing DOJ policy: a June 11, 2025 Civil Division memorandum signed by Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate directing attorneys to 'prioritize and maximally pursue denaturalization proceedings in all cases permitted by law,' listing fraud against private individuals, businesses, or the government as one of ten priority categories, alongside national-security threats and human-rights violations -- a facially neutral, nationality-blind policy. Legal experts, including immigration attorneys and civil-liberties groups (ACLU), argue that publicly announcing and reviewing denaturalization specifically for one national-origin group, rather than applying the same fraud-based criteria neutrally across all naturalized citizens convicted of similar conduct, raises equal-protection concerns distinct from the underlying policy's facial neutrality. Separately, ABC News reported DHS announced termination of Temporary Protected Status for Somalis in the same period this group was being publicly targeted by Trump -- a related but distinct DHS action affecting a different, non-citizen population.
elements_required: A facially neutral federal denaturalization-priority policy already existed (the June 2025 DOJ Civil Division memo), not itself limited to any nationality

The President and White House Press Secretary publicly and repeatedly singled out one national-origin group (Somali-Americans) by name for denaturalization review, rather than describing the policy in nationality-neutral terms

The President's own public statements attributed the underlying fraud to illegal immigration from Somalia, a factual mischaracterization given that the fraud defendants are predominantly naturalized citizens or lawful residents, not people who entered illegally

Legal scholars and civil-liberties organizations identified this as raising Fifth Amendment due-process and Fourteenth Amendment equal-protection concerns distinct from the general denaturalization policy's own constitutionality

No denaturalization proceeding against a specific Somali-American tied to this announcement had actually been filed as of this writing -- the entry documents a threat/review process, not yet a completed enforcement action

rebuttal_anticipated: The underlying DOJ denaturalization-priority policy is facially neutral and was adopted seven months before Trump's Somalia-specific remarks, applying to fraud convictions of any naturalized citizen regardless of national origin; the administration could argue it is simply applying a pre-existing, generally-applicable policy to the specific fraud case currently in the news (the $250M+ Feeding Our Future scheme), not creating a nationality-based policy from scratch. comeback: The distinction between a facially neutral policy and its selective public application matters: the administration's own spokesperson and the President both repeatedly named one nationality specifically in describing the review, rather than describing it in the policy's own neutral fraud-conviction terms, and Trump's own broader remarks ('they hate our country') extended well beyond the fraud-conviction criterion to a generalized characterization of an entire national-origin group. The President's own framing of the underlying fraud as resulting from people who 'came into the country illegally' is also factually inaccurate for a predominantly naturalized-citizen defendant population, undercutting the claim that this is simply neutral fraud-policy enforcement rather than nationality-driven messaging. That no proceeding has yet been filed is itself part of what this entry documents -- a public threat and an active administration review targeting one group by name, which legal experts say would face immediate court challenges if converted into actual filings.

official: Keith Sonderling, Acting Secretary of Labor (nominated for permanent position); also Acting Director, Office of Government Ethics; concurrently held acting roles at IMLS and Commerce during the relevant period
offense_category: Administrative Procedure Act Violation (5 U.S.C. §706(2)(A), arbitrary-and-capricious agency action) and Impoundment Control Act concerns (unilateral termination of congressionally-appropriated grants) — per Rhode Island v. Trump (D.R.I.), in which the court found the IMLS dismantlement actions arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, and the separate ALA v. Sonderling (D.D.C.); NOT criminally charged, resolved via civil litigation (permanent bar, withdrawn appeal, settlement and stipulated dismissal)
incident_summary: **As acting director of the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) beginning March 2025, Sonderling placed many agency staff members on administrative leave, sent termination notices to most of them, began canceling grants and contracts, and fired all members of the National Museum and Library Services Board -- actions carrying out Executive Order 14238, which directed that IMLS be cut to the minimum functions required by law.** A federal judge later blocked these actions. In a suit brought by 21 state attorneys general (Rhode Island v. Trump), the federal district court in Rhode Island found the dismantling actions arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law, set them aside, and permanently barred further steps to carry out the order on November 21, 2025; on April 6, 2026, a federal court granted the administration's request to withdraw its appeal of that ruling. In a separate case in federal court in Washington, D.C., brought by the American Library Association and AFSCME (ALA v. Sonderling), the plaintiffs and DOJ signed a settlement agreement, binding on all parties, on April 9, 2026 that keeps IMLS intact, confirms that terminated grants were reinstated and staff reductions reversed, and records the administration's representation that it will take no further steps to carry out the executive order against IMLS; the parties filed a stipulation dismissing that case without prejudice the same day. Trump announced on June 29, 2026 that he would nominate Sonderling as permanent Labor Secretary, and Sonderling testified at his Senate HELP Committee confirmation hearing on July 16, 2026; the IMLS matter did not derail his nomination or confirmation process. The Senate HELP Committee approved Sonderling's nomination 12-11 on a party-line vote on July 30, 2026 (after an earlier scheduled July 23 vote was postponed for lack of attendance), advancing it to the full Senate floor; the IMLS matter does not appear to have been a stated factor in the committee vote. As of September 24, 2026, the Senate's roll-call record showed no floor vote on the nomination.

The 'consistent with stated policy' framing also doesn't address why the same individual has held five different acting/deputy positions across multiple agencies, several of them at the same time, a structural pattern that itself raises the institutional-design concerns documented in this dataset's Rubio entry.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Possible structural cause: the IMLS actions carried out Executive Order 14238, which targeted several small agencies at once, and the administration put a trusted official already serving elsewhere (the Deputy Labor Secretary, who was also made acting head of the Minority Business Development Agency that same week) in acting control to execute the cuts quickly, with DOGE staff involved. This resembles the concentration of acting roles documented in Rubio's Vacancies Act entry, though the roles and acts there differ. At IMLS the speed did not outrun the courts: judges blocked the layoffs within weeks, and the agency was restored by the November 2025 ruling and the April 2026 settlement described in the companion IMLS dismantlement entry. The pattern reflects an administration-wide approach to agencies targeted for elimination rather than a practice specific to Sonderling.

Trump (the 21-state attorneys general suit) found the IMLS dismantlement actions arbitrary and capricious and contrary to law and permanently barred further dismantling (Memorandum and Order, ECF No. 99, which holds the actions "arbitrary and capricious" and "contrary to law" and vacates them); the administration's appeal was withdrawn at its request on April 6, 2026, and ALA, AFSCME and DOJ signed a settlement agreement in their separate D.C. case on April 9, 2026. The AP's June 29, 2026 nomination story still described the case as on appeal, which was out of date by then. official: Leland Dudek, Acting Commissioner of the Social Security Administration
offense_category: Canceling a State's Vital-Records Service Contract as Admitted Political Retaliation Against Its Governor -- an abuse-of-power and improper-use-of-office claim, not a criminal charge
incident_summary: On March 5, 2025, Acting SSA Commissioner Leland Dudek ordered the cancellation of the agency's longstanding contracts with the State of Maine that automatically processed Social Security numbers for newborns at hospitals and death certificates from funeral homes -- contracts that, if actually terminated, would have forced Maine parents to travel to a federal Social Security office in person to register a newborn. Emails later obtained by the Bangor Daily News showed Dudek ordered the cancellation explicitly as retaliation against Democratic Governor Janet Mills, after watching her publicly clash with President Trump over transgender-athlete policy at a White House event -- **Dudek wrote to staff, 'Please cancel the contracts. While our improper payments will go up, and fraudsters may compromise identities, no money will go from the public trust to a petulant child,' and separately told reporters he had been 'ticked' at Mills for 'not being real cordial to the president.'** SSA reversed the cancellation within 48 hours amid bipartisan backlash and calls for Dudek's resignation, and Dudek apologized to Mainers -- though he later offered additional, non-retaliatory justifications for the brief cancellation in September 2025 reporting.

Dudek's own contemporaneous email and on-the-record remarks admit the decision was motivated by personal irritation at the governor's political conduct, not a stated policy or fraud rationale
The action targeted a Democratic-led state specifically, following a public Trump-Mills confrontation
The action was reversed only after public exposure and bipartisan criticism, not through an independent internal check that caught it beforehand

status: Reversed within 48 hours of the March 5, 2025 order, following public disclosure and bipartisan criticism. Dudek apologized to Mainers. No further contracts or agency action against Maine specifically have been identified in sourcing reviewed as of this entry's addition.

official: John Thune, Senate Majority Leader
offense_category: Inserting an Undisclosed Self-Benefiting Provision Into Must-Pass Government Funding Legislation, Creating a Personal Financial Remedy for Himself and Colleagues Whose Records Were Lawfully Subpoenaed in a Federal Investigation
incident_summary: In November 2025, as Congress finalized the legislative package ending the 43-day government shutdown, **Senate Majority Leader John Thune personally directed staff to insert language into one of the package's full-year spending bills allowing senators (and at least one House member) to sue the federal government for up to $500,000 in statutory damages per violation if their phone or electronic records were subpoenaed or obtained without their knowledge.** The provision followed an October 2025 disclosure, via documents released by Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, that then-Special Counsel Jack Smith's 2023 investigation into efforts to overturn the 2020 election had obtained phone records for eight Republican senators -- Lindsey Graham, Bill Hagerty, Josh Hawley, Dan Sullivan, Tommy Tuberville, Ron Johnson, Cynthia Lummis, and Marsha Blackburn -- around the time of the January 6, 2021 Capitol attack, plus at least one House member, all via lawful grand jury subpoena. The provision was inserted without a standalone vote or public debate and signed into law along with the rest of the funding package. It drew immediate bipartisan criticism once discovered: House Speaker Mike Johnson said he was 'surprised and very frustrated,' calling it 'way out of line' and saying he was 'very angry about it'; Senate Finance Committee Democrat Ron Wyden called it a 'tax dollar giveaway to Republican senators.' Johnson announced the House would hold a standalone vote to strip the provision. The House did so, voting 426-0 to repeal the provision -- a second unanimous House repeal vote followed weeks later after the first stalled -- but Thune has refused to bring the repeal to a Senate floor vote, and Sen. Graham personally blocked a Democratic attempt to force one, arguing senators whose records were 'wrongly' obtained deserved a 'remedy.' As of this entry, the provision remains law, unrepealed, despite two unanimous House votes against it.

official: Scott Bessent, Treasury Secretary / White House
offense_category: Enhanced Financial Surveillance Framed Around an Ethnic Community, Over Internal Treasury Objections -- a facially geographic order (Hennepin and Ramsey counties) launched and publicly framed as a crackdown on alleged fraud in Minneapolis's Somali community, raising civil-liberties and discriminatory-targeting concerns about blanket reporting imposed without individualized suspicion
incident_summary: **John Hurley, Treasury's Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence (the sanctions and anti-money-laundering chief), began telling associates in recent weeks that he was leaving his post after privately objecting to White House-backed plans to crack down on alleged fraud in Minnesota's Somali immigrant community, The Washington Post reported February 25, 2026, citing seven people familiar with the matter.** Bloomberg News had reported on February 15 that Hurley was set to leave after friction with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Per the Post, Hurley had recently conveyed his concerns to Bessent about a project to enhance federal monitoring of international payments from the Minneapolis area, and two of the people said he raised data-privacy concerns; ACAMS's moneylaundering.com, summarizing the Post's report, said he did so before the surveillance commenced. The project was FinCEN's Minnesota Geographic Targeting Order, issued January 8, 2026 and in effect from February 12, 2026, which requires banks and money transmitters in Hennepin and Ramsey counties to report added information on transfers of $3,000 or more going abroad. Career officials who helped formulate the order also objected, viewing it as clumsy and an inefficient way to root out fraud (one person said some saw it as an overtly partisan use of Treasury resources); Hurley shared at least some of their concerns, but they were effectively overruled, two people told the Post. Hurley denied the premise of the Post's article, calling his team "the tip of the spear pushing back to stop Somalia fraud in Minnesota," and an administration official told the Post the Minnesota disagreement was not the only reason he was leaving and that he and Bessent had mutually agreed the role was not the right fit. The Post wrote that his departure underscores how some Trump allies in the federal government are uneasy with the extent of White House directives to deploy law-enforcement tools against Minneapolis's Somali community, part of the administration's broader crackdown on alleged benefits fraud in the state. Hurley's departure follows several other senior Treasury exits since August 2025, including Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender and two successive Bessent chiefs of staff. By April 28, 2026, the Post reported that Hurley had left his post and was expected to be nominated as U.S. representative to the OECD. The underlying financial-surveillance program has continued: FinCEN renewed the order on August 7, 2026, effective August 11, 2026 through February 6, 2027, per FinCEN's order and Treasury's press release; a February 27, 2026 FinCEN order exempting banks from recording or reporting transfers by certain categories of originators was carried into the renewal, which is otherwise unchanged -- the program remains active and has been formally extended past its original term, not ended. The Senate confirmed Hurley as U.S. Ambassador to the OECD on August 7, 2026.
