official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Categorical Clemency for 2020 Election-Subversion Co-Conspirators (Fake Electors, Legal Architects, and Aides), Issued via Sweeping, Ambiguously-Worded Proclamation Language -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the pardon's non-individualized scale, its later-rejected attempted extension beyond its intended targets, and its practical inability to reach the parallel state prosecutions it was seemingly meant to shield.
incident_summary: On November 7, 2025, Trump signed a proclamation granting 'full, complete, and unconditional' federal pardons to 77 people over conduct connected to efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss; U.S. Pardon Attorney Ed Martin publicly released the list on November 10, 2025. Named recipients included Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani, former chief of staff Mark Meadows, attorney Sidney Powell, DOJ official-turned-elector-scheme architect Jeffrey Clark, and lawyers Kenneth Chesebro, Jenna Ellis, and John Eastman, alongside dozens of Republican 'fake electors' from Michigan, Arizona, Nevada, Georgia, and Wisconsin. **The proclamation's operative language was sweeping rather than individualized, granting pardon for conduct relating to the 'advice, creation, organization, execution, submission, support, voting, activities, participation in, or advocacy for or of any slate or proposed slate of Presidential electors, whether or not recognized by any State or State official, in connection with the 2020 Presidential Election,' as well as for 'any conduct relating to their efforts to expose voting fraud and vulnerabilities in the 2020 Presidential Election.'** Because the presidential pardon power under Article II reaches only federal offenses, and none of the named recipients had actually been charged with a federal crime over their 2020-election conduct (Special Counsel Jack Smith's federal case charged Trump himself, not these co-conspirators as defendants), the pardon left the parallel state prosecutions of many of the same people legally untouched: Georgia's 2023 racketeering indictment of Trump and 18 others (including Giuliani, Meadows, Chesebro, Ellis, and Eastman), Arizona's fake-elector indictment of 18 people, and Michigan's and Nevada's own fake-elector cases all continued under state authority the federal pardon has no power to reach. Legal scholars, including Loyola Law School's Justin Levitt (a former DOJ official), warned at the time that the proclamation's broad, non-individualized wording could unintentionally sweep in people Trump did not intend to cover. That warning proved accurate: Matthew Laiss, federally charged in September 2025 with double voting in the 2020 election (in person in Florida and by mail in Bucks County, Pennsylvania), invoked the proclamation's broad language as a defense. The Justice Department itself told the federal court it did not consider Laiss covered, stating it had consulted the Office of the Pardon Attorney and could 'explicitly confirm' Laiss fell outside the proclamation's intended scope. On January 13, 2026, a federal judge ruled the pardon did not apply to Laiss, finding he had not applied for or received the pardon certificate the proclamation's own terms require; Laiss was subsequently found guilty of the underlying voter-fraud charge. A second test case produced the opposite outcome. Harrison Floyd -- an ex-Marine and MMA fighter who worked on Trump's 2020 campaign, one of the 79 people actually named on the November pardon list for his role in the Georgia fake-electors racketeering case -- separately faced a federal charge from a February 2023 incident in which he allegedly rushed at and assaulted two FBI agents (spitting in their faces, per reporting) sent by then-Special Counsel Jack Smith to serve him a subpoena in the federal 2020-election-subversion investigation, an incident with no direct connection to the fake-electors conduct itself. Floyd's attorney, Carlos Salvado, told ABC News in November 2025 the pardon's broad 'any conduct relating to their efforts to expose voting fraud' language might extend to the unrelated assault charge, saying only 'there is an argument.' Unlike the Laiss case, DOJ did not contest the extension: on January 7, 2026, federal prosecutors moved to dismiss the assault charge, a decision reporting tied directly to the clemency order -- meaning the same ambiguous pardon language a federal judge rejected as a shield for Laiss's unrelated voter-fraud conviction was, weeks later, allowed by DOJ itself to end a federal prosecution for physically assaulting FBI agents in the line of duty.

status: The pardon proclamation is final and cannot itself be reversed. The state prosecutions it left unaffected -- including Georgia's racketeering case and Arizona's, Michigan's, and Nevada's fake-elector cases -- remained ongoing under state authority as of this writing. The attempt to extend the pardon's reach to an unrelated federal voter-fraud case failed in court: a federal judge rejected Matthew Laiss's claim to coverage on January 13, 2026, after DOJ's own Pardon Attorney's office told the court on the record it did not consider him covered; Laiss was subsequently found guilty of the underlying double-voting charge. Days later, on February 10-11, 2025, Trump went further and granted Blagojevich a full pardon, formally erasing the corruption convictions his sentence had only previously been commuted for.**

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Using Official U.S. Trade and Sanctions Authority to Attempt to Shield a Foreign Political Ally From a Legitimate Foreign Prosecution -- not itself a domestic criminal charge, addressed here as a foreign-policy/abuse-of-power accountability concern
incident_summary: In a July 9, 2025 letter to Brazil, Trump threatened a 50% tariff on Brazilian goods, explicitly citing and denouncing the ongoing coup-plot prosecution of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro -- an ally Trump has publicly supported -- as a politically motivated "witch hunt." **Trump followed through by executive order, imposing a 40% additional tariff (bringing total duties on many Brazilian goods to 50%) and separately invoking the Global Magnitsky Act -- a sanctions law designed for human-rights abusers and corrupt officials -- against Alexandre de Moraes, the Brazilian Supreme Court justice overseeing the Bolsonaro case, freezing his U.S.-based assets and barring his travel to the United States.** The administration also revoked U.S. visas for 8 of Brazil's 11 Supreme Court justices and other Brazilian officials. In August 2025 the State Department separately revoked the visas of Health Ministry officials tied to the Mais Médicos program, which had brought Cuban doctors to Brazil, citing what it called a Cuban forced-labor scheme, and then the visas of Health Minister Alexandre Padilha's wife and 10-year-old daughter; Padilha's own visa had already expired. Despite this pressure campaign, a five-justice panel of Brazil's Supreme Court convicted Bolsonaro by a 4-1 vote and on September 11, 2025 sentenced him to 27 years and three months in prison; Justice Moraes, the case's lead judge, pointed to "overwhelming evidence" of a plot to assassinate then-President-elect Lula and Moraes himself, part of which he said was printed inside the presidential palace. On September 22, 2025, the U.S. extended the Magnitsky sanctions to Moraes's wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes, and a family-linked company, and revoked the visas of more Brazilian officials, including Attorney General of the Union Jorge Messias, which the White House framed as a further response to the conviction. Brazilian President Lula publicly framed his government's refusal to intervene in the judiciary as a defense of national sovereignty, and his domestic popularity rose amid the confrontation, while Brazil simultaneously expanded trade ties with China as U.S.-Brazil relations strained. In October 2025, the first formal U.S. proposal for negotiating the tariffs, later revealed by O Estado de S. Paulo, contained 21 demands, mostly on trade but including that Brazil hold "free and fair" 2026 elections and not arrest or arbitrarily restrict the participation of "political dissidents," which Brazil's government read as a reference to Bolsonaro; Brazil refused to negotiate those points. Relations then thawed: after an October 26, 2025 Trump-Lula meeting on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit in Kuala Lumpur, which Lula described as "surprisingly good," Lula said Trump had assured him an agreement would be reached, and in November 2025 Trump signed Executive Order 14361 exempting coffee, beef, and certain other agricultural products from the 40% tariff. Bolsonaro began serving his sentence in November 2025 after Justice Moraes declared the case closed at the end of the appeals period. On December 12, 2025, the Treasury removed Moraes, his wife, and the linked company from its sanctions list. On February 20, 2026, after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the emergency-powers law (IEEPA) does not authorize tariffs, Trump signed an order ending all IEEPA tariffs, a category that included the 40% Brazil tariff. In March 2026, Justice Moraes granted Bolsonaro temporary humanitarian house arrest after he was hospitalized with pneumonia, and he extended it in July 2026. A new dispute followed a May 2026 White House meeting that Lula said had improved relations: on June 1, 2026, the U.S. Trade Representative, concluding an investigation opened at Trump's direction in July 2025 under Section 301 of the Trade Act, proposed a 25% tariff on many Brazilian products, citing alleged unfair practices in areas including electronic payments, digital trade, ethanol, anti-corruption enforcement and illegal deforestation. The proposal became entangled with Brazil's October 2026 presidential race: Lula accused Bolsonaro's son Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, a presidential candidate, of lobbying Washington for the tariffs, while Flávio Bolsonaro denied it and asked the administration to delay any decision until after the election. On June 16, 2026, Brazil's Supreme Court sentenced Bolsonaro's son Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former congressman living in the U.S., to four years and two months in prison after finding him guilty of courting U.S. interference in his father's trial through sanctions on the court's justices and tariffs on Brazilian goods; he said he had not been properly notified of the proceedings. On July 15, 2026, USTR imposed the 25% tariff, effective July 22, with exemptions including beef, coffee, rare earths, energy products and aircraft; Lula called it unjustified and said Brazil would invoke its Reciprocity Law and the WTO. This Brazil-specific pressure campaign was part of a broader pattern this tracker documents in a companion entry, which covers parallel U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and its judges over the Netanyahu/Gallant arrest warrants, and informal pressure on France over Marine Le Pen's conviction.
elements_required: Trump's own July 9, 2025 letter explicitly ties the tariff threat to the Bolsonaro prosecution ("This trial should not be taking place... It is a Witch Hunt that should end IMMEDIATELY!"), alongside free-speech complaints and a claim of an unfair trade relationship despite a U.S. trade surplus with Brazil -- a rare case where a foreign prosecution is on the record, in the President's own words, among the stated reasons for a major trade action

The Magnitsky Act sanctions against Justice Moraes apply a human-rights/corruption sanctions authority to a sitting foreign judge for performing his judicial function in a case involving a Trump ally -- a novel and contested use of that authority
The pressure campaign did not achieve its stated goal: Brazil's Supreme Court proceeded to convict and sentence Bolsonaro despite the tariffs and sanctions, a directly observable outcome

U.S. visa revocations targeted 8 of 11 sitting Brazilian Supreme Court justices, an unusually broad diplomatic action against a foreign judiciary as a body, not just the individual judge presiding over the case

incident_summary: The May 2026 executive order documented here had two direct antecedents in late 2025. On November 7, 2025, NPR reported that a CDC committee hand-picked by RFK Jr. was scrutinizing the childhood vaccine schedule after Trump's own complaint that "they pump so much stuff into those beautiful little babies", and that the CDC was investigating splitting up the combined MMR shot; some public-health experts worried the review was part of Kennedy's campaign against vaccines, amid new measles and whooping cough outbreaks. Then, on December 5, 2025, Trump signed a memo directly ordering federal health agencies to reconsider the childhood vaccine schedule and potentially align it with "peer, developed countries," after praising advisers for scrapping the longstanding hepatitis B birth-dose recommendation for newborns; the memo instructed the HHS Secretary and CDC director to revise U.S. standards if they deemed foreign practices "superior" -- the same "peer nations" framing and hepatitis B rollback that recur in the December 2025 HHS assessment and executive order below. On May 29, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14407, directing the CDC and its Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to realign the U.S. childhood vaccine schedule with that December 2025 HHS assessment, which had called for reducing the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11, reasoning that the U.S. recommends more childhood vaccines than "peer nations" such as Denmark and more than twice as many vaccine doses as some European countries. The order followed the CDC's January 2026 overhaul of the immunization schedule under HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a memo by then-acting CDC Director Jim O'Neill that cut the vaccines recommended as routine for children from 17 to 11, limited several to high-risk groups, and moved rotavirus, COVID-19, influenza, hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal shots to shared clinical decision-making -- an overhaul the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts stayed on March 16, 2026, along with the appointments of 13 ACIP members Kennedy named between June 2025 and January 2026 and all votes the panel had taken, leaving the recommendations in place before June 2025 in effect pending litigation (the same underlying ACIP litigation this tracker documents in detail in a separate entry, which should be checked for that litigation's current status rather than this entry). **EO 14407 steers CDC/ACIP toward a specific numerical and substantive vaccine-schedule outcome via presidential directive, notwithstanding that a federal court has already found the government's process for changing the schedule, including bypassing ACIP, disregarded the scientific method, and that the schedule remains under an active judicial stay.** On August 10, 2026, Trump signed a second executive order, EO 14420 ("Delivering Gold Standard Childhood Vaccine Recommendations for Americans"), which reaffirms rather than supersedes EO 14407 and elaborates it into three specific categories: vaccines recommended for all children (including measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, and polio), vaccines for high-risk groups only (including RSV and dengue), and vaccines moved into a shared clinical-decision-making category between parents and doctors (including hepatitis A/B, rotavirus, influenza, and COVID-19). It also states that the combined MMR vaccine should be given as three separate single-disease shots once domestically available (while keeping combination vaccines available), and that childhood immunizations should be given at separate visits where feasible. According to an October 1, 2026 vaccine-policy column published by CIDRAP, Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump's nominee to lead the FDA, helped develop that order, and flu vaccines remain recommended for everyone 6 months and older this season because the order's call to end that recommendation for children has been held up by a legal challenge. EO 14420 is not self-executing: Section 3 directs an HHS Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines to deliver an implementation plan within 90 days, and the order itself states it creates no enforceable right or benefit against the government. The order explicitly acknowledges that implementation of the administration's prior vaccine-schedule directives "has been delayed due to litigation over the composition" of ACIP -- the same litigation covered in detail in the separate entry noted above, which covers the litigation side of the dispute while this entry covers the presidential-directive side. EO 14420 assigns that 90-day implementation plan to the statutory Task Force on Safer Childhood Vaccines, which HHS had revived in August 2025 after it lay dormant since 1998, naming NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya chair, with CDC and FDA representatives. The 90-day deadline runs to approximately November 8, 2026. HHS published a formal Request for Information in the Federal Register on August 24, 2026 (Docket No. HHS-OS-2026-0332), seeking public comment on whether the three categories used in federal vaccine recommendations (routine/universal, risk-based, and shared clinical decision-making) are adequate or should be revised -- a direct follow-on to EO 14420's 90-day implementation-plan mandate. The comment period closed September 20, 2026. On September 18, 2026, speaking in the Oval Office with Kennedy beside him, Trump said his administration would be "demanding" that drug companies split certain childhood vaccines into five smaller doses given at six-month intervals, "so that a small amount of the vaccine gets pumped into the body," and claimed the change would bring a "massive reduction in autism." He offered no evidence, did not say which vaccines he meant, and HHS did not answer CNN's request for details. **Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told CNN the plan "would not work" and would give vaccines "in a manner in which they wouldn't be protective," and extensive scientific studies have found no evidence linking vaccines to autism.** The remarks came a day after Kennedy told a conference of Children's Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group he founded, "you have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House."

incident_summary: **In April 2025, the White House sent a 'de-designation' email to Rochelle Garza, the Democratic chair of the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights (a term she had held since March 17, 2023), seeking to demote her and elevate Republican commissioner Peter Kirsanow as the new chair. Garza refused to step down, citing 42 U.S.C. § 1975's requirement that a chair be designated only with the concurrence of a majority of the Commission's members -- not by unilateral presidential letter -- and declined to recognize a vote on new leadership as procedurally in order.** The White House renewed the attempt in March 2026, when the deputy director of the Office of Presidential Personnel sent a similar letter seeking the same change; Garza again resisted, and the Commission's own website continued to list her as chair as of at least June 12, 2026 (she is documented moderating an official Commission hearing on immigration enforcement in Minnesota that month). The dispute sits against the backdrop of a major, unrelated Supreme Court ruling: on June 29, 2026, the Court decided Trump v. Slaughter 6-3, overruling the 91-year-old Humphrey's Executor v. United States precedent and holding that for-cause removal protections for heads of independent multi-member agencies exercising executive power violate separation of powers. That case arose from Trump's firing of two Democratic FTC commissioners, not from the Civil Rights Commission, but its reasoning substantially strengthens the legal argument that Trump could lawfully remove or override Garza going forward -- a development not yet resolved as of this entry's creation.

offense_category: First Amendment Viewpoint Discrimination — Denial of Press Access (established precedent: Sherrill v. Knight, D.C. Cir. 1977, holding that White House press credential denials must not be arbitrary or based on viewpoint) — civil litigation, not criminal
incident_summary: On Friday, September 18, 2026, Trump announced on Truth Social that he was banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House over their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" The next day, journalists from all three outlets had their credentials pulled and were blocked from entering the White House. **After the outlets sued on September 21, Trump personally defended the ban in Truth Social posts, baselessly claiming the outlets' coverage posed "a threat to our National Security," and wrote that the White House was "instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS,"** adding "Why should I have to give 'access' to such people?" Before the suit, the White House had also removed CNN from its scheduled turn as White House pool representative -- the network had been set to accompany Trump to New York for the United Nations General Assembly -- and the five-network television pool declined to replace it: pool chair Bryan Boughton of Fox News wrote that there would be "no replacement pool put in place," and ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said in a joint statement that "the public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government" and that "no administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting." On September 22, letters from the White House Press Office, filed in court that day with the Justice Department's opposition to the outlets' motion, accused them of behavior "in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information." The letters listed stories on the Iran war, U.S. munitions and missile-interceptor stocks, the East Wing bunker, security funding for the White House ballroom, and a Politico Playbook item on the Republican midterm convention, and gave the outlets until 5 p.m. on September 25 to contest the decision. The Justice Department's brief argued that "access to the White House is a privilege—not a right," asked that the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight precedent be overruled, and urged that the appeals court's reasoning in the AP case, which, in a stay ruling, let the White House weigh viewpoint in the Oval Office and similar restricted spaces, be applied to the whole White House complex. **One of the Politico stories the letters cited, a June report quoting a "senior administration official" who put the odds of a preliminary Iran deal at 80 to 85 percent, reportedly came from Vice President JD Vance speaking on a background press call the White House itself hosted**, according to the media newsletter Status and to HuffPost, which cited a Washington Post report on a recording of the call; on September 21, Vance had publicly called the ban "totally appropriate." Early on September 24, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly granted a 14-day temporary restraining order requiring the White House to restore the revoked hard passes, finding the outlets likely to succeed on their Fifth Amendment due-process claim because the passes were revoked without notice or a chance to be heard, and writing that he was skeptical, on the record before him, that national security was the actual motivation; he also noted that, in most cases, the reporters who wrote the stories cited in the letters did not hold hard passes. Reporters from all three outlets were turned away again that morning and began getting back onto the complex around noon. The five-network pool resumed coverage on September 25, but that night White House guidance left CNN off Air Force One for Trump's September 26 trip to Tennessee, a flight on which it had been scheduled to fly as the TV pool network; the Associated Press noted that Kelly's order addressed hard passes and did not directly address pool duties; the outlets' lawyer said they believe it does. rebuttal_anticipated: The administration's defense in court: access to the White House is "a privilege, not a right"; Sherrill and Karem were wrongly decided and should be overruled; the appeals court's reasoning in the AP case should extend to the whole White House complex; the ban was not retaliatory because other outlets equally critical of the President kept their access; letters sent to the outlets on September 22 gave adequate after-the-fact notice and a chance to respond; and the outlets' reporting threatened national security and breached "standards of professionalism and decorum" -- a broad claim of executive discretion over access rather than a factual rebuttal of the outlets' account.
comeback: Sherrill v. Knight holds that once a general practice of press access exists, it cannot be withdrawn from specific outlets based on the content of their reporting or editorial decisions -- and here the viewpoint-based motive is unusually explicit and self-documented: Trump's own Truth Social post cited "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!" as the reason, and his subsequent Truth Social posts offered no evidence for the separately claimed national-security rationale. The same judge, Timothy Kelly, previously found a materially similar credential revocation (Acosta, 2018) likely unlawful and ordered access restored on an emergency basis. On September 24, 2026, he did so again here, finding the outlets likely to succeed on their due-process claim under Sherrill and Karem v. Trump, and noting that nothing in the record predating the suit suggested national security motivated the revocations, and that most of the reporters behind the stories the White House cited did not hold hard passes. One of the Politico stories the White House cited to justify the ban reportedly quoted Vice President JD Vance himself, speaking anonymously on a background call the White House arranged.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Part of a documented pattern of White House press-access restrictions aimed at outlets whose coverage the President objects to, following the earlier Wiles/AP press-access case, in which the Associated Press was shut out of the Oval Office, Air Force One and other pool spaces after refusing to adopt the "Gulf of America" name. This case is larger in scale -- three outlets' hard passes revoked and their reporters barred from the White House complex entirely, rather than one outlet excluded from specific restricted spaces -- and more direct in how it was announced: in the AP case, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt conveyed the exclusion and told the AP it came at President Trump's direction, while here Trump announced the ban himself on Truth Social and defended it in public remarks. Chief of Staff Susan Wiles is a named defendant in both lawsuits. In court, the Justice Department asked that the appeals court's AP-case reasoning be extended from the Oval Office and similar spaces to the whole White House complex, and that the 1977 precedent protecting reporters' access be overruled, relying in part on a Pentagon press secretary's declaration and an appeals court stay order favoring Pentagon escort rules for reporters. The national-security rationale was raised only after the outlets announced their suit, and Judge Kelly wrote that, on the record before him, he was skeptical it was the actual motivation.

offense_category: Selective Clemency Pattern -- Pardoning Crypto-Industry Figures Convicted of Financial Crimes, Including One Pardon Directly Preceded by a $2 Billion Deal Using the Trump Family's Own Stablecoin -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the pattern's ties to $100M+ crypto-industry campaign spending and, in one case, a direct personal financial benefit to the Trump family
incident_summary: Over 2025, Trump granted three notable pardons to individuals convicted of crypto-linked financial crimes, following a 2024 campaign in which the crypto industry spent more than $100 million to influence the election. On January 21, 2025 -- his first full day in office -- Trump pardoned Ross Ulbricht, founder of the Silk Road dark-web drug marketplace, who was serving a double life sentence for a marketplace prosecutors said facilitated roughly $1 billion in illegal transactions; Trump had promised the pardon at the 2024 Libertarian National Convention while courting crypto-industry support. On March 27, 2025, Trump pardoned BitMEX co-founders Arthur Hayes, Benjamin Delo, and Samuel Reed, along with a former BitMEX executive, all of whom had pleaded guilty in 2022 to Bank Secrecy Act violations for failing to implement anti-money-laundering controls prosecutors said let BitMEX operate as a "money laundering platform"; the pardon was signed quietly and not publicly announced, and separately extended to BitMEX's parent company, HDR Global Trading -- reportedly the first-ever full presidential pardon granted to a corporation -- just before a $100 million fine payment deadline. CBS News reported May 5, 2025 that the Trump family's personal wealth had grown by nearly $3 billion over the prior six months, driven largely by crypto ventures -- including the $TRUMP and $MELANIA meme coins launched days before Trump's inauguration and the family's stake in World Liberty Financial -- with the report separately noting a $2 billion stablecoin deal with a UAE-backed firm, the same MGX/USD1 transaction detailed below in connection with the later CZ Zhao pardon. This broader personal-enrichment picture is the context in which the CZ pardon's specific $2 billion financial dimension sits, not an isolated event. On October 23, 2025, Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, who had pleaded guilty in 2023 to enabling money laundering as Binance's CEO, paid a $50 million personal fine, and served four months in prison as part of Binance's own $4.3 billion DOJ settlement. The CZ pardon carried a documented direct financial dimension the other two lacked: **Abu Dhabi-based investment fund MGX used USD1 -- the stablecoin issued by World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto venture, on which Trump is listed as "Chief Crypto Advocate" and in which a Trump-affiliated entity holds a 60% ownership stake and a claim to 75% of token revenues -- to close a $2 billion investment into Binance, a deal that functioned as a $2 billion effective deposit into World Liberty Financial's stablecoin.** Sen. Elizabeth Warren publicly stated that Zhao "financed President Trump's stablecoin and lobbied for a pardon" and "today, he got it." In late September 2025, ahead of the pardon, Binance hired Checkmate Government Relations -- a firm run by Ches McDowell, a friend of Donald Trump Jr. -- to lobby the White House and Treasury Department specifically on "executive relief" and cryptocurrency policy; Checkmate disclosed being paid $450,000 for that one month of work. Zhao himself told CNBC at Davos in January 2026 that reports of a pardon-for-support deal "do[] not exist at all." Separately, Trump's own 2025 financial disclosure reported more than $550 million in income from World Liberty Financial token sales -- broader venture-wide income not specifically tied to the Binance/MGX transaction documented above, but illustrating the scale of the family's financial stake in the same crypto venture Zhao's pardon and business dealings intersected with. This tracker separately documents a related conflict-of-interest concern involving the same World Liberty Financial/MGX relationship and a July 2026 Commerce Department export-control decision benefiting the UAE, in a companion entry.

comeback: The three pardons are not being treated as a single undifferentiated conspiracy -- the Ulbricht pardon's libertarian/campaign-promise rationale is different in kind from the Zhao pardon, and this entry says so explicitly. offense_category: Contested Exercise of D.C. Home Rule Act Emergency Authority -- Section 740 permits the President to direct D.C.'s police for limited emergency purposes, but the scope, duration, and factual predicate ('crime emergency') of this invocation raised separation-of-powers and home-rule concerns rather than an established statutory violation
status: Federal control of D.C. police lapsed Sept. 10, 2025. Judge Jia Cobb found the Guard deployment likely unlawful Nov. 20, 2025, but the D.C. Circuit stayed that ruling Dec. 17 pending an appeal still unresolved; the deployment is extended through January 2029.
incident_summary: On August 11, 2025, President Trump announced he was placing Washington, D.C.'s Metropolitan Police Department under direct federal control and deploying the National Guard, invoking Section 740 of the D.C. Home Rule Act to declare a "crime emergency." Within about a week, roughly 800 D.C. National Guard troops had been mobilized, with additional state National Guard units en route, alongside roughly 500 newly deployed immigration and other federal agents patrolling the streets and operating checkpoints. Trump said he was acting "to rescue our nation's capital from crime, bloodshed, bedlam and squalor, and worse," but the city's own crime data showed violent crime had been declining for two consecutive years before the declaration: homicides fell 32% in 2024 (from a 2023 peak of 274, the city's highest since 1997, to 187) and continued falling roughly 12% further into 2025. D.C. officials and local commentators characterized the declared emergency as a pretext rather than a response to worsening conditions, noting that the district's justice system was already strained -- including by the administration's own purge of senior federal prosecutors who had worked on January 6 cases, documented separately in this database, and a years-long judicial vacancy backlog in the D.C. courts, which remained short-handed into 2026 (the Senate confirmed six Superior Court and two D.C. Court of Appeals judges on August 7, 2026); according to the D.C. Sentencing Commission, felony case filings in the Superior Court rose 44% in 2025, an increase Bloomberg Law reported coincided with the administration's push for more control over D.C. police and more federal prosecutions in the district. A documented case of wrongful detention arose within the same crackdown-era criminal-justice system: Kristal Rios Esquivel was arrested August 20, 2025 at the National Zoo, accused of trying to enter a restricted birdhouse staff entrance and spitting on a police sergeant during her arrest. She should have been brought to court on August 22 but was not brought before a federal magistrate judge until August 25 -- a three-day delay -- and at that hearing prosecutors did not seek her detention, instead recommending release on minimal conditions. She was ordered released but remained jailed for more than 19 hours afterward, until the afternoon of August 26, about six days after her arrest. **U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui wrote that the D.C. Department of Corrections had refused to release her over a "hit" in the warrant system from the very warrant for which she had appeared on August 25 -- a failure Faruqui called "false imprisonment," noting it was not the first time in the past four months that the court had encountered the problem.** The Department of Corrections said a routine database check had turned up an FBI warrant and that it held her until that warrant was cleared. A DOJ prosecutor ultimately intervened to clear the erroneous database entry. Faruqui questioned why compliance with a release order required such extraordinary effort. Reuters reported on September 4, 2025, based on interviews with nine current and former FBI employees, that the surge pulled FBI agents who normally work out of the public eye into routine, highly visible police work, emerging from unmarked cars in tactical gear -- the employees said as many as 1,000 unmarked FBI vehicles had been used in Washington during highly public scenes. FBI employees said the exposure risked burning vehicles the bureau relies on for undercover work against cartels, violent gangs, and foreign intelligence services; one employee said, "We can't use these cars to go undercover, we can't use them to surveil narcotraffickers and fentanyl suppliers or Russian or Chinese spies or use them to go after violent criminal gangs or terrorists." An FBI spokesman denied the employees' assertions. The surge, justified by the administration as a violent-crime crackdown, drew criticism for featuring many arrests for minor offenses while creating this operational-security cost to the FBI's own national-security and counterintelligence capacity. On September 4, 2025, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued over the National Guard deployment. Federal control of the Metropolitan Police Department lapsed on September 10, 2025, when the 30-day Section 740 period ended without a congressional extension, after Mayor Muriel Bowser ordered continued cooperation with federal law enforcement; the National Guard deployment, which is not subject to that time limit, continued. On November 20, 2025, U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb ruled that the deployment was likely unlawful and blocked it, pausing her order for 21 days to allow an appeal. On November 26, two West Virginia National Guard members were shot while on patrol near the White House; Army Spc. Sarah Beckstrom died the next day, and Trump ordered 500 more troops to Washington. The D.C. Circuit administratively stayed Cobb's ruling on December 4 and, on December 17, a unanimous panel of Judges Patricia Millett, Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao stayed it pending appeal, finding the president likely to succeed in arguing that he holds a unique power to mobilize the Guard in the federal district; the appeal remained pending as of September 2026. By August 2026 the deployment had been extended through January 2029, an extension a Defense Department estimate put at about $1.4 billion, and more than 4,600 military personnel from D.C. and 24 states and territories were still deployed as of August 4, 2026. Crime kept falling: Metropolitan Police Department figures showed overall crime down 20% and homicides down 32% (from 97 to 66) through August 7, 2026 compared with the same period of 2025, though how much of the decline was owed to the surge rather than longer-running local efforts remained disputed.

incident_summary: On March 25, 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14248, 'Preserving and Protecting the Integrity of American Elections,' which sought to require documentary proof of citizenship for federal voter registration, directed the Department of Homeland Security (with the Social Security Administration) to compile state-by-state citizenship lists, and directed states to reject mail/absentee ballots received after Election Day even if postmarked on time. **Military-family voting advocates joined a lawsuit challenging the order in April 2025, arguing the postmark/receipt-deadline change and citizenship-documentation requirements would disproportionately disenfranchise servicemembers and their families stationed abroad or deployed, who already face mail delays military voters have long relied on postmark-based deadlines to accommodate.** Multiple federal courts subsequently ruled against key provisions: a coalition of 19 state attorneys general won a permanent injunction in the District of Massachusetts blocking the citizenship-documentation and mail-ballot-deadline provisions, and a separate ruling permanently blocked the provision requiring the Election Assistance Commission to mandate proof-of-citizenship documents on the federal voter registration form. In August 2026, the Supreme Court handed Trump a procedural win, staying the injunction 6-3 ahead of the November 2026 midterms -- but on standing grounds, finding the states had sued too early and had not yet shown concrete harm, not on the merits of whether the order itself is constitutional. A separate nationwide ruling by a U.S. District Judge in Boston continues to block the U.S. Postal Service specifically from following the order's mail-ballot directives.

offense_category: Rescission of Executive-Branch Ethics Pledge Requirements (Lobbyist Gift Ban and Revolving-Door Restriction) -- no criminal or civil legal violation established; the accountability concern is the removal of a structural anti-corruption safeguard rather than any single unlawful act
incident_summary: On January 20, 2025, his first day back in office, Trump signed Executive Order 14148, rescinding a list of Biden-era executive orders and actions, including Executive Order 13989. **That Biden order had required every executive-branch appointee to sign an ethics pledge committing them not to accept gifts from lobbyists or lobbying organizations, and imposing a two-year "revolving door" ban preventing new appointees from working on regulations or contracts tied to their immediately prior employer or clients. The pledge also barred departing appointees from lobbying senior executive-branch officials until the end of the administration or for two years, whichever was later, and for senior appointees lengthened the one-year ban on contacting their former agency to two years. Rescinding it removed these restrictions for Trump's incoming appointees.** One immediate effect was lifting restrictions that would otherwise have continued to apply to former Biden-administration appointees after they left government, which Politico reported could make it easier for them to move into lobbying and other private-sector jobs. Trump did not issue a replacement ethics pledge or comparable restriction of his own for his administration's appointees, despite this being a step new administrations have typically taken, and none had been issued as of July 2026. That month, a Sludge review of second-quarter lobbying disclosures named former Trump administration officials who had moved into lobbying after leaving: three of them, from the Interior Department, the White House press office and the Vice President's office, were lobbying the agency they had recently left or the White House offices of their recent colleagues, and a fourth, a former White House Senate liaison, was lobbying senators and the Energy and Treasury Departments. Sludge wrote that none of this was illegal, because no ethics pledge or revolving-door restriction of Trump's own was in place to prevent it.

status: The rescission is a completed, standing action. Executive Order 13989's pledge has not been reinstated, and as of September 2026 no replacement ethics pledge for Trump's appointees appears in the Federal Register. This is an ongoing absent safeguard, not an event in progress.
rebuttal_anticipated: Each incoming administration can set its own ethics rules for its appointees, and rescinding a predecessor's executive order is a routine, lawful exercise of presidential authority -- it does not itself authorize or excuse any specific act of corruption, and other legal restrictions on gifts to federal employees (the general federal gift rules under 5 C.F.R. part 2635) remain in place regardless of this pledge.
comeback: This entry does not allege the rescission itself is unlawful -- the accountability question is that Trump removed a specific, self-imposed anti-corruption structure (a lobbyist gift ban and a two-year revolving-door cooling-off period) for his own incoming appointees without replacing it with anything comparable, and that the immediate documented effect freed recently-departed officials from a restriction that had applied to them, while leaving Trump's own appointees under no equivalent commitment.
cause: [TAP Analysis, not sourced] Illustrates a policy-level accountability question rather than a legal violation: on his first day Trump removed a self-imposed ethics safeguard without replacing it, and by mid-2026 some of his own former appointees were lobbying the offices they had recently left, which no pledge barred.
confidence_note: HIGH confidence on the core facts (the EO, what it rescinded, and the absence of a replacement pledge) -- corroborated by COSSA's direct citation of the order text, The Hill, and Campaign Legal Center. The effect on departing Biden-administration appointees rests on Politico's January 22, 2025 reporting, in which ethics lawyer Rob Kelner described restrictions being lifted and Politico predicted easier moves into lobbying and other private-sector jobs; it is not tied to named individual cases. offense_category: Apparent Quid Pro Quo -- a $5 million campaign donation followed within weeks by the President's personal intervention to delay a federal agency's regulatory action benefiting the donor, raising accountability concerns under anti-corruption norms even absent a criminal bribery charge, which requires proof of an explicit agreed exchange not established here
status: Rule delay remained in effect as of this entry's last-verified date, with implementation pushed to at least January 1, 2026; Extremity Care's principal donor made a second, larger ($2.5 million, initially anonymous) donation to Trump's White House ballroom project in October 2025
incident_summary: Extremity Care LLC, which sells 'skin substitute' wound-care products made from placental and other tissue, donated $5 million to the pro-Trump MAGA Inc. super PAC on February 24, 2025 -- a donation not publicly disclosed until July 31, 2025, buried on page 18 of the PAC's mid-year filing. The Biden administration had proposed a CMS rule limiting Medicare coverage of skin substitutes to products 'supported by evidence' of effectiveness, which CMS itself found would have excluded 92% of currently covered products (identifying only 17 with proven scientific validity) -- including Extremity Care's, which cost $7,812 to $11,051 per square inch, compared to $75 to $195 for proven alternatives. Days after the donation, Extremity Care co-owner Oliver Burckhardt attended a Mar-a-Lago donor dinner and spoke with Trump. The next morning, March 1, 2025, Trump posted on Truth Social attacking the rule and claiming, without evidentiary support, that it would cause '431,429 lost limbs annually and 187,286 additional deaths.' CMS, which had already pushed the rule's original effective date from February to April 13, 2025, announced on April 11, 2025 -- 40 days after Trump's post -- a further delay to at least January 1, 2026. **Between April and July 2025 alone, Medicare spent an additional $2.3 billion on skin substitutes while the rule remained blocked, on top of a broader spending surge in the category from a negligible amount in 2014 to more than $10 billion in 2024.** Extremity Care separately retained Trump fundraiser Brian Ballard as a lobbyist for $320,000 annually; Ballard's former employee, Susie Wiles, is Trump's White House Chief of Staff. In October 2025, Burckhardt attended a second Trump donor dinner, this one at the White House Rose Garden, and the New York Times later reported Extremity Care had been an anonymous $2.5 million donor to Trump's White House ballroom construction fund.
elements_required: A specific, substantial donation ($5 million) from a company directly financially interested in a pending federal regulatory action, made shortly before that action was delayed in the donor's favor
Direct, documented donor access to the President (the Mar-a-Lago dinner) preceding the President's own public intervention against the rule
The President's own social-media statement opposing the rule, containing specific numerical claims (limb-loss and death figures) that lack cited evidentiary support
A federal agency (CMS) action -- a further implementation delay -- following within 40 days of the President's public position, benefiting the donor commercially
A quantified financial benefit to the donor and cost to the Medicare program ($2.3 billion in additional spending over roughly three months) resulting from the delay
A second, larger donation from the same donor to a Trump-connected fund (the White House ballroom) later in 2025, initially undisclosed, suggesting a continuing pattern rather than an isolated event

status: Ongoing, not charged: Trump still holds and trades individual stocks, including AI-sector shares, while setting AI policy. Warren and Garcia's questions (due August 28, 2026) have no public answer found; no investigation or finding exists.
incident_summary:
Trump's in-office stock trading as a whole, including the revocable trust his eldest son runs and the scale of his trades, is covered in the entry on his in-office stock trading; this entry follows the part of his and his sons' holdings tied to artificial intelligence. His sons built their own stakes in the artificial-intelligence economy: according to outlets summarizing a later Washington Post analysis, Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump helped launch American Data Centers, a venture aimed at high-performance computing infrastructure, in February 2025; Trump Jr. is a partner at 1789 Capital, whose investments include the AI companies Cerebras Systems, Perplexity and xAI, and which in August 2026 closed a $1.2 billion real estate fund that lists data centers among its targets; and Eric Trump invests through American Ventures in defense, robotics and AI firms. On December 18, 2025, Trump Media & Technology Group, the family's Truth Social company, announced an all-stock merger valued at more than $6 billion with the fusion-power developer TAE Technologies, which TechCrunch reported comes as data centers clamor for more electricity during the AI boom; fusion-industry insiders raised possible conflicts of interest with the Energy Department.

**Several AI-sector trades landed close to government actions or presidential remarks that could lift those same stocks.** According to an August 12, 2026 letter from Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Robert Garcia, ranking member of the House Oversight Committee, citing his May 2026 periodic transaction report: on January 6, 2026, Trump's accounts bought up to $1 million of Nvidia and up to $100,000 of AMD stock, a week before the Commerce Department loosened its export-license policy for the Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X chips to China; on February 10, 2026, the accounts bought at least $1 million of Nvidia stock on the day Vice President JD Vance announced approval of 41,000 more advanced Nvidia chips for a $4 billion data-center project in Armenia; on the same day they bought $1 million to $5 million of Dell stock, nine days before Trump told a Georgia audience to "Go out and buy a Dell Computer"; and after March purchases of Micron stock, Trump called the company "one of the hottest companies" on Fox News. Some, including the January 6 Nvidia purchase, are labeled "unsolicited" in the filing. The letter frames the trades as raising questions, not as proof that Trump directed them; no official body has found that he did. Warren and Garcia asked Trump to name the managers who run his accounts and to say whether he directed specific trades, by August 28, 2026. Trump said in July, as quoted by CNBC, "We have funds that run my money" and "They invest my money, and I don't talk to them." No public answer to the letter's questions was found in the sources reviewed.

Meanwhile Trump has rejected calls to slow AI development. In a September 14, 2026 Truth Social post he wrote that "The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT" and that "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers." On September 20, 2026, the Washington Post published an analysis of his financial disclosures and corporate announcements finding that his "sprawling family business empire has become increasingly intertwined with the boom in artificial intelligence, at the same time that he has resisted calls to slow the development of the technology." According to IBTimes UK, The Herald Business and Adnkronos, which summarized the analysis, the Post counted nearly 30,000 securities transactions in Trump's accounts since he returned to office, including purchases of Dell Technologies, Micron Technology, GE Vernova, Broadcom and Texas Instruments, companies that supply computing hardware or power for AI. Adnkronos and Financial News (South Korea) reported that Don Fox, a former acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, told the Post that no president under the modern conflict-of-interest system has managed his finances this way. White House spokesman Davis Ingle said the investments are managed independently by outside managers using computer-driven portfolios that track market indexes, and that there are "no conflicts of interest."

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Executive Order Stripping Collective Bargaining Rights From Two-Thirds of the Federal Workforce, Allowed to Proceed After an Appeals Court Vacated an Injunction on a Retaliation Challenge -- documents a contested administration action still in litigation, not an allegation of illegality
incident_summary: President Trump signed Executive Order 14251, "Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs," on March 27, 2025, excluding roughly 40 agencies and subdivisions (including Defense, State, Treasury, HHS, and Veterans Affairs) from the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute on stated national-security grounds, eliminating collective bargaining rights for wide swaths of the federal workforce. Federal employee unions sued, arguing the order was actually issued to retaliate against unions for challenging other administration policies, in violation of their free-speech rights. U.S. District Judge James Donato in San Francisco preliminarily enjoined the order on June 24, 2025, but after the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals stayed that injunction on August 1, 2025, allowing enforcement to proceed, agencies moved through August 2025 to terminate union contracts covering hundreds of thousands of workers in quick succession: the EPA said on August 8, 2025 that it would no longer recognize its unions (AFGE, the National Association of Government Employees, the Engineers and Scientists of California, and the National Association of Independent Labor) and that all its contracts were terminated; **USDA notified union leaders on August 12, 2025 that it was ending contracts covering roughly 6,500 FSIS food-safety inspectors and about 1,650 APHIS employees, including roughly 1,500 plant inspectors, prompting a separate union lawsuit arguing that inspection work has nothing to do with national security**; and by August 31, 2025, VA, EPA, and Agriculture Department contracts had all been voided in the same wave (VA's termination specifically is documented in greater depth in this tracker's separate entry on the department's union defiance). Trump then expanded the order's scope: Executive Order 14343, "Further Exclusions From the Federal Labor-Management Relations Program," signed August 28, 2025 (published in the Federal Register September 3, 2025), added agencies including NASA, the U.S. Agency for Global Media, the Patent and Trademark Office's patents office, and the National Weather Service -- NASA's own implementation notice confirmed the agency would stop recognizing certain unions as exclusive bargaining representatives and halt collection of union dues on their behalf. On September 25, 2025, Federal Bureau of Prisons Director William K. Marshall III terminated the agency's collective bargaining agreement covering more than 30,000 correctional officers among its nearly 35,000 employees, represented by the Council of Prison Locals/AFGE, calling the union "an obstacle to progress instead of a partner in it." In Congress, a bipartisan effort to protect Defense Department civilians' bargaining rights via the FY2026 NDAA -- which had passed the House 231-196 in September 2025 -- was stripped from the final compromise bill in December 2025; a source familiar with the negotiations told Government Executive that only Sen. Lisa Murkowski among Senate Republicans ultimately pushed to keep the provision. On December 11, 2025, the House passed standalone legislation, the Protect America's Workforce Act (H.R. 2550), 231-195 with 20 Republicans in favor, to nullify both executive orders and restore bargaining rights; the National Active and Retired Federal Employees Association described the orders as having taken bargaining rights from about one million federal employees. The bill was received in the Senate on December 15, 2025, with no Senate vote recorded in the congressional bill-status records reviewed. On February 26, 2026, a three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit vacated Donato's preliminary injunction, concluding that on the preliminary record the unions had not shown a likelihood of success on their retaliation claim: assuming without deciding that they had made out a prima facie case, the panel found that the order had a legitimate grounding in national security concerns and that the government had shown Trump would have taken the same action even without the unions' protected speech. Judge John Owens, concurring, noted that because the panel was reviewing a preliminary injunction, a fully developed factual record could be materially different. The orders affect the bargaining rights of an estimated two-thirds of the federal civilian workforce. The panel amended its opinion on June 17, 2026, in an order that constituted the mandate of the court and directed that no petition for panel rehearing or rehearing en banc would be permitted, ending Ninth Circuit review of the injunction; no certiorari petition was filed. The panel expressly declined to address the unions' separate claim that the order exceeded the President's authority under 5 U.S.C. Section 7103(b)(1). That claim, the merits of the First Amendment retaliation claim, and the unions' Fifth Amendment claims all remain pending before Donato, where the parties are disputing whether the government must answer the unions' discovery requests before any motion to dismiss. A parallel challenge by the National Treasury Employees Union, argued before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit in December 2025, remained undecided as of September 2026.
elements_required: The executive order eliminated collective bargaining rights for a specifically large share of the federal workforce -- roughly two-thirds, per reporting -- rather than a narrow, security-specific carve-out
Unions specifically alleged retaliatory motive tied to their opposition to other administration policies, a First Amendment theory distinct from a pure policy disagreement
A district court initially found the retaliation theory sufficiently credible to issue an injunction, indicating the claim was not frivolous on its face

The appellate panel's conclusion that the retaliation claim was unlikely to succeed on the preliminary record rested on a but-for analysis (Trump would have acted the same regardless of retaliatory intent) rather than a finding that no retaliatory motive existed at all

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Using U.S. Sanctions Authority to Punish or Pressure Foreign Judges and Courts Over Rulings Touching U.S. Personnel or Political Allies -- a pattern spanning the ICC, Brazil, and France, not itself a domestic criminal charge
incident_summary: Beyond the Brazil-specific sanctions on Justice Alexandre de Moraes over the Bolsonaro prosecution -- documented in full in this tracker's separate entry on that campaign, and lifted on December 12, 2025, when the Treasury removed Moraes, his wife and a linked company from its sanctions list -- Trump's administration built a broader pattern of using U.S. sanctions authority against foreign judges and courts whose rulings touched U.S. personnel or affected political allies. On February 6, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14203 authorizing sanctions against the International Criminal Court, in response to ICC arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant; the order's annex, published February 10, named ICC Chief Prosecutor Karim Khan as its first target. **On June 5, 2025, Secretary of State Rubio named four sitting ICC judges for sanctions -- Beti Hohler (Slovenia) and Reine Alapini-Gansou (Benin), over their role in authorizing the Netanyahu/Gallant warrants, and Solomy Bossa (Uganda) and Luz del Carmen Ibanez Carranza (Peru), over authorizing the ICC's investigation into U.S. personnel in Afghanistan.** The ICC, Amnesty International, and Human Rights Watch condemned the sanctions as an attack on international judicial independence. On July 18, 2025, U.S. District Judge Nancy Torresen in Maine barred the government from penalizing two American human rights advocates who had sued, Matthew Smith and Akila Radhakrishnan, for providing speech-based services to the ICC, finding the order likely violated the First Amendment; the injunction covers only those two plaintiffs and does not lift the sanctions on the designated ICC officials. Rubio added four more designations on August 20, 2025 -- judges Kimberly Prost (Canada) and Nicolas Guillou (France) and Deputy Prosecutors Nazhat Shameem Khan (Fiji) and Mame Mandiaye Niang (Senegal) -- and two more judges, Gocha Lordkipanidze (Georgia) and Erdenebalsuren Damdin (Mongolia), on December 18, 2025, three days after they voted with the majority to reject an Israeli appeal. On August 18, 2026, the State Department sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane and Senior Trial Lawyer Abdoulaye Seye; the ICC said nine of its eighteen judges, both deputy prosecutors, the former prosecutor and one staff member were by then under U.S. sanctions. On September 20-21, 2026, the Wall Street Journal and Reuters reported that the administration was preparing sanctions against the court itself that would prohibit most transactions with it after a grace period. Separately, after a French court convicted National Rally leader Marine Le Pen of embezzling European Union funds and barred her from running for office (March 31, 2025), Trump called her office ban a "very big deal" and wrote on Truth Social, "FREE MARINE LE PEN!" On May 28, 2025, according to French magistrate Magali Lafourcade -- secretary general of France's National Advisory Commission on Human Rights (CNCDH) -- two advisers from the State Department's Bureau of Democracy, Human Rights and Labor, Samuel D. Samson and Christopher J. Anderson, met her in Paris and steered a conversation that began on human rights toward Le Pen's case, seeking "elements indicating that this was a purely political trial to stop her running for president." Lafourcade made her account public in January 2026, on France 5's En societe program (reported by Newsweek) and in an interview with AFP (reported by the Guardian and republished by the Irish Times). She told AFP she immediately reported the exchange to the French foreign ministry -- "which is something I never do, as we are an independent institution and don't report the exchanges we have with diplomats" -- fearing a potential "manipulation of the public debate in France." The State Department did not comment in those reports. On July 7, 2026, the Paris Court of Appeal upheld Le Pen's conviction but cut her ban on holding office to 45 months, 30 of them suspended, leaving her formally eligible to run in 2027; she said she would appeal to the Court of Cassation. No U.S. sanctions against the French judges who tried Le Pen were identified in sourcing reviewed, distinguishing this instance from the ICC and Brazil actions. A Washington Post report (Sept. 12, 2025) said Trump's rebukes of judges and courtroom prosecutors had "extended far beyond the United States' borders," as he and his officials questioned the fairness of foreign court systems, including those of long-standing allies, whose rulings displeased him.

official: Donald Trump, President
offense_category: Selective Clemency Pattern -- Pardoning Convicted Fraudsters (Many Donors/Allies) While Publicly Launching a New Anti-Fraud Enforcement Initiative -- clemency is a constitutional presidential power, not itself unlawful; the accountability claim concerns the pattern's inconsistency and its ties to political/financial support
incident_summary:
The New York Times reported Trump has granted clemency to more than 70 people convicted of fraud across his two terms, including numerous donors and allies, with those pardoned owing a combined $700 million in restitution and fines that the clemency wiped out. Specific documented cases include Philip Esformes, sentenced to 20 years for a $1.3 billion Medicare/Medicaid fraud scheme prosecutors called the largest-ever criminal health care fraud case brought against individuals; Salomon Melgen, a Palm Beach doctor sentenced to 17 years for stealing more than $42 million from Medicare; Trevor Milton, founder of electric-vehicle startup Nikola, pardoned after he and his wife donated $1.8 million to the Trump campaign; and Julio Herrera Velutini, granted clemency after his daughter Isabel Herrera donated $2.5 million in December 2024 and $1 million in July 2025 to the pro-Trump PAC MAGA Inc. Trump's pardon of Republican donor Adam Kidan, and the pardon of former Tennessee state Sen. Brian Kelsey -- a campaign-finance-fraud case rather than a financial-fraud-against-victims case -- are tracked separately in this database as fitting the same pattern.

On April 23, 2025 -- two weeks after being sentenced to 18 months for willfully failing to pay over $10 million in employment and income taxes -- Trump pardoned healthcare executive Paul Walczak. Walczak's mother, GOP donor Elizabeth Fago, had helped spread Ashley Biden's stolen diary during the 2020 campaign to benefit Trump; the New York Times reported Walczak applied for the pardon days after Trump's inauguration, citing his mother's fundraising for Trump and other Republicans, and that Fago was then invited to a $1-million-per-person Mar-a-Lago fundraising dinner less than three weeks before the pardon came through. The sentencing judge had ordered Walczak to pay roughly $4.4 million in restitution alongside his 18-month sentence, declaring there is not a get-out-of-jail-free card for the rich; Trump's pardon relieved Walczak of both the prison time and the entire restitution obligation.

On May 28, 2025, Trump pardoned reality-TV stars Todd and Julie Chrisley, convicted of defrauding banks of more than $30 million and evading federal taxes -- part of a broader late-May 2025 pardon wave tracked in fuller detail in a companion entry in this database. In July 2025, Tim Leiweke, former CEO and co-founder of entertainment-venue developer Oak View Group, was indicted on a federal conspiracy charge for allegedly rigging the bidding process for the $375 million Moody Center arena at the University of Texas at Austin -- allegedly agreeing with a competitor that it would withdraw from the bidding in exchange for subcontracts; Leiweke pleaded not guilty, and Oak View Group itself, not formally charged, separately agreed to pay $15 million in penalties over the underlying conduct. Also in August 2025, former Puerto Rico Governor Wanda Vazquez Garced pleaded guilty to a reduced campaign-finance-violation charge over a scheme to finance her 2020 gubernatorial campaign, in a case that had begun 10 days after she endorsed Trump in October 2020.

**On November 26, 2025 -- less than two weeks after GPB Capital founder David Gentile reported to federal prison to begin a seven-year sentence for a $1.6 billion investor-fraud scheme -- Trump commuted his sentence and eliminated his $15.5 million restitution obligation to more than 10,000 defrauded investors**, per Politico's December 3, 2025 reporting; the sentencing court had received thousands of victim-impact statements, many from elderly retirees describing losing their life savings. The commutation is tracked in fuller detail, including a since-halted DOJ investigation into whether payments were made to secure it, in a companion entry in this database. On December 2, 2025, Trump granted a full and unconditional pardon to Leiweke. The Wall Street Journal reported, per an account Billboard separately confirmed, that a friendly round of golf between Trump and former Republican Congressman Trey Gowdy -- whom Leiweke had hired to lobby on his behalf in the criminal case -- factored into the pardon decision; no direct campaign-donation link comparable to this entry's other cases was identified in sourcing reviewed, making this case's connection to Trump personal/lobbying access rather than documented financial contributions.

The Washington Post's December 19, 2025 investigation put a specific restitution figure on the Milton case for the first time -- prosecutors had argued Milton should pay defrauded investors $660 million, a calculation the sentencing judge never had the chance to finalize before Trump's pardon eliminated the obligation entirely, along with any prison time. The same investigation surfaced a further, previously undocumented case: Marian Morgan, sentenced in 2013 to nearly 34 years for running a Ponzi scheme and ordered to pay $17.5 million to dozens of defrauded investors, most of which remained unpaid -- despite Morgan having told a court in 2021, in a sworn statement, "I want to pay restitution to my victims so they know I am truly sorry for the damage I caused." The Post's reporting also identified at least 20 people who received Trump clemency in 2026 alone who were also forgiven of financial penalties totaling tens of millions of dollars, and quoted Elizabeth Oyer, who served as U.S. Pardon Attorney for three years until being fired two months into Trump's second term, on the pattern's effect: "It's having a detrimental effect on victims and taxpayers, and it's a windfall to the people who committed crimes."

In January 2026, Herrera Velutini's clemency was granted as part of a single pardon covering Vazquez Garced and her two co-defendants, Herrera Velutini and Mark Rossini, in the federal bribery/campaign-finance case described above. A White House official told CBS News the MAGA Inc. donations had nothing to do with the pardon, and the administration's pardon materials characterized the underlying prosecution as politically motivated. On March 16, 2026, Trump signed an executive order establishing a new "Task Force to Eliminate Fraud," to be led by Vice President JD Vance, publicly framing fraud enforcement as an administration priority even as the pardon pattern continued. A further documented example, undated in sourcing reviewed: ProPublica reported Trump pardoned nursing home operator Joseph Schwartz after he had served just three months of a three-year sentence for a $39 million fraud scheme tied to his collapsing chain of care facilities. Families of patients who died or were harmed under Schwartz's ownership had won multimillion-dollar civil judgments against him, but ProPublica found many have recovered nothing, a debt now further complicated by his truncated sentence and clemency.

In May 2026, Trump commuted Marian Morgan's sentence "to time served with no further fines, restitution, probation or other conditions." A bicameral congressional oversight investigation (Sen. Welch, Reps. Min and Ruiz) launched that same month, sending pay-to-play inquiry letters to 17 pardon recipients including several named in this entry; the White House has denied any impropriety. The investigation escalated in June 2026: Welch and Min sent formal records-preservation requests to DOJ's Pardon Attorney, the White House Records Management office, the White House Pardon Czar, and the Secret Service, with a July 24, 2026 compliance deadline.

incident_summary: On November 13, 2024, President-elect Trump nominated former Rep. Matt Gaetz to be Attorney General, the nation's top law-enforcement post overseeing federal sex-trafficking and civil-rights enforcement. Gaetz had faced a federal sex-trafficking investigation beginning in 2021 -- DOJ ultimately declined to bring charges -- but the House Committee on Ethics had separately been conducting its own investigation, effectively derailed when Gaetz resigned from the House the day after his nomination. **The Ethics Committee nonetheless later released its findings, concluding there was 'substantial evidence' Gaetz violated Florida's statutory rape laws, among other findings.** Newly unsealed court records reported by the New York Times on November 13, 2025 (one year after the nomination) detailed the vulnerable circumstances of the minor victim at the center of the case: she was a homeless high school junior living in a shelter with a parent, working at McDonald's, who joined a 'sugar dating' website in an effort to save money for braces, falsely listing her age as 18. She testified she was 17 when she met Greenberg -- a Gaetz associate later convicted in a broader sex-trafficking scheme -- through the site in April 2017, and that she first had sex with Gaetz, who paid her, in July 2017 at a party hosted by lobbyist Chris Dorworth. Gaetz has consistently denied the allegations, telling the Times the account was 'fiction' and that he 'never had sex with this person,' who he said had instead threatened to sue him for $2.3 million. Gaetz withdrew his AG nomination on November 22, 2024, nine days after it was announced, citing a desire to avoid becoming 'a needlessly protracted Washington scuffle' and 'a distraction' to the transition; CNN and other outlets reported the more direct proximate cause was that Trump personally told Gaetz he lacked the Senate votes for confirmation, amid senators' concerns over the same allegations.

incident_summary: **On January 28, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14187, 'Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation,' directing federal agencies to withhold grant funding from medical institutions that provide gender-affirming care -- including puberty blockers, hormone therapy, and certain surgical procedures -- to patients under 19, and directing exclusion of these treatments from Tricare (military health coverage) and calling for restrictions under Medicare and Medicaid.** The order was challenged almost immediately: Lambda Legal filed suit on behalf of PFLAG in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland on February 4, 2025, and on March 4, 2025 the court issued a nationwide preliminary injunction barring the federal government from withholding funding from institutions on the basis that they provide this care to minors. The order has not been enforceable since that injunction. A second front opened in late 2025: a coalition of 19 states and the District of Columbia sued HHS and other federal defendants, filing a motion for summary judgment on January 6, 2026 that challenged an HHS report (referred to in litigation as the 'Kennedy Declaration,' after HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.) cited to justify the restrictions; at oral argument on March 19, 2026 the presiding judge indicated an intent to partially grant the states' request to invalidate that declaration.

offense_category: Presidential Imposition of an Unauthorized Tax Via Proclamation -- a federal court found the $100,000 H-1B visa fee exceeded executive authority, violated the Administrative Procedure Act, and violated separation-of-powers principles by usurping Congress's exclusive taxing authority
incident_summary: In September 2025, Trump announced by proclamation a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa petitions, dramatically increasing the cost of hiring highly skilled foreign workers. A coalition of 20 Democratic state attorneys general sued, and **on June 8, 2026, U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin in Boston ruled the fee unlawful, finding it constituted a tax Trump imposed without congressional authorization -- an authority the Constitution reserves to Congress -- and that the administration's implementation violated both the Administrative Procedure Act and constitutional separation-of-powers principles.** Despite the ruling, the court's order blocking the fee was temporarily paused on June 12, 2026 to allow an appeals court to consider the government's request for a stay; as a result, USCIS was again permitted to collect the $100,000 fee while the First Circuit considered that request, even after a federal court had found it unlawful. On July 24, 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals denied the government's request to stay Judge Sorokin's ruling, finding the administration had not shown it was likely to succeed on the merits; as a result, the fee has been unenforceable nationwide since that denial. Separately, a different lawsuit (brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Association of American Universities) produced the opposite result: in December 2025 the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia upheld the fee, leaving two district courts in direct conflict; that ruling is on appeal before the D.C. Circuit, which heard oral argument on March 9, 2026 and had issued no ruling as of late September 2026. As of August 12, 2026 reporting, the administration was expected to seek emergency relief from the Supreme Court, but no such application had been reported as of late September 2026. Separately, on August 25, 2026, DHS proposed a new $103,265 fee on H-1B cap-subject petitions via notice-and-comment rulemaking rather than presidential proclamation, with comments due September 24, 2026 -- a different mechanism and different actor from the proclamation fee this entry tracks, noted here as forward-looking context. Proclamation 10973's 12-month restriction was due to lapse on September 21, 2026; on September 18, 2026, Trump signed Proclamation 11069 extending it, including the $100,000 payment requirement, for another 12 months, until September 21, 2027.
